name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee US House District 9: Republican Taylor and Democrat Pearson set for general election
description: Republican Memphis state Sen. Brent Taylor and Democratic Memphis state Rep. Justin J. Pearson will face off in the general election for Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District after they won their respective primaries Thursday. Taylor defeated Chapel Hill state Rep. Todd Warner, retired U.S. Army Sergeant Jeremy Thompson and four-time congressional candidate[...]
text:
State Sen. Brent Taylor earned the Republican nomination for Congress in Tennessee's 9th Congressional District and will face Democratic nominee, state Rep. Justin J. Pearson. (Photos: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Republican Memphis state Sen. Brent Taylor and Democratic Memphis state Rep. Justin J. Pearson will face off in the general election for Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District after they won their respective primaries Thursday.
Taylor defeated Chapel Hill state Rep. Todd Warner, retired U.S. Army Sergeant Jeremy Thompson and four-time congressional candidate Charlotte Bergmann.
Pearson won against Memphis state Sen. London Lamar and healthcare executive Jim Torino. The second term state lawmaker swept the Democratic field with just under 65% of the ballots.
State Republicans held a special redistricting session in May to explicitly redraw Tennessee’s 9th U.S. House seat in hopes of flipping control of the seat. The district as it was previously drawn has been represented by Democrats for more than 40 years. The redistricting session followed a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais that struck down a portion of the 1965 Voting Rights Act allowing for the creation of majority minority districts. 

Traditionally, the seat has been drawn to include almost all of Memphis and has been represented by U.S. Rep. Steven Cohen, a Democrat, for the past two decades. After the seat was redrawn, Cohen dropped out of the race. 
The new seat is now an L-shaped district that includes two of the state’s wealthiest suburbs in Nashville and Memphis on its ends, pinning vast swaths of rural Middle and southwest Tennessee counties in between. 
The district’s jagged western edge includes the town of Eads in Shelby County, where Taylor lives, and ends at the Memphis airport.
Taylor and Pearson were the only candidates for either party to raise over $1 million for the election.
Taylor, a former funeral home director, put in over $1 million of his own cash into the race and took just over 46% of Republican votes. He also received the endorsement of President Donald Trump. 
Pearson rose to national prominence after he was temporarily expelled from the state House in 2023 for protesting gun violence on the state House floor. The recognition has allowed him to raise a large amount of money from small donors all across the country. 
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced Wednesday that it was adding Tennessee’s 9th District to its seats in play during the 2026 November midterm election. 
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the district as “Solid Republican” with a Republican plus 9 ranking, the lowest GOP lean of any seat in the state.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn advances to general election, first woman to win party nomination
description: U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn on Thursday advanced to the general election in November, defeating U.S. Rep. John Rose and becoming the first woman to win the Republican nomination for governor.  Despite polls in the final weeks of the campaign showing a tightening race, Blackburn cruised to victory with 43.8% of the primary vote. Rose got […]
text:
U.S. Sen.Marsha Blackburn, photographed on Aug. 6, 2026, will be the Republican gubernatorial candidate in November (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn on Thursday advanced to the general election in November, defeating U.S. Rep. John Rose and becoming the first woman to win the Republican nomination for governor. 
Despite polls in the final weeks of the campaign showing a tightening race, Blackburn cruised to victory with 43.8% of the primary vote.
Rose got 32.7% of the primary vote and state Rep. Monty Fritts of Kingston received 23.4%.
Soon after Blackburn was reelected to her second Senate term in November 2024, she began floating rumors she would run for governor, but didn’t make a formal announcement of her gubernatorial campaign until August 2025. 
She ran her first campaign ad in June, a spot that featured her touting her toughness on threats from China while crushing fortune cookies in a Nashville restaurant decorated to look like a Chinese restaurant. 
Rose, a former state commissioner of agriculture who was elected to Tennessee’s 6th Congressional District in 2018, announced his candidacy in March 2025, but got off to a slow start. 
He gave his campaign $5 million early on but didn’t begin running advertisements until May. He conceded the election to Blackburn around 8:30 p.m. Thursday night and said he would be supporting her in the general election.
“Thanks to this campaign, I gained a deeper love for this state and its people,” Rose told a crowd of about 500 supporters at his Cookeville election party. Rose did not make himself available to reporters and didn’t say whether he would run again in  four years.
Rose received his strongest support from farmers, including people such as Ron Ash of Savannah, who said he backed the congressman because of his “conservative” values and work in agriculture.
The Blackburn juggernaut 
Blackburn’s 30 years in elected office and longtime Republican Party activism built a bulwark too formidable for Rose or Fritts to overcome. 
A native of Mississippi and former image consultant, Blackburn organized the first Young Republicans group outside of East Tennessee in Williamson County in the early 1980s before chairing the Williamson County Republican Party. 
Former Gov. Don Sundquist appointed her as executive director of the Tennessee Film, Entertainment, and Music Commission in 1995, a post she held for two years. 
She was elected to the Tennessee Senate in 1998 and led opposition to Sundquist’s proposal of a state income tax in 2001, before running for and winning the 7th Congressional District seat in 2002. 
When U.S. Sen. Bob Corker announced he would not seek reelection in 2018, Blackburn jumped in the race to replace him, facing off in the general election against former two-term Democratic Gov. Phil Bredesen. According to Open Secrets, a nonpartisan and nonprofit organization that tracks political spending, the race was the seventh most expensive race in the 2018 campaign cycle, with more than $90,000 spent by the candidates and by outside groups. 
Although the race was thought to be competitive, Blackburn defeated Bredesen by 12 percentage points. 
Both Blackburn and Rose have consistently voted with President Donald Trump, with Blackburn becoming one of the first U.S. representatives to endorse him after he announced his candidacy for president in 2015. 
On Jan. 6, 2021, Rose voted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, which was won by Joe Biden.
But Trump declined to endorse either candidate, despite a third-party group, the Tennessee Freedom Fund — a political action group, PAC, affiliated with conservative private school choice group Club For Growth — running TV ads on Blackburn’s behalf featuring footage of her and Trump. 
Blackburn took political heat for refusing to debate or appear in public forums with her two opponents, as well as for leaked documents from a Senate Ethics Committee investigation alleging her campaign manager, Ward Baker, urged Senate staff members to participate in campaign activities, a violation of federal law. 
Only six women have run for governor in Tennessee’s history. Blackburn will face Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilmember, in the general election, making for the state’s first all-woman partisan gubernatorial field.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Division of Elections erroneously removed more than 600 citizens from voter list
description: More than 600 U.S. citizens were mistakenly flagged as possible noncitizens and removed from Alaska’s list of active voters earlier this year, the director of the Alaska Division of Elections said Thursday in a letter responding to questions from state lawmakers. Those citizens were among 3,058 people removed from the list after the division compared […]
text:
Reject stickers await ballot envelopes Wednesday, June 15, 2022 at the Division 1 office of the Alaska Division of Elections in Juneau, Alaska during counting for Alaska's special U.S. House primary election. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)More than 600 U.S. citizens were mistakenly flagged as possible noncitizens and removed from Alaska’s list of active voters earlier this year, the director of the Alaska Division of Elections said Thursday in a letter responding to questions from state lawmakers.
Those citizens were among 3,058 people removed from the list after the division compared its citizenship data to a separate set of records kept by the Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles. 
Someone removed from the voter list may still cast a vote this year, but they will not appear on the register of their local precinct and will have to provide additional identity information in order to cast a “questioned ballot.”
Removal from the active voter list also puts a citizen on the path to being purged altogether from the voter list, an act that would make them ineligible to vote.
After the swath of removals, the Division of Elections sent letters to every affected state resident, and many have responded.
“Approximately 685 voters have contacted the Division and stated they are citizens, despite the inconsistency with the DMV’s records,” Carol Beecher, the division’s director, said in a letter addressed to the chairs of the Alaska House Judiciary Committee and the Alaska State Affairs Committee.
Beecher also said “more than 100 people have reported they are not citizens and requested that their voter registration be cancelled.”
About 350 letters were returned as undeliverable, and another 1,900 affected Alaskans have not responded at all, indicating that they may be unaware that they were removed from the active voter list before the Aug. 18 statewide primary election.
Legislator calls timing of removals ‘very interesting’
In an interview with the Anchorage Daily News earlier this week, and again in Thursday’s letter, Beecher said she will not unilaterally return affected Alaskans to the voter rolls.
The division will instead send out another notice to affected voters, she said.
Beecher’s letter leaves many questions unanswered and raises more. According to the letter, the Division of Elections checked “the entire statewide voter registration list … with DMV records.”
Normally, the two divisions only compare a fraction of the list, and typically only those people who are registered to vote through the federally mandated “motor-voter” program that prompts citizens to register to vote when they get a new driver’s license.
In 2024, for example, DMV and DOE compared just 2,000 records — not the more than 580,000 compared this year, which DMV called “non-routine.”
Legislators asked Beecher the reason for the switch, which took place with no notice, in an election year. Beecher’s letter does not answer.
“It’s kind of interesting that the DOE is essentially spearheading a large-scale voter roll cleanup and list maintenance immediately preceding a primary election with major implications for the state going forward,” said Rep. Ashley Carrick, D-Fairbanks and one of the two legislators to which the letter was addressed.
Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage and the other recipient, said by text message that he was driving Thursday afternoon and had not yet reviewed the letter.
Carrick, speaking broadly, noted that the Alaska Legislature passed a bipartisan elections bill — Senate Bill 64 — that would have improved voter roll list maintenance, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed it.
“A lot of this would have been taken care of with policy that we passed as a legislature in a more routine format, so I think it’s very interesting that those two things are corresponding,” Carrick said.
The Alaska Legislature attempted but failed to override Dunleavy’s veto, with two Republican lawmakers, both from Southeast Alaska, providing the key votes to uphold the governor’s decision.
Poll worker fired for raising concerns
In Anchorage, Lisa Maloney was briefly hired as a temporary poll worker to chair the precinct covering Jewel Lake. On Thursday morning, Beecher fired her after an email exchange in which Maloney raised concerns about the way that poll workers were instructed to handle potential issues with voters flagged by the division as possible noncitizens.
Maloney said it might be misleading for poll workers to tell potential voters to cast a questioned ballot if the poll worker knows the ballot will not be counted.
“You have been provided with instructions on what to do when an individual who is not on the register wants to vote. We are not confident that you will follow these instructions and for that reason we will no longer require your services as a Poll Worker for the August 18 Primary Election or the November 3, General Election,” Beecher wrote.
In a prior email to Beecher, Maloney had said she does not think it is practical for someone removed from the active list to promptly call the Division of Elections on Election Day if they have questions.
By phone, Maloney said she thinks Beecher “seems to have completely lost track of the fact that it’s actually her job to make sure that everybody who should get to vote can. At least, that’s my understanding of the job of the Division of Elections, and that is why I had signed on to be a poll worker.”
Beecher has not responded to an independent list of questions sent to the division by the Alaska Beacon, which requested an interview on July 28 and was denied. 
The division asked for a list of questions, which was sent by email on July 31. The Beacon followed up by email on Tuesday and again Thursday morning. The division has not responded as of Thursday afternoon. 
State legislators requested a list of all 3,058 people removed by the division. The division has not released that list.
The Beacon has an outstanding public records request — due by the end of the day Friday — for a list of all people on the state’s inactive voter list who are flagged as “noncitizens.” 
The division disclosed a similar list last year, which showed 70 noncitizens either voted or attempted to vote in elections over the past decade.
Beecher’s letter to legislators also does not explain why the Division of Elections relied on DMV data rather than data from the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend division, which collects data on citizenship annually. 
Driver’s licenses may be valid for a decade, which means many people were affected by this year’s action because they obtained driver’s licenses before subsequently becoming citizens and registering to vote.
Given the outcome, Beecher said, “the Division has paused additional DMV comparisons while it evaluates this initial effort and incorporates lessons learned. Future comparisons should involve fewer records because this was the first review that involved the entire voter list.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Farm bill stalls, leaving Kansas farm leader concerned about whether it will pass this year
description: TOPEKA — A top Kansas agriculture advocate lost some of his optimism regarding the farm bill after the U.S. Senate Agriculture Committee failed to move the bill forward Thursday. Nick Levendofsky, executive director of the Kansas Farmers Union, said he had hoped the nation would see the much-needed passage of a farm bill this year […]
text:
Nick Levendofsky (right), executive director of the Kansas Farmers Union, is concerned the failure to move a farm bill out of the Senate Agriculture Committee on Aug. 6, 2026, means the bill won't happen this year. He's shown here speaking about agriculture with former U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman during a U.S. Global Leadership Coalition meeting in 2025, in Overland Park. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A top Kansas agriculture advocate lost some of his optimism regarding the farm bill after the U.S. Senate Agriculture Committee failed to move the bill forward Thursday.
Nick Levendofsky, executive director of the Kansas Farmers Union, said he had hoped the nation would see the much-needed passage of a farm bill this year — the first since 2018 — until Thursday afternoon.
“At the end of the day, it boils down to the cuts that were made through reconciliation, primarily on (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program), have caused a lot of division within the committee itself, and there’s pretty tight (voting) margins to begin with,” Levendofsky said, noting that Sen. Mitch McConnell, the Kentucky Republican who fell ill weeks ago, serves on that committee and is not attending.
In the Trump administration reconciliation bill, states will absorb more administrative costs for the SNAP program and bear costs based on the state’s error rate. Advocates have asked to delay the implementation of costs that affect state budgets. The farm bill includes a one-year delay but an increase in the percentage of administrative costs a state would share.
Kansas farmers need a farm bill to pass, Levendofsky said.
“Usually — our hope is anyway — that the Senate tends to be the adults in the room, and that they can kind of come together,” he said. “But I think given the time that we’re in right now and the politics, it’s proving to be even more and more of a challenge.”
The farm bill is a big piece of legislation, Levendofsky said, that touches every part of agriculture and every person in the country.
Given that it’s an election year and legislators are about ready to recess, Levendofsky said, it will probably be another year without a bill passing.
“The world has changed a lot since 2018,” Levendofsky said. “We survived a pandemic. We have seen a lot of challenges with climate change. We’ve seen a lot of challenges with different administrations and different priorities that they bring forward.”
The holdup in the agriculture committee is over one of the priorities outlined in Project 2025, a document created by the Heritage Foundation compiling a conservative agenda, he said. One goal was to cut food assistance programs such as SNAP.
“We’ve got to learn how to put politics aside, and we’ve got to learn how to be more bipartisan and truly compromise on things,” Levendofsky said. “I know that that’s a dirty word in D.C., ‘compromise,’ but that’s how we’ve gotten farm bills in the past, and it’s worked.”
Farm bills help those in the agriculture industry strategize and enjoy some certainty, even as they deal with uncertainty that’s part of the profession.
Levendofsky said a good farm bill needs to keep pace with rising production costs, lessen the expense of crop insurance, and strengthen and modernize programs to reflect the economic realities today.
“There’s got to be some flexibility in there. There’s got to be a better structure to allow for that,” he said. “Disaster assistance is another thing. With more and more extreme weather events, climate change, whatever you want to call it, that is a big issue for a lot of farmers that they’re dealing with.”
For instance, Kansas saw both droughts and floods this year, Levendofsky said. Specifics he’d like to see in the bill include mandatory country of origin labeling for meat and poultry, year-round E-15 or ethanol, and local food procurement funding.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Sunset Veterans Park is now home to the image of an Air Force C-123 aircraft. Here’s why
description: On July 27, an etched image of a renowned C-123 aircraft was installed in Sunset Veterans Park, which is located in Davis County near Hill Air Force Base.  The C-123 gained notoriety due to its use during the Vietnam War, especially as an aircraft used to spray toxic herbicides in an effort to remove tree […]
text:
Two engraved panels were attached to the back of the Agent Orange Memorial at Sunset Veterans Park on July 27, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Nelson Thibault)On July 27, an etched image of a renowned C-123 aircraft was installed in Sunset Veterans Park, which is located in Davis County near Hill Air Force Base. 
The C-123 gained notoriety due to its use during the Vietnam War, especially as an aircraft used to spray toxic herbicides in an effort to remove tree leaves and other foliage that provided enemy concealment. 
While not the only type of aircraft used by the U.S. military for that purpose, the C-123 was the most commonly employed. It sprayed Agent Orange and other toxic herbicides.
Because of its extensive use in chemical dispersal, it’s no wonder that the image of a C-123 appears on a granite panel of a monument honoring veterans harmed by exposure to toxic chemicals.  
That monument is the Agent Orange Memorial, and the panel with a C-123 spraying Agent Orange is prominently located on the back of the memorial above an inscription honoring victims of toxic chemical exposure. 
The inscription reads:
In honor of the warriors who bore the invisible wounds of Agent Orange — and in steadfast recognition of all Veterans exposed to toxic battlefields, from the jungles of Vietnam to the burn pits of the modern era. This memorial stands as a promise: That their sacrifice will never be forgotten, their voices will never be silenced, and those who follow will be protected.
The installation of the monument’s two back panels marks another milestone in the construction of the Agent Orange Memorial, which began in the fall of last year. 
Panels for the front of the memorial have not yet been put in place, but are expected to adorn the stately tribute in the near future. 
In the meantime, the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation will continue its efforts to finish building a monument that pays homage to Utahns who have sacrificed so much for our nation.
Anyone interested in supporting the foundation’s mission can do so by making a donation at agentorangeheroes.org/donate/ or purchasing a personalized memorial brick at bricksrus.com/donorsite/agentorangeheroes.

name: Daily Montanan
title: State says Billings milk plant is fixing problems
description: The Montana Department of Livestock declined to close a Meadow Gold milk facility in Billings despite multiple violations saying Thursday the company had responded to corrective guidance. Bird droppings in a loading dock and repeated violations over residue in production areas were among the issues that prompted Meadow Gold to receive on July 31 a […]
text:
The Meadow Gold milk processing facility in Billings, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).The Montana Department of Livestock declined to close a Meadow Gold milk facility in Billings despite multiple violations saying Thursday the company had responded to corrective guidance.
Bird droppings in a loading dock and repeated violations over residue in production areas were among the issues that prompted Meadow Gold to receive on July 31 a notice of proposed license suspension from the Department of Livestock.
There have been no recalls for products from the facility, which is run by Meadow Gold.
That company, nor its parent company, Dairy Farmers of America, immediately responded to a request for comment from the Daily Montanan.
In a press release Thursday, the agency announced it had reviewed the corrective actions a Meadow Gold facility on the south side of Billings had sent it and “will reinspect to verify all non-compliant issues have been corrected or are in the process of being corrected.” 
It wasn’t immediately clear when those inspections would take place, though a department spokesperson said it could be “as soon as tomorrow (Friday).” The agency press release said it expected that “some issues require time and materials to complete.”
The notice of suspension included results from inspections on June 16 and July 27, which included repeated violations related to birds and residue buildup in tanks at the facility. No illnesses have been reported from the milk.
According to MTN News, the Billings milk consumers have complained about milk going bad before its expiration date since spring and that a cluster of complaints during the summer prompted the state investigation.
In the release, the state defended keeping the facility open, saying neither a temporary or permanent closure of the facility “would benefit the industry, dairy producers, retailers, or consumers.”
“However, it is the responsibility of milk processing facilities to produce safe, wholesome milk for the people of Montana and we will apply regulatory enforcement to ensure the standards set forth by state law and the Pasteurized Milk Ordinance are met,” the Livestock Department press release said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay $567M for youth harm abatement fund
description: New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid at the end of the day Thursday issued a ruling in the state’s pending case against social media giant Meta, ordering the company to pay $567 million for an abatement fund to address the harms it has done to the state’s youth.
text:
New Mexico First Judicial District Chief Judge Bryan Biedscheid listens to testimony on May 22, 2026, the final day of the second phase of New Mexico’s case against Meta, held in Santa Fe. (Photo by Eddie Moore/Albuquerque Journal)New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid at the end of the day Thursday issued a ruling in the state’s pending case against social media giant Meta, ordering the company to pay $567 million for an abatement fund to address the harms it has done to the state’s youth.
The case, which ended with written closing arguments in mid-June centered on the New Mexico Department of Justice’s allegations that Meta’s platforms — including Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp — constitute a “public nuisance” to teen health within the state. Among its list of demands, NMDOJ requested the court order the company to operate differently for its youth users; issue monetary relief; and appoint an independent monitor.
The juryless bench trial followed a Santa Fe jury’s March 24 verdict finding Meta violated New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act, and misled the public on the risks of its sites for underage users’ mental health and risk of sexual exploitation. The verdict, which Meta said it would appeal, ordered the company to pay $375 million in damages.
In his decision, Biedscheid said Meta’s obligations to the abatement fund would last for five years, and include written reports on a semiannual basis as to the status and progress of its compliance with each of the abatement measures the court ordered.
In a news release Thursday evening, the New Mexico Department of Justice said the court’s order “requires real, structural changes, not just promises, and provides the resources New Mexico needs to begin repairing the damage caused by Meta’s conduct.”

The case, Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement, “has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence. Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.”
This breaking news story will be updated.

name: Washington State Standard
title: 2 votes separate WA Democrats in Bellingham-area state Senate race
description: Two votes separate two Democratic hopefuls as they battle for a chance at an open state Senate seat in northwest Washington.  Since election night, Bellingham port commissioner Michael Shepard has seen his lead dwindle over fellow Democrat Eamonn Collins. By Thursday night’s tally, Shepard was ahead 12,856 to Collins’ 12,854. Nearly 49,000 votes have been […[...]
text:
Left, Eamonn Collins and, right, Michael Shepard. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Two votes separate two Democratic hopefuls as they battle for a chance at an open state Senate seat in northwest Washington. 
Since election night, Bellingham port commissioner Michael Shepard has seen his lead dwindle over fellow Democrat Eamonn Collins. By Thursday night’s tally, Shepard was ahead 12,856 to Collins’ 12,854. Nearly 49,000 votes have been counted so far.
Collins was down two-and-a-half percentage points on Tuesday.
More votes will trickle in over the next week, though it’s unclear how many still need to be counted.
A machine recount is required if the difference between two candidates is under 0.5% of the total ballots cast and fewer than 2,000 votes. To trigger a manual recount, candidates have to be separated by fewer than 150 votes and 0.25% of the total votes.
Either candidate in November will face Republican Erika Creydt, a psychologist and Blaine school board member. She’s picked up 44.7% of the primary vote. 
They’re running to represent the 42nd Legislative District, covering north Bellingham and rural Whatcom County, including Ferndale, Lynden and Blaine.
The seat is open after Sen. Sharon Shewmake, D-Bellingham, opted not to seek reelection after serving in the Senate since 2022. She beat a Republican by just 900 votes in 2022. Before that, the seat had long been held by Republicans.
Collins, who previously served as a policy adviser in the U.S. Senate, appears to be the preferred candidate of the left, with support from the Washington Federation of State Employees and the district Democratic Party. 
Shepard also has many union endorsements, as well as the backing of Shewmake and party establishment figures, including Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen. Shepard has also benefited from $7,000 in independent mailers supporting his campaign from the Jackson Legacy Fund, a business-friendly group that tries to elect moderate Democrats.
The primary indicates Democrats have a good shot at holding the seat, as the total of the two Democrats’ votes would be over 52%. The district has been turning bluer in recent years.
Collins didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Before the latest tally late Thursday afternoon, Shepard said “it’s been a real privilege to run and I’m thrilled to have so much support.”
“I think we have two great candidates in this race on the Democratic side,” he added.
Shepard said a key difference between him and Collins is his years of countywide elected experience.
Creydt, the only Republican in the race, leads the fundraising battle, bringing in over $195,000. She’s spent just about all of it. Shepard has raised $104,000 and Collins $73,000.
A fourth candidate, Ryan Bowman, ran with no party affiliation but campaigned on his support of the state’s new income tax on higher earners. He’s earned 2.5% of the primary vote so far.
In another Democrat-on-Democrat battle for an open position, Luc Jasmin III surpassed Pam Kohlmeier for the second spot in the 3rd District race in Spokane for retiring Rep. Timm Ormsby’s seat. Jasmin now leads by nearly one percentage point, after the latest vote count Thursday.
And in the 29th District in Tacoma, Democrat Patrick Stickney leads Natasha Laitila, also a Democrat, by 172 votes for the second spot in that race. Another Democrat, Tacoma Deputy Mayor Joe Bushnell, leads the race for the position opened by Rep. Sharlett Mena seeking an opening in the state Senate.
The top two candidates in Washington primaries advance to the general election regardless of party.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: In Inupiaq, when the weather talks, you listen
description: In winter, Papa would stand at the north-facing window of his home, looking to the open sky and his neighbor’s sleeping garden. “Alapaa,” he would say: “It likes to be cold,” in Inupiaq. He was talking about Sila, the weather. And on January days during my childhood, when we all gathered for supper and the […]
text:
Gulls forage on the Norton Sound beach at Nome on Oct. 2, 2020. Norton Sound is part of the Northern Bering Sea. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)In winter, Papa would stand at the north-facing window of his home, looking to the open sky and his neighbor’s sleeping garden. “Alapaa,” he would say: “It likes to be cold,” in Inupiaq. He was talking about Sila, the weather.
And on January days during my childhood, when we all gathered for supper and the house shook from coastal storms and the snow berms throughout town grew and grew over the season, Papa would say something like “Piqsiġuktuq,” to my Gram, mom, aunties and uncles.
In Inupiaq, piqsiq translates to “stormy.” The syllable ġuk means “likes to” and tuq signifies “it or they.” The string of sounds sounded familiar and comfortable, but I didn’t understand that it translates to “It likes to be stormy.”
Because Papa and Gram were punished, physically and psychologically, for speaking Inupiaq in school classrooms as children, they did not want my mom and her siblings speaking the language and experiencing the deep and unjust shame and pain they carried. Mom and her siblings understood Inupiaq but couldn’t speak it. I grew up not speaking or understanding it. As a kid wearing braids and bobbles, I didn’t have the knowledge that our language is imbued with the Indigenous understanding that the weather, Sila, is living with us. And Sila is boss.
Papa was born with this understanding. In fact, he understood the weather so well he was a traditional weather forecaster. I imagine he learned the signals from his dad, who learned them from his father and the generations before him who made Uņalaqłiq, the southernmost Inupiaq settlement, their homelands. What settlers changed to Unalakleet. He would stand at the beach, look out at the ocean, the current, the clouds and the color and movement of it all, and let Sila decide our days, our week ahead. If wind was coming, we couldn’t hunt ugruk. If Sila said “rain,” we waited to fish for humpies until a good stretch of clear skies arrived for days of hanging and drying. Sila told us, and continues to decide for us, our activities.



Quotation







Our language is imbued with the Indigenous understanding that the weather, Sila, is living with us. And Sila is boss.


– Laureli Ivanoff


Papa was a slight, slender and sinewy man with a full head of gray hair and browline glasses. He moved with purpose, was comfortable with silence, never complained, and always seemed to look ahead. He wore scratchy wool plaid button-up shirts, chewed snuff, and smelled like earth, fresh air and no nonsense. He had the most wrinkled face I’d ever seen, sported a crewcut, had large ears that stuck out, and was the type of man who, when he talked, people listened.
We often ate supper at Papa and Gram’s house. All of us. Aunts, uncles, all the cousins. So many that there weren’t enough chairs, and Papa or Dad would haul a bunch of white 5-gallon buckets from the back porch to fit as many as could sit at the kitchen table. I never wanted to sit on one of those buckets. My legs were too short for my feet to reach the floor, and the raised rims on the lids hurt my thighs.
On those cold or stormy winter days, Gram would stand at the oven and stir a pot of fresh caribou soup. The yeasty smell of baking bread wafted through their small home and softened the talk, as we knew we’d eat fresh bread slathered with Crisco very soon. The oven and all our bodies warmed the room. Some of us young cousins stole away to play in the back bedroom, reserved for grandkids who lived with them, to escape boring adult conversation and the stuffiness. I didn’t know it then, but those conversations I passively heard while thinking of something to do shape my values and mindset today.

THIS TIME OF YEAR, communities throughout coastal Western and Northern Alaska are thinking of and preparing for the coming fall storms. When I was a child, we experienced fall storms, but nothing like what we’re seeing today. I grew up hearing about a major flood in the 1960s. My dad’s dad’s house floated off its foundation and landed in the spot where it still stands, where my uncle and auntie now live. When it landed there, my papa jovially asked the man across the road, “Can I be your neighbor?”
Last fall, Typhoon Halong started in the central Pacific Ocean, southeast of Japan. The storm traveled north and hit Alaska’s entire western coastline, flooding and damaging 45 communities and forcing the total relocation of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok residents, turning them into climate refugees. In response, the governor declared a state disaster emergency, and the president approved a federal disaster declaration.
These floods used to occur once every 100 years or so. Today, the fall storms that bring high water are a threat every year. I chatted with Alaska’s leading climatologist, Rick Thoman, about the frequency of storms. He said the oceans are warming. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting. “They combined to produce a double whammy driving sea-level rise,” he said. “Coastal erosion is aggravated by the longer sea-ice-free season. Warmer oceans can increase also the intensity of storms.” That was likely a factor in the ferocity of the Halong flooding. He said permafrost is thawing only a few feet above sea level in places, and the sinking and settling land can cause catastrophic flooding where it might otherwise have been minor.
As we brace for whatever Sila may bring to us this fall, I often wonder what Papa would say today, looking out of his window. I wonder what he’d think when it rains for days on end and we’re unable to dry our fish like we used to on the fish rack. How we are now drying our fish inside empty bedrooms, garages or hallways, using fans. I wonder what he’d say about the ocean eating the coastline where he and Gram camped during fishing season. I wonder if, standing on the sandy beach, looking west to the horizon, he could see the messages in the signals and predict the weather like he used to. I wonder what kind of conversations I would hear, sitting at the kitchen table. I wonder what Sila would tell him.

name: WyoFile
title: These legislative races could determine the balance of power in Cheyenne
description:
After taking control of the House, the Wyoming Freedom Caucus has set its sights on the Senate.
The post These legislative races could determine the balance of power in Cheyenne appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When lawmakers gavel in for the 69th Wyoming Legislature this January in Cheyenne, there will be new faces in the House and the Senate. Voters will decide just how many when they cast ballots in the Aug. 18 primary election. 
All House districts are on the ballot this year alongside about half of the Senate. Sixty-one of the 79 districts up for election are contested. Out of those contested seats, 35 races will soon be determined by voters. The rest will be decided in the general election. 
WyoFile has highlighted several statehouse races including a House rematch between a Natrona County incumbent and an ousted lawmaker, a race defined by nuclear energy, a former House speaker seeking another term and a Senate showdown between two Crook County ranchers that symbolizes the Republican divide in the statehouse. Those races also represent a larger, pressing question looming over the 2026 election — will voters give the Wyoming Freedom Caucus more power in Cheyenne? 
After most of its top legislative goals failed this year, the caucus, which bills itself as the genuine conservative voice of the state, will attempt to bolster its majority in the House and win control of the Senate. That could have major policy implications, including how institutions like the University of Wyoming and the Wyoming Business Council are funded in the future.
Here are some of the races that will determine their success. 

The House


The caucus got its start in the House in 2020 before Gillette Republican Rep. John Bear led the group to secure the lower chamber’s majority in 2024. Bear, a Navy veteran, is now running for his fourth term in House District 31, which encompasses Gillette’s eastern flank. 
As chair of the House Appropriations Committee, Bear led the charge on taking inspiration from the Trump administration’s efforts to cut federal jobs and spending by “DOGE-ing” Wyoming’s budget. Bear proposed a budget that included major cuts to the Wyoming Business Council, Wyoming Public Media, the University of Wyoming and the Department of Health. 
The Legislature ultimately rejected that proposal — approving instead a budget that included 99% of the recommendations by Gov. Mark Gordon, a frequent Freedom Caucus foil. Bear declared victory nonetheless, according to the Gillette News Record. 
“Had we not pulled back on the reins, what would the spending have been? I think we did a good job at slowing down the growth of the government,” Bear said at a lawmaker event in Gillette. 
Douglas Moore, a longtime energy industry manager, is challenging Bear for the Republican nomination. 
“Campbell County needs a representative who understands how state and federal policies directly impact the families working in our pits, on our ranches, and in our small businesses,” Moore told County 17 in June. “I’m ready to bring that practical, results-driven approach to Cheyenne to protect our way of life.”
Dave Hardesty, an educator and veteran, is seeking signatures to appear as an independent candidate for House District 31 on the general election ballot. 
In Casper, Republican Rep. Tony Locke, an engineer, is seeking his third term for House District 35. The race represents another Natrona County rematch as Chris Dresang, a public school administrator, is also running for the Republican nomination. Locke, a Freedom Caucus ally, beat Dresang in 2024 with 54.4% of the vote. 
During his time in the Legislature, Locke has served as chairman of the House Revenue Committee and championed property tax cuts, including a 25% cut in 2025. While Locke advocated for the state to provide millions in backfill to local governments to reimburse them for lost revenue due to the cuts, he also accused local officials of exaggerating those concerns. 
In his response to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire, Dresang said relief for homeowners needs to be balanced with funding local services. 
“I favor targeted relief for the homeowners who need it most, especially seniors, over blunt, across-the-board cuts that leave counties scrambling or force us to backfill with volatile state revenue, such as an increase in the sales tax,” Dresang said. 
Two Republican women will compete in Cheyenne to represent House District 43 — Rep. Ann Lucas, a retired banker, and Jessica Crowder, a rancher and natural resource policy consultant.  
Lucas, a freshman legislator and Freedom Caucus member, was the leading proponent of a committee bill designed to regulate how books with graphic sexual content are housed and challenged in the state’s public and school libraries. The bill, which critics call a book ban, easily cleared the House but failed to advance in the Senate earlier this year. Lucas partially credited the bill’s failure as a reason to run for a second term, according to the Wyoming Tribune Eagle.
Crowder previously led the Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust and served as a policy advisor under Gov. Matt Mead. In her campaign announcement, Crowder said she will focus on “strengthening Wyoming’s economy, supporting local communities, and preserving the state’s way of life for future generations.” 
It remains to be seen if the caucus will release a slate of candidate endorsements as it did on primary election day in 2024. At least two candidates, however, have announced on social media that they’ve been given such endorsements, including Lyman’s Rep. Joe Webb, who is running for reelection to House District 19, and Karen Weber, who is running as a Republican for Goshen County’s House District 5. 
The latter seat is now held by Rep. Scott Smith, a Freedom Caucus member, who is running for state treasurer. Weber, a rancher, will compete against Joe Speckner, a farmer and attorney, for the Republican nomination. 
Webb, a Freedom Caucus member, is running for his second term against Chad Stephens, who is a veteran and small business owner, according to his campaign website. 
Webb, a retired police officer, was one of several Republican lawmakers to receive a campaign check on the House floor during the 2026 legislative session. “Checkgate” sparked multiple investigations and rule changes.
“Never, at any time has anyone offered me money, anything of value or anything else to vote or not vote a certain way,” Webb said at a House Special Investigation Committee hearing in February. 
More recently, Webb penned an op-ed, pushing back on what he called  “an organized, statewide movement” to oust the Freedom Caucus from the Legislature. 
“We will continue the fight for parental rights, tax reform, government transparency, streamlined infrastructure funding and more,” Webb wrote. “The Freedom Caucus exists for the people of Wyoming.”
In Lander, Republican Rep. Lloyd Larsen, is running for his eighth term in House District 54. Larsen, who retired from the oil and gas construction business, has eight years experience serving on the Appropriations Committee — a powerful panel of lawmakers responsible for crafting the initial budget bill. He’s also become one of the lower chamber’s healthcare policy wonks from his time on the House Labor, Health and Social Services Committee. 
Jeff Martin, a motorcycle shop owner, will challenge Larsen for a second time. In 2022, Martin ran in the general election as an independent candidate, losing to Larsen by 1,085 votes. That year, Martin hosted a GOP political rally in Fremont County after an inside-out day — a common school spirit activity where students wear their clothes inside out — at his granddaughter’s elementary school spurred him into action. 
“We teach our kids to wake up in the morning on time, get to the kitchen table, get some breakfast. We teach them to dress properly, put their shoes on the right feet and get to school,” Martin told WyoFile at the time. “So what’s changed? What is going on?”
In 2024, Martin donated to several Freedom Caucus candidates, according to campaign finance records. He is running as a Republican this year. 

The Senate 


During the most recent legislative session, the Wyoming Senate stood as an obstacle to multiple Freedom Caucus budgetary priorities. In response, the caucus has focused on controlling the upper chamber. Several Freedom Caucus members and allies in the House are running for Senate seats including Powell Republican Rep. Paul Hoeft, a retired mechanic. 
Voters first elected Hoeft to House District 25 in 2024. The one bill Hoeft brought in his first term in office sought to prohibit counties, cities, school districts, special districts and the state government from using taxpayer funds on legislative lobbying. The legislation failed an introduction vote in the House in February with some Freedom Caucus members and allies voting against it. 
Hoeft decided to run for Senate District 19 after Republican Sen. Dan Laursen, who is not seeking reelection, asked Hoeft to run in his place, according to The Powell Tribune. 
He will face R.J. Kost, who previously represented the district from 2019 to 2022, when Laursen won a three-man race in the primary election. Kost, a retired teacher and curriculum coordinator, brought successful legislation in 2022 to formally facilitate the state’s ongoing transition from a traditional analog emergency 911 system to an advanced, digital system. He also served on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Senate Agriculture, State and Public Lands and Water Resources Committee during his time in office. 
One of the most crowded legislative races will see Evanston Sen. Wendy Schuler, a retired educator, compete to retain the Senate District 15 seat against three other Republican women — Jen Hegeman, Tina Johnson and Chris Katzl.   
Schuler is not part of the Freedom Caucus and was challenged by one of its former members, Rep. Bob Wharff, in 2022. The lawmaker is likely best known for her successful 2023 bill that prohibits transgender girls from competing in middle- and high-school girls sports events. Schuler, a longtime coach and former college athlete, also successfully brought a bill in 2025 to establish a similar ban in collegiate athletics. 
Hegeman is a former Evanston City Council member, Johnson is Uinta County Chapter Chair of Moms for Liberty and Katzl is a special education teacher. 
In Sheridan, Rep. Ken Pendergraft, a retired contractor, is running for Senate District 21, which is now held by Senate President Bo Biteman, who is running for U.S. House. 
Voters first elected Pendergraft, a Freedom Caucus member, to House District 29 in 2022. He serves on the House Appropriations Committee and led a subcommittee last year charged with bringing DOGE-like scrutiny to the Wyoming Department of Health’s budget. While the department and healthcare advocates braced for cuts as a result of the subcommittee, ultimately lawmakers voted to fully fund the agency. 
Pendergraft’s primary opponent, Melissa Butcher, is a small business owner in Dayton with 30 years experience as a public process facilitator. 
“As a legislator, I would focus on practical conservative solutions: disciplined budgeting, responsible tax relief, strong infrastructure, workforce development, and policies that support local communities rather than imposing one-size-fits-all mandates from Cheyenne,” Butcher said in her candidate questionnaire. 
While the primary election is Aug. 18, early voting is already underway. 
For more information about candidates in Wyoming’s federal, state and legislative races, check out WyoFile’s 2026 Election Guide.

title: Deficient data means Montana FWP should stop wolf hunting
description: How many wolves are left in Montana? Nobody knows. Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks admitted that its iPOM counting method over-estimated wolf numbers for years. Instead of 1,094 wolves, FWP’s revised iPOM 2.0 method now estimates that Montana’s population is 725 wolves—34% less.  Longtime wolf researchers say the population is closer to 400 wolves.  Either[...]
text:
A gray wolf. (Washington Department of Fish & Wildlife)How many wolves are left in Montana? 
Nobody knows. 
Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks admitted that its iPOM counting method over-estimated wolf numbers for years. Instead of 1,094 wolves, FWP’s revised iPOM 2.0 method now estimates that Montana’s population is 725 wolves—34% less. 
Longtime wolf researchers say the population is closer to 400 wolves. 
Either way, the tipping point has been breached; wolves are in perilous decline. The average pack has plummeted to four wolves, well below a healthy, functioning pack size.
Yet FWP is proposing a quota of 250 wolves and 20 wolves per person. 
In 2025, FWP recorded 328 wolf mortalities including the 247 killed by hunters and trappers. and those killed by vehicle collisions and other causes.
If that scenario is repeated with a 250 quota, there will be 397 survivors. If the reality is 400 wolves left on the landscape, wolves will be effectively exterminated. 
By law (Montana Code Annotated 87-1-901), 450 wolves must be maintained in Montana to ensure 15 breeding pairs. This rule is the core foundational benchmark of the Montana Gray Wolf Conservation and Management Plan 2025.
The history of exaggerated numbers and quotas should trigger the Commission to suspend wolf killing to keep wolves at or above the legal number. This includes not giving FWP and USDA Wildlife Services carte blanche to kill an unlimited number of wolves, as proposed.
FWP’s deeply flawed iPOM was built on four bad models and the iPOM 2.0 does not improve it. Information is hidden; FWP can’t verify it. FWP no longer radio collars wolves and does not collect scat (markers) for genetic individual identification. The iPOM is riddled with bias and not updated with annual variables. FWP depends on phone surveys with game hunters six weeks after hunting season. This means coyotes are mistaken for wolves, the same wolves are counted multiple times, locations are sketchy, packs are guessed at. Relying on anecdotal sightings recollected by hunters untrained in data collection is the antithesis of reliable research. 
FWP chose not to adopt a method similar to Italy’s most accurate Integrated Spatial Model, which uses multiple lines of evidence and non-invasive inputs to determine individual genetic information, pack size and population estimates. Instead, FWP uses numbers which are wrong and irrelevant because wolf survival depends on family social structures and individuals holding families together. 
Wolves are held in the public trust. But as trustee, FWP pays only lip service to societal values, ignoring 74% of Montanans who want wolves on the landscape and hundreds of people who speak out against high quotas and killing methods that amount to persecution.
As the top apex predator, wolves provide humans healthy ecosystems by “culling weak deer and elk, suppressing coyotes that prey on calves/sheep, reducing disease transmission, restoring streamside vegetation that supports songbirds, beavers, trout and insects and reducing deer-vehicle collisions,” wrote Dr. Robert Crabtree, chief scientist, Yellowstone Ecological Research Center. “Naturally formed, larger packs are the key indicator of a healthy ecosystem.”
Deficient data, canine distemper, habitat destruction and catastrophic wildfires, heat and drought signal doom for this keenly intelligent, valuable species.
This is no time for recreationally killing 250 wolves struggling to survive. 
At the Aug. 19 meeting, the Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission can and should place a moratorium on wolf hunting and trapping until a transparent, reliable method of ascertaining wolf packs and wolf population health is established. It is the right thing to do in a time of great uncertainty. 
Poten is the co-founder and board president of Footloose Montana and Heister is the co-founder and executive director of Footloose Montana.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Journalist Georgia Fort, who filmed ICE protest in church, seeks dismissal of federal charges
description: Independent journalist Georgia Fort is asking a judge to dismiss the federal charges brought against her after she livestreamed a protest inside a St. Paul church, arguing the prosecution violates her First Amendment rights and accusing the Justice Department of “vindictive prosecution.” Fort was indicted alongside three other journalists — including former[...]
text:
Journalist Georgia Fort leaves the federal courthouse in downtown St. Paul on Feb. 17, 2026 after pleading not guilty to felony charges stemming from her coverage of a protest at a church. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer) Independent journalist Georgia Fort is asking a judge to dismiss the federal charges brought against her after she livestreamed a protest inside a St. Paul church, arguing the prosecution violates her First Amendment rights and accusing the Justice Department of “vindictive prosecution.”
Fort was indicted alongside three other journalists — including former CNN anchor Don Lemon and his producer Michael Beute — and 34 activists for their involvement in a Jan. 18 protest against President Trump’s immigration crackdown inside Cities Church, which employs a pastor who is an official with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The federal government makes no distinction between journalists and protesters in bringing the two charges: felony conspiracy against the right of religious freedom at a place of worship and a misdemeanor count of injuring, intimidating and interfering with the exercise of right of religious freedom at a place of worship.
The federal charges against journalists — sought by the highest ranks of Trump’s Justice Department — represent an attack on the free press that has alarmed journalists nationwide and led a career prosecutor assigned to the case to quit in disgust.
In three motions filed on Thursday, Fort’s attorneys asked a judge to dismiss the charges, arguing that Fort’s actions are protected by the First Amendment; that prosecutors failed to allege any facts that constitute a crime; and that the government has gone to extreme lengths and “manipulated the law” to target her in an illegal act of “vindictive prosecution.”
“All of the evidence in this case points to the government prosecuting Fort precisely because she is a journalist, and in particular because she engaged in that constitutionally sacred work to amplify a message with which the government vehemently disagrees,” Fort’s attorneys write in a motion seeking dismissal.
Fort has spent nearly 20 years as a journalist, winning several awards — including three regional Emmys — for reporting that often focuses on police brutality. She is also the founder of BLCK Press and the Center for Broadcast Journalism, and has press credentials from both state and federal courts.
The church demonstration was organized nearly two weeks after an immigration agent killed Renee Good, leading to widespread protests. The demonstrators took issue with the church employing an ICE official, David Easterwood, because they found ICE’s tactics irreconcilable with Christian teachings.
The demonstration drew the ire of President Trump and then-Attorney General Pam Bondi said, “We are coming after you if you participated in that. I don’t care if you’re a failed CNN journalist, you have no right to do that in this country. We don’t live in a third world country.”
But the Justice Department struggled to bring charges against Fort, Lemon and some of the demonstrators.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko initially rejected charges against Fort, and then-Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz and the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined the government’s appeals, leading prosecutors to pursue a series of legal maneuvers to secure grand jury indictments instead.
Fort was not able to turn herself in and instead was arrested by federal agents at her home in front of her children, which she livestreamed.
Fort’s attorneys at Ballard Spahr, including a former federal prosecutor, say allowing the prosecution against her to proceed would have a chilling effect on journalists, noting that Fort has already had to curtail her reporting as she mounts a defense.
Fort’s attorneys suspect federal prosecutors erroneously told the grand jury that Fort participated in protest chants to help secure an indictment. In at least 15 search warrants — including for Fort’s work product — the federal government falsely said she chanted along with protesters despite ample video evidence to the contrary.
Prosecutors later conceded Fort did not chant, and the judge has taken the unusual step of reviewing the grand jury transcript, which is typically sealed.
The case has been beset by a series of errors by prosecutors, detailed by the New York Times, which reported 29 defendants were offered a deal to plead to just one misdemeanor. (Fort was not among those offered a deal, according to her attorney.)
Federal prosecutors allege that Fort, Lemon and his producer stood close to the church pastor “in an attempt to oppress and intimidate him,” and that she blocked a minivan from leaving outside the church as she interviewed Nekima Levy Armstrong, a protester and longtime Twin Cities civil rights activist.
But Fort’s attorneys say video evidence contradicts those claims.
Fort’s interaction with the pastor, Jonathan Parnell, amounted to holding a microphone to his mouth as he answered questions from Lemon about the demonstrations. Video also shows Fort interviewing Armstrong in front of a minivan, but it was able to back out without issue.
In sum, what Fort did was journalism, her attorneys write: “Fort was invited into a space open to the public, observed events, video recorded them, conducted interviews, asked questions of key players, sought to include a range of perspectives, and conveyed the information she gathered to her online audience in real time.”
Fort’s attorneys accuse the federal government of targeting Fort for her perceived viewpoint and the topic of her coverage, noting that some parishioners also broadcast the protest inside the church. They also point to incidents in which the federal government encourages favorable coverage of immigration enforcement, noting that federal law enforcement agents interrupt church services and other church functions.
“If the First Amendment is to mean anything, it must halt the government’s prosecution against Fort for doing precisely what it protects: covering and reporting on newsworthy events,” Fort’s attorneys write.

title: Governor seeks public comment on Public Service Commission applicants
description: Five candidates, including a former Montana Public Service Commissioner, filed applications to serve in place of Commissioner Brad Molnar, temporarily suspended from office by Gov. Greg Gianforte. Thursday, Gianforte’s office announced it is seeking comment through Aug. 20 on the applicants. The candidates are the following: Kirk Bushman of House District 48[...]
text:
(Screenshot from a PSC social media page.)Five candidates, including a former Montana Public Service Commissioner, filed applications to serve in place of Commissioner Brad Molnar, temporarily suspended from office by Gov. Greg Gianforte.
Thursday, Gianforte’s office announced it is seeking comment through Aug. 20 on the applicants. The candidates are the following:

Kirk Bushman of House District 48 (Billings area), who served on the Public Service Commission as a Republican from 2013 to 2016 and lists Kestrel Engineering and Sibanye Stillwater as recent employers; 
Nick Fitzmaurice of HD 61 (Bozeman area), energy transition engineer for conservation watchdog Montana Environmental Information Agency;
Nicholas Loos of HD 50 (Billings area), nonprofit Service to Summit president and CEO, and former constituent and veterans liaison for Republican U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke from 2024 to 2025;
John Prinkki of HD 55 (Red Lodge area), former Republican Carbon County Commissioner from 1989 to 2017, and retired small horse ranch operator; and
David Wanzenried of HD 53 (Billings area), former state legislator, most recently a Missoula Democrat in the Senate from 2007 to 2015; consultant from 2012 to present for clients including Mountain Pacific Quality Health, Montana State University — Billings and others.

The Public Service Commission regulates monopoly utilities in Montana. The appointed commissioner will serve for one year alongside four other commissioners elected by district for four-year terms.
All commissioners, including Molnar, are currently Republican, as is Gianforte.
Full applications are available at governor.mt.gov/PSCappointment.
Members of the public may submit comments to caitlin.wagoner@mt.gov or to Attn: Caitlin Wagoner, Governor’s Office, PO Box 200801, Helena, Montana 59620.  
Letters or other comments submitted will be publicly available and posted at governor.mt.gov/PSCappointment.
The position is open because Gianforte temporarily suspended Molnar following an investigation into allegations of professional misconduct and a recommendation from a majority of the PSC.
Molnar is fighting the suspension in district court in Montana.
Both the governor and Molnar have described the suspension as unprecedented in state history, but Gianforte has said Molnar’s actions also were unprecedented.
A report that discussed misconduct allegations against Molnar found he referred to “topless Tuesdays” in the office and retaliated against those who filed complaints.
The report into misconduct included numerous recommendations, including that Molnar complete training on sexual harassment and civility during his suspension.
Public Service Commission spokesperson Michael Turner said agency leadership declined to endorse applicants and will not comment on them.
However, Turner said the governor sought recommendations from the commission, and PSC leadership provided characteristics, skills and experience that “would make for an ideal candidate.”
Editor’s note: This story has been updated with comment from the PSC.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: More than 13,300 Lincoln petition signatures flagged as fraudulent
description: Lancaster County election officials referred to law enforcement more than 13,300 signatures suspected to be fraudulent on three petitions.
text:
The backroom of the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24, 2026. Backers of three petitions seeking to restructure city elections in Lincoln submitted signatures this week to send their ideas to voters in the capital city this November.  (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Lancaster County election officials have referred to law enforcement more than 13,300 signatures suspected to be fraudulent on three petitions seeking to reshape Lincoln elections.
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen confirmed that update to the Nebraska Examiner on Thursday afternoon. His office on Wednesday had provided a report to the Lincoln City Clerk’s Office on the Good Government Lincoln campaign’s petition pages.
An Examiner review of those documents, obtained via a public records request, indicated 67.6% of rejected signatures were flagged as being “suspected fraudulent signatures.” The reports do not specify what led local election officials to flag them as fraudulent.
Twenty unique reasons were given for rejection. “Suspected fraudulent signatures” was listed as the most common, followed by voters not being registered in Nebraska (12.1% of the rejections), not being registered in Lincoln (9.9% of rejections), duplicate signatures (2.1%) or a missing signature from a petition line (2.1%).
Campaign applauds election officials
Campaign leaders said late Thursday afternoon that Lincoln officials still had not responded to their own request for the same records, raising questions of fairness. Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird is a chief opponent of the measures.
In a statement, campaign leader Tony Fulton said the campaign supports the referral of potentially fraudulent signatures to law enforcement and the prosecution of the “fraudsters.”
“We take the citizen-led petition process very seriously and appreciate the work the election commissioner did in flagging these irregularities,” Fulton, a former state senator and former state tax commissioner under former Gov. Pete Ricketts, said. “We look forward to getting answers, and in the meantime remain committed to giving voters a voice on these issues for the November ballot.”
Requests for comment to the offices of Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon and Sheriff Terry Wagner went unanswered. The Lincoln Mayor’s Office declined to comment, as did the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office.


Sept. 1 deadline
The Lincoln petitioners seek three amendments to Lincoln’s city charter to move the dates of city elections to align with statewide elections, allow certain residents within a few miles of city limits to vote in municipal elections, and place term limits on Lincoln City Council members.
The group needs at least 4,981 valid signatures on each petition. Nearly 10,400 total signatures were validated, leaving each measure short of the goal.
Supporters announced Wednesday they would restart signature gathering.
The deadline for a political subdivision to certify a special issue for inclusion on the Nov. 3 ballot is Sept. 1. In this case, that’s Lincoln and the Lincoln City Council.
2024 petition fraud investigation
This is the second petition campaign to face public allegations of fraudulent behavior in the past two years.
The previous saga began Sept. 12, 2024, when former state Sen. John Kuehn of Heartwell, a longtime marijuana opponent, filed a lawsuit challenging the validity of two medical cannabis petitions seeking to legalize and regulate medical cannabis. 
Nebraska Supreme Court Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke listens to arguments from former state Sen. Andrew La Grone of Dunbar. Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. Andrew La Grone, an attorney who is advising the latest campaign, is Kuehn’s lawyer. Jessica Flanagain, a partner with Axiom Strategies and a consultant to Fulton’s group, helped review signatures on Kuehn’s behalf, according to court records.
The following day, Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen certified the petitions for the November 2024 ballot. But that same day, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers and Hall County Attorney Marty Klein announced their offices were jointly investigating “several thousand signatures.” 
They found at least 200 fraudulent signatures before pressing charges, a fraction of the total in the current petition controversy.
The duo announced they had charged Michael K. Egbert of Grand Island with circulator fraud. The following month, prosecutors charged Egbert’s notary, Jacy Todd of York, with two dozen misdemeanors stemming from allegedly improper notarizations. 
Egbert later pleaded guilty to a Class I misdemeanor, down from a Class IV felony, and was fined $250. A jury in February found Todd guilty of one Class I misdemeanor for lying under oath and 23 Class II misdemeanors of “official misconduct.” Todd is appealing. He was assessed nearly $4,000 in fines.
Hall County Attorney Marty Klein, standing, speaks to the jury during the first day of trial before Hall County Judge Alfred Corey, center, against a former notary public, Jacy Todd of York, at left, who is connected to two 2024 statewide medical cannabis ballot measures in Grand Island on Feb. 23, 2026. (Courtesy of Kasey Mintz-Pool/KSNB Local 4)
Hall County Election Commissioner Tracy Overstreet’s office had caught suspected fraudulent signatures obtained by Egbert and rejected them from the beginning. He admitted having used a phone book to identify and illegally add voters to his pages.
When charges were announced, the Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana campaign took a similar approach to Fulton’s and said anyone caught violating the law should be held accountable.
Evnen, whom Hilgers’ office defended in the Kuehn case, essentially joined forces with Kuehn later to challenge tens of thousands of signatures. The primary reasons given were improper circulation of petition pages or improper notarizations.
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong ruled Nov. 26, 2024, that while some signatures had been improperly gathered and shouldn’t have counted, the campaign still had enough to qualify for the ballot. She disqualified any signatures that Egbert gathered. Voters overwhelmingly approved both proposed laws at the Nov. 5, 2024, election.
Kuehn and Evnen appealed to the Nebraska Supreme Court, which has not yet issued a ruling. Oral arguments were Dec. 3.
‘Same legal firepower’
Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana has stood by its efforts and continues to push for implementation. On Thursday, the group said that while Hilgers led a large news conference against the medical cannabis campaign two years ago, he is “nowhere to be found now” in a case involving his allies. He is running for reelection and is a client with Axiom Strategies. He served in the Legislature for two years with La Grone and also two years with Kuehn.
“If simple mistakes warranted subpoenas, lawsuits and years of litigation when it came to medical cannabis, surely this warrants the same response,” the medical cannabis group said.
The statement continued: “Unless he [Hilgers] unleashes the same legal firepower against his allies that he used against patients and families, Nebraskans will know the truth: this was never about protecting elections. It was about using public office to overturn the will of the voters.”

title: Arkansas seeks 2-year reprieve for state’s hybrid Medicaid expansion
