name: Florida Phoenix
title: Amendment 3 rewrite is already underway, Gov. Ron DeSantis says
description: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Thursday that the state will not challenge a Leon County Circuit judge’s finding that the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3 defective and that the Attorney General James Uthmeier is rewriting the language. Appearing during a press conference in Lehigh Acres, DeSantis said he didn’t “necessarily agree” with Judge […]
text:
Former Sen. Jeff Brandes addresses reporters ahead of a hearing on the proposed property tax Amendment 3 in the Leon County Courthouse on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Thursday that the state will not challenge a Leon County Circuit judge’s finding that the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3 defective and that the Attorney General James Uthmeier is rewriting the language.
Appearing during a press conference in Lehigh Acres, DeSantis said he didn’t “necessarily agree” with Judge David Frank’s ruling on the property tax constitutional amendment but said the decision had been made to go ahead and rewrite the summaries.
“I’ve actually seen some of the drafts,” DeSantis said. “It’s going to be very clear for voters what’s on there. It addresses what the judge said even though we don’t necessarily agree with the legal analysis.”
DeSantis added that it will be “straight forward. … People are going to know you are getting tax relief. You’re going to get increased homestead exemptions.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Florida Legislature passed Amendment 3 in the form of HJR 1F in early June. 
The ballot title and summary language Frank found deficient were drafted primarily by the DeSantis administration, which means Uthmeier is redrafting language written by his former boss. (He was DeSantis ‘ chief of staff.) He will have to submit the new version to Frank for review.
“The focus now shifts to the rewrite. The court identified real problems with the ballot language. Whether those concerns have actually been addressed remains to be seen,” Jeff Brandes told the Phoenix in a text.
Brandes and others filed lawsuits challenging the wording of the amendment. A former senator, Brandes said the legal challenge wasn’t filed to preclude Florida voters from weighing in on property tax relief.
“It was about whether the government can sell a constitutional amendment with advocacy instead of explanation,” he said. “I’ll be looking closely at whether the new language gives voters an honest description of what’s in the amendment before drawing any conclusions.”
Another Amendment 3 challenge filed by bipartisan pair of former legislators

‘Political slogan’
The initial lawsuit took aim at phrases in the amendment; for example, the title labeled it “Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes.” Frank agreed with opponents that the title was “akin to a political slogan” and violated Florida law.
Amendment 3 maintains the existing homestead property exemption through this year for resident homeowners. But it increases the homestead exemption for longstanding property owners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.
A proposed constitutional amendment passed by the Legislature cannot be knocked off the ballot. But the title and summary can be challenged in court. 
If passed, Amendment 3 would constitute one of the most significant changes to property taxes in the state in more than a generation. Its projected financial impact would reach up to $12 billion annually beginning in 2031. It has drawn opposition from groups that represent firefighters, sheriffs, and police.
Also, DeSantis repeated Thursday that he will not lead a campaign to pass the amendment because Amendment 3 isn’t what he proposed or advocated for. DeSantis’s proposal would have applied to all property taxes paid by Florida homeowners, even those targeted toward public education. The Legislature was uneasy with that proposal and eliminated school taxes before passing the proposal.
The governor, who first called for property tax changes last year, still praised Amendment 3 as “meaningful” and said if passed it would be the “biggest tax relief in the modern history of Florida.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Democrats say voting rights are in danger again 61 years after passage of Voting Rights Act
description: Thursday marked the 61st anniversary of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, a landmark law prohibiting discrimination in voting based on race, color, or language-minority status.
text:
N.C. House Minority Leader Robert Reives speaks on the anniversary of the Voting Rights Act on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)Democratic lawmakers and advocates gathered in front of the North Carolina legislative building Thursday to defend voting rights against what they say is growing pressure by Republicans to roll back years of progress. 
Thursday marked the 61st anniversary of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, a landmark law prohibiting discrimination in voting based on race, color, or language-minority status. 
But modern legislation hasn’t always reflected those principles, according to House Minority Leader Robert Reives, a Democrat from Chatham County.  
The North Carolina General Assembly went 1,003 days without passing a comprehensive budget, yet the Republican majorities were able to pass other laws Reives said were aimed at weakening the voting power of minority communities. 
Black advocates in NC warn Jim Crow era ‘never ended’ as voting maps shift across South

“At the president’s request, the Republican leaders in the state House and in the state Senate ran us back to session so that we could further gerrymander the most gerrymandered maps in the entire United States,” Reives said. 
In October 2025, lawmakers approved a congressional map designed to make the state’s only toss-up district unwinnable for a Democrat, bringing North Carolina’s 14-member U.S. House delegation from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 11 Republicans and three Democrats.
Previously, a court drew maps for the 2022 election resulting in a 7-7 split between the parties. However, Republicans in 2023 passed a new map leading to 10 Republicans and four Democrats in the 2024 cycle. 
Republicans who drew the two most recent congressional voting maps said they were designed to maximize advantage for their own party, pointing out that partisan gerrymandering is not illegal. But in the process, several Black communities were divided up or “cracked” into Republican districts, diluting their voting power.
Reives also criticized his GOP colleagues for shifting control of the North Carolina Board of Elections to the state auditor — the only state auditor in the country with that power, he said. 
NC Auditor Boliek expressed polling site preferences and looked to boost GOP turnout, messages show.

Following his election in 2024, state Auditor Dave Boliek appointed Republican chairs to lead local elections boards as they switched from Democratic to Republican control. 
“Then the pressure campaign began,” Reives said. “They started moving voting sites, shortening voting hours, eliminating our early voting days entirely, and his staff has continued to push this.”
Sen. Val Applewhite, a Democrat from Cumberland County, spoke out against House Bill 958, a controversial election law measure that passed in the lower chamber on Tuesday. It shortens early voting in primaries from 17 to 10 days, along with other changes. 
Republicans who supported the bill said voter turnout during primaries is too low to require county boards of elections to staff early voting sites for 17 days. 
Democratic Gov. Josh Stein said Wednesday he plans to veto the bill.
Earlier versions of the legislation would’ve required military and overseas voters to include photo identification when mailing in their ballots. Republicans said the change is necessary to maintain election security among overseas voters.  
Applewhite, a retired Air Force veteran, said she recently received a text from her son who’s deployed in the Middle East. He said he was confused about how to cast his ballot. 
Her son, and others in military service, don’t have the luxury of figuring out how to vote while sitting in an air-conditioned office, Applewhite said. Instead, they’re often in harm’s way. 
“Their focus is protecting one another and accomplishing a mission. That reality caused me to ask a simple question: When did we decide that people carrying the greatest burden should also carry more burden when it comes to voting?” Applewhite said. 
North Carolina Voter Protection Alliance Executive Director Terence Everitt reminded listeners that the right to vote is fundamental to American democracy.
Everitt, who resigned from the Senate in April to focus on protecting voting rights, condemned Boliek’s demands for transparency within government while not providing the same from his office when questioned about his involvement with voting plans.
“Confidence in elections is earned through transparency, it’s not by demanding blind trust,” he said.

name: VTDigger
title: Annual recovery summit aims to explain the unexplainable
description:
Organized by people in recovery from substance use disorder, the event brings together an often stigmatized community to share their stories.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Annual recovery summit aims to explain the unexplainable.
text:
Melinda White is one of the organizers of the fifth annual “Coming Together, There is Hope” substance use addiction summit in Essex Junction on Friday, July 31, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
ESSEX JUNCTION — Trying to explain substance use disorder to someone who hasn’t gone through it is like trying to explain the color red to someone who’s colorblind. 
That’s what David Riegel explained to a full room of about 50 people, who filled rows of chairs and kneeled on the floor at the Champlain Valley Exposition. Riegel was one of five speakers on a panel of people in recovery sharing their stories. 
“There are not words for what I experienced in active addiction,” Riegel said at one point during the panel. But still he and others tried to find them. 
The group turned out for the annual Coming Together Summit, an event that started five years ago as an effort to advocate for more resources for people in recovery. Even as organizers say that state resources have improved, the event has become an annual tradition, convening people in recovery, their supporters and anyone who wants to learn, to shed light on a community often stigmatized. 
Vermont has some of the highest rates of substance use in the country, according to the Vermont Department of Health. Rates of alcohol, cannabis and stimulant use among Vermonters outpace the rest of the country, according to the health department’s data. 
Service providers stood behind booths with pamphlets while a slate of speakers gave speeches and presentations throughout the morning. Smaller events were held throughout the afternoon, like a drumming circle and a panel discussion from people in recovery. 

Candles and pens sit near a memorial wall during the fifth annual “Coming Together, There is Hope” substance use addiction summit in Essex Junction on Friday, July 31, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The event grows in size every year, organizers Melinda White and Brad Ferland — who are in long-term recovery themselves — say. They estimated about 2,000 people attended on July 31, including Lt. Gov. John Rodgers and Vermont National Guard Adjutant Gen. Henry “Hank” Harder. 
“It feels like a family reunion,” said White. She’s become friends with the providers and attendees to go every year, she said. 
It’s troubling to see people at their lowest points, to see their “misery” and “defeat,” Christina Reiss, chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont, said in a speech addressing how her work intersects with addiction. 
It wouldn’t be worth it if she didn’t get to see people also turn their lives around, she said. Many people who sit in front of her are facing serious charges and looking at years of jail time, she said. 
“For many people it’s an incredible wake up call,” Reiss said. 
They’re usually people who have gotten in way over their heads and are highly motivated to turn things around, she said. About 70% of people incarcerated in Vermont receive medication assisted treatment for opioid use disorder, according to a 2025 survey from The University of Vermont. 
As Reiss spoke to the room of about 200, attendees were buzzing about down the hall. People in recovery reunited with their groups of friends and counselors who helped them leave drugs or alcohol behind. Families walked around to tables set up by counselors at inpatient treatment centers and harm reduction groups. Many of those counselors were in recovery themselves, or lost someone who couldn’t stay sober. 
In the afternoon, groups of people gathered in small rooms to hear not from state officials or judges, but from people in recovery themselves. One man brought his acoustic guitar and played a cover of “Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door” featuring lyrics he wrote about recovery. 
Riegel, among a panel of four, said he had been in long-term recovery since 2007. For him, he explained, that means he hasn’t had any mood or mind-altering substances that haven’t been prescribed by a doctor. 
He grew up in a loving family, he had friends and he did pretty well in school, he said. But still he never felt good enough. 
When he started drinking after eighth grade, he said, all his problems felt lighter. 

Members of the Abenaki Circle of Courage drum circle perform at the fifth annual “Coming Together, There is Hope” substance use addiction summit in Essex Junction on Friday, July 31, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

“It was this magic elixir that allowed me to move through the world and — for the first time — be comfortable in my own skin,” Riegel said. 
His drinking continued through high school and seeped into his life. 
“Alcohol did more for me than what it did to me,” he said. For a long time the consequences didn’t matter, he said, whether he was getting pulled over for driving drunk or ruining his relationships. 
He realized he couldn’t reach his goals in life if he continued on the same path, he said, but he just couldn’t get sober. Then, “out of desperation,” Riegel went to a treatment facility and started a 12-step program, he said. 
That program turned his life around, he said. Now he spends his days taking care of his parents and running residences for people in recovery, to help them transition out of inpatient programs, he said. He’s the executive director of the Vermont Foundation of Recovery in Essex Junction,  and also directs policy and planning for the Vermont Agency of Human Services. 
Many other recovery coaches were similarly in long-term recovery themselves. 
Paul Mader, who sits on the board for the Vermont Veterans Place, said he developed substance use disorder after serving in the military for about eight years. The Northfield organization provides transitional housing and support for struggling veterans. 
Now he volunteers taking care of other veterans in recovery and is guided by his religious faith. Finding Jesus, he said, helped him “start acting right.”
“You learn how to be a grown ass adult and do the right things and live on tuna and whatever for as long as you need it to get yourself right,” Mader said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Annual recovery summit aims to explain the unexplainable.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The first Black woman to lead the CDC will face an uphill battle in restoring trust
description: This story was originally reported by The 19th.  Dr. Erica Schwartz will be the first Black woman to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, promising that she will show “radical transparency and unwavering scientific integrity” in the role. But she faces political headwinds and practical challenges as she starts the job. Schwartz, who […]
text:
Erica Schwartz testifies during her confirmation hearing to become director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
This story was originally reported by The 19th. 
Dr. Erica Schwartz will be the first Black woman to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, promising that she will show “radical transparency and unwavering scientific integrity” in the role. But she faces political headwinds and practical challenges as she starts the job.
Schwartz, who was confirmed Wednesday by the Senate to run the federal agency that primarily responds to infectious diseases, is expected to balance a public commitment to evidence-based policy and how that might clash with the requests of her new boss, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
A CDC director has typically overseen coordination between the federal government and states during disease outbreaks and other public health emergencies. The job has also entailed approving vaccine policy changes and ensuring accurate health data collection.
But the role has been reshaped under an administration that has questioned trust in government institutions, particularly after a global pandemic that generated right-wing outrage over mask mandates and other COVID-related policies.
President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz — who has served in the U.S. Navy, the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and as chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard — but the CDC reports to HHS. Although Schwartz told senators during a July 15 confirmation hearing that she would “follow the science wherever it leads,” she deflected inquiries on whether she would stand up to Kennedy or Trump if she was asked to act in ways that countered scientific evidence.
“She’s trying to walk the tightrope of keeping all of her bonafides: tons of experience, all the background you would want, good relationship with the medical public health community — while also continuing to have the support of the person and people who nominated her,” said Diana Z. O’Brien, a political science professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies women’s political representation.
Schwartz — who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term — said neither the president nor the secretary would put her in a problematic position, a response that some senators repeatedly challenged given the firing of Schwartz’s predecessor, Susan Monarez. Monarez said Kennedy, an anti-vaccine activist, terminated her after an August 2025 meeting in which she refused to prematurely approve vaccine policy changes. Kennedy has refuted Monarez’s claim.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a doctor who was a key vote for Kennedy’s confirmation but has since criticized several of his policy actions, tried to get Schwartz to commit to standing firm.
“We need a CDC director that will actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization,” he said. “Are you the person? And I’m being very direct here, because obviously I feel like we’ve got thousands of kids hospitalized because people have promoted that immunization is bad, and now kids have died because of it. It is evil to do that, and people persist. You are the bulwark, so I’m asking: Will you have the ability and the firmness to stand up to that political meddling, to say, ‘No, that’s wrong, and this is right?’”
Schwartz responded: “You have my assurances that I will continue to lead by my integrity. I will never compromise on the science. I will always, always have the public’s health in mind.”
Cassidy later voted to advance Schwartz out of the health committee that he chairs, a key step for her nomination to reach a full Senate vote. Most Senate Democrats on the committee voted down her nomination.
Schwartz is taking over a beleaguered agency battling multiple public health emergencies, including a measles outbreak and climbing cases of cyclosporiasis, a parasitic infection which causes explosive diarrhea. That all comes amid proposed budget cuts to the CDC that have led to staff cuts and weakened some public health programs. Morale among employees is reportedly low, particularly after a deadly shooting at its Atlanta headquarters last year that officials say was driven by misinformation.
Nadia E. Brown is a government professor and director of the Women’s and Gender Studies Program at Georgetown University who studies Black women’s politics. She said Schwartz’s nomination reminds her of the glass cliff theory of organizational leadership — the idea that companies appoint underrepresented leaders at times when they are struggling or facing a crisis. Schwartz brings extensive experience to the job, having served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term and more recently working at UnitedHealth Group along with board roles at several health-related companies. She committed to resigning from those roles if confirmed.
Still, Schwartz is Trump’s third nominee for CDC director. Trump withdrew his first pick, Dr. Dave Weldon, amid reports that senators were critical of his anti-vaccine views. His second nominee, Monarez, was approved by the Senate in July 2025 only to be fired a month later. The agency has not had a permanent leader for nearly a year.
“It’s become a polarized position when it wasn’t,” Brown said. “We know that the country is deeply racialized and gendered, and Black women face misogynoir. And so if she fails, there’s already a built-in trope into why she fails, right? But there’s also an already built-in trope about, ‘Well, try her. What else do we have to lose?’”
There may also be some opportunities for Schwartz. During her confirmation hearing she expressed support for the Make America Healthy Again platform that is credited with elevating Kennedy’s profile and later helping Trump return to the White House. Her public backing of healthy eating and tackling chronic disease could help Trump ahead of a midterm election year that is perceived as having limited policy wins.
But O’Brien said that, too, carries pitfalls.
“Black women have not had the opportunity to be the face of Make America Healthy Again, even though in the abstract we should be prioritizing Black women’s health,” she said. “But they’ve not gotten to be the face of that movement, and she may just face an uphill battle with the core MAHA people, even if she’s able to bolster support among CDC and among the broader polity.”
Schwartz is already facing criticism from some of Kennedy’s staunchest supporters. Aaron Siri, an anti-vaccine activist who has served as a personal attorney for Kennedy, reportedly called Schwartz “the queen of mandating vaccines” — a point highlighted during her hearing when Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland asked Schwartz how she would respond to people who do not support vaccine mandates. Schwartz has a history of supporting vaccine mandates for military servicemembers.
“I want to be the CDC director for all Americans. I don’t want to be the CDC director just for Americans that believe in vaccines. I want to be the CDC director for Aaron Siri and people that have concerns about vaccines,” she said.
Almost immediately, Siri responded on social media with a message for Schwartz to “contact my office with proposed dates and we will book a ballroom in DC for a full day ‘open and transparent debate.’”
Schwartz also told lawmakers that mRNA technology — which helped develop COVID-19 vaccines and could address a range of diseases — “is safe and effective.” Kennedy last year canceled federal funding for mRNA vaccine research, claiming the technology poses more risks than benefits for certain respiratory viruses. Public health experts have warned the move could harm the nation’s response to future pandemics.
Brown pointed out that Schwartz as a Black woman needed an impeccable resume — her education includes a medical degree, a master’s degree in public health and a law degree — to even be considered for the job while others in the Trump administration have a history of limited experience for key governmental roles. But those credentials can only get someone so far amid such distrust in science.
“In order to be a Black woman who gets this, she had to come in with an absolutely perfect pedigree,” she said. Normally that would help her, but this is just a very unusual situation where, for the MAHA people, it’s not a good pedigree because it’s too much in the conventional scientific community.”
Adia Wingfield is a sociology professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies racial and gender inequality in the workplace. She said Schwartz’s goal of restoring trust and bringing transparency faces a high bar in this political climate since public trust in a variety of institutions — Congress, media, universities — is declining.
“Certainly the CDC is not immune from that. So taking on the task of restoring trust to an institution that has been besieged for quite some time is a pretty lofty goal. And that’s not to say that she couldn’t achieve it, but that’s just to say that I think the headwinds are probably against anybody taking on that role,” she said.
The challenge may be exacerbated by Schwarz’s race and gender.
“As a Black woman, I think failing or being unable to achieve those goals in the ways that she has set out would take on additional resonance because of how few Black women have held either that position or tend to hold these types of positions in society at large,” Wingfield said. “It becomes reflective of the group membership, not necessarily of the individual, and that allows for drawing attention away from the bigger structural factors that make it difficult to do the job in the first place.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas’ Democratic, GOP nominees for governor seek unity — except with each other
description: The Republican and Democratic nominees for governor in Kansas are labeling their partisan rivals as extremist politicians capable of harming the state.
text:
Sen. Cindy Holscher arrives at an Oct. 13, 2025, forum on redistricting at Shawnee Mission Unitarian Universalist Church in Lenexa. Holscher, who won the Democratic Party's nomination for governor, says Republican gubernatorial nominee Ty Masterson, a senator from Andover, is an extremist conservative. In turn, Masterson is labeling Holscher a leftist extremist. They meet Nov. 3 in the general election to determine who replaces Gov. Laura Kelly. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher preach the gospel of political unity while opening the three-month odyssey to determine Kansas’ next governor by casting their partisan rivals as political extremists.
The gestures of goodwill were designed to bring comfort to voters who didn’t make Holscher or Masterson their first choice in the Tuesday primary election. These obligatory calls for togetherness didn’t inhibit Masterson nor Holscher from urging voters to stand against their major party rivals.
Holscher and Masterson received blessings from second-place finishers in the respective primary campaigns — businessman Phillip Sarnecki on the GOP side and state Sen. Ethan Corson on the Democratic side — after votes were tallied. Masterson said he spoke with Sarnecki and other prominent GOP candidates, while Corson said in a statement he wished Holscher well during the general election campaign.
“We’ve got to come together in this state,” said Masterson, who is a state senator from Andover. “I’m asking all Republicans, independents and commonsense Democrats to join me in the effort to take back Kansas.”
He went on to condemn Holscher’s record as a state legislator and to describe her as a “left-wing extremist.”
“Cindy Holscher would be the most radical progressive governor in the history of Kansas,” Masterson said. “I serve with Cindy Holscher in the state Senate, and I’ve seen firsthand just how far to the left she is.”
Holscher, an Overland Park lawmaker who prevailed without the endorsement of Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, thanked primary opponents Corson and Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog for their “commitment to our state and for their willingness to serve.” Kelly endorsed Corson in the primary.
“Our party is stronger because of the debate we had, and I look forward to working alongside them in the months ahead,” Holscher said. “From this moment forward, we are united, and as we turn our attention to November, the stakes couldn’t be higher. Our state cannot afford another extremist like Ty Masterson.”
In a step toward electoral harmony, Kelly made a peace offering to Holscher after she worked diligently to assist Corson’s bid for the Democratic nomination.
“We cannot let Kansas go backwards,” Kelly said. “I ask all Kansans, regardless of political party, to unite and move our state forward by electing Cindy Holscher this November. If Ty Masterson is elected, he will take our state back to the dark days of Sam Brownback, to the days of chronically underfunded schools, fiscal mismanagement and crumbling roads and bridges — the very problems I ran for governor to solve.”
Kelly is completing her second and final term as governor after defeating Republican gubernatorial nominee Kris Kobach in 2018 and GOP gubernatorial nominee Derek Schmidt in 2022.
“For decades, Laura Kelly has tirelessly served the people of our state, and I’m grateful and honored that she has endorsed our campaign,” Holscher said. “As governor she has moved our state forward while blocking a host of disastrous policies put forward by extremist Ty Masterson.”
She said Kelly understood the urgency of mobilizing Democrats, independents and Republicans to make certain Masterson didn’t ride President Donald Trump’s endorsement to victory on Nov. 3.
On Election night, Masterson thanked his family and campaign staff for handling the primary contest the “right way.” He said his campaign didn’t put out “negative garbage” against his GOP challengers on the primary, but acknowledged political action committees and dark money groups did.
“I can’t go without thanking President Trump. He loves this country,” Masterson said. “Occasionally, God raises somebody up that kind of  becomes greater than themselves, right, and does more than a single human being can do.”
Unofficial results reported by the Kansas secretary of state’s office show Masterson received 43% of the vote in a seven-candidate Republican primary. Sarnecki netted 22% while state Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt had 14% and Secretary of State Scott Schwab had 11%. Holscher collected 49% of the Democratic Party vote with Corson earning 39% and Skoog receiving 13%.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Some data centers are building their own power plants. In Oklahoma, most want to plug into the grid
description: Oklahoma passed a law last year allowing energy-hungry facilities to build their own power. But as data center announcements sprout up across Oklahoma, most include plans to work with local utilities. Last month, Gov. Kevin Stitt and some Oklahoma electric utilities signed a federal pledge to protect household ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge dire[...]
text:
Transmission lines are pictured in central Oklahoma. (Photo by Chloe Bennett-Steele/StateImpact Oklahoma)Oklahoma passed a law last year allowing energy-hungry facilities to build their own power. But as data center announcements sprout up across Oklahoma, most include plans to work with local utilities.


Last month, Gov. Kevin Stitt and some Oklahoma electric utilities signed a federal pledge to protect household ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge directs data center developers to pay their own way and invest in surrounding communities.
Part of the document states companies must buy the massive amount of electricity they require, add more power to the grid or supply it on-site.
“You’re going to be building your own data centers, and you’re going to be building your own electric plants,” said President Donald Trump. “You’re essentially becoming a utility.”
The pledge is one of many ways officials are responding to public pushback against hyperscale data centers.
Oklahoma has its own version of a ratepayer protection pledge, a law requiring electricity suppliers to create separate terms and conditions for large-scale energy consumers like data centers and increase transparency. State regulators are currently reviewing large-load tariffs from utilities intended to prevent households from shouldering grid connection costs for companies like Google and Meta.
The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities. Rep. Brad Boles, R-Marlow, co-authored the legislation.
“What we realized is in Oklahoma, our state law is kind of vague; it doesn’t really say that companies can provide their own power generation,” Boles, who is running for a seat on the Corporation Commission, said. “It doesn’t say they can’t either, but it doesn’t say that they can.”
“ So we wanted to provide clarity that if a large load comes to Oklahoma and they want to provide their own power generation, that they would have the ability to do that,” he said.
The bill was expected to generate billions of dollars in private investment and alleviate pressure from the electric grid. Growing demand, supercharged by large-load consumers like data centers, is expected to outpace supply within the Southwest Power Pool’s territory. The organization operates the electric grid in Oklahoma and 16 other states.
But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid. Experts say the state’s grid system is likely more reliable than depending on behind-the-meter generation. Building a power plant is costly and can take years to complete.
“ I don’t readily, actually, believe that any data center company wants to also be in the power business,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin.
Still, some AI companies are investing in behind-the-meter natural gas plants in states like neighboring Texas to accelerate the pace of buildout. Those plants are expected to emit significant amounts of pollution, an analysis from the Texas Tribune and Floodlight shows.
Why Oklahoma isn’t seeing an influx of behind-the-meter projects for data centers 

	Data centers typically have backup generators on site, should they temporarily lose connection. Some companies are adding power to the grid with new energy projects.
Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company’s three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater. Google is building two solar farms to add energy generation.
Christi Woodworth,  OG&E’s chief communications officer, said companies are eyeing the state’s relatively low electricity costs and reliability.
“They’ve got to make a decision about if they want to build or bring their own generation,” she said. “That effectively puts them on an island, right? They take on all of that risk themselves, and they have to decide if that’s something that they want to do.”
“The folks we’re talking with are very interested in connecting to the grid.”
The company is in “a handful” of other discussions with large-load projects, Woodworth said, but no plans are public yet.
Last year, officials announced a project in Chickasha and celebrated the state’s new behind-the-meter law. The Chickasha Airport Industrial Park could one day be home to a data center and power plant, but no firm plans have been made public. A manufacturing firm in the Tulsa Port of Catoosa announced early this year it plans to build its power on-site. A news release says the company specializes in aerospace, energy and advanced manufacturing.
Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN’s Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities.
The Kiowa facility is the state’s largest proposed data center, according to energy analytics firm Cleanview. In an email, Jason Date, associate director of development, said the company plans to secure its power through Public Service Company of Oklahoma.
“Like the vast majority of homes and businesses, IREN’s facilities use grid power because it is the most efficient and reliable way to source electricity,” he said.
A delay in critical infrastructure delivery is also an obstacle for data center developers. Getting a natural gas plant, the typical energy source for behind-the-meter data center projects, can currently take years.
“If you’re not in line right now, you’re probably not getting one until the 2030s,” Rhodes said.
Some companies instead are turning to used products to avoid the mile-long backlog.
“ I’ve heard of companies looking to buy used cruise ship engines,” Rhodes said. “I heard one the other day of someone trying to string together a bunch of used helicopter engines.”
Oklahoma’s behind-the-meter law requires developers to have natural gas as part of their plant. Other sources, including solar and wind, could be used in conjunction. When asked about the natural gas requirement, Boles said it was included to support the oil and gas industry.
“We felt like, as Oklahomans, it’s important to ensure that natural gas has a seat at the table,” he said.
According to an analysis from Cleanview, Oklahoma has fewer than 30 data centersplanned for the state as of early August. Texas has hundreds in its queue, Rhodes said, meaning more developers are racing to supply power. Should tech companies continue showing interest in Oklahoma, it’s possible more behind-the-meter projects could be announced.
Boles said he expects more interest in the future.
“Like anything, it takes time,” Boles said. “If you’re to build a facility with behind-the-meter, it may take three to five years to get the power infrastructure built.”
“I think we’re not going to really know for sure how many companies are utilizing this until a few years down the road.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Goodlander calls for feds to investigate Sununu Center amid ongoing allegations
description: U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander waded into the ongoing controversy at the Sununu Youth Services Center this week as she called on federal prosecutors to open their own investigation into the Manchester juvenile justice facility. The Office of the Child Advocate first raised concerns about staff being potentially abusive toward the facility’s underage detainees i[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander speaks at an event at Waypoint in Manchester on July 8, 2025. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander waded into the ongoing controversy at the Sununu Youth Services Center this week as she called on federal prosecutors to open their own investigation into the Manchester juvenile justice facility.
The Office of the Child Advocate first raised concerns about staff being potentially abusive toward the facility’s underage detainees in a March letter to lawmakers. The Disability Rights Center-NH, the Department of Justice, and a state Senate ad hoc committee all launched parallel investigations. 
The investigations have uncovered a series of allegations, including children being denied education and access to the outdoors during an overrestrictive lockdown; illegal restraints resulting in at least one broken bone; children forced to urinate on the floor of their cells; unwarranted strip searches; and dried blood found on the building’s walls. Additionally, a child was hospitalized after a fight with another resident, investigators revealed. This all comes as staff members have struggled to manage the growing aggression of residents toward them.
Now, Goodlander, a Democrat who represents the western half of the state, is asking U.S. Attorney Erin Creegan and the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division to launch its own investigation. She wrote in an open letter that the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act gives them authority to investigate and “determine whether a pattern or practice at the facility has deprived children in state custody of their constitutional or federal rights.”
The New Hampshire Department of Justice’s investigation — which was criticized by the Office of the Child Advocate for putting too much blame on the children — ended last month with a final report that concluded there were staffing issues and general leadership failures but no evidence of physical abuse against youth by facility staff. 
The state Senate committee’s final report was harsher and recommended sweeping changes, including a near-total ban on strip searches; increased staff training; restructuring of the Division for Children, Youth, and Families; more cameras in the facility; and traits to look for in new leadership. The Office of the Child Advocate and the Disability Rights Center’s investigations are ongoing, but the two watchdog agencies’ initial letters somewhat contradict the Department of Justice’s final assessment.
Goodlander, in her letter, writes that a “neutral federal assessment … is well suited to resolve the divergence between the two watchdogs’ findings and the State’s conclusions.”
Attorney General John Formella, who leads the New Hampshire Department of Justice, said in a statement: “The New Hampshire Department of Justice follows the facts, enforces the law, and pursues justice without fear or favor. The State continues to work to strengthen safety and security at the facility. The New Hampshire Department of Justice remains focused on accountability, transparency, and protecting children.”
Goodlander’s team did not respond to the Bulletin’s emailed question about whether it reached out to DHHS, which operates the facility, before releasing the letter. Creegan’s office did not respond to emailed questions.
This year’s allegations are the latest in a long history of abuse and neglect at the Sununu Youth Services Center, which was formerly known as the Youth Detention Center, or YDC, and has been involved in hundreds of lawsuits spanning decades.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Despite community pushback, MaineHealth announces closure of Damariscotta birthing center
description: The closure of a birthing center at a Damariscotta hospital is moving forward, the MaineHealth Board of Trustees announced Thursday, despite months of community opposition and concern about worsening health access for rural Mainers. In a statement Thursday, MaineHealth announced it would transition inpatient labor and delivery services from Lincoln Hospital[...]
text:
Maine Medical Center in Portland, Maine. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)The closure of a birthing center at a Damariscotta hospital is moving forward, the MaineHealth Board of Trustees announced Thursday, despite months of community opposition and concern about worsening health access for rural Mainers.
In a statement Thursday, MaineHealth announced it would transition inpatient labor and delivery services from Lincoln Hospital to Mid Coast Hospital in Brunswick beginning Dec. 18. 
As part of the plan, the board also committed that MaineHealth will not close any additional labor and delivery centers in the statewide health network in the next two years. The closure of the Lincoln unit marks the 12th birthing center to close in Maine since 2015, and it leaves Lincoln County, as well as neighboring Waldo and Sagadahoc counties, without any operating birthing units. 
“We pursued every reasonable path we could identify because this decision was never about whether labor and delivery matters — it absolutely does,” MaineHealth CEO Andrew Mueller said in a press statement. “It came down to one responsibility: determining whether we could continue providing safe, reliable care for every mother and every baby, every day and every night.”
Mueller added that providing this care “requires highly specialized teams that are available around the clock and prepared to respond immediately to routine deliveries and unexpected emergencies. We concluded that we could no longer consistently ensure that level of staffing and clinical coverage at Lincoln Hospital over the long term.”
Comprehensive prenatal and postpartum care will continue at Lincoln Hospital, which also plans to expand local gynecologic outpatient and surgical services.
Save Miles Labor and Delivery, a local group that organized in opposition to the planned closure, wrote on social media after the announcement, “One of the most harmful decisions our community will ever see. Cowardice. Plain and simple.” 
“They have ignored the voice of our governor, politicians on all sides, the local ambulance service, businesses, far and wide, and they are creating a maternity desert in Lincoln County,” they added. “This isn’t a hospital, it’s a morgue.”
Gov. Janet Mills sent a letter to the chair of the board of trustees last week asking the hospital to push the decision back two years in order to “meaningfully engage the community on the issues at hand” and to “allow for full consideration of alternatives to closure,” the Press Herald reported.
The decision also comes one day after Lincoln County resident Corinna Stum filed a lawsuit against MaineHealth seeking to prevent the closure. 
MaineHealth sued over potential closure of labor and delivery unit

Stum, who is pregnant and scheduled to deliver at Lincoln Hospital in January, asked for an emergency injunction while the court assesses whether the nonprofit violated its legal obligation to serve the public and was, as the lawsuit alleges, non-transparent in its review process.
Under the consolidation plan, the board notes that Lincoln and Mid Coast hospitals “will operate as one coordinated regional OB/GYN and certified nurse midwife team, giving patients access to a broader clinical team while allowing them to receive all care other than labor and delivery close to home.” 
Mid Coast Hospital is situated 24 miles south of the Miles Campus in Damariscotta, a 40-minute drive along Route 1 that can become very congested during the summer months.
MaineHealth notes that patients who prefer to deliver at Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport or another hospital of their choosing “will also be supported in transferring their obstetrical care.” 
In the wake of MaineHealth’s announcement this past spring that it was deciding whether to close the unit, a group of community members formed The Miles Delivers Action Coalition, which conducted extensive independent research into the hospital’s claims of lower birth volumes and challenges with workforce recruitment, as well as hospital finances, demographic trends, available funding opportunities and more.
The coalition also hosted a rally and march in Portland on Saturday, which drew nurses, doctors, activists and state leaders, including Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree and U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson.
In a statement Thursday, Pingree said she disagreed with the board’s decision.
“Moms, babies and families in Lincoln County will suffer for it. Women will still be giving birth, just farther from home, with less time to spare and fewer safety nets if something goes wrong,” she said. 
Pingree said if elected she would bring physicians, hospital leaders, physicians, families, and state policy experts together “to develop a real plan for how we maintain maternity care across this state, ensuring the safety of moms and babies,” including her promise of a one-year moratorium on labor and delivery closures on Day One.
“Families in Maine deserve better than a system that closes doors one county at a time,” she added.

text:
A pile of ruined furniture sits outside of Pop’s Furniture in Buckhannon, West Virginia, on Thursday. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)People in Upshur and Lewis counties who lost employment because of last month’s deadly storms and flooding are eligible for disaster unemployment assistance, Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s office and Workforce West Virginia announced Thursday.
The Trump administration approved a major disaster declaration for those two counties earlier this week. 
Storms on July 21 and 22 brought 9 tornadoes and up to about 7 inches of rain in some areas of the state, leading to flash flooding. central West Virginia was among the hardest hit. Flooding killed two people in Upshur County. FEMA is still reviewing damage in five other West Virginia counties: Barbour, Doddridge, Harrison, Pleasants and Ritchie, officials said. 
“Recovery doesn’t end when the floodwaters recede,” Morrisey said in the news release. “We’ll continue working with our federal, state and local partners to make sure the people of Lewis and Upshur counties have the resources they need to recover. Disaster Unemployment Assistance is another important step in helping affected workers and businesses get back on their feet.”
Benefits are available to those living or working in Upshur or Lewis counties who lost their jobs due to the storms July 21 and 22, and to self-employed workers, including farmers who are usually not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
Applicants are required to give proof of past earnings, such as business records or bank statements and income tax forms, no more than 21 days after the application has been filed. Claims must be filed by Oct. 2, 2026.
“Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA) applies to losses incurred during the incident period of July 21, 2026 to July 22, 2026 for eligible people impacted by the severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes, flooding, landslides and mudslides,” Scott Adkins, acting Commissioner of WorkForce West Virginia, said in the news release. “Full-time workers, part-time workers, and self-employed part-time individuals can be eligible for benefits. The last payable week of this emergency benefit ends February 6, 2027 as long as your unemployment or loss of self-employment continues as a result of the disaster. Eligibility for DUA benefits will be determined on a week-to-week basis for each week you file your claim.”
People who are unemployed due to the storms must contact Workforce West Virginia by email during the work day at ucpolicy@wv.gov phone 304-558-3340.

text:
Indianapolis City-County Councilor Joshua Bain will become the next member of the powerful Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. (Photo from Bain's LinkedIn)Gov. Mike Braun on Thursday named his next pick for Indiana’s Utility Regulatory Commission, shortly after a nominating panel released a trio of finalists and three days after he fired former Commissioner Andy Zay.
Indianapolis City-County Councilor Joshua Bain, who has represented the southwest corner of Marion County since 2020, will fill the vacant seat. His appointment is effective immediately. A caucus will be held to fill his seat.
“I have been clear (that) affordability is my top priority for Hoosiers. As families and businesses continue to feel the pressure of rising costs, it’s essential that we have leaders who will be ratepayer conscience,” Braun said in a news release.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“Joshua Bain brings experience in energy policy, environmental stewardship, and collaboration across government and local communities,” the governor continued. “I am confident he will serve with integrity and keep affordability and the public interest at the forefront of every decision.”
Bain has worked as executive director of legislative and intergovernmental affairs for the Indiana Department of Environmental Management since February, according to his LinkedIn.
He was previously at the Center for Energy Education, and has also worked in virtual customer support, as a legislative assistant for the Indiana House, and as a field manager for the House’s Republican Campaign Committee.
The five-member IURC can have up to three members of the same political party. Bain, who is a Republican, will maintain a GOP majority.
The commissioner job comes with a salary of about $152,000.
Zay was fired Monday for allegedly “failing to file a required financial disclosure after his removal as Chair, improperly awarding payments and personal gifts to employees, and directing staff to alter a public meeting agenda without consulting the new Chair,” according to the State Personnel Department.
Commissioners are appointed to four-year terms and can only be dismissed “for cause” under Indiana law. But Braun, in his comments to reporters, has focused on a June vote to raise rates for AES Indiana customers.
IURC head, governor talk Zay firing and AES hike reconsideration

Zay joined Commissioners David Veleta and David Ziegner to support the $71 million hike. Commissioner Bob Deig voted in opposition and now-Chair Anthony Swinger recused himself after working on the case in his previous job at the Office of Utility Consumer Counselor.
Counselor Abby Gray, whose office represents ratepayers in IURC matters, has petitioned regulators to reconsider the increase or rehear the case.
The IURC was set to vote Wednesday on the petition. But Swinger pulled the case from the agenda, citing a lack of consensus. Regulators have until Sept. 8 to make a decision on the petition. Shifting membership on the five-member body could affect the results.
Last month, Braun selected attorney Joby Jerrells to replace Veleta, who announced plans to resign shortly after the original AES Indiana vote.
Veleta’s last day at the IURC is Aug. 14, with Jerrells starting work Aug. 17.
With Zay out, Ziegner will be the only remaining commissioner who approved the rate increase. He’s also set to become the only one appointed before Braun took office in early 2025.

title: Dane Co. judge says absentee voting system discriminates against people with disabilities
description: A Dane County judge found that Wisconsin’s absentee voting system discriminates against voters with print disabilities by forcing them to have someone else assist them with filling out their ballots — undermining the secrecy of their vote.  In a ruling issued Tuesday, Judge Everett Mitchell sided with Disability Rights Wisconsin and the League of Women […]
text:
RALEIGH, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 17: Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. North Carolina will send out absentee ballots to military and overseas citizens by September 20. Other absentee ballots will be sent by September 24 to voters who requested ballots by mail. Early voting begins October 17. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)A Dane County judge found that Wisconsin’s absentee voting system discriminates against voters with print disabilities by forcing them to have someone else assist them with filling out their ballots — undermining the secrecy of their vote. 
In a ruling issued Tuesday, Judge Everett Mitchell sided with Disability Rights Wisconsin and the League of Women Voters who had brought the lawsuit against the state Elections Commission to ensure that voters who have trouble seeing, reading or filling out their ballot can request, receive, vote and return an absentee ballot on their own. 
The groups, and four voters with disabilities, brought the lawsuit in April 2024 and were represented by the voting rights focused firm Law Forward, arguing that the state’s existing system violates the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Rehabilitation Act. 
In his decision, Mitchell wrote that WEC must follow the ADA’s requirement to accommodate voters with disabilities and that the current system allowing people with print disabilities to have someone else fill out their ballots denies the voters “the equal opportunity to vote absentee privately and independently.” 
While he agreed that the current system is discriminatory, Mitchell did not grant the request that disabled voters be allowed to cast their absentee ballots electronically, writing that “there remains a genuine dispute of material fact with respect to whether their proposed accommodation is reasonable.” 
Further hearings will be held in the case to determine the best solution.

title: 22 years later, Mark Sanford brings pigs back to the Statehouse, this time over DC spending
description: COLUMBIA — More than two decades after then-Gov. Mark Sanford carried two piglets into the Statehouse to protest the state budget, the now-U.S. Senate candidate reproduced the stunt — at least, as close as he could — to show he’s the best candidate to fight overspending in Washington. The former governor and 1st District congressman […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Mark Sanford holds a piglet on the steps of the Statehouse Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. It echoed the time in 2004 that Sanford, then the governor, brought a pair of piglets he called Pork and Barrel into the state House chamber to protest the General Assembly's override of his budget vetoes. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — More than two decades after then-Gov. Mark Sanford carried two piglets into the Statehouse to protest the state budget, the now-U.S. Senate candidate reproduced the stunt — at least, as close as he could — to show he’s the best candidate to fight overspending in Washington.
The former governor and 1st District congressman is among 10 candidates competing in the special GOP primary to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on November general election ballots.
Early voting ends at 5 p.m. Friday for the Aug. 11 primary. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the top two vote-getters advance to an Aug. 25 runoff.
Sanford argues what distinguishes him in the crowded field is his demonstrated resolve to combat deficits. In 2004, that included carrying “Pork” and “Barrel” into the Statehouse as a visual representation of what he called waste and opposition to how quickly legislators dispensed with his attempted cuts.
His administration “got into the weeds” of spending, he said, noting he was the first governor to create a real budget proposal ahead of the legislative process.
“Should I go to Washington, I would get in and look under the hood as I did in Columbia at the way money is being spent,” he said in another Statehouse news conference with swine.

U.S. Senate candidate Mark Sanford and his sister Sarah Sanford hold a pair of piglets, nicknamed Debt and Deficit, on the steps of the Statehouse Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. It echoed the time in 2004 that Sanford, then the governor, brought a pair of piglets he called Pork and Barrel into the state House chamber to protest the General Assembly’s override of his budget vetoes. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

This time, he talked to reporters outside and brought three pigs: A 400-pound pig stayed in a pen pulled by a trailer onto the grounds.
He again held a small pig under each arm, but only briefly, as one squealed so loudly, he couldn’t talk above it. The kunekune swine calmed down when his sister took one.
“I begin with pig math,” he said, noting that if Pork and Barrel had lived for the last 22 years, they could’ve had 880 piglets, based on normal reproduction. He equated their offspring to compounded interest.
“We’ve seen that math at work against us in Washington, D.C.,” he said. “Pig math doesn’t work for any of us as taxpayers. It will hurt every one of us.”
He’s been preaching against growing the national deficit for decades. As governor, that included refusing South Carolina’s $700 million share of federal stimulus money approved by Congress in 2009 to help states deal with Great Recession-caused holes — until an order by the state Supreme Court forced him to request the aid.

U.S. Senate candidate Mark Sanford touted his record as a fiscal hawk Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, bringing Porky, a 400-pound Berkshire pig to the steps of the Statehouse. It echoed the time in 2004 that Sanford, then the governor, brought a pair of piglets into the state House chamber to protest the General Assembly’s override of his budget vetoes. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

That’s another example of the public spats between the GOP-controlled Legislature and Republican governor, who often used props as he took his arguments directly to the public. In 2005, he used a horse-drawn carriage as the backdrop, as he argued that South Carolina’s government still operated like it was the 19th century.
The defecating piglets, which received national attention, provided arguably his most memorable complaint about spending.
In May 2004, he stood outside House chambers with a piglet in each arm a day after the chamber overturned more than 100 of his vetoes in less than two hours. The squealing piglets — along with the mess they made on the carpet — infuriated legislators, who continued to overturn his vetoes that day and throughout his tenure. In 2006, ahead of his re-election, Sanford vetoed the entire budget package, which legislators overrode even easier.
And while Sanford’s office created the first detailed executive budget — rather than broad proposals that didn’t balance spending, as prior administrations — his recommendations were largely discarded by the Legislature.
Asked Thursday how he would be more successful as a senator, he acknowledged that he “had many, many vetoes not sustained.”
But what’s not remembered about the pig story, he said, is that it worked.
Due to lower-than-expected tax collections the previous year (2002-03), lawmakers needed to dig out of a $155 million deficit. While mostly covering it, the budget that Sanford protested with poo on his jacket still left a $16 million hole.
“People got it back home: ‘You’re right,'” he said of how South Carolinians responded.
Legislators were “putting pork barrel spending ahead of a constitutional requirement” to balance the budget, he said.
Ultimately, the debt was erased when the 2003-04 fiscal year unexpectedly closed with higher-than-expected revenues.
Sanford recognized Thursday that his concerns about the federal deficit didn’t gain traction in the past. But with the national debt now at $39.8 trillion, and unaffordability putting the American Dream out of reach for many, he believes voters get it now.
Earlier this year, Sanford jumped into the open contest for the 1st District in an effort to win back the coastal congressional seat he held before and after his tenure as governor. He ended that bid a month later, saying he planned to form a nonprofit focused on bringing the debt down.
He’s still in the process of creating that nonprofit. What becomes of those plans depends on the outcome of the upcoming contests, he said Thursday.

title: McConnell says he has been discharged from rehab
description: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell says he has been discharged from a rehabilitation program after a seven-week absence from the Senate.  McConnell, 84, was hospitalized in June and said on July 12 he would enter a rehabilitation center.  “Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home. Elaine and I […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, left, with his wife, former Secretary of Labor and Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao, on Sunday, July 26. (Provided by McConnell's office)U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell says he has been discharged from a rehabilitation program after a seven-week absence from the Senate. 
McConnell, 84, was hospitalized in June and said on July 12 he would enter a rehabilitation center. 
“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home. Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff,” McConnell said in a Thursday afternoon statement.
 “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business,” he continued. 
On Thursday, McConnell was not present at an Agriculture Committee committee to advance the farm bill to the Senate floor. He had attempted to cast a vote by proxy but Senate rules prevented it. 
Throughout his public absence, speculation about McConnell’s vitality ran rampant online and his office shared photos of him with his wife, former Secretary of Labor and Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao. 
Among those calling for greater transparency about McConnell’s health was Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. He sent a letter to McConnell last week asking for “provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.” 
Beshear faced many calls nationally to declare McConnell’s seat vacant. However, legal experts have previously told the Lantern Beshear has no authority to take any action on McConnell’s seat until the senator has resigned or died.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska, neighbors Iowa and Missouri join state list tied to cyclosporiasis outbreak
description: LINCOLN — Federal officials have added Nebraska to the growing list of states with residents who are part of a national outbreak tied to the parasite cyclospora that can cause lengthy gastrointestinal illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that at least 92 Nebraska cases have been directly tied to the ongoing outbreak […]
text:
Nebraska's Douglas County Health Department on Monday notes a sudden rise in cyclospora infections among county residents. On July 17, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it has linked an outbreak of cyclosporiasis in five states to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taco Bell restaurants. (Photo courtesy Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)LINCOLN — Federal officials have added Nebraska to the growing list of states with residents who are part of a national outbreak tied to the parasite cyclospora that can cause lengthy gastrointestinal illness.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that at least 92 Nebraska cases have been directly tied to the ongoing outbreak that has grown to more than 6,000 linked cases across 15 states. 
Health investigators have determined that iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico and recalled by Taylor Farms de Mexico is the most probable cause of the outbreak. Other states newly identified in the outbreak are Iowa, Missouri, Arkansas, North Carolina and New Hampshire. 
The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services as well as the Douglas and Lincoln-Lancaster County health departments released media statements Thursday confirming Nebraska’s inclusion. 
Cases of cyclospora in Douglas, the state’s largest county, have been rising fast in recent weeks. A spokesperson said the county has confirmed 71 cases since the outbreak began.
While 46 confirmed cases have been reported in Lancaster County since June, health director Kerry Kernen said the team is working with state and federal partners to determine how many are linked to the national outbreak.
“We conducted in-depth interviews with residents who became ill and looked for potential commonalities among cases,” Kernan said. “Information gathered in our investigations showed a correlation with the shredded iceberg lettuce.”
According to federal health officials, illnesses linked to this outbreak began on June 22 and onset dates have continued through July 31, so it is possible more cases will surface. The CDC reports at least 278 hospitalizations. Two deaths have been reported in Michigan. 
Symptoms of the illness, called cyclosporiasis, include watery diarrhea that can last weeks to months, fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, bloating, cramping and nausea. Less common symptoms include low-grade fever and vomiting.  
Fresh vegetables and fruit are usually associated with cyclospora outbreaks, health officials said. People become sick when they eat food or drink water contaminated with the parasite. The illness does not spread from one person to another. 
Unlike viruses and bacteria, cyclospora is a parasite, making outbreaks more difficult to investigate, according to the state DHHS. Standard laboratory methods that can quickly connect illnesses are less effective for parasites so public health officials rely on  interviews with patients, epidemiologic analysis  and coordination among various health partners to identify a common source, the agency said. 
Dr. Timothy Tesmer, DHHS chief medical officer, emphasized that the state food supply is safe, yet he encouraged Nebraskans to “use proper food handling practices, exercise caution with certain produce and, when possible, choose locally sourced produce.”
The DHHS said that the risk to the general public remains low, and that recalled products have been removed from store shelves. Tesmer said Nebraska continues to work closely with local health departments and federal health officials to identify additional cases and protect Nebraskans’ health.

name: National
title: More states ban child marriage, though it’s still legal in most of the US
description: After authorities rescued 16 children last month who had been confined to a single room in a home in rural Ohio, attention turned to their mother, who had been 15 and pregnant when she married their father. The child endangerment case has recharged a national conversation around child marriage, which is defined by the United […]
text:
Since 2018, 17 states have barred marriage before age 18, but most states still allow minors to wed with parental or judicial approval. (Photo by Anna Claire Vollers/Stateline)
After authorities rescued 16 children last month who had been confined to a single room in a home in rural Ohio, attention turned to their mother, who had been 15 and pregnant when she married their father.
The child endangerment case has recharged a national conversation around child marriage, which is defined by the United Nations as any marriage involving someone under age 18.
Earlier this year two Ohio state senators — one Democrat, one Republican — introduced a bill that would require Ohio residents to be at least 18 to get married. Current state law allows 17-year-olds to marry with court approval. The bill passed out of a Senate committee in June but didn’t get a full Senate vote before lawmakers adjourned for the summer.
Until the last decade, marriage under age 18 was legal in all 50 states. In 2018, Delaware and New Jersey became the first states to outright ban it. More states followed: Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Rhode Island, New York, Massachusetts, Vermont, Connecticut, Michigan, Washington, Virginia, New Hampshire, Washington, D.C., Maine, Oregon, Missouri and most recently, Oklahoma, have banned it since 2020.
Vinton County children endangerment case increases interest in bill to ban child marriage in Ohio

In May, Oklahoma passed a Republican-sponsored bill that removed all exceptions for a person under 18 to marry.
“Oklahoma children must be able to grow up free from coercion and exploitation, and it is our duty to guarantee those protections are enacted and enforced,” said Oklahoma state Sen. Warren Hamilton, a Republican who sponsored the bill, in a May statement.
Hamilton  said the law protects minors from forced marriage and helps prevent child trafficking and exploitation, ensuring “that no minor, even those who are close to adulthood, is placed in a marriage that puts their safety or well-being at risk.”
In 33 states, marriage under 18 is still allowed with varying restrictions, such as requiring parental consent or court approval for marriage involving someone aged 15-17. Only three states — California, Mississippi and New Mexico — do not specify a minimum age for marriage.
As of 2021, the most recent year for which data is available, Nevada, Idaho and Utah had the highest rates of child marriage, according to a 2025 study by Unchained At Last, a nonprofit that advocates for the end of child marriage. Nevada’s rate — 6 per 1,000 minors — was nearly twice that of Idaho and Utah. Maine, New Hampshire and Rhode Island had the lowest rates, at less than 0.2 per 1,000 minors. The U.S average was more than 2 per 1,000 girls and 0.31 per 1,000 boys.
Between 2000 and 2021, nearly 315,000 children under age 18 were legally wed, according to the group. Most of those were girls wed to adult men.
Advocates for ending child marriage point to research that has found lifelong consequences for those involved, including greater vulnerability to sexual and domestic violence, worse health outcomes, higher likelihood of dropping out of high school, greater risk of poverty and higher divorce rates.
A 2022 study from researchers at McGill University found that the proportion of child marriages that met the definition of a sex crime varied across states from 1% to more than 50%.
Oklahoma’s bipartisan bill sailed through the Senate earlier this year but encountered fierce opposition in the House, where it passed by a single vote.
Some Republican lawmakers argued that the measure amounted to government overreach and would increase the number of babies born out of wedlock. One Oklahoma Republican lawmaker who opposed the bill said it would take away parents’ rights to give permission for a teen to marry.
Republican lawmakers in states including Missouri have made similar arguments. One Missouri Republican legislator said he believed banning child marriage would result in more abortions, reported the Missouri Independent.
Oklahoma Democratic state Rep. Michelle McCane told her colleagues earlier this year that she gave birth at 15 and that her life would have been far different if her mother had let her marry the person she “picked in eighth grade.” She pointed out that married minors can’t legally seek a divorce or stay at a domestic violence shelter.

“I don’t know about you all, but please think back to who you picked in eighth, ninth, 10th grade, and I think many of you would be very disappointed to be saddled with that person for the rest of your life,” McCane said.
Children under 18 typically lack the legal rights that give adults agency in a marriage, such as being able to file for divorce or to file court actions in their own name.
While Republicans have been divided recently on the issue, underage marriage bans have drawn criticism from liberal groups in the past. The American Civil Liberties Union and Planned Parenthood opposed a 2017 California bill to ban marriage before age 18, arguing it intruded on the fundamental rights of marriage.
This week, a bill in California that would raise the minimum marriage age to 18 with no exceptions is headed to a vote in the state Senate.
One of the advocates pushing for the bill this year in California is Courtney Stodden, a model and singer who, at age 16, married a 51-year-old actor.
“I cannot rewrite my childhood, but I can spend the rest of my life helping rewrite the future for children who deserve more freedom, more protection, and more choices than I had,” Stodden wrote on social media in a July post supporting the California bill.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.
