name: Alabama Reflector
title: Voting Rights Act commemoration comes with warnings after Supreme Court rulings
description: The Southern Poverty Law Center Thursday commemorated the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act amid ongoing attacks on the landmark legislation.  Speakers at the event celebrated the impact of the law, which reversed decades of disenfranchisement across the South, but warned of recent attempts to roll back progress on voting rights. “For generations, Bl[...]
text:
President Lyndon B. Johnson and Martin Luther King, Jr., Clarence Mitchell, and Patricia Roberts Harris exchange greetings after the signing of the Voting Rights Act on Aug. 6, 1965 in Washington, D.C. Speakers at an SPLC-sponsored event Thursday marked the 61st anniversary of the law, which has been gutted by recent Supreme Court rulings. (Courtesy of the LBJ Library)The Southern Poverty Law Center Thursday commemorated the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act amid ongoing attacks on the landmark legislation. 
Speakers at the event celebrated the impact of the law, which reversed decades of disenfranchisement across the South, but warned of recent attempts to roll back progress on voting rights.
“For generations, Black people were denied full participation in our democracy,” said Tafeni English-Relf, state director of Alabama for the SPLC. “And it was the passage of the Voting Rights Act that allowed those barriers to be broken down.”
The Voting Rights Act was passed months after peaceful voting rights marchers were attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, an event known as Bloody Sunday. The attack led to the Selma-to-Montgomery March and sparked congressional action.
The law abolished barriers such as literacy and qualification tests, and allowed the U.S. Attorney General to challenge poll taxes in state and local elections. Within six months of President Lyndon Johnson signing the measure on Aug. 6, 1965, the number of Black registered voters in Alabama doubled from 110,000 to about 228,000. 
However, the U.S. Supreme Court’s rulings in Shelby County v. Holder in 2013 and Louisiana v. Callais this spring wiped out key enforcement provisions of the law and allowed states to erect new barriers to voting. 
The Holder ruling eliminated Section 5 of the law, which required states with histories of voting discrimination to have election law changes reviewed and approved by the U.S. Department of Justice. Callais made challenges to legislative maps under Section 2 considerably more difficult.  
Tafeni English-Relf, Alabama state director for the Southern Poverty Law Center, speaks with reporters on Thursday, August 6, 2026, about the significance of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. She says that efforts to undermine its provisions go back to 2013 in the case of Shelby County v. Holder. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)
“While we are celebrating today, we must also tell the truth, that the progress we celebrate has not always been protected,” said Shalela Dowdy, a plaintiff in Allen v. Milligan that sought to add a second congressional Black district in the state. “The Voting Rights Act has been weakened. Section 5 has been gutted. Section 2 has been narrowed.”
Since Shelby County v. Holder, the disparity in voter participation between Black and white voters in Alabama has increased.
Associate U.S. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito wrote in the Callais majority opinion that those who would challenge election laws as racially discriminatory must prove there was intent to discriminate against minority voters, instead of showing discriminatory effects of a law. 
The decision allowed Alabama to use a 2023 congressional map previously ruled racially discriminatory by the courts. The move substantially redrew Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, currently represented by U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, and reduced its Black Voting Age Population from about 49% to under 40%. 
At the event, SPLC announced the “We Decide” campaign to mobilize voters and increase voter participation in Alabama. This includes multiple days of canvassing starting in late August, along with community block parties in September.
“The Voting Rights Act was never meant to be a final chapter in American democracy,” said Jerome Dees, policy director for the SPLC. “It was the foundation for what could come next. So today, we honor that legacy by recommitting ourselves to the ongoing work of ensuring that every Alabamian has both the opportunity and the power to help shape our future.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: How to bring candidates of different parties together? Take them to a pre-K classroom.
description: Few people could stand before a crowd of childcare providers and advocates, having just toured classrooms brimming with cheery toddlers, and not pledge more funding for early education programs and educators. Indeed, all four gubernatorial candidates who attended the Thursday morning forum at Children’s Friend in Providence were emphatic that the state can a[...]
text:
Clockwise from top left: Gubernatorial candidates Ken Block, an independent; Aaron Guckian, a Republican; Jay Gotra, an independent; and Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a Democrat, participated in a gubernatorial forum at Children's Friend in Providence on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photos by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)Few people could stand before a crowd of childcare providers and advocates, having just toured classrooms brimming with cheery toddlers, and not pledge more funding for early education programs and educators.
Indeed, all four gubernatorial candidates who attended the Thursday morning forum at Children’s Friend in Providence were emphatic that the state can and should do more to support its youngest residents and the people who care for them. The hourlong event was heavy on promises but scant on details as participants Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a Democrat; Aaron Guckian, a Republican; and independents Ken Block and Jay Gotra answered the same four questions from moderator Ian Donnis, a political reporter for Ocean State Media.
All seven gubernatorial candidates who met the 1,000 signature threshold to qualify for the ballot were invited to attend the event organized by Children’s Friend and RIght from the Start, a legislative and budget campaign centered on children and families. The other three, Gov. Dan McKee, Republican Elaine Pelino and independent Christopher Reynolds never responded to the invitation, said Kaycie Green, a spokesperson for Children’s Friend. Rhode Island Current also contacted McKee, Pelino and Reynolds independently; none responded to requests for comment on their absence.
Despite the partisan differences between the participating candidates, they came together on the need for Rhode Island to maximize federal funding for early childhood development, education, and associated programs like nutrition and home visitation. 
“We should be fully funding every match available on a yearly basis,” said Block, 60, a software engineer who lives in Barrington. “We leave hundreds of millions on the table because we are not fully funding and taking advantage of federal matches across all programs.” 
Even with the enticement of a 2-to-1 match, state lawmakers have not always maxed out contributions from state coffers amid competing budget priorities.
Rhode Island’s fiscal 2027 budget, for example, marks the first annual state spending plan in which lawmakers invested the maximum state funding for a federal program providing trained home visitors to pregnant women and families. The $787,000 in state funds included in this year’s budget comes with a $2.4 million federal match.
Asked by Donnis where they would find the money to max out state contributions to programs like Head Start and Medicaid, all four candidates suggested there was too much being spent in other areas.
Guckian, 49, of East Greenwich, echoed the familiar conservative refrain about “bloat” in the $15.2 billion state budget. An aide to then-Gov. Don Carcieri and the former executive director of the Rhode Island Dental Association, Guckian proposed a combination of modern technology and an incentive program that offers a small portion of saved revenue to the people who find ways to improve government efficiency as solutions.
Gotra, 44, an East Greenwich resident, said that eliminating “waste” in government would free up funds for childcare services. But the first-time candidate whose now-defunct solar sales company is the subject of a predatory sales lawsuit by the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office, sidestepped Donnis’ follow-up question about where he would propose cuts.
“Bloated budgets are not a one-person problem, so one person can’t solve that,” Gotra said.
Foulkes singled out the Rhode Island Department of Transportation, which despite its $1.1 billion budget and 700-person payroll has not kept Rhode Island from ranking dead last in infrastructure conditions in a string of surveys
Foulkes, 62, of Providence also proposed adding a state worker devoted to maximizing federal funds across programs, replicating a similar position in Massachusetts.
The former CVS Pharmacy president took aim at the Trump administration for threatening to dismantle or substantially restrict eligibility to key social safety net programs, including those for early childhood development.
Workers wanted 
Ample program funding is not the only obstacle facing families and children. Candidates were also asked for proposed solutions to the shortage of critical childcare providers and educators. Children’s Friend has struggled to fill the eight pre-K and Head Start classrooms at its Berkshire Street location because it can’t find enough workers.
Increasing childcare providers’ wages was a common proposal across gubernatorial candidates, along with improved training programs to grow the pool of future educators and social service providers. Foulkes, the only woman to participate, stressed the value of high school vocational programs that cater to industries beyond plumbing, automotive and other male-dominated fields.
“We should also be training in fields that young girls want to be in, and I want more young boys in this field,” she said.
Block, whose wife is an educator, suggested improving students’ academic performance would set them up for early childhood development careers, among other industries. 
But the grand fix to an underfunded, understaffed and unpredictable system proved elusive.
“Put everyone in the room and lock the door and just give them bread and water and say let’s solve the problem,” Block suggested. 
Guckian’s take? “No one’s listening. We need to communicate more and listen.”
Rather than closing statements, the forum was capped off with a string of pre-K students filing into the room to present thank you cards to the participants. 
Early voting begins on Aug. 20, ahead of a Sept. 9 primary. The general election is Nov. 3.








Republican gubernatorial candidate Aaron Guckian (right) meets with childcare advocates outside of Children's Friend in Providence on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)









Independent gubernatorial candidate Jay Gotra talks with staffers at Children’s Friend in Providence on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)









David Caprio, president and CEO of Children's Friend, leads a tour of the nonprofit's Berkshire Street facility in Providence. Behind him is Helena Buonanno Foulkes, Democratic gubernatorial candidate. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)









Ken Block, an independent candidate for governor, looks over a thank you card from a pre-K student at the end of a gubernatorial forum at Children’s Friend in Providence on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)









Democratic gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes (left) accepts a thank you card from a student at Children's Friend in Providence following a gubernatorial forum on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Fancy Farm focused on next year’s election, not midterms
description: FANCY FARM, Ky. – The three-day political cavalcade that ends at the Fancy Farm Picnic was less about this year than next year. Yes, the picnic’s political speaking featured the first faceoff of candidates to succeed retiring Sen. Mitch McConnell, and they had vigorous exchanges – with each other and the largely Republican crowd stoked […]
text:
US Rep. James Comer shakes hands with a supporter on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)FANCY FARM, Ky. – The three-day political cavalcade that ends at the Fancy Farm Picnic was less about this year than next year.
Yes, the picnic’s political speaking featured the first faceoff of candidates to succeed retiring Sen. Mitch McConnell, and they had vigorous exchanges – with each other and the largely Republican crowd stoked by First District U.S. Rep. James Comer.
But with the Senate race uncompetitive, the signal events of the weekend were (1) a GOP lineup behind Comer for governor next year and (2) the first four joint appearances of the Democratic candidates: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, former senior adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear. They faced off at the Paducah labor lunch and Democratic events in Calvert City and Mayfield, then at the picnic, where they had a give-and-take with Comer.
Comer was the toast of several Republican events, as his fellow partisans endorsed his likely candidacy; an airplane flew a banner over the picnic reading “Run Comer Run.” The final speaker, Secretary of State Michael Adams, made real news by announcing that he wouldn’t run for governor and is for Comer. Following state Senate President Robert Stivers’ announcement last week that he wouldn’t run, Comer is ready to waltz to the nomination after his expected re-election to Congress over Democrat John “Drew” Williams – who gave the most substantive speech at the picnic but is the definition of an underdog.
With Comer on track, the big question I got from Republicans was how his potential opponents were matching up, and it was intriguing. Adkins, 66, and Coleman, 44, are of different generations, styles and backgrounds, but both are running on the popularity of what Coleman (but no one else) calls “the Beshear-Coleman administration.”
For now, they’re mainly shadow-boxing, but signaling themes and memes. Both cite record economic development under Beshear, but Adkins told the Democratic dinner he was “in the room” for negotiations with job creators and noted his 41 years’ experience in state government. Coleman’s standard speech goes back that long to share credit with Martha Layne Collins, “the only woman who’s ever served as governor of Kentucky – so far. And I think it’s time we changed that.”
At the picnic, where personal jabs are expected, Coleman had the punchiest lines, and even joined Republicans in throwing shade on Beshear and his absence (to see his son play his final baseball games before college): “I really tried to get him here. I even told him Fancy Farm was in New Hampshire.” Did she clear that line with her boss? She wouldn’t say.
Coleman got in a shot at Comer, alluding to his 2015 primary loss to ex-Gov. Matt Bevin, saying he “went from losing to criminals to protecting them in D.C.” She also dealt with a blemish on her record that Comer noted, helping her hairdresser get unemployment benefits in the pandemic: “I do want to apologize for helping her during Covid, because it’s actually [state Auditor] Allison Ball’s hairdresser that needed all the help she could get.” 
If that was the closest thing to a catfight, this was the closest to a dogfight: Adkins had no laugh lines but charged that Comer announced grants under the 2022 infrastructure law, which Comer voted against. Comer supporters chanted “liar, liar” but Adkins was correct. Afterward, Comer dismissed the charge, noting that he voted for the program’s most recent appropriation, which funded the grants.
Adkins’ charge came after his riff about Republicans “hurting people,” with points punctuated by “I think that’s wrong; how about you?” After Democratic cheers, he introduced the next point: “If that wasn’t enough . . .” He said nothing about Coleman, and she said nothing about him.
At more than one event, Coleman and Adkins decried Washington “chaos” but didn’t mention President Trump, who carried the state three times by about 30 percentage points.
Trump’s most recent job rating in the state is about even, and on Saturday no Republicans mentioned him except Comer, who wants the president’s endorsement for governor. At the picnic, he mentioned Trump’s most popular policy, “secure the border and deport the criminal illegals.”
Democratic Senate nominee Charles Booker was the only Democrat who mentioned the president, calling Republican nominee Andy Barr “a bootleg version of Donald Trump” in a well-crafted, energetic speech that struggled with the almost-constant Republican noisemaking. Booker’s no socialist, as Barr and others claimed, but he had a good opening line for the hecklers: “Even if you boo, I’m gonna make sure you have high-quality health care.”
On a broader front, though, Booker looked feckless. His campaign had relatively little presence at the picnic, beyond supporters’ signs, and his attempt at a call-and-response chant (“give Barr the boot”) with his supporters, which he promoted at a Democratic event hours earlier, went nowhere.
So, while Booker may keep inspiring his supporters, the only real statewide race now is for governor. Primary election day is May 18, 2027.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Tlaib introduces bill to prevent data sharing from TSA to federal immigration authorities
description: A new bill introduced Tuesday by U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) would ban the Transportation and Security Administration from sharing passenger information with federal immigration agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.  The legislation was introduced after American Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog or[...]
text:
TSA Precheck line in McNamara Terminal at Detroit Metropolitan Airport in Romulus. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA new bill introduced Tuesday by U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) would ban the Transportation and Security Administration from sharing passenger information with federal immigration agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection. 
The legislation was introduced after American Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog organization, released a Memorandum of Agreement between TSA and ICE that they obtained via the Freedom of Information Act, which details a data-sharing agreement between the two agencies. The specifics of what will be shared by each agency were all redacted in the released document.
Tlaib raised concerns that the details in the agreement, which was signed in May 2025, go against the sworn testimony of acting TSA Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill in January 2025, in which she testified that, regarding passenger information, TSA does not “send the information to ICE; we help ICE check against [TSA] information.”
“When people fly, they should be able to trust that TSA won’t divulge their sensitive information or use it for political retaliation,” Tlaib said in a press release from her office. “TSA has broken that trust in a gross violation of people’s First Amendment rights. This data sharing should terrify all of us. It does nothing to make us safer, but rather endangers the basic rights of all Americans and worsens our mass surveillance crisis.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The legislation specifically states that the Secretary of Homeland Security would not be able to access specified information, which is defined as information directly from TSA or “personally identifiable information of a flight passenger” that comes “from a private sector entity that brokers such data,” for the functions of ICE or CBP.
It also would make it so that the Secretary of Homeland Security could not deny, suspend or terminate someone’s enrollment in a program such as TSA PreCheck or Global Entry based on their “participation in an activity protected by the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States,” including anti-ICE protests.
“TSA is proud to support our DHS partners in our shared mission to secure the homeland,” a TSA spokesperson wrote in response to the legislation. “SOPD Administrator McNeill’s testimony confirms that commitment.”
“As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific terror attacks of 9/11, it’s not shocking that some in the Democrat Party would want to neuter the Department of Homeland Security’s ability to protect Americans from terrorists,” the TSA statement continued. “DHS was established to prevent information silos that could create blind spots against threats.”
Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit), member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, attends a field hearing in Minneapolis–Saint Paul about ICE activities there. Jan. 16, 2025 | Photo from Office of Rashida Tlaib
The legislation has 25 Democratic co-sponsors, including U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit). It was referred to the House Homeland Security Committee, where it is unlikely to get a hearing in the Republican-led Congress.
Regardless, a coalition of 65 organizations — ranging from local to national groups — endorsed the legislation, according to Tlaib’s press release. 
“Handing travelers’ private information over to immigration agents isn’t about safety or security. It’s about turbocharging the already violent and deadly immigration enforcement happening in real time across the country that has claimed the lives of neighbors and fathers like Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastian Guerrero,” said Juliana Macedo do Nascimento, Deputy Director of Advocacy and Campaigns at United We Dream. “As immigration enforcement exploits databases, expands surveillance, and targets travelers across the country, Congress has a mandate to protect the safety and rights of the American people from the administration’s growing overreach and put an end to the cycle of tragedy that follows when communities are forced to live under fear. We urge Congress to pass the No TSA Data for ICE Act now.”

title: Beshear expands K-12 to another KY school district
description: Gov. Andy Beshear is expanding Kentucky’s “Pre-K for All” pilot program again — this time to his dad’s hometown of Dawson Springs.  About 160 children will be enrolled through the Dawson Springs Independent School District, Beshear announced Thursday.  “This is a town that’s been through a lot. It’s been through a level of heartbreak that’s […]
text:
In this aerial view of Dawson Springs on Dec. 13, 2021, homes are heavily damaged from a tornado three days prior. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Gov. Andy Beshear is expanding Kentucky’s “Pre-K for All” pilot program again — this time to his dad’s hometown of Dawson Springs. 
About 160 children will be enrolled through the Dawson Springs Independent School District, Beshear announced Thursday. 
“This is a town that’s been through a lot. It’s been through a level of heartbreak that’s hard to comprehend from the 2021 tornadoes, but they are building back with strength,” Beshear said. “And this news adds to their progress because Pre-K is not just a win for our kids, but also for families and local businesses in a community.” 
Lenny Whalen, the superintendent of Dawson Springs Schools, said early education has “immediate and lasting effects” for children and communities. 
“We’re looking to have a stronger kindergarten, have stronger reading and math skills, and be more likely to graduate high school and possibly go into college or other skilled trades,” Whalen said. “That’s 160 kids less likely to be chronically absent or have behavior issues.” 
This news brings the school districts with Pre-K programs to 5. They are:

Dawson Springs Independent School District
Franklin County Schools 
Glasgow Independent Schools in Barren County
Rockcastle County Schools
Robertson County Schools

Kentucky governor expands pre-K pilot programs for two more school systems

In June 2025, Beshear signed an executive order establishing the Pre-K for All Advisory Committee to explore support for universal pre-kindergarten programs in Kentucky. After meeting for several months, the committee recommended that Kentucky phase in expanded access to pre-K over several years.
A fall report from that committee also found about 48% of Kentucky’s kids are ready to learn when they reach kindergarten.

name: VTDigger
title: In Chittenden Southeast Senate primary, incumbents and challengers alike pivot platforms to affordability
description:
In the wealthy blue district, affordability — for healthcare, education and businesses — have become top issues. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In Chittenden Southeast Senate primary, incumbents and challengers alike pivot platforms to affordability.
text:
Clockwise from top left: Sen. Thomas Chittenden, Joanna Grossman, Elizabeth Hunt, Sen. Ginny Lyons and Sen. Kesha Ram Hinsdale are candidates seeking a seat in Chittenden Southeast Senate district and competing in the Aug. 11 Democratic primary. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger and courtesy of the Hunt and Grossman campaigns.
When the three Democrats representing the Chittenden Southeast Senate district first ran as a united incumbent bloc three primaries ago, they cited a need for experience amid high political turnover. 
Now, that turnover has only deepened in the Vermont Senate. But new candidates see it as a reason for fresh leadership rather than consistency. As a result, a competitive primary this year has incumbents and challengers alike focusing more on economic development as voters express greater frustration over affordability. 
“I never thought I would be the person to run, and that started to change last year when the political climate seemed to get more dire,” candidate and political strategist Joanna Grossman said. 
Federal funding cuts hitting the state, frustration over Vermont’s sweeping education reform law and a perceived lack of small business representation in the Senate all pushed Grossman, a longtime campaign manager but first time candidate, to run. She joins pediatrician and fellow political newcomer Elizabeth Hunt on the ballot, facing off against the three incumbent Democrats — Sens. Thomas Chittenden of South Burlington, Ginny Lyons of Williston and Kesha Ram Hinsdale of Shelburne, who have cross-endorsed each other in an effort to hold their seats. The five candidates, who all made themselves available for interviews, are vying for three seats in the Aug. 11 Democratic primary. Two Republicans — Bruce Roy and Javen Sears — are running in the GOP primary.  
In the wealthy blue district — which spans Bolton, Charlotte, Hinesburg, Jericho, Richmond, St. George, Shelburne, South Burlington, Williston, Underhill and the southern tip of Burlington —  healthcare, education and small business ownership have emerged as top issues for all candidates. The focus on affordability has left topics like gun control and climate change that once drew candidates’ attention to take a backseat. But the candidates differ in their vision for what this economic change looks like and what policies fit best to address them. 
The Issues 
Some Vermonters this year have paid double or more than what they previously paid for health insurance amid the expiration of federal health insurance subsidies, demographic challenges and soaring underlying hospital and prescription drug costs. That’s made healthcare affordability a key issue for voters, the candidates said.
A veteran Senator in the race, Lyons introduced a bill last session, S.190, aimed at addressing the issue by fast-tracking the state’s ability to use a tool called reference-based pricing to lower what hospitals charge for certain services. That effort would have targeted two groups of insurance customers: public school employees and people buying plans on Vermont’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Gov. Phil Scott vetoed the bill this June, but even challengers of Lyons in the race applauded her efforts with the bill. 
“It’s an interest in healthcare,” Lyons said, describing voters’ focus this year. “I think it’s a result of the work that I, in particular, have done and others have done to raise the issue about what we can do and how we can reduce some of the administrative burdens and increase some of the access to care, particularly primary care across the state.” 

READ MORE

A former biology professor and current chair of the Senate Health and Welfare Committee, Lyons said her unique background as a scientist and her long experience in the Senate are why she is best to address the issue of healthcare affordability.
But Hunt, the pediatrician, who is largely supportive of Lyons’ bill, believes the steep healthcare-related affordability challenges facing Vermont require a new perspective. She has seen the concern firsthand while working with children and families, an experience that she said pushed her to run. To address healthcare costs, she’s proposed an examination of the Green Mountain Care Board, the state’s main healthcare regulator, to audit how money is spent by the board and how it can be more effective, as well as expanding Vermont’s Blueprint for Health, a program that invests in primary care clinics.
For Grossman, who is the community relations director at Phoenix Books, the impacts of rising healthcare costs have been particularly seen in small businesses. She said she would have pushed for a bill, H.585, introduced last session, that would have advanced site-neutral billing, a policy that sets payment for certain medical services equally regardless of the hospital setting.    
While working for the local bookstore chain, Grossman said she became focused on supporting small businesses. She pointed to her opposition to a proposed Amazon warehouse in Essex as a moment that illuminated her interest in economic development. 
The warehouse, Grossman believes, would have been “actively displacing Vermont businesses and Vermont retailers” and “devastating to the Vermont economy.” 
Chittenden, who also described himself as pro-business and is vice chair of the Senate Finance Committee, holds the opposite position. To him, the facility presented an opportunity to “bring in-state supply chain efficiency and private funding for infrastructure upgrades while making delivery of goods more affordable for both Vermont consumers and Vermont small businesses that use Amazon regularly,” he wrote in an email to VTDigger.  
Their differences on the issue highlights a larger distinction in how the two candidates view being pro-business. Grossman describes herself specifically as pro-small business, while Chittenden said he wants more state politicians to realize that “medium and large businesses are good for Vermont too.”
While Chittenden said he has always been a “pro-growth” candidate, his Senate platform, compared to previous years, has shifted from a focus on gun control and climate change to a prioritization of economic growth. 
“I will say the results of the 2024 election put that conversation into a place where it was harder to advance sensible reforms,” he said of gun control and climate change policies, referencing Republicans gains in the Vermont Senate two years ago. 
For Chittenden, tax burdens, including housing costs, are why small businesses are struggling — an issue he extended to the education system. 
“If we want property tax relief, we need to restructure our system in a sensible way that Vermonters can afford,” he said. “And that’s what the big conversation has been over the last two years.”
Education dominated the last legislative session, as Gov. Scott and the Legislature agreed to an  education reform compromise that seeks to facilitate voluntary school district mergers. Chittenden, who voted for the legislation, said he supports the push to improve equity for students no matter where they live but has also criticized the bill for overriding local control of school spending. Lyons also voted yes on the controversial bill, but has emphasized that it will require ongoing local work.  
For Ram Hinsdale, who voted yes as well, the bill presented an opportunity to “bend the cost curve,” but looking ahead, she said she is most interested in investing in technical education. Technical education centers in the district faced a rise in student demand that they were unable to meet this past school year, according to data from the Center for Technology, Essex, one of the two career and technical centers in Chittenden County. Hinsdale said she is focused on finding solutions to meet that demand, describing technical education as a “lucrative” path.
That, alongside housing, are her biggest priorities, she said. 
Chittenden County has seen historically low rental vacancy rates in recent years. Though that rate has risen this summer, indicating a slightly healthier rental market, the rate is still an issue, and younger Vermonters report rising costs steering them away from homeownership.
Across the board, the candidates said they support the construction of higher density units as a solution. Grossman said she wants to make sure Vermont residents get their first choice of units on the market, while Hunt believes land could be used more efficiently to support housing demands. 
Ram Hinsdale cited a need for better use of state and federal dollars for housing programs amid a crackdown on federal spending from the Trump administration. 
“I look back at the pandemic when we had federal dollars to pay for the motel program,” she said, referencing the state’s program that pays for some people who are homeless to stay in hotels. “We didn’t stretch those dollars as far as we could have because the governor’s team did not negotiate the price of those motel rooms.”
This climate of uncertainty with federal funding has led Grossman to see Vermont as a refuge, one that needs to become more economically self reliant to be preserved. 
“We’re seeing federal overreach encroaching here in Vermont. We need to shore up Vermont. We need to protect it,” she said.
While Grossman and Hunt believe these unique challenges require a new voice, Chittenden, Ram Hinsdale and Lyons believe it’s all the more reason why experience is needed in the race. 
“I have grown a tremendous respect for seniority and service and longevity,” Chittenden said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear to issue executive order to protect against ‘harmful impacts’ of data centers
description: Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear says he’s signing an executive order to protect Kentuckians “against any harmful impacts from potential data centers,” directing the state utility regulator and environmental protection officials to take specific actions on data centers.  During a Thursday press conference, Beshear said economic wins “can never come at t[...]
text:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, center, said Thursday he's signing an executive order to protect Kentuckians against the potential impacts of data centers. Kentucky Public Service Commission Chair Angie Hatton, left, and Energy and Environment Cabinet John Lyons, right, stood next to Beshear. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer).Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear says he’s signing an executive order to protect Kentuckians “against any harmful impacts from potential data centers,” directing the state utility regulator and environmental protection officials to take specific actions on data centers. 
During a Thursday press conference, Beshear said economic wins “can never come at the cost of the health and safety of our families or the communities we call home.” He stood next to Angie Hatton, the chair of state utility regulator Kentucky Public Service Commission, and John Lyons, the secretary of the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet. 
“Any company looking at Kentucky, at minimum, is required to demonstrate they will be good neighbors. They must invest responsibly, operate transparently, and work in partnership with our people and our communities,” Beshear said. “They will be held to the same high standards we demand of any potential partner, and they must prove that their investment will deliver lasting benefits to Kentucky’s working families.”
Beshear said his executive order would direct the Energy and Environment Cabinet, which issues permits to industrial sites that set limits on air and water pollution, to deny permits to any data center site that would negatively impact air quality; water quality, usage and supply; federally protected wetlands and “natural resources”. 
He said data center developers would also have to submit an “initial energy plan” to the cabinet explaining how the developer would protect businesses and residents from rising utility bills while not “imposing any additional costs on our families.” 
The Democrat said the order would also direct the Kentucky Public Service Commission to deny requests from utilities that would increase rates “to recover costs caused by the development or operations of a data center.” 
“The governor’s executive order and his directive are clear. The cabinet simply will not permit, not issue a permit that’s not protective of human health, our natural resources, and the environment,” said Lyons, the Energy and Environment Cabinet secretary. 
Hatton, the chair of the PSC, said it was important for the state to learn lessons from other states “that maybe have not implemented data centers in the most effective way to protect ratepayers.” 
“I’m grateful that we have guidance like this that will provide a framework that allows us, if we allow data centers to develop in our state, that they’re done in a thoughtful and deliberate way, and in a way that allows us to protect Kentucky families and ratepayers of every class,” Hatton said. 
This story will be updated.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As industry faces rising costs, there’s hope new Pa. Farm Bureau leadership brings positive change
description: Last month, the president of the state’s largest farm organization resigned. Members believe fresh leadership could help infuse energy into the organization.
text:
New leadership at the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau could be a fresh start for an industry grappling with surging bankruptcies, rising costs and stifling tariffs. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Ethan Young is a summer intern for the Pennsylvania Legislative Correspondents Association, and a rising senior at the University of Pennsylvania. 
It’s been a difficult time for many Pennsylvania farmers. And it’s been a tumultuous stretch for leadership at the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau. 
Last month, Chris Hoffman resigned as president of the state’s largest farm organization to take a position at the U.S Department of Agriculture (USDA). Hoffman’s position had been modified in April as the board considered removing him in response to an “internal investigation about staff turnover.” 
Across the industry, bankruptcies have surged, costs have increased due to tariffs as well as the war with Iran. The conflict has led to rising prices for diesel fuel and fertilizer.
In light of those headwinds, Pennsylvania Farm Bureau members are hoping for a fresh start, optimistic that new leadership could help infuse energy into the organization’s members and bring about policy changes they say have traditionally received less focus.
Tommy Nagle, who oversees a diversified farming operation in Cambria County and a former Farm Bureau vice president, has since assumed the duties of president. A formal election for a new leader will take place in November. 
Brandon Mytrysak on his Indiana County farm on Dec. 18, 2025. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
A third-generation Christmas tree farmer from Indiana County, Brandon Mytrysak hopes Nagle, or whoever ultimately leads the organization, pushes legislation and policy changes that benefit traditional agriculture operations. 
“When it comes to research and funding and all that kind of stuff, we kind of get left out of a lot of the different programs because we are specialty crops,” Mytrysak said. “I would hope, or would love, to see the Farm Bureau continue to help push legislation or policy change to include the special crop growers, to help us succeed as well as everybody else.”
Mytrysak, who is also a board member of the Indiana County Farm Bureau, wants to look at the changes as a positive thing. New people in positions of power, he said, may bring fresh ideas and a “different wavelength” that could elevate the organization. 
A changing industry
Amanda Butterfield, who has been a dairy farmer in Somerset County for 16 years, hopes the next generation of leaders can be diversified, especially regarding age. She also hopes they will work to bring more young people into the ranks of the organization and the industry. 
“Looking at Pennsylvania Farm Bureau’s leadership, it’s been basically white, male, older. We do need to have some diversity in there. We need to have youth represented in there,” said Butterfield, who runs a cow-calf operation. “There’s potential there for opportunity to look at what will attract younger people to farming and get them involved.”
Nagle, in a statement, said there are “absolutely” efforts to bring younger people into Farm Bureau leadership. 
Interim Pennsylvania Farm Bureau President Tommy Nagle speaks during a roundtable conversation at Way Fruit Farm on July 22, 2026. (Photo from PACasst)
He said the Young Ag Professionals program, for members ages 18 to 35 offers “various leadership development opportunities for young people that are involved in agriculture, or want to be involved in agriculture.” A member from the initiative also holds a seat on the state board of directors. 
Butterfield would also like the Farm Bureau to start asking tougher questions of the Trump administration and its policies which she said have cost farmers “quite a bit of money.”
The organization “is supposed to be our voice,” she said. “I’m not seeing that voice showing up in Washington and asking questions.”
Ahead of the November election — where Nagle plans to run for a full term — he said there have been no disruptions to organization’s advocacy efforts at the state or federal level. 
“Pennsylvania Farm Bureau is structured that if there is a change in leadership, our grassroots members and our staff is prepared to do what it has always done,” he said in a statement. “Nothing changes as far as our lobbying efforts are concerned.”
Nagle said he’s working to launch new initiatives that help offer relief for the rising costs. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That rising cost of production is the biggest challenge the industry currently faces, according to Tom Croner, whose family has been farming land in Somerset County since 1773. 
At age 82, Croner would like to see a mix of both younger and older farmers involved in decision-making at the Farm Bureau, an organization he estimates he has been involved with since the 1960s.
“There is wisdom that can be offered by older generations again because of perspectives and historic knowledge,” Corner, who is currently in the grain industry, said. “But we’re always facing a new set of dynamics, so we have to be prepared and able to change course if needed.”
William Thiele, a sixth-generation dairy farmer from Butler County and Farm Bureau board member, has practically been a farmer since he was born. 
His grandfather was farming during World War II. In the 1980s, his dad witnessed widespread consolidation of the industry. Now, Thiele faces weather extremes, inflation, and other challenges as he operates Thiele Dairy Farm. 

“There’s always going to be unique challenges to each generation,” Thiele said. But, like the obstacles his dad and grandfather overcame, he is confident his generation will persevere. 
“That’s how I view agriculture as a whole,” he said. “It’s going to move forward through all these challenges. You just got to roll with the punches and adapt to what is the biggest challenge in our current era.”
While it may take time to adjust to new leadership, “ultimately it’s going to make a stronger Farm Bureau because we’ll look past this and say ‘okay, we need to get stuff done,’” he said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: No on 3 campaign focuses on the pain for renters if property tax cut passes
description: A survey of 1,400 Floridians shows the proposed constitutional amendment to reduce property taxes on homestead properties gets 74% support, well more than the 60% required for passage. However, the survey from the James Madison Institute also shows how support for the measure drops to 55% when voters are informed passage of the amendment could mean […]
text:
A Consumer Affairs Journal of Consumer Research analysis rates Florida the worst state in the nation for renters, and that the cost of rent takes up 37.4% of the typical income. That means Florida renters are the most cost-burdened in the country. (Photo by Barbara Barrett/Stateline)A survey of 1,400 Floridians shows the proposed constitutional amendment to reduce property taxes on homestead properties gets 74% support, well more than the 60% required for passage.
However, the survey from the James Madison Institute also shows how support for the measure drops to 55% when voters are informed passage of the amendment could mean less funding for local government services — meaning it would fail at the polls if the voting matches the survey finding.
“Education equals opposition when it comes to this amendment,” said Jackson Peel, communications director for Save Our Services — No on 3, in a Zoom conference call Thursday. “When people hear what this bad policy will do to their communities, they reject it. They don’t like what it stands for.”
Save Our Services No on 3 is a statewide coalition formed to oppose Amendment 3, which if approved in November would increase the homestead exemption for property owners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. State economists project its passage would cut funding to local governments by up to $12 billion annually beginning in 2031.
The measure has drawn opposition from groups representing law enforcement, local government officials from both political parties, as well as the Florida Democratic Party.
Save Our Services highlighted how passage would specifically hurt renters. That’s because local governments may seek to close shortfalls in revenue by increasing taxes on non-homestead properties, including rental units. The measure does call for reducing the assessment-growth cap for non-homestead residential and commercial properties from 10% to 5%.
“Renters are not going to receive the homestead exemption. A landlord might get a tax benefit, but there is absolutely no guarantee that a renter sees a lower rent payment,” said state Rep. Rob Long, D-Boynton Beach.
“At the same time, cities are going to have to increase fire assessments, utility charges, or other fees to keep services running. And those costs will likely still be passed along to tenants. So, the landlord might get a tax benefit while the tenant gets no guarantee and they’re still going to get a higher bill probably.”
Hard-pressed renters
Kelly Lynch works in Gainesville but can’t afford to live there. Instead, she lives in the city of Bronson in Levy County, making a more than 20 mile commute every day. The mother of two said she and her husband dream of home ownership, which is why a rent and cost of living increase would deal a significant blow to that dream.
“I know plenty of people that work full time. Single moms living in Gainesville that would honestly face eviction or homelessness if their rent increases or their cost of living increases any more,” she said. “None of us can comfortably afford an increase.”
Florida was rated the worst state in the nation for renters, according to a Consumer Affairs Journal of Consumer Research analysis published in April. The report said the cost of rent takes up 37.4% of the typical income, meaning that Florida renters are the most cost-burdened in the country.
A circuit court judge in Tallahassee ruled earlier this week that Amendment 3’s ballot summary language is misleading, and he has given Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier until Aug. 14 to rewrite significant portions of the ballot and summary title of the proposal.

title: Cyclospora cases rise in Kansas, following report of two deaths nationally
description: TOPEKA — Kansas cases of a gastrointestinal illness typically caused by an organism on produce rose to 615 as of Wednesday, up about 150 cases from last week, according to a state infectious disease dashboard. Cyclosporiasis cases nationally rose to more than 6,300 and two deaths linked to the outbreak occurred in Michigan, the Centers […]
text:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says national cases of Cyclospora, a gastrointestinal illness linked to produce, have risen to more than 6,300 and two deaths were reported nationwide. (Photo by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)TOPEKA — Kansas cases of a gastrointestinal illness typically caused by an organism on produce rose to 615 as of Wednesday, up about 150 cases from last week, according to a state infectious disease dashboard.
Cyclosporiasis cases nationally rose to more than 6,300 and two deaths linked to the outbreak occurred in Michigan, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported. The nation’s top health agency added six new states to those affected by the outbreak, bringing the total to 15.
“The true number of sick people in this multistate outbreak is likely higher than the number reported, and the outbreak may not be limited to the states with known illnesses,” according to a U.S. Food and Drug Administration page that details the ongoing investigation. “This is because some people recover without medical care and are not tested for cyclospora. In addition, recent illnesses may not yet be reported because it can take as long as 6 weeks to determine if a sick person is part of a cyclospora outbreak.”
The infection is a caused by the cyclospora parasite and causes gastrointestinal upset that frequently includes watery diarrhea, fatigue and loss of appetite.
Lettuce products were determined by CDC and state health departments to account for at least some cases in the outbreak, and most of that product has been removed from shelves.
“We expect cases to increase as we continue to work through interviews to identify sources of the illness,” said Jill Bronaugh, spokeswoman for the Kansas Department of Health and Environment. “The iceberg lettuce that was initially associated with some of the cases should no longer be available at restaurants or retail stores. Since the lettuce does not account for all of the cases, state and federal public health officials will continue to investigate other possible food sources attributing to the illnesses.”
The 15 states associated with the outbreak are Arkansas, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, according to the FDA.

name: VTDigger
title: Local development corporation wins bid for former Montpelier post office
description:
The final auction price of $540,000 was far under the federal government’s initial asking price.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Local development corporation wins bid for former Montpelier post office.
text:
The building that houses the former Montpelier post office is up for auction. Seen on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A local development corporation spearheaded by the Foundation for a Resilient Montpelier has won the auction for 87 State Street, the former Montpelier Post Office building and longtime downtown staple, the foundation’s Executive Director Jon Copans said Thursday. 
“This is a transformational piece of property and opportunity for our community, and now we’re on a path — a pretty clear path — to having site control,” Copans said. “And so that feels like a positive development for Montpelier, that ultimately, the 87 State Street Local Development Corporation will be carrying this project forward.”
The winning bid of $540,000 was well under the federal government’s original asking price of $2.4 million. The Foundation originally walked away from a potential sale at that price after uncovering evidence of environmental contamination throughout the building. 
“The gamble that we took when we stepped away” was that they would be able to get the property at a lower price, Copans said. 
The property suffered damage in the July 2023 flood, forcing the U.S. Postal Service to relocate to another location on Main Street. From the time the federal government announced the sale, the Foundation, once called the Montpelier Commission for Recovery and Resilience, has had an interest in developing the property into a flood-resilient site for both housing and commercial use. 
The Foundation approached the U.S. General Services Administration during the “negotiated sale” process, a time when local and state entities can get an early opportunity to purchase federal property. But they found a 2023 report from Clay Point Associates, Inc. that revealed widespread contamination from PCBs, Copans told VTDigger in June.
The Foundation walked away from that negotiation. Instead, it put together a coalition of ten local entities that form the newly created local development corporation, which includes Vermont Mutual Insurance Group, Union Mutual Insurance, National Life and Central Vermont Economic Development Corporation, among others, Copans said. 
The local development group also secured an award through the Rural Industry Development Program to defray the cost of the building, a Vermont Agency of Commerce and Community Development program, Copans said. 

READ MORE

“Everyone has said yes when asked about their participation, and that participation has a lot of different — flavors, let’s say,” he said. “But people have been really generous in stepping forward to help us with this project.”
Copans said in June that the Foundation was interested in turning the parking lot behind the building into housing, helping to alleviate the city’s housing struggles, while continuing to use the building itself as office space. 
But the first order of business, he told VTDigger Thursday, will be getting into the site to perform a more thorough environmental assessment. 
“Before we make any other decisions about the building and how to proceed, we’ve really got to understand what the scope of that contamination is, and what kind of a plan and what kind of a cost is entailed in cleaning it up,” he said. 
This story will be updated.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Moms’ Equal Pay Day’ highlights the struggles faced by many Mississippians
description: Cassandra Welchin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, speaks at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Feb. 13, 2025. Welchin emphasized the importance of the “Secure the Bag” initiative, which advocates for fair wages, paid leave and economic policies that support Black women and working families.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

Every day across Mississippi, mothers wake up early, get their children ready for school, go to work and do everything they can to provide for their families. Yet despite their hard work, far too many still face impossible choices: paying the rent or keeping the lights on, covering childcare or buying groceries, replacing a child’s school uniform or filling a prescription. No parent should have to make those decisions simply because her work is undervalued.
At Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, we see these realities every day. The stories we hear from mothers across our state remind us that the wage gap isn’t an abstract policy debate. It’s a daily struggle that affects whether families can remain stable and whether children have the opportunity to thrive.
That is why Moms’ Equal Pay Day, which is recognized today, is more than a date on the calendar. It marks how far into the following year mothers must work – added with their pay from the previous year – to earn what fathers earned the previous year.
According to the National Women’s Law Center’s most recent Mothers’ Wage Gap report, last updated in May 2025, mothers working full-time, year-round earn approximately 74 cents for every dollar earned by fathers. In Mississippi, that figure drops to approximately 67 cents on the dollar, and the gap widens even further for mothers working part-time or part-year.
For many mothers – especially single mothers who are often their family’s sole provider – that gap translates into fewer opportunities to build savings, absorb unexpected expenses and create long-term financial stability.
Our mission at Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable is to build the political, economic and social power of Black women and girls throughout Mississippi. While we advocate for long-term policy solutions, we also recognize that families facing emergencies cannot wait for legislation to catch up. They need support today.
That understanding gave rise to our Community Outreach and Relief Resources Initiative, CORRI, which helps families weather unexpected hardship with dignity while we continue advocating for lasting economic opportunity.
One of CORRI’s signature efforts, Quarters Because We Care, began as a practical response to families facing extraordinary circumstances during the Jackson water crisis and has grown into a lifeline for parents struggling to keep their households together. Through CORRI, Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable provides emergency support – from laundry services to rent, utility and childcare assistance – that often determines whether a working parent can remain employed.
Clean clothes may seem like a small thing until you’re the parent trying to report to work or send your child to school with dignity. Economic justice is often built on meeting these everyday needs.
The impact of Quarters Because We Care is reflected in what participants tell us. One of the most common responses we hear is: “Thank you. I only came in to wash a couple of loads of laundry – whether it was my children’s school uniforms or my work clothes. Because your organization provided this service, I can now use those resources for other things my family needs.”
Many participants return later the same day or the following day to finish the rest of their laundry because they know they have a safe, welcoming place where they can meet an essential need without added financial stress.
Through the Quarters Because We Care program, the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable provides struggling families with help for basic needs like laundry services, rent, utility and childcare assistance. Credit: Courtesy photo
The families we serve come from every corner of Mississippi. They are teachers, restaurant workers, social workers, government employees and, at times, people experiencing homelessness. Their circumstances differ, but they all share the same determination: to provide for themselves and their families with dignity.
Programs like Quarters Because We Care give families room to breathe – allowing them to redirect scarce dollars toward groceries, gas, school supplies, utilities or rent while preserving dignity, restoring hope and reminding them they are not facing these challenges alone.
That program is just one example of how CORRI responds when families face immediate hardship. Our Emergency Assistance Program provides another critical safety net, helping parents bridge temporary financial crises before they become long-term setbacks.
We regularly hear from mothers whose financial stability has been disrupted almost overnight. One mother lost her childcare voucher, threatening her ability to continue working. Another welcomed a new baby while unpaid maternity leave reduced her household to a single income. In both cases, emergency assistance helped prevent temporary setbacks from becoming lasting financial crises by easing concerns about utility shutoffs, eviction and other immediate hardships, allowing parents to focus on caring for their families while regaining stability.
These stories remind us that the wage gap is not simply about unequal paychecks. It is about unequal opportunity. It is about whether families can build savings, purchase homes, afford healthcare, invest in education or recover when life inevitably brings unexpected challenges.
While Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable will continue meeting immediate needs through programs like CORRI, we know firsthand that emergency assistance alone cannot solve the structural inequities that leave too many working mothers one unexpected expense away from financial crisis.
When mothers are paid less than they have earned, the impact extends far beyond individual families. Employers lose valuable talent, local economies lose spending power and communities lose the stability that comes when working families have the opportunity to thrive.
That is why we continue advocating for policies that strengthen economic security for Mississippi’s families, including raising the state’s minimum wage, which has remained at $7.25 per hour for 17 years; strengthening equal pay protections by prohibiting employers from relying on salary history; expanding pay transparency and protecting workers who discuss wages from retaliation; strengthening protections against pay discrimination; and expanding access to affordable healthcare so mothers can remain healthy, employed and able to care for their families.
These are not partisan ideas. They are practical investments in Mississippi’s workforce, businesses, children and future.
Moms’ Equal Pay Day should challenge all of us – not simply to acknowledge the wage gap, but to ask what we are willing to do about it.
Every mother deserves the opportunity to provide for her family without having to work harder simply to earn less. Every child deserves the stability that comes when the youngster’s parent is paid fairly.
When we invest in mothers, we invest in stronger children, stronger communities and a stronger Mississippi. Closing the wage gap is about more than equal pay. It’s about ensuring every family has the opportunity not simply to survive, but to build a secure future for generations to come.

Cassandra Welchlin is executive director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable. A licensed social worker, advocate and mother, she has spent more than 20 years advancing policies that strengthen economic security and health for Mississippi women and families.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Questions arise about Pasco state Rep. Kevin Steele’s run for Congress in Hillsborough County
description: Pasco County Republican state lawmaker Kevin Steele has emphasized his Hillsborough County roots since entering the race for the Republican nomination for Congressional District 14. That’s because the newly redrawn congressional seat is set exclusively in Hillsborough, far from the area he now represents in the Florida House of Representatives. Federal law d[...]
text:
Pasco County state GOP Rep. Kevin Steele speaking in Plant City on Aug.t 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Pasco County Republican state lawmaker Kevin Steele has emphasized his Hillsborough County roots since entering the race for the Republican nomination for Congressional District 14. That’s because the newly redrawn congressional seat is set exclusively in Hillsborough, far from the area he now represents in the Florida House of Representatives.
Federal law does not require a member of Congress to live in the district he or she represents. However, state law says a state lawmaker must live in the district he or she represents.
The CD 14 seat has been held for the past 20 years by Tampa Democrat Kathy Castor. But after it was redistricted from an area she won by 15 points in 2024 to one that Donald Trump won by more than 10 points that same year, Steele and seven other Republicans filed to run for the seat.
When asked by the Phoenix Tuesday night whether he intended to move from Pasco to Hillsborough if elected to the seat in November, he said he already lived in and had voted in the district. He posted a photo on social media Monday with members of his family at the Jan Platt Library in South Tampa, the first day of early voting in the county.
Records show Steele is registered to vote in Hillsborough County. However, he still has a homestead exemption at his Dade City home in Pasco County, where he serves as a state representative in District 55.
According to his most recent Form 6 financial disclosure filed July 1, under the description of assets, he lists his “Residence and Land” as the street address of his home in Dade City, but instead of Dade City he lists the city as Tampa. However, the street he lists as his residence does not exist in Tampa.
State law says House candidates or incumbents must live and be registered to vote in the districts in which they were running at the time of the election and maintain a residence in the district for the entire term to which they are elected. Lawmakers are allowed to own multiple homes but can only have one principal, or legal, residence.
Florida House rules also say they consider a lawmaker’s legal residence to be the one listed on official documents or mentioned in statements to others, voter registration records, homestead exemption paperwork, and a driver’s license; where a lawmaker receives mail; or where a spouse and minor children live and attend school.
Steele did not respond to a request for comment.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Lawsuit seeks Missouri ballot spot for amendment limiting changes to voter-approved initiatives
description: A campaign seeking to make it harder for lawmakers to alter voter-approved initiatives sued Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Thursday, asking a judge to overturn his decision blocking the proposed constitutional amendment from the November ballot. The lawsuit, filed in Cole County Circuit Court by three Missourians who signed the Respect Missouri Voters p[...]
text:
Volunteers with Respect Missouri Voters collect signatures during the No Kings demonstration at the Missouri State Capitol in Jefferson City in October 2025.  Respect Missouri Voters is the intiative petition campaign for a constitutional amendment that would make it harder for the General Assembly to overturn citizen-led ballot measures (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A campaign seeking to make it harder for lawmakers to alter voter-approved initiatives sued Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Thursday, asking a judge to overturn his decision blocking the proposed constitutional amendment from the November ballot.
The lawsuit, filed in Cole County Circuit Court by three Missourians who signed the Respect Missouri Voters petition, also challenges Hoskins’ attempt to withdraw and replace a ballot title his office certified nearly a year ago — before supporters collected hundreds of thousands of signatures.
It is the second lawsuit filed this week challenging Hoskins’ refusal to certify a citizen petition for the Nov. 3 ballot.
On Tuesday, Hoskins declared both the Respect Missouri Voters initiative and a referendum seeking to overturn Missouri’s new congressional map insufficient. People Not Politicians, the campaign behind the redistricting referendum, sued later that day.
Respect Missouri Voters filed its lawsuit Thursday morning.
“Hundreds of thousands of citizens, far more than required, signed to demand that the Respect Missouri Voters Amendment appear on the ballot,” Toni Easter, a volunteer and co-founder of the group, said after Hoskins announced his decision.
Hoskins could not immediately be reached for comment Thursday.
Referendum campaign asks court to block new Missouri map from November election

Respect Missouri Voters submitted its petition to Hoskins’ office May 3 after a yearlong campaign aimed at limiting lawmakers’ ability to change measures approved through the initiative process.
The campaign says it collected more than 367,000 signatures. Its lawsuit says more than 330,000 were submitted to the secretary of state.
A constitutional amendment requires signatures equal to 8% of the votes cast in the most recent gubernatorial election in six of Missouri’s eight congressional districts. The lawsuit says the petition needed 177,713 valid signatures across six districts.
Hoskins did not cite an insufficient number of valid signatures when he rejected the petition Tuesday.
Instead, he concluded the proposal violated constitutional requirements limiting initiative petitions to a single subject and changes to a single article of the Missouri Constitution.
His decision relied on a legal opinion from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, who also argued parts of the proposal impermissibly restricted future legislatures and raised questions under the U.S. Constitution’s guarantee of a republican form of government.
The proposed amendment would declare initiative and referendum powers a fundamental right, preserve existing signature and statewide majority requirements and prevent lawmakers from weakening the initiative process.
It would also prohibit lawmakers from changing or repealing laws enacted through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both the Missouri House and Senate or a public vote.
The protections would apply to citizen-initiated laws and constitutional amendments approved after Jan. 1, 2010, as well as laws rejected by voters through referendum after that date. The restrictions would apply to legislative action taken after the amendment takes effect, meaning they would not automatically undo changes lawmakers made before then.
The lawsuit argues all of those provisions share one “reasonably narrow and identifiable central and controlling purpose” and amend only Article III of the Missouri Constitution.
But the dispute also centers on decisions Hoskins and the attorney general made before supporters ever began gathering signatures.
Former Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who held the office at the time, approved the petition as to form on July 31, 2025. Hoskins approved the petition’s form the same day and certified its official ballot title on Sept. 9.
No one challenged that ballot title during the 10-day period allowed under state law.
Supporters then circulated petitions bearing the title Hoskins had certified.
When Hoskins rejected the petition Tuesday, however, his certificate of insufficiency also purported to withdraw the September ballot title and certify a new one.
The lawsuit argues state law gives the secretary of state no authority to do that at the end of the petition process.
It points to a 2024 Missouri Supreme Court ruling arising from the abortion-rights amendment voters approved that year.
In that case, then-Secretary of State Jay Ashcroft attempted to reverse earlier decisions approving the form of the petition after a Cole County judge ordered the amendment removed from the ballot.
The Supreme Court said Ashcroft’s attempt was “a nullity and of no effect” and held that the secretary was not entitled to reassess matters he had previously approved.
The Respect Missouri Voters lawsuit argues Hoskins is bound by the same principle.
“The secretary is not entitled to re-assess matters of form that he [has] already approved,” the lawsuit states, quoting the 2024 decision.
The lawsuit asks a judge to reverse Hoskins’ certificate of insufficiency, order him to declare the petition sufficient and place it on the November ballot using the title certified last September.
The case comes days after Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected Amendment 4, a measure placed on Tuesday’s ballot by lawmakers that would have required citizen-led constitutional amendments to win a majority statewide and in each of Missouri’s eight congressional districts.
Respect Missouri Voters was among the groups campaigning against Amendment 4.
Tuesday was also the statutory deadline for Hoskins to decide whether citizen petitions had enough support and otherwise complied with state law to qualify for November.
Under state law, lawsuits challenging those decisions must be moved to the front of the court docket and decided “as quickly as possible.”
There is another deadline looming.
No court may order a measure added to the Nov. 3 ballot after Sept. 8, eight weeks before Election Day.
That leaves Respect Missouri Voters and People Not Politicians less than five weeks to win their cases if their proposals are to appear before voters this fall.

name: Delaware
title: First State Educate launches onboarding initiative for new school board members
description: Statewide program will provide governance training, mentoring and professional support as newly elected members begin making decisions affecting students, families and taxpayers By George D. Rotsch, Editor Delaware LIVE WILMINGTON, Del. — First State Educate has launched a statewide onboarding initiative that provides governance resources, professional learn[...]
text:
Statewide program will provide governance training, mentoring and professional support as newly elected members begin making decisions affecting students, families and taxpayers
By George D. Rotsch, Editor Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — First State Educate has launched a statewide onboarding initiative that provides governance resources, professional learning and ongoing support for Delaware’s newly elected school board members.
Julia Keleher, Executive Director of First State Educate, said the initiative is designed to help new members understand their responsibilities before they begin making decisions involving district budgets, superintendent leadership, student achievement, public policy and the use of taxpayer dollars.
School board members often take office only weeks after winning an election. Although they immediately assume responsibility for major policy and financial decisions, many begin their service with limited formal preparation for their governance role.
Keleher said the initiative will help new members begin their service with a clearer understanding of how an effective school board operates and how individual members can contribute to the board’s success.
Starting with governance
School boards establish district policies, approve budgets, hire and evaluate superintendents, and set the strategic direction of local school systems.
Board members are not responsible for managing the daily operations of schools. That work is generally handled by the superintendent and district administrators.
Understanding that distinction can help board members focus on long-term goals, student outcomes, financial oversight and accountability rather than becoming involved in routine management decisions.
Keleher said effective onboarding can also help new members understand meeting procedures, legal responsibilities, public accountability requirements and the importance of working collaboratively with other members of the board.
Resources, mentoring and professional learning
The First State Educate initiative includes a board onboarding framework, governance resources and continuing professional learning opportunities. The initiative is intended to provide support beyond a member’s first weeks in office. Keleher said ongoing professional learning can help board members respond to changing academic, financial and community challenges throughout their terms.
Keleher said the program also includes a partnership with Wilmington University and a governance credentialing pathway that allows board members to publicly demonstrate a commitment to effective school governance.
First State Educate also offers an opportunity to create a mentoring component that can connect newly elected members with experienced education and governance leaders.
Better preparation can also help members ask stronger questions, evaluate information more carefully and build productive relationships with superintendents, fellow board members and the public.
Why residents should care
Strong school boards benefit more than the people seated at the board table.
Board decisions influence classroom resources, academic programs, school safety, transportation, employee contracts, taxes and the long-term financial health of a district. Those decisions affect students, families, educators, property owners and businesses throughout the community.
Keleher said a well-prepared board is more likely to remain focused on measurable goals, responsible spending and student achievement.  Citizens can expect a more meaningful discussion at board meetings, more focus on the highest priorities and a better exchange of ideas between the community and leaders in the school.
Delaware residents also have a role in strengthening local school governance. Community members can learn who serves on their board, attend meetings, review agendas, follow budget discussions and communicate constructively with elected members.
Residents should not wait until a controversial vote or financial crisis to begin paying attention. Understanding how a board operates before disagreements arise can lead to better public discussions and more informed community participation.
Keleher said the initiative is intended to help board members start strong while giving Delaware residents additional opportunities to understand, follow and support the work of their local school boards.
To Go Box

What: First State Educate’s statewide school board onboarding initiative
Purpose: To provide newly elected Delaware school board members with governance resources, mentoring and continuing professional learning
Program components: A board onboarding framework, governance materials, a Wilmington University partnership, mentoring opportunities and a possible governance credentialing pathway
Who benefits: School board members, students, families, educators and taxpayers
Learn more: Visit First State Educate’s website for school board resources, educational programs and community discussion opportunities.
