name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC needs an alternate route to less traffic and more housing
description: South Carolinians are fed up with traffic, understandably blaming explosive population growth. Road congestion’s real driver is less obvious: a sprawling, government-mandated development pattern that leaves taxpayers on the hook for infrastructure maintenance costs that localities will struggle to pay. The Palmetto State should return to traditional, natural[...]
text:
According to U.S. Census commuting data, about one in five workers employed in Charleston County in 2023 lived more than 50 miles away, amounting to more than 50,000 long-distance commuters. (Getty Images)South Carolinians are fed up with traffic, understandably blaming explosive population growth.
Road congestion’s real driver is less obvious: a sprawling, government-mandated development pattern that leaves taxpayers on the hook for infrastructure maintenance costs that localities will struggle to pay.
The Palmetto State should return to traditional, natural growth patterns that strengthen local finances, make homes more abundant and affordable, and reduce traffic by letting people choose to drive less.
Mount Pleasant did not have much traffic in the 1990s and 2000s, when I grew up there. As a College of Charleston student, I easily visited my parents across the Cooper River. I only became acquainted with the stresses of heavy traffic after moving to the Washington, D.C., area.
When I brought my girlfriend to the Lowcountry in 2016 to propose, I was curious to see how smartphone navigation would optimize my driving routes. I quickly realized there was typically only one direct route between wherever I was and where I wanted to go. Detouring required making a huge loop. Happily, traffic still seemed fairly tame.
The Lowcountry has much worse traffic now, and it is easy to see why: A simple road network has inherent chokepoints.
Desperate to appease public anger about congestion, Mount Pleasant’s government banned new multifamily housing, including townhouses, for seven years back in 2017.
Results and public discourse show that policy failed.
Unfortunately, my hometown’s housing ban likely worsened its traffic problem by pushing more people who work in Charleston or Mount Pleasant to live in places farther out.
According to U.S. Census commuting data, about one in five workers employed in Charleston County in 2023 lived more than 50 miles away, amounting to more than 50,000 long-distance commuters. Living closer to their jobs would mean less driving for them and less traffic for everyone.
Most of South Carolina’s new housing is sprawling development at the edges of metropolitan areas: a limited number of large, expensive homes on government-mandated large lots.
“Drive until you qualify”— families buying a home with a mortgage they can barely afford at the edge of a metro area — keeps extending South Carolinians’ commutes.
Young parents in particular waste hours on jammed highways, commuting between a home they can afford and a job to pay for it.
Folks born and raised in the state who want a family of their own are increasingly forced to move, saying goodbye to their hometowns, relatives, and lifelong friends. They cannot compete with affluent newcomers for the limited supply of homes.
Spread-out housing stresses public budgets too. On a per-acre basis, it requires more physical infrastructure — such as roads and utility lines — while generating less property tax revenue.
The grassroots organization Strong Towns studies municipal finances, including road networks. It finds that such neighborhoods generate insufficient tax revenue to cover the long-term maintenance of their extensive infrastructure.
When the bill comes due, localities allow new development at their periphery to pump up new tax revenue. New development finances old — what Strong Towns calls “the growth Ponzi scheme.”
This is a familiar story in South Carolina, where road funding has become a major state budget issue.
There is probably no simple formula for fixing South Carolina’s housing shortage.
But the state’s fiscally sound neighborhoods of the future probably resemble Mount Pleasant’s colonial-era Old Village. Its street grid and small lots let many residents walk or bike, supporting local businesses — and reducing and diffusing traffic.
Strengthening private property rights and allowing traditional housing types would lead to additional family-friendly communities for people who want to live in them, generating less traffic elsewhere.
Regulation is the predominant barrier to building new places with the same basic ingredients as Old Village or even Charleston’s historic districts, where children can play in the streets and extended families keep old traditions alive.
South Carolina’s current growth pattern maximizes traffic. Its cultural heritage offers an alternate route forward.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Attorney General Jeff Jackson joins two dozen states in lawsuit over new Trump tariffs
description: North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson has joined 24 Democratic-led states in suing the Trump administration over the latest round of sweeping tariffs. The U.S. Supreme Court invalidated Trump’s first round of tariffs in February, ruling that the executive branch doesn’t have the power to impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers[...]
text:
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson shares details of his latest lawsuit involving the Trump administration during a August 4, 2026, N.C. Council of State meeting. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson has joined 24 Democratic-led states in suing the Trump administration over the latest round of sweeping tariffs.
The U.S. Supreme Court invalidated Trump’s first round of tariffs in February, ruling that the executive branch doesn’t have the power to impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Trump criticized the ruling, and in July, he ordered a new round of tariffs of up to 12.5% on countries his administration claims are engaging in unfair or discriminatory trade practices.
Jackson said the new tariffs on 80 countries will impact nearly all U.S. imports and cost the average North Carolina family approximately $1,100 per year.
“These tariffs are hurting families, farmers, and business owners,” said Jackson in a statement on Tuesday. “They’re illegal, and they’re making things harder for North Carolinians who are working around the clock to keep the lights on, pay rent, and afford gas.”
Jackson said North Carolinians paid nearly $3.5 billion in tariffs last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act before the Supreme Court ruled against the administration.
And while business owners and importers have applied for refunds, over half of those levies collected prior to the court’s ruling remain unreturned, according to the free-market think tank Tax Foundation.
The lawsuit filed this week argues that the latest round of tariffs exceeds the administration’s legal authority and violates the Administrative Procedure Act.
Jackson is joined in the suit by the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania and the Attorneys General of Oregon, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin.
FEMA, DHS grant conditions draw second suit
This is the second suit in as many days that Jackson has filed against the Trump administration.
On Tuesday, Jackson told members of the North Carolina Council of State that his office has also filed suit against the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Department of Homeland Security for threatening to withhold more than $1  billion that has been promised to states for disaster response and counterterrorism efforts.
“This is bomb squads, hurricane response, active shooter response. They are attempting to impose new conditions on the receipt of those funds,” Jackson said.
Jackson said one condition would allow DHS to terminate any federal grant at any time, for any reason.
Jeff Jackson blasts FEMA funding freeze at flooded Hillsborough facility

A second condition would withhold federal money unless states change how they administer elections. According to the attorney general, at least 13 counties in North Carolina would be forced to replace voting equipment that has already been certified by the State Board of Elections.
The suit maintains that Homeland Security is “using hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funds as a cudgel” to impose the current administration’s preferred policies.
Jackson said the conditions are plainly in violation of the instructions with which Congress gave the money to FEMA.
Jackson is joined in this suit by many of the same attorneys general suing over the tariffs.
“This is the second time we have had to sue FEMA over something like this. We were successful last year, I anticipate that we will be successful this year,” Jackson said on Tuesday.
The attorney general won $17 million for N.C. in a similar suit against FEMA and DHS last December. In that case, the court found the federal government’s conditions on the grants were not “consistent with Congressional intent or FEMA’s mission.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Former Holy Cross Hospital CEO Kevin Sexton tapped to lead HSCRC
description: Kevin Sexton, former president and CEO of Holy Cross Health hospitals, has been tapped to chair a powerful state commission charged with setting hospital rates in Maryland, the Moore administration announced Thursday.
text:
A sign outside an Iowa hospital. Health officials in Maryland were optimistic about the selection of Kevin Sexton to run the state's Health Services Cost Review Commission as it prepares to launch a new model of rate setting for hospitals in the state. (Photo by Cecilia Lynch/USDA)Kevin Sexton, former president and CEO of Holy Cross Health hospitals, has been tapped to chair a powerful state commission charged with setting hospital rates in Maryland, the Moore administration announced Thursday.
Sexton’s nomination comes at a critical time for the Health Services Cost Review Commission, as it prepares to implement a new rate-setting model that will limit some of the state’s authority to regulate hospital prices, a new model that has taken two years of negotiations between two federal administrations.
“Kevin brings the strong leadership abilities, effective communication skills, and expertise needed to successfully empower our communities to achieve health and well-being at this transformative time for healthcare in Maryland,” Gov. Wes Moore (D) said in a statement announcing the appointment.
Sexton, whose appointment still needs Senate approval, will serve as an interim appointee until the legislature convenes in January. He has been nominated to a four-year term, replacing former Chair Joshua Sharfstein, who stepped down in July after serving a single term.
Former Holy Cross hospital CEO and President Kevin Sexton. (Photo courtesy of Holy Cross Health)
“I look forward to working with my fellow commissioners, our dedicated staff, and all of our stakeholders to manage this transition and move forward in a way that benefits all Marylanders,” Sexton said in a written statement Thursday.
Fortunately, he’s already familiar with the often complex and intricate policy decisions at the HSCRC. Sexton was first appointed to the commission back in 2003 and moved up to become vice chair in 2005, where he served for six years.
He also served from 1998 to 2018 as president and CEO of Holy Cross Hospital, with facilities in Silver Spring, Gaithersburg, Germantown and other locations. During his time at Holy Cross, he “oversaw a strategic restructuring that established the Holy Cross Health Network, managing community health centers and prenatal care facilities for the uninsured,” according to a press release from the governor’s office.
Emily Holliman, regional president for Kaiser Permanente of the Mid-Atlantic States, called Sexton a “highly respected and trusted leader in Maryland’s health care community.”
“Throughout his tenure at Holy Cross Hospital, Kevin demonstrated an unwavering commitment to the communities he served and a strong dedication to collaboration and innovation that advanced access, quality, and care delivery,” she said in a written statement.
In 2019, Sexton joined the Primary Care Coalition, which advocates for a stronger primary care network in Maryland. In 2024, he was selected to chair the coalition’s board of directors.
Representatives and advocates from various arms of the healthcare industry said Sexton’s experience will be crucial as the state builds a new hospital rate-setting system.
“Kevin has a deep understanding of Maryland’s healthcare system and has consistently demonstrated a collaborative approach that values the perspectives of physicians and other stakeholders,” said Gene Ransom, CEO of MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society. “We look forward to working with Chairman Sexton to continue advancing high-quality, patient-centered healthcare across Maryland.”
His main challenge as the new chair will be leading the HSCRC as it moves to a new hospital rate-setting model that will limit the state’s ability to set Medicare costs, an authority it’s had for more than 40 years.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The previous model, called the Total Cost of Care, expired at the end of 2025, leading into the Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design system, also called the AHEAD model.
The Total Cost of Care system gave Maryland officials authority to regulate hospital costs across all payers in the system, which include private insurance, Medicaid and Medicare. The Health Service Cost Review Commission determines those rates.
State officials had signed an agreement in 2024 with the Biden administration that would have largely kept the state’s authority to regulate all payers intact. But the Trump administration decided early last year to renegotiate the terms of that agreement.
The final version of the AHEAD model will remove the state’s authority to set rates in 2028 while emphasizing improvements in community health and competition in Maryland’s healthcare system, among other priorities.
The AHEAD model also aims to improve overall population health in Maryland by strengthening the state’s primary care system to prevent illnesses and catch health issues early.
Sexton’s background makes for a “well-rounded” candidate to lead the commission once more, according to Melony G. Griffith, president and CEO of the Maryland Hospital Association, in a written statement.
Matthew Celentano, executive director for the League of Life & Health Insurers of Maryland, agreed.
“As we embark on the next phase of AHEAD model implementation, affordability for Maryland consumers must stay at the forefront of all health care discussions, and Kevin is the right person to lead that effort,” Celentano said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Huntington community organizers start ballot initiative to prohibit Flock cameras
description: Weeks after Huntington City Council voted to move forward with the purchase of a $2.1 million Flock surveillance system, organizers against the proposal are starting an effort that, if successful, would prohibit the devices in the city.
text:
Protestors gather outside of Huntington City Hall as they respond in opposition to Flock Safety items listed on the Huntington City Council agenda on Monday, July 13, 2026, in downtown Huntington. (Photo by Ryan Fischer/The Herald-Dispatch)Weeks after Huntington City Council voted to move forward with the purchase of a $2.1 million Flock surveillance system, organizers against the proposal are starting an effort that, if successful, would prohibit the devices in the city. 
The Huntington Community Action Group launched its “Get the Flock Out” ballot initiative at a rally Wednesday at Marshall University. The group wants to pass an ordinance prohibiting mass surveillance systems in the city. One provision of the ordinance would require the city to void the contracts with Flock Safety it approved last month. 
Council members voted 6-4 to approve the contracts for audio detection, live video cameras, drone services and license plate recognition at a July 14 meeting that stretched several hours into the early morning. More than 50 people spoke against using the contracts with Flock, a company that’s been criticized for privacy and civil liberties concerns in other municipalities where they’ve contracted. Huntington Community Action Group also led a rally against the systems before the council meeting. 
According to the ACLU, between 80,000 and 100,000 Flock devices have been installed on urban and rural areas of highways. The automated license plate readers are more powerful than typical license plate readers and analyze the make, model and color of cars they see, along with other identifiers like scratches and dents, and even pedestrians passing by, according to the ACLU.
The systems analyze recordings and upload data to a national surveillance platform and store it in a way that’s accessible by law enforcement and Flock users everywhere, according to ACLU. 
During the meeting, Huntington Mayor Patrick Farrell spoke in support of the Flock system, saying the devices would lead to convictions of people harming the community. He said license plate readers had been used in another city to arrest a man suspected in the shooting death of Huntington resident Jackie Harper on July 7. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia filed a lawsuit against the city over the cameras in Cabell County Circuit Court, alleging the city neglected key procedural matters in awarding the contract.
Matthew Lebo, HCAG’s treasurer and an organizer within its Democracy Task Group, told West Virginia Watch Wednesday afternoon that the organization’s rally that evening would serve as canvassing training for volunteers who will go door-to-door in the city collecting signatures for the ballot initiative.
“That is where most of our energy has been spent the past week, creating the materials and training we need to go door-to-door,” Lebo said. “In addition to that, we are going to be sending people to special events with a couple clipboards to do some crowd canvassing, and we will be arranging a regular series of special events, rallies, and town halls across Huntington, also to collect signatures.”
According to the Huntington city charter, initiative petitions must be signed by at least 10% of the number of registered voters during the last municipal election. 
Chrisa Hayes, communications director for the city of Huntington, said that 13,574 ballots were cast during the 2024 city mayoral race. She declined to comment on the initiative. 
Lebo said the organization’s goal is to collect 4,000 Huntington signatures — or a little more than 10% of the 27,000 Huntington residents who were registered to vote during that election. The extra signatures will account for those the city invalidates for various reasons, like signatures not matching, or a voter not updating their address, or believing they lived within the city limits when they don’t, he said. 
The organization hopes to collect the signatures by the end of September, though that deadline is not a requirement in the city charter.  
If the city deems the petition to have the sufficient number of signatures, city council must consider the proposed ordinance within 60 days, according to the charter. If council does not approve the ordinance or changes it, it must refer the ordinance to a vote by the city. The election must then take place between 30 days and one year later. If there’s no regular election during that time frame, the city must provide a special election on the proposed ordinance. 
The ballot initiative is also being supported by the ACLU-WV, West Virginia Citizen Action Group and West Virginia Can’t Wait. 
Lebo said the group is learning the ballot initiative process as it goes along. There’s not a template for the process other than what’s in city charter and state code, he said. The group wrote a letter to the city’s attorney for guidance, but got no response, he said.
“We have asked for a template petition,” he said. “We have submitted Freedom of Information Act requests, trying to find template petitions. There are none. We are building this ship as we sail it.”
Lebo said he’s been surprised by how excited people are to support the work to reject Flock. Several times in the past month, he said, he’s walked into city businesses and heard people talking about it, or people have recognised him from a city council meeting or town hall organizing meeting, he said. 
Posts about Flock cameras on the group’s social media page have received about 140,000 views and more than 13,000 engagements. The organization’s number of followers have quadrupled in the last month, he said. 
“There is so much public excitement, not and not just from Huntington either,” he said. “Our organizing and the pressure we are applying in Huntington is rippling out throughout the region.”

After the July 14 meeting, city leaders in Barboursville and Ironton, Ohio have come against the use of Flock cameras. St. Albans voted to reject the systems. The backlash led to Putnam County officials pausing the implementation of the Flock cameras that they had already purchased, but not installed. 
“People are so fired up in Huntington to ban mass surveillance that everyone in the region seems to be taking notice,” Lebo said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: ‘The Bird-Watchers’ of Memphis: tracking ICE flights and documenting detainees In shackles
description: This story was originally published by the Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis.  On a Saturday morning in July, Joni Laney, a 73-year-old retired English teacher, parked her car in a small lot overlooking Wilson Air Center near Memphis International Airport. She had received word from her group of fellow volunteers that a flight there […]
text:
Handcuffed and shackled detainees are unloaded from a van and ushered onto a waiting jet last month at Wilson Air Center in Memphis. (by Meghnad Bose)
This story was originally published by the Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis. 
On a Saturday morning in July, Joni Laney, a 73-year-old retired English teacher, parked her car in a small lot overlooking Wilson Air Center near Memphis International Airport. She had received word from her group of fellow volunteers that a flight there was going to be used to transport several detainees held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Laney had shown up, as she has done numerous times over the past few months, to document what would transpire. On this occasion, Laney invited me to come along and see for myself the manner in which ICE treated its detainees in transit. Seated in her car, and attempting to be as inconspicuous as possible, we kept watch as a bus and a van — both vehicles white and unmarked — stood next to a stationary Bombardier plane registered to an ICE contractor.
“Oh gosh, can you see the shackles? Oh my God,” Laney gasped as a group of women detainees stepped out of the van, their hands and feet in shackles and chains running around their waists. “Three, four…,” she kept count of the number of detainees who got out of the van and made their way to the aircraft in front of them.
Moments earlier, a larger number of male detainees had similarly exited the bus. Laney documented the details carefully, as well as she could from the distance we were at, across a barbed wire fence bordering the air center.
“I’m a bird-watcher,” she told me. That’s what she and her group of just under ten like-minded individuals call themselves — The Bird-Watchers — as they go about tracking ICE flights in Memphis and documenting the manner in which detainees are transported on them.
Many of The Bird-Watchers, like Joni, are retired Memphians. For months, they have painstakingly collected evidence of the harsh conditions in which ICE detainees are moved, bound in shackles and chains.
“It must violate most safety regulations to have that many people shackled (on a plane)”, said Jim West, a 75-year-old retired physician and bioethicist, and another of The Bird-Watchers. “They’d never be able to evacuate if they had to.”
“(ICE) treats them as though they’re non-human at every point,” said Laney, “and every time they’re moved, the airplane gets money, ICE gets money, the prison gets money, (private prison contractor) CoreCivic gets money — I mean it’s just like a revolving door of money.”
Protesters who gathered Tuesday at a rally outside Wilson Air Center echoed those sentiments.
“And we can’t forget, too, that the reason all of this is happening is (because) someone thinks we’re less than” human, Latina activist Gisela Guerrero said.
 Pressure on the Wilsons
A plane registered to an ICE contractor sits on the tarmac at Wilson Air Center. (by Meghnad Bose)
Now, following that money trail, The Bird-Watchers are seeking to pressure the owners of the private air center where the flights are boarded, seeking to stop it from profiting from ICE operations.
At the heart of the row over ICE flights in Memphis is one of the city’s most famous business families, the Wilsons of Holiday Inn fame.
Wilson Air Center is a fixed-base operator or FBO, which is a company authorized to provide aviation services for certain private aircraft. The private enterprise was founded in 1996 by Robert Wilson, also known as Bob, son of the late Kemmons Wilson, the founder of the Holiday Inn chain of hotels. The Wilson Air Center proclaims on its website that “our Memphis location is home of one of the world’s largest aircraft canopies, and is touted by the aviation industry as among the top fixed base operations in the United States for the quality of its services and the comfort and design of its facilities.” The enterprise also has facilities in Houston and Chattanooga.
Now, as The Bird-Watchers and other advocacy groups protest Wilson Air Center’s continued operations with regard to ICE flights, the financial ties between the air center and the federal agency or its contractors have come into question.
On the day that I accompanied Laney to document the detainee transfer at the air center, the flight in question was a Bombardier registered by CSI Aviation, a private air charter company that received a $1.6 billion contract over one year from the Department of Homeland Security “for enforcement and removal operations under the ICE Air Program”. It is unclear whether the services of the Wilson Air Center were requisitioned by DHS, ICE, CSI Aviation or some other agency or contractor. Wilson Air Center did not respond to The Institute’s requests for comment.
Vecindarios 901, a grassroots rapid response group that works on immigrants’ issues in Memphis, has joined The Bird-Watchers’ call to pressure the Wilsons to drop their ICE flight operations. In a statement, the group said that Memphians are joining “a nationwide movement against ICE flights operating in our communities, and against the companies secretly servicing and profiting off the inhumane systems hurting our people.”
“People around the country are sending them emails, asking them to make the same move that other companies around the county are being asked to make,” Blake Burr, one of the co-founders of Vecindarios 901, told The Institute. Burr, who is also part of the group of Bird-Watchers, added that, as a Memphian, she felt that the Wilson family would want to be remembered in a different way, with a positive legacy.
Joni Laney watches the action at Wilson Air Center from her car. (by Meghnad Bose)
Behind the scenes, The Bird-Watchers said they have spent weeks trying to reach out to Bob Wilson’s extended family, trying to persuade them to use their influence to get Wilson Air Center to drop its ICE flight operations. Laney, for one, said she managed to have a phone conversation with Spence Wilson Sr., son of Kemmons, brother to Robert and chairman emeritus of Kemmons Wilson Companies. Laney said that in the conversation, Spence referred to the air center’s operations as a business proposition and pushed back against her protestations.
“They’re a charitable family in lots of ways,” said another Bird-Watcher, who requested to not be identified by name due to her work on tracking ICE flights, “but then at the same time, you know, here they are profiting off human misery.”
 A meticulous process
Every morning, a retired teacher in her seventies who joined The Bird-Watchers a few months ago, wakes up early and gets to work. Her tasks — detainee searches and database updates — are the start of a meticulous process that The Bird-Watchers have nearly perfected over their time working together.
The retired teacher, who requested that she not be named due to fears of retaliation over her work, logs on to an online database of detainees held at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason. There, she manually searches for the names of the detainees.
“I am the one who every single morning spends up to three hours searching through Mason’s database one at a time to find out who is new there and who has left”, she told The Institute. “I don’t get everyone because they don’t make it easy. It’s a tedious process.”
“All these ways to find people was all brand new to me,” she said. But now, the searcher said that she has a long-term database of about 3,500 detainees who were there at the facility at some point since it reopened in September 2025, and over 800 names of detainees who were held there in July.
“I have a sheet for every month and so I have who at the beginning of the month started there, who comes there, and then I keep a database in the same sheet of those who are leaving. And so I can look at my sheet and I can tell you what day they came, I can tell you what day they left,” said the searcher.
When a large tranche of names that was there the previous day suddenly no longer appears the next day, she said it’s a sign that there would likely be a flight that will transfer them out of Memphis from Wilson Air Center.
“Because these planes are leaving at like nine o’clock, I get up really early to make sure we know how many people are going to be on the planes.”
As the searcher hands off this information to The Bird-Watchers, the next stage gets underway — flight tracking. On cue, a resident of Midtown Memphis who specializes in flight tracking for The Bird-Watchers, begins her part of the process.
Before she got involved with The Bird-Watchers, she had never tracked a flight before. “I didn’t know that was possible,” she told The Institute. Now, she scans multiple flight tracking websites, including a real-time flight monitoring site focused on ICE flight paths. She zeroes in on flights near Memphis International Airport, and tries to confirm whether there is a flight registered by an ICE contractor that is in the vicinity.
It’s not always easy to track the flights. “There’s like five of them (flight trackers) you have to kind of look between because they hide a lot of the flights — they have them on special lists so they don’t show up on trackers the same way.”
But when she needs help, she reaches out to a national group of ICE flight watchers who have been performing similar tasks elsewhere in the country. “The national group is helpful,” she said. “If there’s something I can’t figure out, I can ask.”
Over the past five months, The Bird-Watchers have tracked around 50 such ICE flights leaving Memphis. Most of them head toward Alexandria airport in Louisiana, she said, due to it being a hub for multiple detention centers in that Deep South state.
Once the flight details are confirmed by the tracking specialist, the details are promptly shared with the group. Finally, the last leg kicks off — Bird-Watchers must go in person to vantage points near the Wilson Air Center, and document what takes place.
West, the retired physician, and Laney, the retired teacher, are among those who are tasked with this final stretch. Both of them have been near Wilson on these observation trips on numerous occasions. Each time, it hits them just as hard.
“When you go and watch it, it just tears at your gut to see these people that have been separated from their families,” said West. He shares photos and videos from his trips documenting detainees bound in shackles. A majority have no criminal conviction yet are treated like criminals, eliciting sharp and emotional reactions.
“It’s like watching a death train,” said the flight tracking specialist, “You’re watching people get torn away from their families — some of them are going (to be sent) back to very dangerous situations. It’s not safe for them to go back.”
But for The Bird-Watchers, it reinforces the need for the work they do.
“I think it’s important to bear witness,” said the searcher, adding that they have been sharing the details on social media. “But also, we want to verify what they (ICE) are actually doing. Like I had no idea they were shackled, hands and feet.”
“It makes me want to scream because it’s not right,” she added. “They’re not getting the criminals. They’re getting somebody’s mommy and somebody’s daddy and somebody’s grandpa.”
 Most Memphis detainees transferred out of state
The scene outside Wilson Air Center last month. (by Meghnad Bose)
Under the Trump administration, an overwhelming majority of immigrants listed as having been detained by ICE in Memphis end up in detention facilities in neighboring states such as Louisiana, according to The Institute’s analysis of data provided by ICE in response to a public records request by the Deportation Data Project.
Of the 2,529 ICE detainees listed as having been detained first in the Memphis Hold Room since the day President Trump took office in January 2025, over half of them — 1,291 detainees, or 51% — had their final detention stint in Louisiana. Only 15%, or 374 of the detainees, had their final detention stint within Tennessee, either at the Memphis Hold Room itself or the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason.
Vecindarios 901 said in a statement that these transfers of detainees are “designed to punish and wear down migrants in detention, forcing legal counsel to constantly recalibrate and families to wonder where their loved ones are being held and how they are being treated.” The statement added, “As habeas corpus petitions can only be filed in the jurisdiction of a person’s physical location, ICE can effectively prevent habeas filings with constant relocations and no transparency.”
DHS and ICE did not respond to The Institute’s request for comment.
Even as these “shuffle flights” continue, so do the efforts of those such as The Bird-Watchers of Memphis. And their pressure on private partners of ICE flights, such as Wilson Air Center, is also increasing.
“The reason I started doing this work was because I have a five-year-old grandson,” said the retired teacher who performs the early morning detainee database searches. “When he’s old and says, ‘What did you do when all this was going on?’ I want to be able to tell him, ‘I fought against this. I did something, I didn’t just sit and tsk tsk at the news.”
Erika Konig contributed to this article.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Great Plains Food Bank sees record numbers seeking food assistance
description: More than 186,000 people accepted help from the Great Plains Food Bank’s network of food pantries in the past year, a new record for the organization.  The food bank, serving North Dakota and Clay County, Minnesota, said one in four people in the region relied on the network during the fiscal year that ended June […]
text:
John Hoffman, a volunteer at the Dream Center in Bismarck, moves boxes of food from a pallet to a shelf in the facility storage area on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor) More than 186,000 people accepted help from the Great Plains Food Bank’s network of food pantries in the past year, a new record for the organization. 
The food bank, serving North Dakota and Clay County, Minnesota, said one in four people in the region relied on the network during the fiscal year that ended June 30, said Ann Prifrel, CEO of Great Plains Food Bank. 
The total number of people using the food bank increased 16% compared to the previous fiscal year, according to the nonprofit food shelf.
More Americans are hungry in the face of federal cuts, rising grocery prices

“Our neighbors are struggling to make ends meet,” Prifel said in an interview.
She said increasing costs for food, gas, insurance and other necessities are driving people to reach out for food assistance from the organization.
“Working people are turning to the Great Plains Food Bank for help,” Prifrel said. She added the food bank itself has also experienced those increasing gas costs, but people who have made financial and food donations across their network have allowed them to continue helping those in need.
Cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program last year played a role in the increased demand, Prifrel said. She said she was grateful for the state of North Dakota providing more than $900,000 in funding during the federal government shutdown to help get the organization through a difficult time until the government reopened.
Linda Roberson, a volunteer at the Dream Center in Bismarck, cuts mushrooms next to other volunteers preparing meals in the kitchen of the facility on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“The challenge is really at the federal level right now,” she said. A family she spoke to that was receiving about $200 per month in SNAP benefits last year has been receiving about $25 per month since the government reopened last November.
Prifrel said the food bank has also seen a decrease in support from federal programs that provide food to the organization.
The Great Plains Food Bank distributed about 15.4 million pounds of food in the past fiscal year, a 4.5% increase. That’s despite a reduction to The Emergency Food Assistance Program, a federal food assistance program that provided the Great Plains Food Bank with nearly 1 million fewer pounds of food last year, she said.
“That’s challenging for us, and if we didn’t have such great supporters, if we didn’t have the communities really being aware of the need, we’d be in trouble,” Prifrel said. “There have been cuts to these really important federal programs that have impacted us.”
With the reduction in food provided by the federal government, the Great Plains Food Bank needed to purchase more surplus food from producers, distributors and retailers, using their own funds to cover the cost, she said
“The need is growing and we need to grow our response as well,” she said.
The Dream Center in Bismarck, part of the Great Plains Food Bank network, also experienced a record-breaking year in providing food and meals to the community, said Jim Barnhardt, executive director.
Vira Doll, a volunteer at the Dream Center in Bismarck, opens boxes of food on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Barnhardt said the center provided 1.25 million meals last year through hot meals, sack lunches and food box distribution.
If a person loses a job, has a problem with their vehicle or a medical issue, people have to make difficult choices between addressing those problems and eating, he said. 
“If we can help people with their grocery bills, so they have the money to pay their rent, to repair the car, to buy shoes for the kids … that’s a huge savings these days, especially when you go to the grocery store and look at that $7 per pound hamburger,” Barnhardt said.
Leaders of the Great Plains Food Bank are hoping to expand operations in the Fargo area with a new, larger facility that would also serve as a community center in the future, Prifrel said. She added the organization also wants to expand operations to schools and medical clinics in an effort to serve people in their communities.
The Great Plains Food Bank is a member of Feeding America, a nationwide hunger relief charity that provides surplus food and grocery donations from producers and manufacturers.  
The number of food insecure North Dakotans increased from about 36,000 in 2020 to more than 91,000 in 2024, according to Feeding America. The most recent figures also showed a 23% increase in childhood food insecurity, Prifel noted.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Ethics Commission commissioners want closer look at ‘revolving door’ issue
description: The Alabama Ethics Commission Wednesday delayed consideration of an advisory opinion that said the state’s ethics laws do not prevent a former state agency worker from establishing a business with clients seeking to contract with the same state agency. Several members expressed concerns that the opinion would clash with precedent. The commission has previous[...]
text:
The Alabama Ethics Commission holds a regular meeting on June 3, 2026 in Montgomery. Members of the commission Wednesday delayed consideration of an advisory opinion relating to a retiring state employee's plans to open a consulting business. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Ethics Commission Wednesday delayed consideration of an advisory opinion that said the state’s ethics laws do not prevent a former state agency worker from establishing a business with clients seeking to contract with the same state agency.
Several members expressed concerns that the opinion would clash with precedent. The commission has previously said the Alabama Ethics Act does not prohibit an individual previously employed with a state agency from hiring someone to deal directly with the agency. But the state’s “revolving door” provision prevents that individual from representing clients directly with the agency who want to provide services.
“I don’t see much of a difference,” said Carole Smitherman, one of the commissioners, during the meeting. “There is a thin line there.”
The opinion concerns Antwionne Dunklin, a product licensing director with the Alabama Department of Insurance, who plans to retire in the next year or so, according to Brian Paterson, chief counsel for the Alabama Ethics Commission.
After retiring, Dunklin plans to start a consulting firm providing services to the department and to clients conducting business before it.
The Alabama Ethics Act does not prohibit someone from providing paid services to an agency that previously employed them, according to Paterson. Previous advisory opinions have said that state law does not prohibit former public employees from starting consulting businesses so long as the individual does not deal directly with the agency when representing their clients’ interests until two years after leaving their post.
Current commissioners took issue with that interpretation by previous commissioners.
“I see a distinction in the situation where a government employee goes to work for a large company that has hundreds of employees, the ALDOT (Alabama Department of Transportation) scenario, versus a situation where an employee leaves, forms a business that has one employee, and tells that employee to solicit work,” said Greg Pierce, vice chair of the commission, during the meeting.
Paterson said staff would evaluate the matter further for commissioners to consider at the next meeting.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama lawmakers should learn from Arizona’s SNAP crisis
description: When Dee McDonald renewed her family’s benefits under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) last fall, she had no reason to think the process would leave her choosing between paying the rent and feeding the three grandsons she is raising. Months passed without assistance. McDonald told The New York Times she relied on food banks, […]
text:
A sign in a convenience store along Barlowe Road in Hyattsville, Maryland, on Oct. 28, 2025, advertises that it accepts SNAP benefits. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)When Dee McDonald renewed her family’s benefits under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) last fall, she had no reason to think the process would leave her choosing between paying the rent and feeding the three grandsons she is raising.
Months passed without assistance. McDonald told The New York Times she relied on food banks, stretched every grocery dollar and skipped meals while trying to resolve a paperwork problem with Arizona’s SNAP system.
Her family never stopped qualifying for help. The system simply failed to deliver it.
McDonald’s experience was not an isolated bureaucratic mishap. It was one glimpse of a statewide crisis.
Since Congress enacted HR 1 last summer, nearly 440,000 Arizonans have lost SNAP assistance, also known as food stamps — roughly half of all participants. More than 180,000 are children.
The decline far exceeds estimates of those directly affected by new eligibility restrictions. This suggests many eligible people are being caught in a system struggling with complicated rules and pressure to reduce errors and future costs. Arizona has issued $600 million less in SNAP benefits since July 2025, even as food bank traffic surges.
Alabama should take notice. Arizona shows what can happen when sweeping federal changes collide with an underfunded, overburdened system.
About 1 in 8 Alabamians — roughly 650,000 — use SNAP to help keep food on the table. The federal government has fully funded these benefits for decades. But under HR 1, the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), most states must pay for 5% to 15% of SNAP benefits starting in 2028 based on a flawed measure called the payment error rate. The law will require Alabama to cover 10% of SNAP benefits, or about $174 million a year.
This enormous cost shift is based on the misinterpretation of what payment error rates actually measure. Error rates do not measure fraud. Instead, they measure underpayments and overpayments that agencies — including Alabama’s Department of Human Resources (DHR) — make while administering SNAP.
As in Arizona, SNAP participation is falling in Alabama despite higher food prices and persistently high food insecurity and because of decades of unbending food apartheid. Since July 2025, nearly 82,000 fewer Alabamians, including about 23,000 children, are receiving SNAP benefits to help keep food on the table. That number is almost enough to fill Jordan-Hare Stadium.
Much of this decrease is due to SNAP participants’ struggles to navigate HR 1’s new red-tape barriers, including expanded work reporting and verification rules. These requirements have forced DHR staff to manage more calls, applications and paperwork. Additionally, HR 1 now requires states to cover 75% of SNAP administrative costs, up from the previous 50%.
In short, the federal government has told Alabama to reduce its SNAP error rate while cutting federal funding and making the program more complicated to administer. And if state legislators don’t allocate $174 million for SNAP benefits next year, Alabama could be forced to end its participation in SNAP entirely.
That is how a fiscal cost shift becomes a hunger crisis.
Without the funding needed to continue providing SNAP benefits, Alabamians risk losing the stabilizing power that SNAP offers for families, local grocers and retailers, farmers and the broader community.
Alabama has many revenue options to cover new SNAP costs. One would be to increase the state cigarette tax. Another would be to limit or end the state’s federal income tax deduction — a skewed tax loophole that overwhelmingly benefits Alabama’s wealthiest households — and redirect some of that revenue to fund SNAP.
Ultimately, Congress should reverse these harmful new SNAP cost shifts. At minimum, federal lawmakers should give states enough time and resources to implement them without pushing eligible families out.
Over the weekend, U.S. House Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman inaccurately claimed his Farm Bill draft would give “additional time to strengthen administration of SNAP benefits and reduce payment error rates.” Alabama would not get additional time to reduce error rates, but our lawmakers would get additional time to address the revenue gap the One Big Beautiful Bill Act created for our state budget.
As the Farm Bill moves toward committee markup on Thursday, Aug. 6, it appears our state administrators still will have to put paperwork over people beginning this year. Ultimately, we would get a payment plan, with less than optimal “payment error” rates.
Supporting state departments as they work to reduce their payment error rate would give Alabama an opportunity to reduce the cost of the program. Giving states until at least 2029 to prepare would protect families’ access to food while preserving SNAP spending that supports farmers, grocers and local economies.
Arizona’s experience is a cautionary tale. Alabama still has time not to repeat it — but only if state and federal leaders act before the warning becomes another crisis.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey’s listening tour won’t fix West Virginia’s water issues, but that was never the point
description: Beautiful clean water. Four counties. Two days. Hardly any notice.That describes the water listening tour that Gov. Morrisey announced.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey is going on a listening tour of Southern West Virginia to hear residents' concerns about drinking water. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)Beautiful clean water. Four counties. Two days. Hardly any notice.
That describes the water listening tour that Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday morning with Marshall President Brad Smith in Huntington, West Virginia, an area we all of course associate with bad water, I guess? 
The governor said he would drive across Southern West Virginia for two days to listen to local government representatives, business owners and residents about their concerns regarding water access in their communities.
By the time you read this, Morrisey’s political road show — I mean, water listening tour — will already be over. 
I watched some clips from reporters and community members who attended, and some of it didn’t go well. But to be honest, there was more attendance than I expected given the short notice. The public response wasn’t much better. To sum it up, many of the posts I saw on social media from the southern coalfields and across West Virginia seem as confused as I was about the timing and sincerity of the whole ordeal. 
To be clear, I think the governor and other politicians doing stuff like this can be good. Elected offiials hosting town halls is a net positive, and I’m sure it’s not easy to sit there and have people voice their displeasure with you. That is what they signed up for when they ran for office.
But why host a water road show now, and do it this way? Why not give the working class people who are dealing with water problems in Southern West Virginia an adequate heads up so they can rearrange their day?
As reporters and others have mentioned, West Virginia’s water issues have been well documented. There are years of first person accounts and media reports, as well as official government estimates that indicate billions of dollars in need.
There are no simple or cheap solutions to the issue. Some people don’t want to be hooked up to utility water. Some people struggle to maintain their well water systems. Some communities don’t have the same ratepayer base to maintain their local public service district water systems. Then there’s the epidemic of perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances and other pollution that industry dumps into our streams and groundwater that can be costly to treat. 
Don’t forget all of the efforts that President Donald Trump is doing (and that Morrisey is applauding) to threaten drinking water quality as he rolls back environmental protections. Or that the accomplishment that Morrisey ties himself closest to is his recruitment of data centers to West Virginia. It’s a little strange to focus on beautiful clean water while you ask mega-polluters to come to West Virginians’ backyards and rural areas. 
There was no way that a two-day tour was going to get to the heart of the water issue. But that was never the point. 
If there was genuine interest, the governor’s team would have worked long ago with the grassroots groups and residents who have been asking for help. I don’t recall the governor supporting From Below’s request for $250 million in drinking water appropriations this session, or even throwing a bone at some of the supermajority’s attempts to make headway on the issue. Earlier this summer, Reps. Riley Moore and Carol Miller requested $250 million in federal appropriations for the water crisis in West Virginia. Perhaps the governor supported it quietly. I’m betting he didn’t. Either way, it seems he’s late to the party and that this fits his agenda now. 
To me, it feels like the governor can’t be troubled to do something unless it fits nicely on a podium sign. I’m sure there will be a new sign next week and “beautiful clean water” will go to storage until it’s relevant again.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: The League of RI Businesses made a play to sidestep campaign finance limits. Now, it’s game time.
description: Vanessa Lopez knew the odds were stacked against her. A first-time candidate going up against a three-term incumbent, Lopez realized she needed outside help to succeed in her Democratic primary challenge against Sen. Meghan Kallman for the District 15 seat representing Pawtucket and Providence.  “I have no one in my corner, so I was like, […]
text:
The League of RI Businesses used multiple, related PACs to donate $10,000 to Democratic Senate District 19 candidate James Metivier. Checks from each PAC are displayed during a March 30 fundraiser for Metivier at Phantom Farms Brewing in Cumberland. (Courtesy of The League of RI Businesses).Vanessa Lopez knew the odds were stacked against her.
A first-time candidate going up against a three-term incumbent, Lopez realized she needed outside help to succeed in her Democratic primary challenge against Sen. Meghan Kallman for the District 15 seat representing Pawtucket and Providence. 
“I have no one in my corner, so I was like, ‘how the heck am I going to do this,’” Lopez, 37, said in an interview. 
Enter The League of RI Businesses. The political group born out of a gun rights campaign was recruiting state legislative candidates to fill open seats and challenge incumbents whose records did not align with its “pro-business” platform. And, under an unprecedented maneuver to create 40 political action committees — one for each city and town plus a statewide organization — The League advertised up to $1 million in donations per year per endorsed candidate, circumventing state campaign finance laws that cap annual donations at $2,000 per candidate. 
No one has received a seven-figure donation from The League yet. But the execution of its multi-PAC strategy is coming into play for a handful of its chosen candidates, including Lopez.
A $10,000 cash infusion, divided into five, equal $2,000 donations from League PACs, was transferred to Lopez’ campaign account on March 18, according to campaign reports submitted to the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Lopez is also fundraising on her own — reporting $1,800 in donations in the second quarter — but the bulk of her $10,218 campaign balance as of June 30 comes from The League.
“This actually gives me a chance to play the game,” said Lopez, a self-employed videographer and graphic designer. “If I didn’t have the resources, even if I had the good ideas, I wouldn’t be able to compete.”
The loophole has already been employed by seasoned political strategists to a much lesser, and less vocal degree. Amica, Bally’s Corp., and the state teachers’ union all have two PACs apiece, according to state campaign finance data. The Providence firefighters union has four PACS. The union representing local and state government and public school workers has five PACS. 
“It’s a legitimate tool,” said David Levesque, cofounder of The League and the organizer of all 40 PACs. “If people don’t like the law, change the law.”
Which is what good government groups tried to do during the 2026 legislative session. The pair of bills backed by Common Cause Rhode Island and the Rhode Island Board of Elections sought to apply the existing, $2,000 donation limits to multiple political action committees when controlled by the same person or group — replicating the rules in place for federal elections. The bills failed to advance out of committee in both chambers. 
The League of RI Businesses is encouraging anonymous donations to its 501(c)4 and political action committees. State law lets donors who contribute less than $200 per candidate or organization remain anonymous. (Graphic courtesy of The League of RI Businesses)
Incognito mode 
The League lined up a 23-candidate roster and built its cash reserves, openly encouraging donations of up to $9,900. A $9,900 contribution split between 40 PACs, with a 20% cut for the 501(c)4, comes out to $198 per PAC — just below the $200 limit that lets donors remain anonymous in campaign finance reports, under state law.
“As soon as you say who you’re going to vote for, there’s somebody that doesn’t like that person, and then all of a sudden, you lost the contract, or your neighbor is mad,” said Levesque, a Narragansett resident who owns Brewed Awakenings coffee houses.   
The statewide PAC — one of the 40 — has raised nearly $60,000 since fundraising began in May 2025. Roughly 10% comes from under $200, anonymous donations.
Over the same time period, the organization has spent nearly $100,000. Half of that, $50,000, was funneled to five League-endorsed candidates who are running Democratic legislative primaries: Lopez; Mark Mesrobian, the Democratic challenger in Senate District 36; James Metivier, the Democratic challenger in Senate District 19; Leah Boisclair, the Democratic challenger in House District 36; and Kevin Hoyle, one of two Democrats in the primary for the open House District 32 seat. All but Hoyle are running against incumbent Democratic legislators.
“We’re looking at races we think are winnable,” Levesque explained. “If we can win these five races, that would really change the course of the state of Rhode Island.”



Quotation







This actually gives me a chance to play the game. If I didn’t have the resources, even if I had the good ideas, I wouldn’t be able to compete.


– Senate District 15 candidate Vanessa Lopez on campaign contributions from The League of RI Businesses


Kallman, the incumbent facing Lopez in Senate District 15, is a progressive Democrat whose work on restrictions on federal immigration authorities rankled Levesque.
“She spends more time out of the district than in the district, going to Minnesota to talk about ICE,” Levesque said. 
Kallman, along with two other Democratic lawmakers, spent two days in Minneapolis in January, invited to participate in a nonprofit conference meant to draw upon the lessons learned from interactions between federal immigration authorities and people in Minnesota. Three people were shot by ICE agents in and around Minneapolis in January 2025, two of whom died.
Kallman dismissed Levesque’s criticisms about her travels as “nonsense,” while defending her record on supporting protections for Rhode Islanders in interactions with immigration authorities.
“My focus on ICE is absolutely an indicator of what’s important in people’s lives right now,” Kallman, 42, a professor at the University of Massachusetts Boston, said. “Rhode Island has a really important job in protecting our neighbors. I am very proud I am a member of the General Assembly that continues to do that.”
Lopez, who is of Cape Verdean and Puerto Rican descent, did not comment on Kallman’s stance on immigration. A self-described “common-sense candidate,” her website names housing, healthcare and education as top priorities — all topics Kallman has also addressed during her time on Smith Hill. But their proposed solutions differ: Lopez denounces rent stabilization for its effect on landlords, while Kallman has championed stronger protections for renters. Lopez denounced the millionaire’s tax included in the fiscal 2027 budget which she believes will drive out employers and jobs, while Kallman advocates for an even more wide sweeping set of taxes on top earners. Lopez also opposed the assault-style weapons ban approved by lawmakers, including Kallman, in 2025, framing her stance as a matter of self-defense.
The League of RI Businesses organized a fundraiser wine tasting at Gasbarro’s Wines on Federal Hill in Providence on Wednesday, Nov. 19, 2025. From left, John Loughlin, a Republican candidate for lieutenant governor; Laura Turini, a Democratic candidate for state Senate District 35; David Levesque, co-founder of The League; Leah Boisclair, a Democratic candidate for House District 36; and Mark Mesrobian, a Democratic candidate for Senate District 36. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Democrats, divided 
Ideological differences characterize other League-backed candidates and their Democratic primary opponents.
Mesrobian, a Narragansett entrepreneur who is challenging Sen. Alana DiMario in the primary for the Senate seat spanning North Kingstown and Narragansett, espouses a business-centric platform focused on cutting taxes and red tape. Mesrobian received $10,500 from The League through six of its PACs in November and December.
Cumberland Town Councilor James Metivier, challenging Pearson in the Democratic primary for the Senate District 19 seat spanning parts of Cumberland and Lincoln, stresses the need to curtail state spending. Metivier received $10,000 from five of  The League’s PACs on March 30. 
Metivier and Mesrobian each declined to comment on criticism about The League’s campaign finance strategy because they did not know enough about it.
Metivier, 60, a retired IT manager for Amica Mutual Insurance Co., noted he has not spent any of The League’s donations, though he is likely to on campaign mailers. He raised $1,400 in donations from individuals in the second quarter of the year, and has $27,800 cash on hand.
Mesrobian, 58, general manager of members-only Bonnet Shore Beach Club, received $36,000 in donations during the the three-month period that ended June 30, He has over $107,000 cash on hand — more than double the $44,000 balance of DiMario, who raised $14,000 in the second quarter.
“Their contribution is not really that significant to me,” Mesrobian said of The League’s donations. 
It is for Kevin Hoyle. The first-time candidate for the open House District 32 seat representing North Kingstown raised $125 in the second quarter. But he has $66,000 in his account, thanks to a $10,000 series of PAC donations from The League in March, and a $50,000 personal loan. 
“You can’t bitch about $10,000,” said Hoyle. “The nice thing is, there’s no strings attached. It’s not like I am being told I have to vote this way or that to take the money.”
A retired entrepreneur who went back to school for a master’s degree in law studies after selling his software development company because he was “bored,” Hoyle, 67, is running against Robert Craven Jr. for the seat formerly held by Craven Jr.’s father. 
Neither has held elected office, but Hoyle framed himself as the underdog, challenging an incumbent name with political ties. Craven Jr., 32, who works as policy director for the Rhode Island General Treasurer’s office, sees Hoyle’s financial boost from The League as a philosophical problem rather than a practical one. He’s confident he can win on his own record and merits.
But, “As someone vying for the public trust in running for office, I think candidates should value transparency,” Craven Jr. said. “We have campaign finance laws to make sure we know where money is going in politics.”
Kallman, Pearson, DiMario expressed similar concerns with The League’s strategy.
“If their donors are embarrassed enough about what they’re up to, maybe they should reconsider,” Kallman said.
Unintended consequences 
Kallman and DiMario were among the 14 senators who voted against a 2023 bill that became law without the governor’s signature raising campaign contribution limits from $1,000 to $2,000 per year, while upping the threshold for donations to remain anonymous from $100 to $200.
“I think it should be the strength of candidates’ ideas rather than how much money they can put in to getting their name out there,” DiMario said.
Pearson, then-Senate Majority Leader, voted for the bill, but said it was never intended to be used the way The League has done.
“We need to close that loophole,” Pearson, 38, a Citizens Bank executive, said.



Quotation







As someone vying for the public trust in running for office, I think candidates should value transparency. We have campaign finance laws to make sure we know where money is going in politics.


– Robert Craven Jr., a Democrat running for the open House District 32 seat in North Kingstown


A dozen sitting state legislators, mostly Democrats, have received donations from The League’s PACs within the last year, though none were more than $2,000 per candidate per calendar year. 
Rep. Marie Hopkins, a first-term Warwick Republican, received the most: $2,000 in December plus $1,000 and a $800 in-kind donation in March. Deputy House Majority Leader Thomas Noret, a Coventry Democrat, received $400 while Senate Minority Whip David Tikoian received $250. Tikoian, a North Smithfield Democrat, also donated $1,250 to The League’s PACs and $250 to Mesrobian in 2025, according to his campaign finance reports.
John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island, hopes The League’s unabashed application of state campaign finance rules will spur state lawmakers to restrict campaign donations by related PACs in the 2027 session. DiMario has already committed to reintroduce the bill next year.
Second-quarter campaign reports from The League PACs include the following description below each anonymous donation: “Tandem donations from individuals in RI that don’t want the Crazies to target them. :)”
“It certainly helps our case that they’re rubbing the public’s nose in it,” Marion said. “It’s immature and unprofessional and not smart politically.”
Thornton also clocked the comments on The League’s campaign reports but said there wasn’t anything he could do.
“As long as they’re complying with disclosure requirements and the limitations on contributions, we don’t have jurisdiction,” Thornton said.
But, he continued, “I do think this is an area of the law that needs to be tightened.” 
Early voting begins on Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado history rhymes
description: Daily life in early Colorado history can seem alien to modern observers.  In 1876, the year of statehood, it could take weeks for mail to arrive in Breckenridge, then a hamlet of 250 people that was accessible by wagon road. Denver’s daily newspaper contained numerous items about who in town had gone on vacation and […]
text:
A locomotive on the Atchison, Topeka, & Santa Fe Railroad in southern Colorado is pictured in this 1880s photograph. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, MCC-3176)Daily life in early Colorado history can seem alien to modern observers. 
In 1876, the year of statehood, it could take weeks for mail to arrive in Breckenridge, then a hamlet of 250 people that was accessible by wagon road. Denver’s daily newspaper contained numerous items about who in town had gone on vacation and who had arrived to visit. Beer was 10 cents a glass. Needless to say, there was no screen time.
Click the image to see Newsline’s special reporting project on 150 years of Colorado statehood.
But in other ways, 15 decades of events affirms the adage about how history doesn’t repeat, it rhymes.
Newsline this year, as part of Colorado at 150, is publishing stories about the Colorado of 1876, and it recently completed a special reporting series, Fifty for 150, comprising 50 stories about events that helped define Colorado since the proclamation of its statehood. Part of what makes these articles fascinating is how different life used to be, but they also recount episodes that resonate hauntingly with modern times.
Colorado is the site of several infamous mass shootings, including those that occurred at Columbine High School, an Aurora movie theater, and the Club Q nightclub in Colorado Springs. Gun violence prevention is a perennial topic at the Legislature, and deadly shootings are up in Denver this year. But the state has a long history of gun violence, a report by Chase Woodruff revealed. 
“Between 1862 and 1872, research has estimated, the homicide rate in Colorado’s Central City averaged 68 per 100,000 residents per year — a higher rate of deadly violence than plagues even the most dangerous U.S. cities today,” Woodruff wrote. In the American West, he wrote, “Shootings by law enforcement officers were common, as were acts of quasi- or extrajudicial violence by sheriff’s posses or other vigilante groups.”
In 1870s Colorado, a populist movement developed against railroad corporations, which through lobbying and bribery shielded themselves from government interference and established the template of Gilded Age inequality and corruption. Swap out railroad barons for tech oligarchs and you’ve got a modern echo of that former dominance, as today’s grassroots backlash to toxic wealth, as well as timidity before it, resembles the varied response to corporate magnates of the late 19th century.
A recurring theme throughout Colorado history is the mistreatment of vulnerable people and communities. The most extreme example of this kind of abuse involves the Ute people and the government’s egregious betrayal of them. An 1868 treaty promised them “absolute and undisturbed use and occupation” of most of the Western Slope, but the U.S. government broke that promise four years later as gold and silver prospectors began to trespass in the region, which is thought to have sustained the Utes and ancestor cultures for as many as 13,000 years. Today, Ute tribes occupy two small reservations in southwestern Colorado.
An 1874 photograph taken in Washington, D.C., during a visit by a delegation of Utes from Colorado. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-19251)
In 1880, a white mob attacked Chinese residents in Denver and burned and raided most of their businesses. The police did little to stop this mass act of bigotry.
During World War II, Colorado was the site of an incarceration camp for Japanese Americans who were falsely suspected of disloyalty and forcibly removed from their homes. The camp in Granada held more than 7,000 people. 
In one of the most astonishing moments of state history, Gov. Edwin “Big Ed” Johnson in 1936, during the Great Depression, deployed National Guard troops to the border with New Mexico to turn back “indigent” people. The move came during a time when many in Colorado scapegoated Mexicans for economic stress.
Sound familiar? This and other instances of discrimination prefigured the immigration enforcement horrors unleashed by the Trump administration. Most Coloradans oppose the mass deportations carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, but too many leaders in the state have behaved with the kind of complicity and cowardice that has always been necessary for government discrimination to occur and which is always condemned by subsequent generations.
As it happens, ICE’s history of harassing Coloradans goes back to its earliest years. In 2006, it launched the largest instance of workplace immigration enforcement in U.S. history. One of the sites targeted in the operation was a meatpacking plant in Greeley.  
The Fifty for 150 series also highlights people and moments in which Coloradans can take pride, such as a Boulder County clerk’s watershed actions to advance LGBTQ+ rights, a governor’s intervention on behalf of striking miners in 1894, the passage of a civil rights law in 1895, and Chicano Movement leadership in the 1960s.
In every case, the verses of history have something to say today, as we inscribe fresh lines that future Coloradans will read as new rhymes.
