name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo rallies with Trump, defends taking care of billionaires
description: Any doubt about Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo’s allegiance to President Donald Trump was put to rest Wednesday as they appeared on stage together at a rally in Las Vegas. Lombardo, a first-term Republican governor up for re-election this year, was criticized for not attending a Trump rally earlier this year in April. At that time, […]
text:
“He has always taken my phone call,” Gov. Joe Lombardo said of President Donald Trump at a rally in Las Vegas on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Any doubt about Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo’s allegiance to President Donald Trump was put to rest Wednesday as they appeared on stage together at a rally in Las Vegas.
Lombardo, a first-term Republican governor up for re-election this year, was criticized for not attending a Trump rally earlier this year in April. At that time, Lombardo’s campaign said he would be meeting with Trump privately, though his staff confirmed later the two did not meet. Lombardo’s absence fueled political analyses that Lombardo wants to distance himself from Trump and his economic policies without losing the MAGA base.
But Lombardo appeared enthusiastic while on stage during a campaign-style rally at Red Rock Casino in Las Vegas on Wednesday – first as one of several opening speakers before Trump’s arrival, then again toward the end of the president’s hour-long speech when he was invited up.
Lombardo used his time on stage to defend Trump for “taking care of his billionaire friends.”
“Quite often when the press and the media runs him down, they think about, you know, he’s taking care of his billionaire friends,” Lombardo said. “Those billionaire friends provide jobs. Unless you take care of them, those jobs are absent.”
He continued, “The government does not have the ability to hand out infinite amounts of money. That’s not how economies work. That’s why they’re pushing socialism so hard.”
Lombardo did not name drop any billionaires in his brief comment. But Trump directly addressed two that he said were in attendance: Frank Fertitta, the CEO and chairman of Red Rocks Resorts (the parent company of Station Casinos), and Phil Ruffin, the owner of Treasure Island. Trump also cracked a joke about Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, being mad about an anti-electric vehicle policy.
Frank Fertitta, his brother Lorenzo Fertitta, and companies have donated several millions of dollars to Lombardo’s gubernatorial campaign. Another billionaire, Robert Bigelow, the owner of Budget Suites, heavily bankrolled Lombardo’s successful 2022 gubernatorial campaign.
Lombardo this election season has a massive fundraising advantage, in large part to donations from billionaires and their corporations.
In his on-stage comments before Trump’s arrival, Lombardo told the crowd that he and the president have had “productive conversations.”
“He has always taken my phone call,” Lombardo said. “He’s always taken my phone call, and that’s the way the partnership at the state level needs to be with at the federal level.”
The governor said he “spoke directly” to Trump about the potential loss of a thousand  solar industry jobs and that Trump took action because of it.
On his end, Trump briefly praised Lombardo, saying he’s “doing a great job.”
“Will you please win by a big number?” he joked.
Lombardo is facing Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford this November. Lombardo referenced Ford, painting him as a radical who wants to raise taxes, embraces democratic socialist policies and is aligned with California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Ford on Wednesday called Lombardo “a human doormat for Trump.”
“Trump is in Las Vegas campaigning with Joe Lombardo and together they’re sharing a stage and trying to gaslight voters about the reality of the Lombardo-Trump economy raising costs on Nevadans,” Ford said in a statement. “Lombardo and Trump have spent their tenure catering to billionaires who are raising costs on Nevadans instead of lowering costs for working families.”
The Nevada State Democratic Party ahead of Trump’s visit unveiled billboards attacking Lombardo’s relationship with Trump. The Culinary Union held a press event to highlight what they and others have dubbed “the Trump slump.”
“Trump’s tariffs, chaotic immigration and mass deportation policy, the war in Iran, and high grocery and gas prices are hurting working families and driving away the Canadian, Mexican, Southern California, and international tourism Nevada depends on,” said Ted Pappageorge, secretary-treasurer for the Culinary Union, in a statement Wednesday.
Gallup surveys from July suggest “Americans remain broadly pessimistic about the economy.” Here in Nevada, tourism numbers remain sluggish.
But Trump acknowledged none of that, instead saying that the economy was booming and families thriving. He highlighted his “no tax on tips” policy, which he claims a beautiful waitress suggested to him while serving him dinner before a Las Vegas rally in 2024. That provision, along with “no tax on overtime” and “no tax on social security” policies, were passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year.
Trump brought on stage with him a Las Vegas family of four, which included two kids with “Trump accounts,” tax-advantaged accounts seeded with $1,000 from the federal government. He also brought up a Teamsters Local 631 member who came on stage and said he’d lost a lot during a recent divorce but his tax refund was large enough he could buy a house.
 Others in attendance

In addition to inviting Lombardo on stage with him, Trump gave shoutouts to numerous Republicans who will be on the ballot this November, including attorney general candidate Adriana Fralick Guzman, secretary of state candidate Jim Marchant, Congressional District 2 candidate David Flippo, Congressional District 3 candidate Marty O’Donnell, and Congressional  District 1 candidate Carrie Buck. All attended the rally.
Cody Whipple, the Republican nominee for Congressional District 4, was at the rally but was not mentioned. Whipple has not been endorsed by Trump, as the others have.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Instead of installing more EV chargers, Florida DOT dreams of flying cars
description: I watched a lot of cartoons as a kid. None was more visually stunning than “The Jetsons.” It focused on a family coping with life in a streamlined future filled with snazzy gadgets. George Jetson, for instance, commutes to work in a flying car that’s quieter than your average vacuum cleaner. When he lands, George […]
text:
The Skytrax facility in Auburndale is where the Florida DOT plans to test its "flying car" technology — if it ever gets any. (Photo via FDOT)I watched a lot of cartoons as a kid. None was more visually stunning than “The Jetsons.” It focused on a family coping with life in a streamlined future filled with snazzy gadgets.
George Jetson, for instance, commutes to work in a flying car that’s quieter than your average vacuum cleaner. When he lands, George folds his vehicle up into a briefcase he then carries into his office. No need for roads OR parking!
Jared Perdue via FDOT
Apparently, Gov. Ron DeSantis and his Department of Transportation secretary, Jared Perdue, fell under the spell of this cartoon, too. Now they want to make it real using millions in federal funding intended for a different purpose.
The Miami Herald broke the story over the weekend. The headline said, “Florida wants to use cash meant for electric car chargers on flying cars instead.”
There’s just one problem with this plan: Flying cars do not exist.
For years the Florida DOT has been sitting on $197 million in federal grant money that it was supposed to spend on new chargers for electric cars and trucks. Now, the Herald says, the DOT has plans to steer (sorry!) that money to something bizarre. It wants to “build what it calls an ‘Aerial Highway Network’ that includes places the futuristic aircraft can charge, take off, and land.”
In the secret nine-page plan that the Herald got hold of, the DOT says the state is taking “a bold step in building an entirely new mode of transportation.” My hard-headed Cracker forebears would call this “buying a pig in a poke” — throwing money at something that’s not real.
“The Florida Department of Transportation will not waste taxpayer dollars and spend it on everyday passenger vehicles,” the DOT wrote in its flying-cars-are-cool report.
Of course, that’s exactly what the DOT promised the federal government the agency WOULD do with that money. It promised to spend it on chargers needed for the growing number of everyday electric vehicles.
The agency never mentioned that it would instead blow that cash on some cockamamie contraption conjured up by a 1960s Hanna-Barbera cartoon. They never brought up their plans to build 32 landing pads across the state and use state funds to supplement the federal grant.
I suspect DeSantis and Perdue know this looks bad. They’ve been trying for months to hide the DOT document from the public.
As the Herald explained, “The state’s flying-car pivot only came to light after the Miami Herald filed a records request in January, which went unfulfilled until the newspaper’s lawyer got involved.”
Stephen A. Smith via SACE
“It’s a complete misappropriation of these funds,” said Stephen A. Smith, executive director of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. “This just shows how of touch their decision-making is.”
Smith suspects he knows who the beneficiaries will be. It’s not the average Florida driver. Instead, he said, “This is a giveaway to the people who need it the least.”
 Roads vs. politics
The millions of taxpayer dollars at stake here came from one of the worst-named bills ever considered by Congress.
The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which passed in 2021, included language to expand the nation’s fast-charging network for electric cars and trucks. The provision called for adding more chargers within a mile of all interstate highways. That would help EV drivers travel greater distances without getting stranded.
It wasn’t intended as a total government giveaway. Businesses that received the funding, such as Buc-ees and Wawa, would get enough to cover about 80% of the costs. They would be required to put up the other 20%.
Florida’s DOT submitted a plan for spending the money properly, and the federal government approved it. After all, drivers in Florida have really fallen in love with EVs.
A report last year noted that Florida leads all other Southeastern states in the number of EVs sold — roughly half a million in 2024. This is a good thing.
It’s not just that EVs are cleaner for the air and offer a way to combat that thing about the climate that DeSantis doesn’t want us to mention. Given the soaring cost of gas since the start of the Iran War, you can understand why drivers might prefer vehicles that don’t require a second mortgage to fill the tank.
Leighanne Boone with her Tesla, via subject
“Every time the gas prices go up, I say thank you that my price is always the same,” said Leighanne Boone of the Sustainable Tallahassee Ride Electric Club. “I plug in every night.”
What Florida lacks is sufficient public places for rapid charging on the road. As the Herald pointed out, “Florida boasts the second-highest number of EVs in the country but still falls behind the national average on chargers per vehicle.”
“We definitely need more charging infrastructure,” Boone told me. Range anxiety is a deterrent for potential buyers, she explained. Greater availability “will encourage the average driver to go electric.”
The website the Florida DOT put up, via screen grab
Instead of spending the money for more chargers the way it promised, the DOT put it aside. Meanwhile, the agency set up a website called “Roads Are Not For Politics.” Contrary to its name, the site features a list of culture-war complaints, such as “COVID tyranny.” It also offers off-base criticism of EVs.
In the DOT press release about this (which has since been removed), DeSantis said, “We listen to Floridians and meet their needs. Roads are not for politics.”
Except they weren’t listening to Floridians OR meeting their needs. They were playing politics. And now they want to go back on their word to the feds and spend the money on something that hasn’t been built yet.
And I mean spending a LOT. The DOT’s secret plan estimates that each of the 32 landing pads would cost about $5.6 million to build. That’s after going through testing at the DOT’s 775-acre Auburndale test track, the Suntrax Center.
The plan calls for building these landing pads near airports, luxury apartment buildings, and golf courses. All that’s missing is a listing of such hoity-toity locations as Miami’s Indian Creek Island, aka the “Billionaires’ Bunker,” and the Ocean Reef Club in North Key Largo.
Meanwhile, the growing number of EV drivers have to keep scanning the exit ramps and hope they spot a place to pull over and charge.
“It’s disappointing,” Boone said.
 Former trailblazer
I watched a Florida DOT video touting this flying car foofaraw, complete with AI mockups of what they might look like. The video didn’t mention where the money would come from, just how groovy it would be.
“It’s an opportunity to introduce a new mode of transportation to the world,” Perdue said, as giddy as Olivia Newton-John soaring into the clouds in John Travolta’s flying car at the end of “Grease.”
Florida once fancied itself as a trailblazer in aviation.
Tony Jannus prepares for takeoff in 1914, via State Library and Archives of Florida.
In 1914, Tony Jannus flew a local politician from St. Petersburg to Tampa via seaplane, inaugurating the first regular commercial airline service in the nation. The ticket cost $400 and the ride lasted 22 minutes. No word on whether the airline lost the passenger’s luggage.
That same year, the Navy established its first flight training base in Pensacola. It’s still there. The Blue Angels stunt flying team is based at NAS Pensacola and recently sent hats, tents, and chairs flying during a too-low practice run over the beach.
So perhaps it makes sense that the DOT’s looking to the skies, now that our roads are so consistently clogged. It’s as if the agency is giving up on ever freeing our asphalt from those frustrating traffic jams.
“As Florida’s surface transportation networks reach capacity, and right of way is constrained,” it says, “additional modes of transportation are required to maintain economic development goals as well as quality of life for residents and visitors.”
People — especially people stuck in traffic — have been dreaming of taking off in flying cars for years. But we’re still waiting for the Jetsons’ car-briefcase combo.
“NASA had an air taxi program they were working on back in the 1980s,” recalled David King of Arizona State University, a transportation planning expert. So far, the only place you can see any “air taxis” is in the Bruce Willis science-fiction movie “The Fifth Element.”
 Glorified helicopters
I had a lengthy conversation with King, who displayed an encyclopedic knowledge of the “flying car” phenomenon. It’s been a hot topic in Arizona in recent years, he said, and now has begun showing up in other states.
David King via ASU.
“There’s a lot of enthusiasm about this,” he told me. “Strangely, it’s become a partisan Issue. It’s been seized on by people who think government shouldn’t be involved in mass transit, but it’s all about an unproven technology that, as of August 2026, is not currently available.”
While flying cars sound good on paper, King said, there are lots of details still to be worked out.  For one thing, he said, forget about them relieving highway congestion.
The perpetually-under-construction Interstate 4, for instance, draws 180,000 to 200,000 vehicles a day. If and when the flying taxis DO appear, they can’t carry much, he said. Because of the weight of the battery, they can carry no more than three passengers and one pilot.
All the trucks have to keep their tires on the ground. These flying cars can’t carry freight the way 18-wheelers do.
You won’t travel far in your glorified helicopter, King said. Because the batteries are depleted after 40 minutes, “they just won’t stay in the air too long.”
Traveling to and from the 32 launch pads will still require use of land vehicles, he pointed out. And you may have to travel quite a ways because of the Federal Aviation Administration.
“As of now, the FAA will not approve any operations over populated areas,” King told me. “You can’t just put one of these things in the air and start flying.”
King used a transportation-related metaphor to describe the Florida DOT’s secretly swiping EV money to use for flying cars: “They’re putting the cart before the horse.”
Flying car concept from DOT video via screen grab.
 Try a trebuchet
This kind of creative accounting has been a hallmark of the DeSantis administration.
I’m not just talking about the Hope Florida scandal. You remember that one — $10 million from a Medicaid settlement wound up in the hands of political consultants hired to counter the drive to legalize weed.
Remember, too, how DeSantis took $20 million from a disaster relief fund designed to cope with hurricane damage and instead used it to build a destructive immigrant detention camp in the Everglades. A lot of the no-bid contracts went to his donors, too.
Speaking of donors, don’t forget how he cajoled the Cabinet into spending $83 million from the Florida Wildlife Corridor fund on four acres of land in Destin that was nowhere near the wildlife corridor. The seller just happened to be one of his campaign contributors, making this transaction look more like a payback than a payment.
Usually when I call the governor’s office seeking a comment on one of these scandals, his spokespeople don’t even acknowledge receiving the inquiry. But this time, to my surprise, I got an immediate reply.
One of the governor’s spokespeople said he would refer my question to Perdue of DOT. And he did, too. I never got a response from Perdue’s people. Maybe they’re standing on a launch pad in Auburndale, waiting for George Jetson to pick them up for work.
Because I am at heart a problem-solver, I have a proposal for DeSantis and Perdue. It’s based on something that happened when my kids were in Boy Scouts.
A couple of teenage Scouts built a medieval siege engine called a “trebuchet.” It’s basically a fancy catapult. The boys would roll it out at various events and use it to hurl things like a Barney the Dinosaur toy a long distance.
I think the DOT should spend $1 million of its EV funds to build at Skytrax the most impressive trebuchet ever constructed. DeSantis and Perdue can put a Hot Wheels toy in the pouch. DOT employees can hurl the payload as far as possible and claim they finally created a flying car.
Then they can spend the remaining $196 million on what they SHOULD have spent it on in the first place.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Climate change doesn’t care if you believe in it. But CT is paying the price
description: Sooner or later, more people will be forced to confront the reality that climate change is not someone else’s problem, it is everyone’s problem.
text:
Every day, it seems, brings another headline about an extreme weather event. A wildfire destroys homes. A heat wave shatters temperature records. Floodwaters overwhelm communities. A hurricane grows stronger and more destructive. We have become accustomed to scrolling past these disasters, watching them unfold on the news and then moving on with our day. 
None of this is normal.
The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record. Europe just saw its worst heat wave in recorded history that set all time heat records and killed more than 10,000 people, and caused the worst heat stress ever in half of the continent’s largest cities.
In both the United States and Canada, this summer’s heat and drought is driving longer and more intense wildfire seasons, including the more than 800 wildfires across Canada and northern Minnesota that caused dangerous levels of ozone and air pollution. In Connecticut Air Quality Index levels hit over 200 for days, which is considered hazardous.
 Climate change is no longer a distant threat. It is today’s reality. 
 As Connecticut residents were breathing dirty smogged air in July, the climate misinformation grew. But the facts speak for themselves:   Climate   change, including increased heat, extended drought, and a thirsty atmosphere,   has been a key driver   in increasing the risk and extent of wildfires in the western United States during the last two decades.      Research shows that climate change is creating warmer, drier conditions that contribute to longer and more intense wildfire seasons. Rising temperatures and increased atmospheric drying caused by human-induced climate change have made forest vegetation and other fuels drier during the fire season, increasing the risk and severity of wildfires. 
 For decades, the oil and gas industry has perpetuated the fraud that natural gas is clean and a climate solution, despite knowing that it is a significant source of air pollution and a major contributor to climate change. 
 The gas industry knew as early as 1907 that methane gas was a source of respiratory problems when burned indoors, and by the 1950s it knew that gas caused problems in outdoor air.   Beginning in the 1960s, the oil and gas industry learned of another threat, emerging science showed that natural gas was a potentially significant contributor to methane in the atmosphere. 
 As fossil fuel companies and their representatives closely monitored scientific developments on methane, the chemical name for natural gas, they also learned that it was a potent greenhouse gas and damaging for the climate. The gas industry ignored these warnings and did everything they could to escape accountability while continuing to keep us reliant on this fossil fuel. 
 For some people, climate change remains an abstract debate, until the wildfire reaches their backyard, their home floods, or extreme heat threatens their health and livelihood. But climate change does not wait for people to believe in it. It does not care about political boundaries, state lines, or ideology. The impacts are already here, and sooner or later, more people will be forced to confront the reality that climate change is not someone else’s problem, it is everyone’s problem. 
Connecticut is not immune to climate change and our state has been facing the costly effect.
 While communities are paying the price of worsening climate disasters, Big Oil continues to rake in record profits. Families are paying more for energy, while communities are forced to bear the rising costs of wildfire smoke, extreme heat, flooding, and other climate impacts. The companies that helped fuel this crisis should not be allowed to continue profiting while the public pays the bill. When is enough enough? 
 Big Oil shouldn’t profit while our communities pay the cost. It’s time to   make polluters pay  .  
Julianna Larue is Chapter Organizer for Sierra Club Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Waterbury’s water main breaks: A century of aging infrastructure
description: The recent failures beneath Waterbury's streets were not isolated incidents but warnings from an aging infrastructure network.
text:
When another major water main broke beneath Tompkins Street on July 29, more than 5,100 homes and businesses across Waterbury lost running water. Residents in the Bunker Hill, Town Plot, and the Country Club neighborhoods were informed that they could be without service for days. 
At the same time, city crews worked around the clock to repair the damaged transmission main. Once repairs were completed, a second water-main break occurred beneath Tompkins Street, impacting more than 15,000 homes and businesses while under a boil-water advisory. 
For many residents, the disruption was frustrating but not surprising. After multiple major water emergencies in less than a year, a growing question has emerged:
Why does this keep happening?
The answer isn’t a lack of effort from city workers. Instead, it lies beneath the streets of the Brass City.
Waterbury’s water system dates back more than 150 years. The Waterbury Water Company was incorporated in 1859, and the city’s first municipal water system was approved in 1867. 
While the water system has expanded and has been modernized since then, portions of its infrastructure that we’re seeing today were installed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Some transmission mains still in service date back to 1895, 1901, and 1905, while another 42-inch transmission main was installed in 1960. Many of these pipes have now exceeded their expected service lives.  
Age alone does not guarantee failure, but it rapidly increases the risk, and as it continues to age, we’re going to keep seeing more water main breaks across the city. Older cast-iron and prestressed concrete pipes become more susceptible to corrosion, shifting soil, freezing temperatures, increased water pressure, and decades of wear and tear. As these materials weaken, they can trigger catastrophic breaks capable of disrupting water service for entire sections of the city, like we’re seeing today.
In September 2025, a 30-inch transmission main on Huntingdon Avenue failed after an aging air-relief device malfunctioned. The incident led to widespread service interruptions and a boil-water advisory that remained in effect until laboratory testing confirmed the water was safe. During repairs, crews also discovered that an aging isolation valve could no longer be completely closed, complicating the emergency response.
Only months later, Waterbury experienced one of the most significant infrastructure failures in its history. In December 2025, a leak from a deteriorating 10-inch pipe installed in 1901 washed away the soil supporting a nearby 36-inch transmission main on Thomaston Avenue. Eventually, the larger pipe collapsed, leaving nearly 100,000 residents in Waterbury, Watertown, and Wolcott without water for several days. Schools closed, businesses shut down, bottled water distribution sites were established across the city, and the Connecticut National Guard assisted local emergency operations. 

Water pours from a water main break on Thomaston Avenue in Waterbury on Dec 13, 2025 Credit: Mark Pazniokas / CT Mirror

City officials announced that emergency repairs, overtime, bottled water distribution, and related response efforts cost millions of dollars, claiming investments have been made to strengthen the system. Including rehabilitation of two miles of Waterbury’s 42-inch transmission main through a slip-lining project completed in early 2026. The city has also fast-tracked work on valve replacements, pump upgrades, and system modernization..
These projects are encouraging, but they should represent the beginning, not the end, of Waterbury’s infrastructure strategy.
Instead of waiting for another major break, the city should be investing in a long-term pipe replacement program. Every transmission main should be evaluated according to its age, material, break history, and importance to the overall water system. The oldest transmission lines, specifically those installed before World War I, should receive priority for replacement before they fail.
Funding remains the greatest challenge, but it is not an impossible one. Waterbury has already included $18 million in Bureau of Water capital improvements within its current five-year Capital Improvement Plan, while other projects have been proposed through Connecticut’s Drinking Water State Revolving Fund. Continued pursuit of state and federal infrastructure grants will be crucial if the city hopes to replace aging mains without placing the entire financial burden on ratepayers.
Water main breaks are often described as emergencies, but in reality, they are symptoms of a much larger problem. The recent failures beneath Huntingdon Avenue, Thomaston Avenue, and now Tompkins Street were not isolated incidents; they were warnings from an aging infrastructure network that has served Waterbury for generations.
The city’s water system helped build Waterbury into the community it is today. Now, more than a century later, Waterbury faces a choice: Continue short-term responses to emergencies or make the investments necessary to rebuild the system before the next major break occurs.
If recent history has shown anything, it is that replacing aging infrastructure before it fails will almost certainly cost less than repairing it after yet another disaster strikes, and that next disaster is certain if we don’t do something about our water system infrastructure now.
Tavares Anderson lives in Waterbury.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: New districts scramble candidate qualifying for Louisiana’s US House races
description: Louisiana’s current U.S. House races might appear similar to those underway just three months ago before the May 16 congressional primary was canceled, but they’re not.
text:
Those hoping to run for Congress in Louisiana are qualifying for office this week. (Photo by Matthew Perschall for Louisiana Illuminator)New political districts. New candidates. New election date. 
Louisiana’s current U.S. House races might appear similar to those underway just three months ago before the May 16 congressional primary was canceled, but they’re not. 

Gov. Jeff Landry and state lawmakers dramatically altered Louisiana’s congressional district boundaries after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in a landmark redistricting case allowed them to eliminate one of the state’s two majority-Black seats. Now, candidates who were originally running in the 5th District centered in Northeast Louisiana are competing in the 6th District, which runs down to Lafourche Parish. 
For example, two Republican candidates, state Rep. Mike Echols of Monroe and state Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge, were originally opponents in the 5th District race. But the congressional map reworking put Edmonds’ house in the 6th District, so they are no longer running against each other. 
“With the twists and turns of this race, we’ve added some additional parishes [to the 5th District], which has been extraordinary,” Echols said shortly after qualifying Wednesday. 
The political district changes might also put the two candidates with the most campaign cash on hand in different races. 

Echols and state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, have $1 million and $2 million in campaign funding in the bank, respectively. That’s at least three times more than any other candidate considering a run in either race, according to federal campaign finance reports filed in July. 
Until the middle of May, the two men were running against each other in the 5th District, but it’s thought that Miguez might now join the 6th District race. The Baton Rouge house Miguez bought in March flipped from the 5th to the 6th District in the latest congressional map revisions, making it easier for him to run against Edmonds. 
Miguez, who represents an Acadiana state Senate district outside the boundaries of both U.S. House seats, hasn’t clarified whether he’s still running for Congress and, if so, what district he will choose. He didn’t answer calls or text messages to his cell phone Wednesday. 

If Miguez does run, Edmonds said will be happy to take him on in the 6th District. With $323,000 in his campaign account, Edmonds has a fraction of Miguez’s money but a longer history in the area where he’s running. 
“I’m not new to this district,” Edmonds said after signing up to run for office Wednesday. “My family, my grandchildren, all are here, not 100 miles away.” 
The recent changes to the congressional district boundaries have brought at least two candidates into the 5th District race. State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, and state Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, signed up to run Wednesday. 

Both candidates had not considered running for Congress before the map change. Until the end of May, their homes had been in the 4th District, represented by U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Benton, who they wouldn’t want to challenge. 
Two lower-profile candidates have also been affected by the new map. 

Walter “Rocky” Beach of Gonzales, who’s not affiliated with a political party, signed up for the 2nd District race against incumbent U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, D-New Orleans.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

Beach said he lived in the 2nd District under the map used earlier this year but was drawn out of the district when the boundaries changed in May. Congressional candidates are not required to live in their districts, but it can make it harder for them to attract voter support. 
Michael Mebruer, a Republican running in the 6th District, said he was in the same position as Beach when he qualified Wednesday. His St. Francisville residence is in the 5th District, but he will now run in the 6th District because it includes Baton Rouge, where he said he feels more at home. 

Congressional candidates will also meet in an open “jungle” primary  Nov. 3, with all candidates competing against each other on one ballot. The May 15 election was supposed to be a closed partisan primary, where Democrats and Republicans were on two separate ballots. But the format changed when Gov. Jeff Landry issued an executive order to postpone those races after the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling in Callais v. Louisiana in April.
Several candidates who signed up to run for Congress Wednesday said they didn’t intend to alter the way they would campaign, even if the primary election format was different.

“So far it hasn’t changed much about the way I talk to people,” said Dan McKay, a Democrat from Bunkie running in the 5th District. 

Others said it means they need a broader message to appeal to voters other than members of their own political party.

“We’re sending mail to everybody now instead of just one party,” Echols said. 

Other candidates said shifting the U.S. House elections from May to November has been difficult for their campaigns in general. 

Lauren Jewett, a Metairie Democrat running against House Majority Leader Steve Scalise in the 1st District, said she had to collect a second round of signatures for her nominating petition to qualify as a candidate again. 
“The rules were changed in the middle of the game, and everyday voters and candidates like me — people without large teams of voters and lobbyists — were the ones left scrambling to figure out what district we now belong to,” Jewett said Wednesday. “This is not what democracy looks like.” 

Jewett and Conrad Cable of Farmerville, a Democrat running against Johnson in the 4th District, will also have to go through their party’s nominating process again in late August. Both had secured Democratic nominations ahead of the May election but now need to campaign for their party’s support a second time. 
Cable said he almost ended his election bid in May after the first primary was canceled. 

“It disenfranchised me to the point where I felt like giving up,” he said Wednesday. “Instead, I dug in my heels and we kept this campaign alive through grit and determination.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Leaderboard jostled in WA legislative races with latest vote tally
description: A second day of ballot counting didn’t go well for a former Washington state lawmaker pursuing a comeback, but it did for a Republican legislator seeking a second term. Across the state, margins grew and shrank in other closely watched contests with Wednesday’s tally. More changes will come until the primary results are final later […]
text:
The Washington state Capitol in Olympia. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)A second day of ballot counting didn’t go well for a former Washington state lawmaker pursuing a comeback, but it did for a Republican legislator seeking a second term.
Across the state, margins grew and shrank in other closely watched contests with Wednesday’s tally. More changes will come until the primary results are final later this month.
Freshman Rep. Brian Burnett, R-Wenatchee, moved ahead of Democrat Stacy Willoughby after trailing on election night in their duel in the 12th Legislative District.
Burnett, a former county sheriff, led Willoughby, a first-time candidate and financial services professional, by 108 votes. He had 50.1% to her 49.8% in the Republican-leaning district that stretches west from Chelan County to the city of Monroe in Snohomish County. Her advantage was 46 votes on Tuesday.
In the battle for the other House seat, two Republicans, Rep. Mike Steele and Adam James, received a combined 67% of votes cast. As of Wednesday, Steele and Democrat Maggie Adams will advance to the general election.
Meanwhile, ex-state representative Robert Sutherland, a conservative Republican, slipped to third place in the race to succeed retiring Rep. Carolyn Eslick in the 39th District.
Democrat Ida Keeley leads with 46.4%, followed by Republican Steve Ewing with 25.8% and Sutherland with 25.2%. Ewing trailed by 26 votes on Tuesday but moved in front by 148 on Wednesday. Sutherland is trying to return to the district he represented for two terms before getting unseated in 2022.
In Pierce County, Democrat Krista Perez expanded her advantage on Rep. Melanie Morgan, D-Parkland, in the 29th District.
Perez, who led by just five votes on election night, was ahead by 366 after Wednesday. She had 48.7% to Morgan’s 46%. As they are the only candidates, the two will face off in November.
Meanwhile, the race for the other House seat is a tight one. Democrats Joe Bushnell and Patrick Stickney are ahead, but less than 700 votes separate the top four candidates.
Bushnell has 22%, followed by Stickney with 20.5%, Democrat Natasha Laitila with 18.4% and Republican Darek Blum with 17.5%. Bushnell holds a 229-vote lead and is only 688 votes ahead of Blum.
In King County, Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, increased her lead on Redmond City Councilmember Jessica Forsythe in the 48th District after Wednesday’s count.
Walen had 50.9% to Forsythe’s 46.5% as the difference between them stood at 715, up from the 618-vote margin on Tuesday. They are the only candidates in the race and will meet in November.
Little changed in the 32nd District that straddles the border of Snohomish and King counties, where a Democrat state representative is trying to oust the incumbent Democrat senator.
Rep. Cindy Ryu widened her lead on Sen. Jesse Salomon in a battle of two established lawmakers. Ryu has 41.6% of the vote to Salomon’s 38.5%. Both will advance to the general election in this solid Democratic district.
In the contest to replace Ryu, Shoreline City Councilmember Keith Scully maintained the top position with 25.3% of the vote. Attorney Danica Noble is in second with 23.1%, followed by Republican Lisa Rezac with 20.6%
In Spokane County, only a few hundred votes separate a trio of candidates seeking to replace Democrat Rep. Timm Ormsby of Spokane, who is retiring after two decades representing the 3rd District.
Republican Natalie Poulson leads with 33.2%, followed by Democrats Pam Kohlmeier with 31.6% and Luc Jasmin III with 31.1%. Poulson held a 413-vote lead over Kohlmeier and only 551 votes separated her from Jasmin.
Ballot counting continues Thursday with counties facing an Aug. 18 deadline to certify results. The secretary of state will certify the 2026 primary election results by Aug. 21.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: US Senate candidates make final pitch to primary voters at Farmfest debate
description: MORGAN, REDWOOD COUNTY — If there’s one thing farmers can always agree on, it’s that times are tough. The four leading Democratic and Republican candidates for U.S. Senate acknowledged the tribulations facing farmers at the annual Farmfest, during a final debate on Wednesday before the Aug. 11 primary. Their assessments of the causes and cures […]
text:
From left, Rep. Angie Craig, Michelle Tafoya, and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, prepare for the candidate forum for U.S. Senate at Farmfest in Morgan, Minn., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)MORGAN, REDWOOD COUNTY — If there’s one thing farmers can always agree on, it’s that times are tough.
The four leading Democratic and Republican candidates for U.S. Senate acknowledged the tribulations facing farmers at the annual Farmfest, during a final debate on Wednesday before the Aug. 11 primary.
Their assessments of the causes and cures of agriculture’s ills diverged significantly, however.
U.S. Rep. Angie Craig, Democrat of the 2nd District, and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the DFL-endorsed candidate, blamed the Trump administration’s across-the-board tariffs and the war in Iran for causing costs to soar and demand to crater. They advocated for passing a full farm bill rather than the skinny version moving through Congress.
Republican candidate Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter, said overregulation was strangling farmers and that Trump’s trade conflicts would yield better deals down the road. Royce White, a former NBA player, said he wants to end farm subsidies and called the farm bill an example of “uniparty dominance.”
Although Republicans haven’t won a statewide office in two decades, many in the party see Tafoya’s Senate run as their best shot in years at ending their losing streak and foiling Democrats’ hopes of reclaiming control of Congress.
Yet they face the significant headwinds of running in the same party as a deeply unpopular president. While Trump has enjoyed strong support from farmers and rural voters overall, that support appears to be waning with persistent inflation and economic uncertainty.
Farmfest, the state’s premier agricultural expo, doubles as an important political stomping ground, where politicians try to court a crucial voting bloc perusing the latest seeds and agricultural machinery.
Adam Schwarze, Republican-endorsed candidate for US Senate, listens to the candidate forum he was excluded from due to low polling numbers at Farmfest in Morgan, Minn., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Adam Schwarze, the Republican-endorsed candidate, was conspicuously absent from the debate because he didn’t meet the polling threshold of 15% in an independent poll. In a July KSTP poll, just 5% of Republican voters said they supported Schwarze while 41% backed Tafoya and 10% supported White, who was down 5 percentage points from the previous month’s poll that qualified him for the debate.
Schwarze blasted the Farmfest organizers for excluding him, describing it in an interview with the Reformer as a ploy by the “D.C. apparatus” to tip the scales in favor of Tafoya. Schwarze issued a press release claiming the debate was canceled, but nevertheless watched it from a front-row seat with his supporters in campaign T-shirts.
Craig, Flanagan and Tafoya all said they supported allowing the year-round sale of E15 — gasoline with 15% ethanol — which would drive up demand for corn. White said only vaguely that “we have to deconstruct the administrative state.”
Craig boasted that she introduced the bill to permit E15 to be sold in the summer, which is prohibited because of smog concerns, and accused Trump of blocking its passage despite voicing support for it.
“The reason why we haven’t been able to get year-round E15 across the finish line is because the Trump administration is in the pocket of Big Oil,” Craig said. “They keep being Lucy with the football.”
Craig was able to show off the knowledge she’s developed as a member of the House Agriculture Committee, where she now serves as the ranking Democrat. She casually dropped in jargon like the need for a “12-title, five-year farm bill,” and decried the Trump administration’s cuts to “APHIS,” the acronym for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, whose importance is magnified with the rise of the New World screwworm.
She said Trump’s trade wars have forced farmers to accept government assistance to stay afloat amid economic turmoil and uncertainty.
“What we need is good farm policy, not ad hoc assistance,” Craig said.
Tafoya acknowledged the pain global trade wars were causing farmers but framed it as a necessary sacrifice to secure more favorable long-term trade agreements.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There should be short-term bridge assistance to farmers to get through those disruptions,” Tafoya said.
Tafoya blamed overregulation as the biggest impediment to farmers, and also hammered Democrats for the defrauding of social service programs — a topic Republicans aim to make the focus of the 2026 elections.
Trump’s push for mass deportation has hurt farmers, who rely on immigrant labor, though it remains popular among Republicans.
Craig and Flanagan both said they support providing a pathway to legal residency or citizenship to law-abiding workers in the country without authorization.
“I think we can have an immigration system where we have secure borders, but we also have an immigration system that is grounded in safety and dignity and humanity,” Flanagan said.
Flanagan also pointed to her biography — she’s the child of a single mother who used food stamps — to criticize the Trump administration for its cuts to the SNAP program, which is administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Tafoya said she supports expanding visas for guest workers under the bipartisan Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act though said she does not support “amnesty.” White said all people in the country without authorization must be deported.
White, who was the 2024 GOP Senate nominee, avoided getting near the weeds of farm policy and instead spoke to larger right-wing themes like “uniparty dominance,” mass deportation of “foreign invaders,” and transgender athletes in women’s sports.
He did make one agricultural policy position clear: ending subsidies to farmers, which he compared to a heroin addiction.
“It’s never easy to get off the heroin, to get off the drugs. It’s no easier for farmers to get off of the subsidies from the federal government than it is for the welfare ward down in the Twin Cities,” White said.
In response to a question about using farmland for renewable energy and data centers, White said the Chinese Communist Party must be stripped of farmland in America and accused Democrats of suffering from “suicidal empathy.”
“The nexus between radical left Marxism, like my opponents at the end of the table, and radical Islam is the propensity to self-destruction and suicide,” White said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: A tale of Anatevka — and small town Alaska
description: Recent federal immigration enforcement events in Juneau, mirrored in small towns and big cities across America, bring to mind the musical Fiddler on the Roof and the fictional shtetl of Anatevka in early 20th century Russia. There, villagers eke out an existence largely isolated from the political currents of the outside world, hoping to be […]
text:
Image courtesy Bruce BotelhoRecent federal immigration enforcement events in Juneau, mirrored in small towns and big cities across America, bring to mind the musical Fiddler on the Roof and the fictional shtetl of Anatevka in early 20th century Russia. There, villagers eke out an existence largely isolated from the political currents of the outside world, hoping to be ignored by distant rulers whose policies could upend their lives. At one point the village rabbi is asked whether there is a proper blessing for the Tsar. He replies: “Of course. . . May God bless and keep the Tsar . . . far away from us!” Unfortunately, the Tsar’s regime does come for them, ordering all Jews to be expelled from Anatevka.
President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown has emphasized detention, expedited removal and sharply curtailed avenues for asylum or humanitarian relief against people with no meaningful political voice who are trying to survive under a regime that sees them as expendable or suspect. And now the Tsar has come to Juneau.
Juneau is a close-knit community. Our residents are passionate about many things and, being a government town of sorts, we particularly argue over politics. But we also recognize that much of what Juneau is today was built by foreign labor: in the mines, the canneries and all manner of enterprise. And when we encounter a health care worker who happens to be from Haiti, or a construction worker who is Guatemalan, or a chef who is Mexican or a handyman from Ukraine, we don’t ask them for their identity papers. They are our neighbors and we judge them for their willingness to work, their competence and their desire to belong.
We can readily accept the idea of removing “the worst of the worst,” but these are not the people who are disappearing from our streets. Being “undocumented” is now a crime. A young man from Peru with a wife and special-needs child was removed from the community after being arrested and charged with refusal to take a breathalyzer test‚ removed well before his state court trial date — or an Ecuadorian arrested for driving with a broken headlight and without a valid license, leading to an ICE detainer order and his ultimate removal from the country. Nearly an entire Haitian community was compelled to leave after repeated text threats from ICE that said “we will find you” after prematurely terminating their temporary protected status. In recent days a visitor from Mexico with a valid visa was boxed in by two black SUVs as he tried to exit the parking lot of our local Fred Meyers store. The vehicle was searched and, because nothing was found and his papers were “in order,” he was released.   
Not surprisingly, these interventions cause panic, not just among the undocumented, but any residents who are foreign-born or who are awaiting actions on asylum or permanent residency applications. The Trump administration has intentionally slow-rolled these actions, leaving many in a regulatory purgatory. Everyday decisions now become real-time risk assessments:   Do I accompany my children to school? Is it safe to go shopping? Should I forgo needed surgery in Anchorage because I might be detained at the airport?
In recent days there has been a new twist. Recreational boaters that I know have been stopped on the water by agents on small Coast Guard vessels who demand identification from all on board “for security checks.” These are not the typical safety checks that the Coast Guard regularly provides. It is a more ominous development whose on-land equivalent is randomly pulling over a car on a public highway and demanding to see identifications of all passengers.   
A dear friend recently sent a screenshot of a street sign in Philadelphia that captures the horror we are allowing to play out in our country without halt: “Somewhere in America, a little girl is hiding in an attic, writing about I.C.E.” This nation should choose a different path, one that resists gratuitous cruelty and insists on due process and basic humanity.
The incidents referred to in this commentary are recalled firsthand by the author as part of his immigration advocacy work.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Housing forum for South Omaha turns to immigration-related concerns
description: OMAHA — A South Omaha-focused forum hosted by a nonprofit housing agency drew about 80 people and provoked concerns ranging from a need for more “blue-collar” jobs, affordable houses versus apartments and local voices on public boards and in policy-making offices.    But the most impassioned discussion centered on treatment of immigrants — including communit[...]
text:
Nebraska state Sens. Dunixi Guereca, speaking, and Margo Juarez, both of whom represent South Omaha neighborhoods, were featured guests at a Habitat for Humanity of Omaha gathering Tuesday evening intended to hear what is on the minds of South Omaha residents. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A South Omaha-focused forum hosted by a nonprofit housing agency drew about 80 people and provoked concerns ranging from a need for more “blue-collar” jobs, affordable houses versus apartments and local voices on public boards and in policy-making offices.   
Volunteers go over blueprints for building an affordable house. (Photo courtesy of Habitat for Humanity of Omaha)
But the most impassioned discussion centered on treatment of immigrants — including community fallout from ramped-up detentions as well as what some described as rent gouging of newcomers.
Organized by Habitat for Humanity of Omaha, the event was part of its “Key Conversations” series that connects residents and their public representatives in a quest to build stronger communities. Recent other meetings highlighted as a speaker Mayor John Ewing Jr. and, on another occasion, North Omaha lawmakers Ashlei Spivey and Terrell McKinney.
Tuesday night’s event featured state Sens. Margo Juarez and Dunixi Guereca, whose constituents include South Omahans.  Business owner Jamie Gutierrez helped moderate. Habitat homeowners and staff also spoke about the road to attaining homeownership.
 ‘Impacts the economy’  

Ricardo Castro, a South Omaha Realtor and business owner, was an audience member who raised concerns about homeowners and even landlords who he said increasingly are being detained and deported. 
Castro, in an interview, elaborated on migrants he knows who recently were stopped at South Omaha gas stations and apprehended by immigration agents, leaving little to no time for them to resolve issues about homes, properties or businesses they’ve invested in.
“It’s happening more often,” he said, adding that enforcement tactics have stoked fear and disrupted commercial activity.
Both Guereca and Juarez, noting that they represent areas recognized as historical landing places for immigrants, said it was not surprising that conversation pivoted to the impact of heightened enforcement during President Donald Trump’s second term.
“It’s something that people are living,” Guereca said after the meeting, adding that fear and impact ripples to employers, church congregations and neighborhoods. “It’s absolutely going to be front of mind.” 
Said Juarez : “It impacts the economy, no doubt about it.”
The two lawmakers, both in the second year of their first four-year term, told the group that immigration-related bills each had introduced were squelched in committee before reaching debate on the legislative floor.
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota on Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
They spoke of their frustration in trying to advance such state legislation and said it was important for advocacy groups and others to continue to educate migrants on their rights and for residents to raise their voices.
“The reality is that in Lincoln and in D.C., they are not friends of the immigrant community,” said Guereca. “We have to be our own friends. We have to be our own support system.”
One stalled bill introduced by Guereca focused on local and state law enforcement agencies entering into 287(g) agreements with the federal government to enforce immigration laws. The proposal required prior notification to a local governing body and called for a public hearing.
Col. Bryan Waugh, who leads the Nebraska State Patrol under Gov. Jim Pillen, said during a public hearing earlier this year that those new requirements could “unintentionally hinder public safety operations, delay time-sensitive decision-making and create administrative burdens.”
Also this year, Juarez introduced a bill to stop mask-wearing by immigration agents in Nebraska. A similar proposal came from state Sen. Megan Hunt of Omaha, who said legislation also would stop ICE impersonators from concealing their faces to try to commit crimes. Both proposals died in committee.
Juarez spoke about a bill she made her priority last year, which in part sought to allow immigrants who have legal permission to work in the U.S. but lack permanent residency access to unemployment insurance benefits their employers pay into. That bill was crushed under the weight of a Trump administration threat that the state could lose hundreds of millions of dollars in federal aid.
 Blue-collar workers

Shirley Robertson, who works with a local nonprofit that helps migrant families, said rental costs for some older houses are getting “out of control” and in some cases feel like “abuse.” 
Longtime South Omaha native and merchant Marge Stoysich said she’d like to see more on-the-job training opportunities for workers who don’t go to college.
“What happened to good-paying jobs for blue-collar workers?” she asked. “We need more in South Omaha.”
Ricardo Castro, business owner and realtor, comments during the meeting that drew about 80 people. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Juarez said job creation or replacement becomes more of an issue with the shutdown of the WK Kellogg Co. production plant at 96th and F streets in Omaha. The closure was announced in August 2024 and layoffs have occurred in phases, with the final 450 workers losing jobs in July and August. The plant had operated since 1942.
Guereca, acknowledging that not all young people are college-bound, said part of the answer is “holding accountable” the Nebraska Department of Economic Development to help drive to the state a variety of jobs.
He noted there still are thousands of job vacancies in the Lincoln and Omaha area. He said he was frustrated on the campaign trail to hear big business and trade groups lament about a need for workers, yet people in his district say there’s no work.
“Let’s find a way to connect the community with those job availabilities,” Guereca said. 
Nebraska needs population growth to fuel the economy and workforce, Guereca said in an interview. With domestic growth not meeting that demand, he said elected officials should look at reforming the immigration legal system.
 Shape housing policy, neighborhoods 

In response to a question from an audience member, he and Juarez noted the importance of representation on boards, commissions and local elected offices. Guereca recounted when certain Douglas County officials last year sought to rent part of the Omaha-based county jail to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for use as migrant detention beds.
Roger Garcia, County Board chair and outspoken critic of ICE, led a movement to steer clear of that idea, Guereca recalled, reinforcing the value of representation and participation.
Gutierrez, CEO of Midwest Maintenance in South Omaha and member of the Habitat board, welcomed the variety of topics addressed during the forum at the agency’s headquarters in north downtown. She said such discussions help shape housing programs, neighborhoods and can lead to a more thriving community and state.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Sen. Kevin Corbin won’t seek Edwards’ congressional seat in November
description: Longtime North Carolina state lawmaker Sen. Kevin Corbin, R-Macon, announced Wednesday evening he will not run to replace U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot on November. Instead, he says he will continue his reelection campaign for state Senate. Edwards withdrew from his reelection bid early Wednesday morning under pressure from Republican colleagues afte[...]
text:
N.C. Senator Kevin Corbin, R-Macon. (Courtesy photo)Longtime North Carolina state lawmaker Sen. Kevin Corbin, R-Macon, announced Wednesday evening he will not run to replace U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot on November. Instead, he says he will continue his reelection campaign for state Senate.
Edwards withdrew from his reelection bid early Wednesday morning under pressure from Republican colleagues after a U.S. House Ethics report found evidence he had engaged in inappropriate conduct toward two women staffers in his office. Edwards has denied wrongdoing.
The NCGOP’s 11th Congressional District Executive Committee is expected to choose a replacement for Edwards within the coming week.
Edwards’ abrupt withdrawal leaves western NC Republicans scrambling

Corbin, along with Sens. Ralph Hise, R-Mitchell and Tim Moffitt, R-Henderson, were the top names floated by political observers Wednesday as potential replacements, along with several state House members.
Moffitt told NC Newsline Wednesday afternoon he is considering entering the race.
Corbin told NC Newsline earlier Wednesday he was “still processing” the news and had not decided whether to throw his hat in the ring. By the evening, he had made up his mind.
“After discussing this tremendous opportunity with my wife, Beth, and our family, and spending considerable time in prayer, I believe my work in the North Carolina Senate is not yet finished,” Corbin said in a statement.
Corbin said he has made commitments to his constituents, the Governor’s Task Force on Helene recovery, and Senate leaders who made him chairman of the chamber’s education committee.
“For that reason, I do not believe the timing is right for me to seek federal office,” Corbin said. “I am sincerely honored to have been considered and grateful to everyone who offered their confidence, encouragement and support.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Supporters of Arkansas direct democracy effort file suit over rejection of ballot measure petitions
description: Supporters of a proposal to strengthen direct democracy asked the Arkansas Supreme Court Wednesday to order the secretary of state to verify signatures submitted in favor of putting the measure on the November ballot. The lawsuit asks the court to reverse Secretary of State Cole Jester’s rejection of the petitions for the proposed constitutional amendment, [[...]
text:
Protestors sign petitions at the No Kings March in Little Rock, Arkansas on Saturday, March 28, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Supporters of a proposal to strengthen direct democracy asked the Arkansas Supreme Court Wednesday to order the secretary of state to verify signatures submitted in favor of putting the measure on the November ballot.
The lawsuit asks the court to reverse Secretary of State Cole Jester’s rejection of the petitions for the proposed constitutional amendment, which would prohibit lawmakers from amending or repealing constitutional amendments approved by Arkansans and require voters to approve new laws that affect this process.
Jester, a Republican, last week told the proposed constitutional amendment’s sponsors that 19,924 petition pages submitted to his office had an incorrect ballot name on them.
“We’re asking the Arkansas Supreme Court to let the voters decide this ballot measure, not Secretary Jester,” said Alexander Jones, one of the attorneys representing the seven petitioners in their legal complaint.

BallotMeasureSuit 
At least 90,704 valid signatures from registered voters must be submitted for a proposed constitutional amendment to qualify for the ballot. The ballot question committee Protect AR Rights submitted 95,111 signatures, according to the complaint, but Jester said his office would not count any signatures under a different name than the one Attorney General Tim Griffin approved.
The popular name Griffin’s office certified last year was “The Arkansas Ballot Measure Rights Amendment.” The name attached to the signature pages was “The Ballot Measure Rights Amendment of 2026,” which Jester’s office shared online.
These changes did not create “any material confusion to Petitioners or the other lawful voters who signed petitions in support of” the proposed amendment, the complaint states.
The petitioners argue in the complaint that rejecting all signatures because of non-material changes to the petitions infringes on Arkansans’ right to amend the state’s constitution.
“Secretary Jester’s erroneous decision that the petition is insufficient has stifled Petitioners’ voices and limited their rights to express themselves,” the complaint states.
Protect AR Rights submitted petitions to Jester’s office on the July 3 deadline. Jester told the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette that his office immediately found a problem with the popular name circulated on the petitions. The state constitution requires the secretary of state to notify ballot question committees “without delay” if there is a problem with the petitions.
Additionally, a bipartisan 2025 law dictates that the secretary of state cannot determine signatures are insufficient because of a “failure of form,” the complaint states.
Griffin’s office will represent Jester in the case before the Supreme Court. The attorney general maintains that Jester’s rejection of the petitions “was proper and in accordance with Arkansas law,” Griffin spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said Wednesday.
Jester spokesperson Samantha Boyd didn’t comment directly on the lawsuit but defended Arkansas’ elections as the most “free and fair” in the nation “because we focus on integrity and the rule of law.”

UPDATED: Paperwork errors will keep proposed Arkansas abortion amendment off ballot

 

The petitioners asked the Supreme Court to direct Jester “to employ the least restrictive means available” to address “any non-material or insubstantial non-compliance on the face of the petitions.”
State law allows a 30-day cure period if a ballot question committee’s initial submission contains valid signatures equal to at least 75% of the overall required number of signatures and 75% of the required number from at least 15 counties. The petitioners asked the Supreme Court to order Jester’s office to allow the 30-day cure period if needed.
This is the second time in just over two years that supporters of proposed constitutional amendments have asked the Supreme Court to overrule the secretary of state’s rejection of petition signatures. The high court in 2024 upheld then-Secretary of State John Thurston’s rejection of petitions submitted for an abortion rights ballot measure. 
Arkansas’ Supreme Court is nonpartisan, but Republican-linked justices hold five of the seven seats on the court.

name: Daily Montanan
title: State auditor suspends Kalispell bail bondsman
description: State Auditor James Brown suspended the license of a Kalispell bail bondsman after an investigation found evidence the bondsman traded services for sexual favors and exploited people in other ways. Signed on Monday, the suspension order said bail bondsman Laine Kendall Callahan disputed the allegation he used his position in exchange for personal favors incl[...]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images. State Auditor James Brown suspended the license of a Kalispell bail bondsman after an investigation found evidence the bondsman traded services for sexual favors and exploited people in other ways.
Signed on Monday, the suspension order said bail bondsman Laine Kendall Callahan disputed the allegation he used his position in exchange for personal favors including sexual acts.
Callahan could not be reached for comment by email Wednesday about whether he plans to contest the suspension.
The Auditor’s Office also could not be reached about whether it received a request for a hearing from Callahan, who has 21 days from Aug. 3 to challenge the suspension.
However, in the order, Brown said he plans to seek full and permanent license revocation because the bondsman’s operations “pose a substantial and ongoing risk of harm to the public.”
The order said Callahan issued 133 bonds for more than $1 million in a four-month period ending March 2026, and the volume of business and concerns about his conduct span multiple years.
A news release from the Auditor’s Office outlined the following allegations:

Callahan compelled a witness to perform oral sex to “work off” what she owed him on a bond, and the witness complied because she believed her bond would be revoked if she didn’t.
Callahan had another witness perform unlicensed work as a bail agent to work off debt he owed on a bond; the witness alleged he received monetary kickbacks to promote Callahan’s services inside the jail, having referred more than 300 people.
Callahan routinely took possession of vehicle titles as collateral for bail bonds without proper documentation, authorization or timely return of titles after bond obligations were satisfied.

The suspension order said Callahan admitted he collected less than 10% on bonds at times and entered into payment plans for them. It said he also admitted he doesn’t separate client funds from his personal and business funds.
In a statement, Brown, commissioner of securities and insurance, said he acted swiftly to protect the public.
“When a bail bondsman fails to comply with the requirements of Montana’s laws and regulations, the public loses trust in our justice system,” Brown said.
The news release said victims of a scam or fraud as well as their advocates can reach out to the agency for assistance at (406) 444-2040 and sign up for commissioner of securities and insurance advisories at csimt.gov.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota State Penitentiary loses fourth warden in five years amid senior staff shake-up
description: The South Dakota Department of Corrections has lost its fourth penitentiary warden since 2021 amid staffing changes that also include the departure of two other high-ranking officials. Joseph Roemmich, who came to South Dakota from New Mexico just over a year ago to oversee the employees and inmates at the oldest parts of the penitentiary […]
text:
The South Dakota State Penitentiary, pictured on March 27, 2024. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Department of Corrections has lost its fourth penitentiary warden since 2021 amid staffing changes that also include the departure of two other high-ranking officials.

Joseph Roemmich, who came to South Dakota from New Mexico just over a year ago to oversee the employees and inmates at the oldest parts of the penitentiary in Sioux Falls, is no longer employed by the state, according to department spokesman Michael Winder. He also confirmed the departures of Director of Prison Operations Amber Pirraglia and Maj. Cody Hanson.
State hires New Mexico-based warden of for-profit detention center to run state penitentiary

Pirraglia was Roemmich’s superior. In addition to Sioux Falls, Pirraglia oversaw prisons in Springfield, Yankton, Pierre and Rapid City. She had previously worked in corrections in Colorado, and came to South Dakota shortly after the hiring of another Colorado transplant, former Corrections Secretary Kellie Wasko.
Wasko hired Roemmich last year, a few months before she resigned. Gov. Larry Rhoden hired Secretary Nick Lamb, who’d worked most recently in Iowa, to succeed Wasko. 
Hanson, who worked for the prison system prior to Wasko’s arrival, was an administrative major at the prison who’d testified to lawmakers as an advocate for a new men’s prison. He’d also helped lead media tours of the penitentiary.
Tabatha Benting, warden of the maximum security Jameson Annex, located on the state penitentiary campus, is now serving as penitentiary warden.
Winder did not offer departure dates or other details on the circumstances surrounding the exit of the three employees. 
A statement from Lamb on Wednesday said staffing changes are part of a broader effort to improve operations across the prison system, though he did not mention any staff members by name. The statement noted the expansion of community service work by inmates, the adoption of a prison seminary program and additional training programs, the expansion of educational partnerships with Southeast Technical College and Western Dakota Technical College, and a tightening of parole supervision.
“I have been evaluating the agency operations, and we are making some personnel changes consistent with the agency’s mission and the steps we’re taking,” Lamb wrote.
Rhoden, in a separate statement, said he’s “proud of the work” Lamb’s done in his first nine months on the job and called him “a strong leader” who “clearly shares my mission to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free.”
History of shake-ups amid debate over new construction
The state split warden duties in Sioux Falls into two positions last year. Prior to Roemmich’s arrival, the entire state penitentiary campus — which includes the 1881 penitentiary complex, the Jameson Annex and a separate work release center — was supervised by a single warden.

From left, former South Dakota State Penitentiary Warden Joe Roemmich, Maj. Jarod Hettich, former Director of Prison Operations Amber Pirraglia and Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb pose in a social media photo posted in February to congratulate Hettich on a promotion. (South Dakota Department of Corrections photo)

Roemmich’s predecessor, Teresa Bittinger, served less than two years and oversaw a period of controversy and unrest, which included lockdowns and a temporary shutdown of tablet-based inmate communications. She was appointed in 2023 to replace Dan Sullivan, who also served fewer than two years. He replaced Darin Young, ousted in a staff shake-up initiated by then-Gov. Kristi Noem in 2021.
State lawmakers voted last fall to replace the oldest parts of the penitentiary, which was built prior to South Dakota statehood, with a $650 million facility now under construction on the eastern side of Sioux Falls. The other two prison buildings on the penitentiary campus, located on a hill overlooking Falls Park less than a mile from downtown Sioux Falls, will continue to house inmates when the new prison complex opens in 2029.
Commission member: Loss of institutional knowledge is concerning
Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, is chair of the state’s Corrections Commission. The group is meant to offer guidance on corrections policy, and to approve any spending decisions on prison industries.
The loss of so many leaders is a concern for Wittman. Beyond the wardens, other long-term employees — including Doug Clark, the former deputy corrections secretary who served as interim warden after Young’s departure — have left the prison system over the past five years.
“There’s no real institutional knowledge left,” Wittman said. 
Wittman would like to see the commission move toward monthly meetings and address questions about leadership and institutional knowledge, as well as employee retention more broadly, but said it had been difficult to get traction during Wasko’s term.
The former secretary had sought to limit the commission’s scope of discussion and access to information, and some of the commission’s work has been taken on by the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force. 
The latter group was formed following the Legislature’s prison funding vote, with a promise from Gov. Rhoden to address the state’s high reoffense rate. 
Lamb has appeared at both of the Corrections Commission meetings held since Wasko’s departure, introducing himself in the first and offering rundowns of the task force’s discussion points during the second.
Wittman said she expects the next Corrections Commission meeting to take place within the next few months. The next meeting of the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force is scheduled for Aug. 19.
