title: Delaware State Chamber names 2026 Superstars in Business winners
description: Food Bank of Delaware, Synergy Consultants, First Ascent Design and GGA Construction are among the organizations recognized for leadership, growth and community impact. WILMINGTON, Del. — Four Delaware organizations have been named the 2026 winners of the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce’s Marvin S. Gilman Superstars in Business Awards. The Food Bank of De[...]
text:
Food Bank of Delaware, Synergy Consultants, First Ascent Design and GGA Construction are among the organizations recognized for leadership, growth and community impact.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Four Delaware organizations have been named the 2026 winners of the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce’s Marvin S. Gilman Superstars in Business Awards.
The Food Bank of Delaware, Synergy Consultants & Psychotherapy Practice, First Ascent Design and GGA Construction will be honored Oct. 29 during an awards ceremony at the Chase Center on the Riverfront in Wilmington.
The annual program, presented by the State Chamber and its Small Business Alliance, recognizes small businesses and nonprofit organizations for strong business practices, leadership and contributions to their communities.
The awards honor the legacy of Marvin S. Gilman, a Delaware small-business leader remembered for his ethics, community involvement and commitment to encouraging other entrepreneurs.
Since the program began in 1998, it has recognized organizations that have operated for at least three years and meet employee-based standards for small businesses. Awards of Excellence are also presented to organizations demonstrating notable performance and leadership.
Food Bank of Delaware
The Food Bank of Delaware was selected as the winner in the nonprofit category.
The statewide organization provides food assistance while also working to address the causes of hunger and poverty. It distributes millions of pounds of food annually through more than 600 community partners.
The organization also provides workforce training and other programs intended to help Delaware residents achieve greater financial and personal stability.
Synergy Consultants & Psychotherapy Practice
Synergy Consultants & Psychotherapy Practice was selected in the category for businesses with one to 10 employees.
The outpatient mental health practice serves individuals, couples and families. It offers evidence-based therapy for anxiety, depression, trauma, grief and major life transitions.
The practice also trains future clinicians and participates in community wellness programs, outreach efforts and partnerships.
First Ascent Design
First Ascent Design was selected in the category for businesses with 11 to 40 employees.
The Wilmington-based digital marketing agency provides branding, website development, digital advertising, search engine optimization and content marketing services.
During its 11 years in business, First Ascent has worked with nearly 300 businesses, nonprofit organizations and educational institutions in Delaware and other states.
GGA Construction
GGA Construction was selected in the category for businesses with 41 to 150 employees.
The Delaware-based company has offices in Middletown and Rehoboth Beach and specializes in commercial construction projects throughout the region.
Its portfolio includes health care facilities, schools, multifamily housing, hotels, restaurants, senior living communities, recreational facilities and other commercial developments.
Awards of Excellence announced
Four additional organizations will receive Awards of Excellence.
Sunday Breakfast Mission was selected in the nonprofit category. Integrity Nursing LLC was recognized in the category for businesses with one to 10 employees.
Delmarva Central Railroad was selected in the category for businesses with 11 to 40 employees, and AKA Advisory was recognized in the category for businesses with 41 to 150 employees.
Schell Brothers CEO to deliver keynote
Chris Schell, founder and CEO of Schell Brothers, will serve as the keynote speaker for the Oct. 29 ceremony.
Schell Brothers has grown from its Delaware roots into one of the nation’s largest privately owned homebuilders, with operations in Delaware, Virginia, Tennessee and Idaho.
Schell earned a mechanical engineering degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and an MBA from Harvard Business School. He began his career in finance, developing automated futures trading software, before entering the homebuilding industry.
He founded Schell Brothers with a company culture centered on employee and customer happiness.
Schell has served on the University of Delaware Board of Trustees and the Economic Advisory Council for the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia. He currently serves on the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce Board of Governors.
The Superstars in Business awards ceremony will be held Thursday, Oct. 29, at the Chase Center on the Riverfront in Wilmington.
Additional information is available through the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Three Kansas House incumbents — two Democrats, one Republican — fall in primary election
description: TOPEKA — Rep. Henry Helgerson’s lengthy career in the Kansas Legislature will come to an involuntary end after losing the Democratic primary election as three Kansas House incumbents fell short in campaigns for reelection. Helgerson, the most prominent fiscal conservative among House Democrats, was ousted Tuesday by Brandon Whipple, a former Wichita mayor wh[...]
text:
Rep. Henry Helgerson, a Wichita Democrat, lost his primary election to former Wichita Mayor Brandon Whipple, who secured 61% of the Democratic Party vote in the 83rd District race. Helgerson, a fiscal conservative, ruffled Republican and Democratic colleagues during a 30-year career in the Legislature by focusing attention on questionable spending practices. In this Feb. 12, 2026, image, Helgerson reminded House members of risks to burning quickly through state treasury reserve funding. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Rep. Henry Helgerson’s lengthy career in the Kansas Legislature will come to an involuntary end after losing the Democratic primary election as three Kansas House incumbents fell short in campaigns for reelection.
Helgerson, the most prominent fiscal conservative among House Democrats, was ousted Tuesday by Brandon Whipple, a former Wichita mayor who previously served in the House. Elsewhere in Wichita, Democratic Rep. Ford Carr, a two-term incumbent, lost the primary to Bonita Gooch, owner and publisher of the Community Voice. Whipple faces GOP nominee Zachary Werhan in November, but Gooch has a clear path in the general election because no Republican filed in her district.
In southeast Kansas, retired pastor Dan Muter of Pittsburg dispatched Mulberry Republican Rep. Ken Collins, who has served in the House since 2019. Muter’s opponent in the fall will be Democrat Avery Rowland of Girard.
Helgerson, who has served 29 years in the House and one year in the Senate, said he was disappointed the primary campaign didn’t focus on consequential issues, including an approaching state budget shortfall, loss of federal funding and pressure to address property taxes. Instead, Helgerson said, he was unfairly portrayed as an opponent of abortion rights.
“Which is ironic,” Helgerson said. “I’ve gotten hammered for being pro-choice for my 30 years in politics.”
Unofficial results from the Kansas secretary of state indicated that in these three House contests Whipple prevailed by securing 61% of the Democratic primary vote in the 83rd District, Gooch earned 70% of the vote among Democrats in the 84th District and Muter controlled 58% of the Republican votes cast in the 2nd District.
 
Mulberry state Rep. Ken Collins, on the right in this March 2022 photo, lost a primary contest Tuesday to Republican challenger Dan Muter, a retired minister from Pittsburg who was endorsed by political action committees of the Kansas Chamber and Kansas Farm Bureau. Muter faces Democrat Avery Rowland of Girard in the November general election. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Special interest fight
Muter, who served as a minister for 30 years, previously sought public office when a vacancy was created in the Kansas Senate by a member’s resignation. He wasn’t appointed to that opening in 2023, but pivoted to the House and the challenge of Collins. Before the primary, Muter warned voters special interests were behind the flood of advertising designed to benefit Collins.
“Ken hasn’t had to spend one dime on all the mailers, the internet and TV ads, the handbills and the college kids paid to distribute them, the texts and all the other advertising on his behalf. Not one dime,” Muter said. “They’re all paid for by the American Conservative Fund. Every dime. They’re paying for his campaign in gratitude for his past support and to ensure his future support.”
The American Conservative Fund devoted approximately $486,000 to eight Kansas House primary races in a quest to support legislation favorable to a coalition of sports betting platforms.
Muter said that if elected in November, “I won’t be bought by big, greedy corporate interests.”
Overall, more than 150 Kansas House candidates automatically advanced to the general election because they didn’t have a Republican or Democratic primary opponent. The entire 125-member House is up for grabs in 2026, while the Kansas Senate has two special elections because of resignations from that chamber. The full Senate will be on ballots in 2028.
Voters also nominated Republican Al Jirak of Wichita for the November ballot to compete for the seat held by House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican who won the GOP nomination for state insurance commissioner. Jirak captured 61% of the vote to defeat former Rep. Carl Maughan of Colwich, who chose not to seek reelection to the House in 2024 after he was arrested in Shawnee County on a drunken driving charge. Maughan ended up with 22% of the vote. Jirak faces Democrat Amanda Mogol of Wichita in November.
 
Narrow primary victories
In the 42nd District, Republican Rep. Lance Neelly of Tonganoxie was hanging by a 25-vote thread following the preliminary count on Tuesday night. He had 1,622 votes against GOP challenger Mike Stieben’s 1,597.
It is close enough there could be ramifications for the review of provisional ballots issued to voters because the person’s name wasn’t in the poll book, an individual requested an advance ballot but voted in person or the prospective voter was unable to present an acceptable photo ID at the polling station. Winner of the primary would be opposed by Democrat Brandon Wendt of Tonganoxie.
Stieben, a Tonganoxie resident and chairman of the Leavenworth County Commission, proposed a cap on property tax increases and a freeze on property taxes for anyone older than 65. He opposed a Tonganoxie data center project and urged repeal of a state law granting 20-year tax breaks for developers of the projects, a incentive that Neelly voted for in the House.
“Neelly would not debate during the election,” Stieben said. “He has been running a campaign from his basement.”
Neelly said voters in the district were focused during the primary on property taxes — by a 10-to-1 margin over other topics. The Legislature eliminated a 1.5-mill property tax for state building construction, but the state continued to collect the 20 mills of property tax revenue passed on to support Kansas public school districts.
“I’m a firm believer in local control, but the (local government) spending is too much,” Neelly said.
Elsewhere, there was a tight GOP battle in the 35th District for the opportunity to take on Democratic Rep. Wanda Brownlee Paige of Kansas City, Kansas. Republican Alex Sanchez defeated Lisa Walker Yeager by 34 votes. There were only 282 GOP votes cast in the primary with Sanchez locking up 158 and Yeager netting 124.
The decision by Osage City Republican Rep. Brad Barrett not to seek reelection in the 76th District set off a three-person primary in which the top two contenders were separated by 63 votes. Russel Stukey of Waverly had 1,781 votes compared to Art Freund’s 1,718. The other GOP candidate, Mark Weiser of Osage City, had 597 votes.
Freund, of Lebo, said he was distressed the Right Future for Kansas political action committee, which he linked to construction and energy interests, waded into the House contest.
“Let me be plain: I’m running for House District 76 because I believe our representative should answer to you, not to a stack of PAC checks,” he said. “PACs don’t spend thousands because they’re excited about your gravel roads or your grocery bill. They spend because they want access, influence and someone who will take their calls before yours.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Reeves announces pilot programs to improve rural health for Mississippi
description: Gov. Tate Reeves talks about Mississippi's Rural Health Transformation Program plan during a press conference at the Walter Sillers Building in Jackson on Tuesday, Oct. 4, 2025.
text:
Gov. Tate Reeves announced Wednesday new pilot programs aimed to combat obesity, eliminate obstetric care deserts and expand mental health services in rural Mississippi. 
The programs will be funded with federal Rural Health Transformation Program dollars. The Mississippi State Department of Health will oversee the projects designed to reduce obesity through Make America Healthy Again movement principles, track chronic conditions through remote patient-care monitoring and deploy mobile clinics to areas lacking access to prenatal or obstetric care. 
The Department of Mental Health will launch a new telehealth program for veterans and first responders, expand crisis diversion centers to provide an alternative to emergency departments and jails for people experiencing mental health crises and expand access to evidence-based training programs for behavioral healthcare staff. 
“This is not a collection of individual or separate projects,” said Reeves, who spearheaded the state’s application for the federal dollars last fall and is overseeing their distribution. “It’s one, coordinated project.”
In December, Mississippi was awarded nearly $206 million as a part of the Rural Health Transformation Program. States will receive payments over five years as a part of the national $50 billion program, which was designed to support rural health care and offset the disproportionate impact rural hospitals are expected to face as a result of federal spending cuts Congress passed into law last summer. 
Mississippi’s plan included a statewide rural health assessment and other initiatives focused on coordinating care, strengthening the workforce, creating a statewide health information exchange, expanding telehealth opportunities and improving infrastructure. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approved Mississippi’s program budget in April. Mississippi must obligate the funds by October and spend them by September 30, 2027. 
Reeves said the state received 726 applications from 236 organizations for the initial three grant opportunities offered as a part of the program. Applications for the initiatives, which focus on facility improvements, upgrading technology systems and increasing telehealth capacity, were due by July 15. Reeves said applicants requested more than $676 million in funding for $81.7 million in available funds.
“The need is greater than the funding available in the first round,” Reeves said during a Wednesday press conference that was broadcast on social media.
Richard Grimes, program director for Mississippi’s Rural Health Transformation Program Office, said state agencies will be responsible for the scoring and evaluation of the grant applications, keeping a firewall between program administration and scorekeeping. 
Decisions about funding will be made using a scoring rubric designed to identify the projects that will make the greatest difference for rural Mississippians. The first three grant programs’ applications have begun being evaluated by independent reviewers, whose recommendations will be vetted by the Mississippi State Department of Health.
The program’s office currently seeks applications for workforce development and psychiatric emergency services grant opportunities. Applications are due by August 17 and will be reviewed by the state Department of Mental Health and Accelerate Mississippi, the state’s workforce development agency.
The state has also released requests for proposals for an assessment of the emergency medical system’s capacity and expertise to begin designing a health information exchange, Reeves said. 
Grant recipients will be required to pay for most projects upfront and then be reimbursed, though there may be some exceptions. Reeves said his office will work with awardees to ensure the process is not burdensome.
“The reimbursement’s going to happen as soon as humanly possible,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lost SNAP? What to know about CT grocery card benefit
description: Some Connecticut residents who have recently lost SNAP assistance can now qualify for $300 in grocery store gift cards. Here's what to know.
text:
State officials announced on Tuesday that some Connecticut residents who have recently lost food stamps can now qualify for $300 in grocery store gift cards.
But not everyone who has lost SNAP qualifies.
The program is specifically aimed at people who have lost benefits under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, in recent months due to new federal work requirements for “Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents.”
Since July 2025, around 35,000 people in Connecticut have lost SNAP, according to the state Department of Social Services. That includes nearly 18,900 children who have lost access to federal nutrition benefits since July 2025 and 1,745 refugees and asylum seekers. 
Here’s what to know about the funds being offered and who is eligible.
What is the benefit and why is it being offered?
The new funds will provide $300 in spending power for each household member who has lost SNAP. The benefits are being distributed as prepaid virtual grocery store cards, and can be used anywhere that SNAP is accepted. 
Though Connecticut residents who qualify will be able to apply for the cards anytime between now and December, they will only receive the card one time.
Tens of thousands of people have been removed from the rolls since late fall because of rule changes ordered last summer by the federal government. Veterans, unhoused people, young adults transitioning out of foster care and parents of minor children age 14 and older no longer are exempt from work requirements. Federal officials also cut SNAP benefits for certain categories of legal immigrants. 
Who qualifies? 
The funds are available to people who lost SNAP due to the new work requirements, and who don’t have a disability that prevents them from working. This includes veterans, people who are homeless, those between the age of 55 and 64 years old, young adults under age 24 who are transitioning out of foster care, and parents of minor children age 14 and older. 
Though people with refugee status and asylum seekers who do not have green cards have also lost SNAP under new federal rules, these groups do not qualify. Lamont’s spokesperson said the administration has made other funds available to address the needs this population might have.
“Governor Lamont recently allocated $3 million from the Federal Cuts Response Fund to ensure our refugee agencies can continue serving the needs of those populations in the face of dramatic reductions in funding from the federal government,” Cathryn Vaulman said.
The governor earlier this year also sent nearly $25 million from state surplus to food banks and pantries. Another $4.7 million went to the United Way of Connecticut’s 2-1-1 information line and to nonprofit community action agencies, which help SNAP recipients navigate new eligibility rules and find additional forms of aid.
The Lamont administration also added 50 new positions to an understaffed social services department to help residents with SNAP and other assistance programs.
But food bank officials have said they can offset only a fraction of the need created when so many lose SNAP benefits. 
To learn more about who may qualify, Connecticut residents can contact a local Community Action Agency. Those groups are responsible for distributing the gift cards.
What should people do if they are concerned about losing their SNAP benefits?
State officials said on Tuesday that of the 35,000 who have lost SNAP over the last nine or so months, around 5,000 Connecticut residents have been successfully re-enrolled in the program, with some complying with the new work rules that require recipients to work and/or volunteer at least 80 hours a month.
State officials say it’s not always easy to navigate the program, and Connecticut residents should reach out if they are in doubt. 
“It becomes kind of a tangled web of unraveling who is eligible, why they lost eligibility, and what they can do,” said Daniel Giacomi, the director of program oversight and grants administration at the Department of Social Services.  
For questions, DSS recommends visiting your local Community Action Agency. A list of CAA’s can be found here: https://www.cafca.org/agencies/

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Republicans, Democrats agree Rep. Edwards made right call withdrawing from NC-11 race
description: A U.S. House Ethics Committee report detailed his inappropriate conduct toward two young women who worked in his office.
text:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) listens during a  House Budget Committee meeting on Capitol Hill on May 16, 2025 in Washington, D.C.  (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)Democrats and Republicans alike applauded U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards’ withdrawal from his reelection campaign Wednesday after the U.S. House Ethics Committee recommended his censure, followed by pressure from his party. 
Edwards, who has represented North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District since 2023, dropped out of the race after the committee’s Monday report, which detailed his inappropriate conduct toward two young women who worked in his office. 
“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” Edwards said in a statement early Wednesday morning. “I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life.”
Both of the state’s Republican senators praised that move. 
Multiple outlets reported Tuesday that U.S. Sen. Ted Budd told Edwards the race was unwinnable.
NC Rep. Edwards drops reelection campaign following ethics probe, urging of Republican colleagues

Budd said Wednesday morning that Edwards “did the right thing” by withdrawing.
“He has been a fighter for the people of Western North Carolina as they work to recover from the impacts of Hurricane Helene, and I know he’ll continue to advocate for disaster funding for the remainder of his time in D.C.,” Budd said. 
“Chuck Edwards made the right decision to drop out of the race for himself and his family,” U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis said in a statement Wednesday.
Edwards was set to face Democrat Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, on the ballot in November. 
Ager said on Wednesday his “heart goes out to the young women” who took on roles on Capitol Hill to serve their community. 
“No matter who we face in November, I’m confident we can win this race and deliver what I’ve been talking about since day one: Hurricane Helene recovery, lower costs, and an end to the corruption in Washington,” he said in a statement. 
Political observers considered Ager a formidable opponent to take on Edwards. Ager’s grandfather previously represented the 11th district from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991, after a stint in the state legislature. His brother Eric Ager serves in the North Carolina House. 
Even before the March primary election, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee pledged resources and fundraising support to Ager in February, adding him to its “Red to Blue” program. Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its assessment of the district from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up” at the end of July. 
Two North Carolina US House races are now toss-ups, top forecaster says

On Wednesday, the DCCC called for Edwards to resign from the remainder of his term. 
DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus said if Edwards is unfit to run for reelection, he isn’t fit to serve in Congress either.
“The decision to serve out the remainder of his term is not for North Carolina’s working families, it is clearly designed to protect House Republicans’ ever dwindling majority,” Andrus said in a statement. “Chuck Edwards must resign immediately, otherwise House Republicans should preserve what is left of their integrity and expel him from Congress.”
Under the North Carolina Republican Party’s plan of organization, the 11th Congressional District Executive Committee is responsible for selecting a new candidate for the November ballot. 
NCGOP chair Jason Simmons said the group is prepared to move through the process “quickly and efficiently.”
“The District Executive Committee will fulfill its responsibility under our rules to nominate a candidate who will fight for lower taxes, secure our border, strengthen our economy, and stand up for the values of the people of the 11th District,” he said in a statement. 
Several sitting state House and Senate Republicans from western North Carolina are already being discussed as potential replacements.  
Edwards’ abrupt withdrawal leaves western NC Republicans scrambling

North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall said he was confident the committee’s candidate would win the election. 
He said he doesn’t yet know which House members are interested in the seat. 
“It seems clear that [Edwards] made the right decision. That seat is obviously important, and we need to make sure the folks out there have the right representation,” Hall told reporters Wednesday. “I don’t want to lose anybody within our caucus, but at the same time, the members we have out there are all very talented folks.”
The district has long been considered safely red, with President Donald Trump winning by 9.5 points in 2024. But recent polls show flagging Republican support in the district. 
“NC-11 is a Republican seat and will remain that way this November,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Reilly Richardson said. 
Edwards isn’t the district’s first controversial congressman  — former U.S. Reps. Madison Cawthorne and Mark Meadows held the seat before Edwards.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Two debates, three candidates and four takeaways from Providence’s mayoral race
description: After several months of campaigning, it’s obvious Providence Mayor Brett Smiley and his Democratic primary opponent, state Rep. David Morales, disagree about many things. On the fate of three elephants, however, the two men are more aligned. The question of whether Roger Williams Park Zoo should replace its three departing African elephants came up during […[...]
text:
Providence Mayor Brett Smiley, left, state Rep. David Morales, center, and Republican mayoral candidate Dave Talan participate in a forum at South Providence Library on Aug. 4, 2026. The event was organized by the League of Women Voters of Rhode Island and Community Libraries of Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)After several months of campaigning, it’s obvious Providence Mayor Brett Smiley and his Democratic primary opponent, state Rep. David Morales, disagree about many things.
On the fate of three elephants, however, the two men are more aligned.
The question of whether Roger Williams Park Zoo should replace its three departing African elephants came up during a Tuesday morning debate at WPRO’s studios in East Providence, where radio host and journalist Bill Bartholomew questioned the two Democratic candidates for over an hour.
The elephants — Alice, Ginny and Kate — are getting long in the tooth and will move to a sanctuary in Tennessee next year. The relocation plan, Smiley said, is “humane and just,” noting that elephants are social animals and their new home will allow them to age among a bigger herd. 
Bartholomew asked if new elephants should be brought in. Both candidates agreed they shouldn’t. 
It would not be the only time Smiley and Morales agreed on Tuesday, nor would it be their only debate that day. That evening, Smiley and Morales met again at South Providence Library, this time joined by Republican mayoral candidate Dave Talan for the third and final round of a debate series jointly organized by the League of Women Voters of Rhode Island and Community Libraries of Providence. 
Below, four highlights from Tuesday’s doubleheader.
Time, money and morality 
Both debates saw Smiley follow the same orbit of argument, one that characterizes Morales as a redundant problem-solver who ignores the Smiley administration’s existing solutions, realistic timelines or accurate calculations of what certain projects could cost. 
Morales, meanwhile, has centered his campaign on addressing housing affordability, frequently citing it as a moral obligation of city government. The unequal impacts of pollution, policing and poor city services are just a few areas where the Smiley administration has fallen short for many residents, Morales argued again Tuesday. 
These two approaches are crystallized in the pair’s signature disagreement: A rent stabilization ordinance Smiley vetoed earlier this year — one Morales has promised to resurrect if elected.

“It was also sort of a bad version of what I believe is a bad policy,” Smiley said of the Providence City Council’s failed proposal to cap annual rent increases at 4% and create a new bureaucracy to administer the proposed law. 
Morales responded with Zillow-based estimates that Providence rents “have increased by over 40% since 2020, which would have been prevented if we had rent stabilization in place,” and added, “Rent increases are serving as eviction notices for so many working people in the city of Providence.”
At the evening debate, Morales added a personal barb to the policy feud.
“When you’re vetoing rent stabilization while your third home in Tiverton is being built, I don’t blame you for being out of touch with your community,” he said.
Smiley offered his own retort later in the night when Morales floated the idea of a bond-funded home repair program. The city already has one, Smiley said.
“Rep. Morales, you don’t have to worry about doing a bond because it’s in this year’s budget,” Smiley said. 
The money-time divide surfaced again over Rhode Island Recycled Metals. Smiley defended the city’s court efforts to shut down the polluting scrapyard on Allens Avenue, which he noted is “unlicensed” and “unpermitted.”
Morales thought eminent domain might be an option for the city to seize the land directly so it could be remediated.
“Eminent domain is a fine idea, but you’ve got to pay for it,” Smiley replied. “And so, if you want $15 million of your taxpayer dollars going into the pocket of the owners of Rhode Island Recycled Metals, then go the eminent domain route.” 
Not on the same wavelength
The evening’s forum was not without acrimony, but the morning’s radio debate sans Talan was where the two opponents sparred most directly.
Policing, like housing, continues to provoke some of the duo’s fiercest exchanges.
Smiley confronted Morales over his participation in a 2021 police accountability rally, where Morales made the remarks that Smiley’s campaign has since used as evidence that the state rep wanted to defund the police. 
“Did he change his mind right before he declared his candidacy, or did he change his mind years ago?” Smiley said.
Morales clarified Tuesday that he did not want to increase the city police budget after officers had pepper-sprayed a crowd, which included children, during a neighborhood dispute in 2021. He reiterated that he had never advocated for emptying police coffers entirely — then pivoted to the Smiley TV ad which made the defunding claim. 
“My opponent has spent over $400,000 on television ads that have darkened the color of my skin, and hundreds of thousands more on mailers with racial undertones designed to make you believe that a young brown man is going to make Providence less safe,” Morales said. “And these are just desperate attacks that one would expect to see from a MAGA Republican during these times.”
“Did your campaign darken Rep. Morales’ skin in that ad?” Bartholomew asked Smiley.
“We did not alter his image,” Smiley replied. 
The mayor went back on offense to critique Morales’ public safety platform, arguing it would duplicate much of what Providence already does.
“It would have been helpful if he had learned a little bit about what Providence Police do before publishing that report,” Smiley said.
Morales did, however, give a number for the ideal size of the department under his administration: about 456 officers, roughly the current headcount, with recruitment focused on mitigating an anticipated “wave of retirements.”
Talan offered a third lane — sometimes
The only Republican in Tuesday night’s debate and the only candidate not competing in the Sept. 9 primary is Talan, whose most common refrain is a tune of fiscal conservatism. 
He told voters Tuesday, as he has before, that his goal is not to spend more of their money or to spend their money injudiciously. 
“As a Republican, you’re almost never going to hear me tonight talk about spending more money on anything,” he said.
But Talan would make one exception for snow removal. The capital city should meet or exceed state payments to contractors with the trucks needed to move behemoth-sized snowpiles, like those that clogged Providence streets and sidewalks during the winter’s historic blizzard.
Talan also gave the most unequivocal answer to a question on which his rivals hedged.
When an audience member asked which of the three candidates would pledge not to raise taxes, Smiley said he “can’t make that commitment.” Morales said his administration would “intend not to.”
Talan answered, “Definite no.”
Providence mayoral candidates debate housing, ICE and their vision for city’s future

His other distinctive proposal concerned school transportation: Talan wants to save Providence taxpayers an estimated $10 million annually, he said, by increasing the number of neighborhood schools and decreasing the number of children bused across the city from about 9,000 to 4,500.
The Republican was not always in his own lane, and agreed with both Democrats that Rhode Island Recycled Metals should be closed. He also thought Smiley was right on rent stabilization and a policy barring municipal cooperation with ICE. 
Talan had at least one successful punchline Tuesday night.
Morales rephrased, if not softened, his MAGA remark about Smiley’s campaign from earlier in the day, telling the crowd he feels like he’s “running against a Republican with these types of tactics.”
Talan’s retort had the crowd laughing. 
“Running against a Republican is not a bad thing, actually,” he said. “Unfortunately, as a registered Republican, I miss out on getting Mayor Smiley’s daily mailing.”
Attendees speak with Providence Mayor Brett Smiley, left, and Republican candidate Dave Talan following a mayoral forum at South Providence Library on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
A not-so-captive audience
The candidates had some problems with brevity Tuesday night. They repeatedly stretched the answers to questions meant to yield only a “yes” or a “no” or a single word. 
“You have to only use one word because I am afraid of the audience throwing things at me,” joked moderator Amanda Blount when she asked candidates to use but a single utterance to describe their campaign.
Morales went first. 
“Housing affordability,” he said. 
Next up was Smiley.
“Forgive me,” he said, “I’m afraid I’m going to do the same: Public schools.”
And Talan, extending the bit: “Education. School choice.”
To Blount’s point, the standing-room crowd had been lively, with both their questions, applause, laughter and the occasional shout or groan of disapproval.
At one point, Morales invoked Smiley’s 2022 campaign pledge to make Providence the “best-run city in America.”
“Does it feel like Providence is the best run city in America?” he asked the crowd.
He received a “No,” then a “Yes,” in quick succession.
A later interruption was different, and the forum stopped for several minutes when a woman repeatedly confronted Smiley over claims and concerns she said city officials had ignored. Both organizers and members of the crowd asked her to wait her turn, and after three or so minutes of back and forth, she left the room. 
The next audience member pivoted to mental health, homelessness and other public-safety concerns.
“I’ll just say the disruption I’m sure was hard for a lot of people,” Smiley began in his answer. “When you are the mayor, whoever the mayor is, you become the face of government. And obviously we hope she gets the services that she needs and finds peace.”

name: VTDigger
title: A shrinking market for low-grade wood threatens Vermont’s forests
description:
With one of the last buyers of hemlock pulpwood gone, good forest management could become too costly to sustain — putting habitat, climate resilience and rural jobs all at risk.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A shrinking market for low-grade wood threatens Vermont’s forests.
text:
This commentary is by Rob Riley, president of the Northern Forest Center; Danielle Fitzko, commissioner of the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation; Dana Doran, executive director of Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast; Kate Forrer, executive director of the Vermont Woodlands Association; Jamey Fidel, vice president for Vermont at the National Audubon Society/Audubon Vermont; Steve Hardy, president of the Vermont Forest Products Association; Tracy Zschau, president and CEO of the Vermont Land Trust; state Rep. Jed Lipsky, Lamoille-1; Abby Long, executive director of the Northeast Kingdom Collaborative; Tara Miller, forest and wildlife program director at the Vermont Natural Resources Council; and Eve Frankel, state director of the Nature Conservancy in Vermont.
Recent news coverage about the end of pulping operations at Finch Paper has understandably focused on how it is bad for logging contractors and the forest products industry. As organizations and associations focused on the future of Vermont forests, we agree — those impacts are significant. But the story is more than that: This is bad news for everyone who cares about sustaining Vermont’s forests.
Yes, producing logs and fiber to turn into products we need is often a goal of forest management, but so are the following benefits: improving wildlife habitat, biodiversity, climate resilience, recreational trails, carbon storage, protecting against pests and diseases, addressing introduced invasive plants, managing fire danger and improving the overall health and diversity of forests.
Our organizations may prioritize the benefits on this list differently, but we agree on one thing: Without buyers for the wood forest management generates, good forest management activities become economically difficult, or impossible, to carry out. And without sustainable management, we believe Vermont will lose the forest benefits we care about, and — worst case — significant forest acreage.
This is why the Finch news is bad for all Vermonters, even those who may think they don’t care about, or even oppose, logging. As VTDigger reported, Finch was one of the last remaining buyers of hemlock pulpwood from Vermont. Overall, the mill purchased an average of approximately 2,000 tons of both softwood and hardwood roundwood a week from our state. There are no other options that can quickly replace this market for low-grade wood, which is a part of all forestry operations. That means a lot of things.
Near term, it means Vermont will lose logging and trucking contractors, as well as foresters, the people who manage the forests, harvest wood and truck wood to mills. It means Vermont landowners will have fewer — or no — market options when they want to improve their forests through management: fewer people to do the work and fewer ways to pay for it.

READ MORE

Longer term, it will mean that less forest management happens in Vermont, including on the more than 2 million acres enrolled in the Current Use Program, which keeps forestland undeveloped. Substandard practices such as “high grading” forests for higher-quality sawlog timber may be the result of limited wood markets. Poor management practices might be the short-term solution to making ends meet, with serious long-term costs in the form of degraded timber stands that require time and money to remedy. As a result, this increases the pressure on some landowners to seek other sources of income that may involve parcelization, development or permanent forest conversion. This is an outcome that unites us in concern.
Vermont, New England and the United States rely on wood for building materials, paper, packaging and fuel. With over 75% of its land under forest cover, Vermont should be a wood-producing powerhouse — not a state increasingly reliant on timber shipped in from away. Yet due to investment, trade and policy factors that have been building for decades, that wood is increasingly coming from other parts of the world. As part of a broader approach, we call on innovators, researchers and policymakers to take the Finch news as both a warning and an invitation.
Vermont has an opportunity to invest in a wider mix of forest products and markets, from advanced wood products and innovative fiber manufacturing to modern and efficient wood energy and other emerging uses for low-grade wood. Creating diverse, resilient and appropriately scaled markets will provide stability and help Vermont’s logging and trucking contractors, mills and forest products businesses thrive while giving landowners practical options for caring for their forests. In doing so, we can support rural communities, wildlife habitat, climate resilience, outdoor recreation and the many benefits Vermont’s forests provide.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A shrinking market for low-grade wood threatens Vermont’s forests.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lynn Fitch kicks off governor campaign with promise to speed up income tax phase-out
description: Attorney General Lynn Fitch speaks with reporters about her campaign for governor during an event at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026.
text:
Attorney General Lynn Fitch kicked off her statewide tour promoting her 2027 campaign for governor by promising to speed up the income tax elimination, improve the state’s healthcare outcomes and work to make Mississippi more affordable.
Speaking at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in downtown Jackson on Wednesday, Fitch described herself as aligned with President Donald Trump and said she wants to make Mississippi the “leader in conservative governance.”
“Together, we will make a bold and sustaining change for Mississippi,” Fitch said. “That is how we make the most of this moment in time. That is how we make Mississippi the nation’s leader. That is how we give you and your family the best future.” 
In 2025, the Legislature passed a bill to phase out Mississippi’s income tax, which Republican Gov. Tate Reeves signed into law. 
Mississippi is currently reducing its income tax rate to 4% from a previously passed tax cut being phased in. Beginning next year, the new law will reduce that rate by .25% over four years until it reaches 3%. In 2031, the tax will  be reduced incrementally each year as certain revenue “growth triggers” are met. 
Lawmakers have predicted that the income tax could be eliminated in roughly 13 years if the revenue growth triggers are met.  
As state lawmakers cut taxes, they are facing tough funding choices. During the 2026 session, the Legislature adopted a $7.4 billion state budget in which the Division of Medicaid was funded through excess cash reserves. Legislative leaders said they did not give public teachers a large pay raise because of the Division of Medicaid’s funding needs. 
Fitch told reporters that she would be “very diligent” and look for the “correct revenue stream” to responsibly speed up the elimination of the income tax. 
Attorney General Lynn Fitch is greeted by supporters before discussing her campaign for governor during an event at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/ Mississippi Today
“If you’re not paying your personal income tax, that is a huge benefit for you,” Fitch said. “That’s a huge benefit for the workforce as we attract businesses.” 
Fitch is the first woman to serve as attorney general in Mississippi. If elected, she would be the first female governor in the state’s history. 
With Fitch as the state’s top legal officer, attorneys from her office argued the landmark  Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision that overturned national abortion rights, and now abortion is almost entirely banned in Mississippi and in multiple other states. 
Fitch’s role in that case has made her a lightning rod for supporters of abortion rights, as well as a champion of the anti-abortion movement. Mississippi has some of the worst maternal health and infant mortality outcomes in the nation. 
She told supporters at the Jackson event that she wants to promote policies that improve Mississippi’s health outcomes. When asked how she would do that, she pointed to her record on suing pharmacy benefit managers on behalf of the state. PBMs oversee prescription drug plans for employer and have been accused of driving up drug prices.
“I don’t mind going after these big companies like the pharmacy benefit managers who are not doing the right thing,” Fitch said. 
Wednesday’s event in Jackson was the first of a multiple appearances across the state over three days where Fitch will tout her plans and qualifications to succeed Reeves, who is constitutionally prohibited from seeking a third term in 2027.
Fitch, a Holly Springs native, was elected to two terms as state treasurer before being elected attorney general in 2019. She began her legal career in the attorney general’s office as a special assistant attorney general. 
She has also served as executive director of the Mississippi State Personnel Board, worked in private practice and was deputy executive director of the Mississippi Department of Employment Security.
Fitch joins what’s expected to be a crowded Republican primary for governor. So far, Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson and former House Speaker Philip Gunn have announced they’re running for governor. 
Other possible contenders for governor are state Auditor Shad White, Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann, former U.S. Rep. Gregg Harper, businessman and radio talk show host Gerard Gibert and billionaire businessman Tommy Duff.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Senate panel approves Blumenthal’s Kids Online Safety Act
description: The unanimous vote moves KOSA to the Senate floor. But lawmakers will need to work out differences with the House, which passed its own bill.
text:
At a May rally in Washington, advocates supporting the Senate’s version of a bipartisan kids online safety bill pleaded with U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, to once again bring it before his committee, as Congress’ schedule was filling up fast ahead of election season.
Cruz, a supporter of the bill, vowed to do so, without a firm commitment on the date. Dozens of attendees, including mothers who attribute their children’s death to social media harms, chanted, “Mark it up, mark it up!” U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., one of the authors of the Kids Online Safety Act, or KOSA, joined in on those calls.
Three months later, the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation took it up. At a Wednesday hearing, the panel voted to once again approve KOSA through a unanimous voice vote, sending it back to the Senate floor for consideration.

U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks at a May rally in support of the Senate version of the Kids Online Safety Act. Attendees pressed Cruz to hold a vote on KOSA in the Senate Commerce committee. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

It’s another major step forward for the legislation, but it sets up a clash with the House, which recently passed its own version as part of the Kids Internet and Digital Safety (KIDS) Act. Blumenthal and proponents of the Senate bill argue the latter is a watered-down alternative.
“I think we have enormously powerful momentum,” Blumenthal said in an interview from the U.S. Capitol following Wednesday’s committee vote. “The House passed a version which is basically toothless and a pale imitation of what we need in KOSA to protect children.”
“The parents who were at the committee meeting today are going to be once again our most important advocates,” he continued, “and their plea should not be turned aside or denied.”
The Senate’s bill, sponsored by Blumenthal and GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, has gone through a number of revisions to gain more support over the years. It’s also been marked up and passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee a few times. KOSA got closest in 2024 when it passed the Senate in an overwhelming 91-3 vote, but the House never took it up.
But because it didn’t fully make it through Congress at the time, the bill started from square one at the start of the current session. Getting out of committee is the first step in the process.
KOSA was one of five bills focused on online safety for minors, as well as some related to artificial intelligence and age verification, on the docket at Wednesday’s hearing. The committee postponed taking up a larger AI legislative framework at the markup and plans to do so after the August recess.
The Senate version of KOSA aims to put in place stricter settings by allowing children and parents to disable addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay of videos, enable privacy settings and opt out of algorithmic recommendations. The platforms that would need to comply include social media, online video games, messaging sites and video streaming services.
The “duty of care” section, to hold platforms legally responsible for mitigating certain harms to minors, has come under scrutiny before, though it has been revised and narrowed in newer iterations of the Senate bill.
It’s one of the central tenets of KOSA that’s divided the lower and upper houses of Congress. It would require companies to “exercise reasonable care” when designing a platform to mitigate a defined list of potential harms to minors, including certain mental health disorders, substance use disorders and physical and sexual abuse.
Supporters of the Senate bill argue a duty of care is needed to hold major tech and social media companies accountable. Blackburn, a KOSA sponsor who sits on the Senate Commerce Committee, commended the work of parent advocates who have helped her and Blumenthal work on the bill for several years. “They have turned their grief into action,” she said.

Parent groups advocate for the Kids Online Safety Act at a Mother’s Day rally held in D.C. on May 12, 2026. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

During the hour-long hearing, senators on the committee applauded the work of the parents and families who have devoted time to the issue. One senator asked if they could recognize that work by having parents stand up and say the name of their child.
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, had an amendment to attach his bill, which seeks to incentivize tech companies to advertise mental health resources and services for minors. But he withdrew it so the committee could pass a clean version of KOSA, with the hopes of getting his legislation into a larger online safety package.
Still, challenges lie ahead for KOSA. As online protections for children remain a priority for Congress, the House and Senate are split over how to address the issue. If KOSA clears the full Senate again, lawmakers in both chambers will need to work through the differences.
“While there are important differences between the Senate and House versions of KOSA, the bill’s success in both chambers shows that our leaders in Congress agree far more than they disagree when it comes to kids’ online safety — including that states should be able to continue to pass and enforce their own laws,” Fairplay Executive Director Josh Golin said in a statement. “We call on leaders in both chambers to work together to pass the strongest possible version of KOSA this year.”
On top of that, scheduling remains a major hurdle.
At the end of the week, the Senate will join the House in a month-long recess. Congress returns in September with only a few weeks to address priority bills, including must-pass legislation to fund the government after Sept. 30. Lawmakers will then be out again through the November midterm elections. That leaves Congress with a short lame-duck session before the holidays and the end of another session.
Critics of the Senate legislation have voiced concerns around free speech. Criticism has also stemmed from some LGBTQ+ advocates who argue it could ultimately limit access to critical services for vulnerable children and communities. (Other LGBTQ+ groups have dropped their opposition after a past revision to address concerns).
Groups such as the Center for Democracy and Technology and Electronic Frontier Foundation argue the Senate’s KOSA would incentivize age verification systems and say Congress should instead pursue legislation more focused on things like data privacy and consumer protection.
“Legislative proposals that would enact meaningful data minimization restrictions and other data privacy protections either for everyone or, at a minimum, beginning with enhancing protections for children would help to address some of the root causes animating the concerns for kids’ safety online,” the Center for Democracy and Technology wrote in a letter ahead of the hearing to Cruz and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee.
Meanwhile, the House passed a package of online safety reforms in July that included a version of KOSA that removes the controversial duty of care provision. U.S. Rep. Jim Himes was Connecticut’s only House member to vote for the KIDS Act.
Supporters of the House bill have taken issue with the duty of care, citing potential First Amendment and censorship concerns.
But Blumenthal has been vehemently opposed to the House’s efforts, noting that KOSA is focused on design and is “content neutral.” He has previously said it would not allow enforcers like the Federal Trade Commission or state attorneys general to sue over content or speech.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong is also opposed to the House version of KOSA.
After the House bill passed last month, Blumenthal and Blackburn called it “dead on arrival.”
“The Senate cannot and will not accept the version that the House passed earlier,” Blackburn said at Wednesday’s hearing. “It’s a very pale imitation of the Senate version and therefore it’s a pale imitation of Big Tech accountability. The parents have waited a long time.”
Blumenthal echoed that sentiment.
“I’m very hopeful that our conversations with leadership as well as with members of the House will be productive,” Blumenthal said. “We’re going to work as long as hard as possible to get it done as quickly as possible.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: FERC signs off on new gas pipeline to go across Mississippi
description: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission announced the approval of the project Friday, reasoning that the new infrastructure would serve a need for additional gas transportation in the southeastern United States.
text:
A federal agency has approved a set of proposals to build a new natural gas pipeline system that will span the width of Mississippi.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission announced the approval Friday, reasoning that the new infrastructure would serve a need for additional gas transportation in the southeastern United States. The decision came despite protests from environmental groups and landowners in the impacted states, which also include Alabama and Georgia.
The new pipeline, a joint project between Tennessee Gas Pipeline Co. and Southern Natural Gas Co., will take gas from an existing network and send it from Greenville across Mississippi to Butler, Alabama. The line will go through Washington, Humphreys, Holmes, Attala, Leake, Neshoba, Newton, Lauderdale and Clarke counties. New compressor stations will also be built in Humphreys, Attala and Lauderdale counties.
The 206 miles of new pipeline will provide up to 1.5 billion cubic feet a day of added transportation  capacity, according to FERC. The $1.7-billion project is set to create 750 temporary jobs and 15 permanent positions, according to Kinder Morgan, the applicants’ parent company.
Credit: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
Environmental groups, including in Mississippi, expressed concern over the more than 2,000 water bodies the pipeline’s route crosses, as well as surrounding wildlife habitat and air quality. The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians, whose reservation in Neshoba County is adjacent to the pipeline’s route, said it received limited consultation over the proposal and told Mississippi Today it didn’t think there was enough consideration of impacts to historical artifacts. 
“The pipeline would split my property, and I do not believe the company has offered fair options for landowners other than a one-time payment,” Trevor Langston, a Leake County property owner, wrote in a recent comment submitted to FERC. “That payment does not adequately account for the long-term loss of use, value, and impact to the property over the years.
“This land has been passed down through my family, and we do not wish to lose it to a gas line.”
FERC, the federal body in charge of regulating interstate transport of energy sources, such as natural gas, said the pipeline’s route largely overlaps with or is near existing rights-of-way. The commission, in the July 31 order, wrote that the companies “have taken appropriate steps to minimize adverse economic impacts on landowners and surrounding communities affected by the” pipeline project.
“The Commission finds that there is no basis to conclude that property sales, demand, and development decisions would be significantly impacted on land surrounding proposed project facilities,” FERC wrote. “As for use and enjoyment of property, we find that Applicants’ route design, co-location, as well as the mitigation measures prescribed in this order adequately address these impacts.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Governors and lawmakers say they’re getting serious about states’ rights
description: At major gatherings in recent days, state authority was a major focus. Govs and lawmakers agreed the federal government has grown too powerful
text:
OKLAHOMA CITY — State leaders of both parties say the federal government — including the president — wields too much power, and they want to see more authority returned to the states.
Bipartisan groups of governors and state lawmakers held major gatherings in recent days where issues of state authority became a major focus. They agreed the federal government had grown too powerful and pushed for states to maintain control over elections, energy, education and other issues. 
During President Donald Trump’s second term, state leaders have heightened focus on federalism, the uniquely American system created by the framers of the Constitution to share power between Washington, D.C., and the states.
But governors and lawmakers said it requires bipartisan cooperation across the states to reset the balance of power.
Utah Republican Gov. Spencer Cox said it’s easy for state leaders to champion states’ rights when the opposing political party controls the levers of federal power. But a truer test of federalism likely lies in how states approach it when their own party controls Washington.  
“And that’s why I’m proud to have Republicans who still believe it even when the president is doing things that they want,” Cox told Stateline.
Cox, who was in Oklahoma City this weekend for the National Governors Association summer meeting, has long championed a rebalancing of state and federal powers. He and other leaders argue that a renewed focus on federalism could help lower the national political temperature. By shifting more political decisions to the states, some officials envision a nation less subject to blue-red swings that change the entire course of federal law enforcement, environmental policy and business regulation. 
In Utah, state officials are looking to lead a national movement to bring more authority back to the states. Cox said too many political issues have become nationalized, driving vitriol and polarization as a sharply-divided Congress acts on few policy issues. 
“That means that the president becomes even more important than they were ever meant to be,” Cox said, “and then these big elections every four years feel kind of life or death.”
Cox said recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions have empowered states. But he said liberal and conservative states alike must push to take more authority from the federal government. 
“We have to demand it,” he said. “We have to talk to our members of Congress about it, let them know that we don’t want the feds playing such a major role.”
The bipartisan association of governors is in the process of updating its internal policies on federalism. Last revised years ago, NGA’s current policies speak about challenges such as unfunded mandates, in which the federal government requires states to meet new rules without providing money to achieve them.
The updated policy will address pressing issues such as artificial intelligence regulation — an ongoing state-federal conflict over jurisdiction — and the primacy of each state to control its own National Guard — an issue that sparked major concerns about state sovereignty last year.
The revised policy will remind governors of the inherent authority of states in pushing back against the federal government, said John Dinan, a professor and chair of the department of politics & international affairs at Wake Forest University in North Carolina. Dinan, a federalism scholar, is consulting with NGA on its federalism work. 
Dinan said both political parties have leaned on federalism principles opportunistically over the years — depending on which party enjoyed national power. But now, he sees strong agreement between Republicans and Democrats to strengthen the role of states.
“It’s attracting interest from people across the ideological spectrum,” he said.
States say they should lead
In Oklahoma City, governors sought to showcase a bipartisanship that has nearly vanished in national politics. 
Governors said their states could compete with each other, experiment with programs and adopt wildly distinct policies — without being divisive or disrespectful. 
In particular, Oklahoma Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt and Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore emphasized their close friendship. Moore wore cowboy boots as he assumed leadership of the national association from Stitt at the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum.
In opening the meeting, Stitt recalled President Abraham Lincoln’s second inaugural address, given near the end of the Civil War. The 16th president famously pushed for national unity by calling for “malice toward none” and “charity for all.”
“Think about that,” Stitt said. “After years of war, Lincoln didn’t focus on settling scores or getting revenge. He focused on putting our country back together. His commitment to unity saved our country.”
Like Lincoln, Stitt said the nation’s governors don’t shy away from fractures and disagreements. They debate and share ideas, while also embracing the role of diverse policies across the states. 
“When states lead, America succeeds,” Stitt said. “There’s not a one-size-fits-all for a country as diverse as America.”
As one example, several governors pointed to the recent dramatic climb in Mississippi’s student reading and language scores.
“Mississippi really turned the entire country around when it comes to the science of reading,” said North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat. “And that was because one state went out there and figured something else out and we’re now all aggressively copying it.”
Stein, along with Vermont Republican Gov. Phil Scott, have been working on revising the association’s federalism policies. Both of those states were among a coalition that recently sued the federal government over attempts to withhold federal disaster aid. Trump officials sought to condition more than $1 billion in funding on states moving away from electronic ballot counting ahead of November’s midterms. 
“Which has nothing to do with disaster recovery and also offends federalism because elections administration is to be left to the states,” Stein said in Oklahoma City. “The federal government shouldn’t be dictating how states conduct their elections.”
‘We don’t want a king’
Just days before the governors met, thousands of state lawmakers assembled in Chicago for the National Conference of State Legislatures annual summit.
At that meeting, lawmakers of both parties also emphasized the important role of states in reining in a federal government they say has grown too powerful. 
Michelle Woods, vice president of the state-federal affairs division at NCSL, characterized the current moment as one of the most consequential ever for state and federal relationships. She cited executive orders coming from the White House and upheaval in federal spending and policy. 
“Federalism is no longer simply a constitutional principle that we’re going to debate,” she said during a panel discussion on the topic. “It’s the reality that state legislators are navigating every day.”
Maryland state Del. David Moon, the Democratic majority leader, kicked off his remarks on the panel noting how his state had to pivot to “basic debt collection” from the federal government at a time when it has sought to punish blue states and withhold previously approved federal funds. 
Moon pushed for legislation in Annapolis this year, which Moore signed into law in April, that allows the state to place liens on federal property or withhold revenue payments to Washington if officials determine the feds are withholding funds in defiance of court decisions.
Despite current high-profile clashes with the feds, Moon said he was optimistic that the nation could return to more traditional state-federal relationships after Trump leaves office. 
“I think we are witnessing an outlier moment with respect to federalism and some of these interesting expansions of federal power, “ he said. “…But the truth of the matter is, whether we get there is really determined by all of us.”
Utah state Rep. Ken Ivory, a Republican, said state leaders nationwide must start by educating themselves of the constitutional limits of federal power. He said orientation for newly elected lawmakers often teaches how to navigate their capitols or enroll in state insurance — rather than emphasizing the legal fundamentals.
“If we’re going to restore federalism, we have to know very clearly what state jurisdiction is versus the limits of federal power,” he said. “We have to know our powers to do that — to push back.”
Ivory leads Utah’s Federalism Commission, which lawmakers hope will connect state officials and agency staff from across the country to bring more authority back to the states. He said state Republicans and Democrats must stand together on states’ rights — even when they strongly disagree on individual state policies.
“We felt very strongly that if federalism is purely a partisan exercise, it’s not federalism, and it’s just seeking advantage, gaining advantage, and it actually undermines the concept,” he said. “And so, we kind of have a saying that we don’t want a red king or a blue king. We don’t want a king.” 
This story was first published Aug. 5, 2026 by Stateline.

title: Michigan Republicans rally behind ticket after divisive gubernatorial primary
description: Republicans gathered in Macomb County Wednesday for a Unity Luncheon, stirring up support heading into the general election cycle the morning after the primary election, which included a contentious GOP gubernatorial contest. “To those who supported me, thank you. Those who didn’t, I’m going to continue to work to earn your trust each and every […]
text:
Michael Bouchard, the GOP nominee for Michigan's 10th Congressional District, at the GOP Unity Luncheon. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Republicans gathered in Macomb County Wednesday for a Unity Luncheon, stirring up support heading into the general election cycle the morning after the primary election, which included a contentious GOP gubernatorial contest.
“To those who supported me, thank you. Those who didn’t, I’m going to continue to work to earn your trust each and every single day,” said U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Twp.), who won that competitive gubernatorial primary. “Today marks Michigan’s comeback.”
U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township), the conference chair of the Republican Party, said to the crowd, “I’m here to tell you, we are here to put Michigan back on the map, and that’s exactly what we intend to do with some of our candidates today in Congress.”
U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) speaks at the GOP Unity Luncheon. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Senate nominee Mike Rogers speaks to supporters at the GOP Unity Luncheon. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. The GOP Unity Luncheon was held in Macomb County the day after the primary election. Aug. 5, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. 
The event was hosted by U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who was unopposed in his primary, and included speeches by James, as well as Attorney General and Secretary of State nominees Doug Lloyd and Anthony Forlini. Also speaking were congressional nominees Terri DeBoer, Ethan Baker and Michael Bouchard, nominees in the 3rd, 11th and 10th Districts, respectively, as well as Thomas Smith, who won the 8th District despite suspending his campaign in mid-July.
“Love of country is why we win. It’s because we know that our country is at a crossroads,” Bouchard said. “We stand for American ideals, and in November we will deliver real solutions for our country.”
Others in the crowd included Republican state legislators Sen. Ruth Johnson (R-Holly) and Rep. Donni Steele (R-Orion Township), as well as Oakland County GOP Chair Vance Patrick, who was an ardent supporter of Perry Johnson in his failed gubernatorial primary bid.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Edwards’ abrupt withdrawal leaves western NC Republicans scrambling
description: As the dust settles on U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards’ 3:35 a.m. withdrawal from his reelection campaign, western N.C. Republicans and observers are gaming out the best option to replace him on the November ballot. The replacement will be chosen by the NCGOP’s 11th Congressional District Executive Committee. It’s expected to meet next week to make […]
text:
Republican Congressman Chuck Edwards holds local town hall meeting with constituents. (Photo Credit: Sean Rayford/Getty Images)As the dust settles on U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards’ 3:35 a.m. withdrawal from his reelection campaign, western N.C. Republicans and observers are gaming out the best option to replace him on the November ballot.
The replacement will be chosen by the NCGOP’s 11th Congressional District Executive Committee. It’s expected to meet next week to make its choice, according to NCGOP Chairman Jason Simmons.
The typical choice in a situation like this would be a sitting state lawmaker in or near the 11th Congressional District. Several powerful lawmakers come to mind, says Western Carolina political scientist Chris Cooper, including longtime Sens. Ralph Hise, R-Mitchell, Kevin Corbin, R-Macon, and Tim Moffitt, R-Henderson, who previously represented the area in the state House. Other potential choices could include Rep. Jake Johnson, R-Polk, Rep. Karl Gillespie, R-Macon, and Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson.
The question, Cooper says, is which one wants to trade a safe legislative seat to take on a strong, well-funded Democratic opponent in a district that’s trending blue in what’s already likely to be a tough year for Republicans.
Two North Carolina US House races are now toss-ups, top forecaster says

“This is not the same district it was last cycle or the cycle before,” Cooper said. “It’s far from a guarantee that a Republican is going to win this seat. They’ve got to uproot their life. They’ve got to not just campaign, but they’ve got to fundraise when they’re already behind the eight ball.”
Cooper said the committee could also choose one of the two primary opponents Edwards defeated in 2022 and 2024.
“It’s very possible that the folks in power positions in the Senate don’t want to lose that power, and the party’s left with somebody with not a lot else to do,” Cooper said.
But Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer doesn’t think western N.C. Republicans will have any shortage of hopefuls drawn by the allure of Washington power.
“If anybody’s got a friend or an ally or an acquaintance on that committee, they’re probably going to be vying for it,” Bitzer said. “It’s probably easier to put the list together of who may not be considering it than considering it.”
‘It’s a very short runway’
NC Newsline reached out Wednesday morning to Hise, Moffitt, Corbin and Johnson to ask whether they’re interested in running to replace Edwards.
Corbin was the first to respond. He said he had “a ton of phone calls” from people urging him to run for the spot.
“I appreciate the people’s thoughts. I’m considering it,” Corbin said. “I’m still trying to process it like everyone else.”
“If I throw my name in the ring, I would run to win, so I have to decide: Do I want to go to Washington? And so that would affect my family and my time at home and all that. So I need to talk with my family about that,” Corbin said.
He said he also feels responsible to his district, and he isn’t eager to give up the seniority he has in the N.C. Senate.
Whoever is selected, Corbin noted, will have to start from scratch on fundraising as well as campaigning.
“It’s a very short runway to consider,” Corbin said, “and that’s all part of the decision.”
None of the other potential candidates NC Newsline contacted responded by publication time.
What to watch for
If Republicans can secure a strong replacement candidate, Bitzer says, they can probably keep the race at status quo. But Democrats will benefit if the new campaign isn’t operational by Labor Day.
“You’ve got to go from zero to a congressional campaign in a very quick time period,” Bitzer said.
Cooper’s watching who’s chosen to run the new campaign.
“It’s not just who gets the nod, but who their consultant is,” Cooper said “Paul Shumaker is running Edwards’ campaign. He’s obviously the most seasoned Republican consultant in North Carolina. If the next candidate gets a Paul Shumaker, then they’re going to be able to hit the ground running quicker, right?”
Bitzer’s waiting to see whether RNC money will come in to help the new candidate. While the GOP has a strong fundraising advantage nationally, it also has a lot of seats it needs to defend this cycle.
“I think the money flow will be the big signal,” Bitzer said. “I think that that’s an early indication of is this a viable, hard-fought campaign, or do they see resources needing to go to defend other seats?”
