text:
Kansas State Board of Education candidates, from left, Destry Brown, Jean Clifford and Jim McMullen prevail in unofficial Aug. 4 primary results. (Kansas Reflector composite from photos submitted by the candidates)TOPEKA — Unofficial GOP primary results as of Wednesday morning place an attorney, a retired superintendent and a former Kansas Board of Education member one step closer to overseeing K-12 public schools.
While Republicans Jim McMullen, Destry Brown and Jean Clifford consider next steps ahead of the November general election, their primary opponents reflect on their campaigns.
Seven Republican candidates appeared on the Kansas primary ballot on Aug. 4 across three district races. For two other seats, the Republican candidate was uncontested. No Democrats faced a primary opponent.
The primary results set the state for a Republican and Democrat to face off in November for each of the five open seats.
Kansas voters reelect five of 10 education board seats every two years. This year, none of the incumbents chose to seek reelection. Because most members whose terms won’t end until 2028 are Democrats, the November election could flip the board’s GOP majority.
 
Eastern district
In the race to represent most of Johnson and Miami counties on the state board, McMullen, an attorney and former Blue Valley school district board member from Johnson County, prevailed with 64% of votes and all precincts reporting.
“I’ve been beating the same drum for five years,” McMullen said. “When I was on the Blue Valley school board, at least the Republican voters, they know I’m not really a mystery.”
His core message, he said, is promoting “foundational” education, a view he plans to continue campaigning on.
“That foundational purpose is to develop students to be great speakers, to be great readers and to be great writers,” he said.
He will face Amy Diediker, an Olathe Democrat and former teacher, in November.
The 1776 Project PAC, a conservative organization promoting state and school board candidates in multiple states, endorsed McMullen and opponents of Brown and Clifford.
His primary opponent, Steve Roberts, a former math teacher and state board member and current driver for Uber and Lyft, called the 1776 Project PAC’s endorsement of McMullen decisive.
“The lesson I think I’m taking away,” Roberts said, “is that money is the No. 1 factor in winning elections these days.”
Roberts has lost bids for state treasurer, Congress and the Blue Valley school district board within the last four years. He said his career in politics is over and plans to retire to the classroom as a teacher.
Both candidates have received criticism over controversial speech. Roberts used the N-word in a state board meeting in April 2013, and the Blue Valley school board in 2022 stripped McMullen’s vice president title over his social media posts against transgender advocacy. He lost reelection in 2025.
 
Southeastern district
Brown, the former Fort Scott school district superintendent, received 43% of votes to represent the southeast corner of Kansas on the state board. Behind him, Kristian Gerken, a Paola school board member endorsed by the 1776 Project PAC, took 36%. Renee Slinkard, a retired teacher, received 21%.
Brown said his concern with empowering local control resonated with voters. He wants to take that message to the northern part of his district.
“​​It’s kind of hard to decide what is the best strategy,” he said. “But I’ve had a lot of volunteers helping me down here in southeast Kansas, and I need to work on getting more people involved in the north.”
He will challenge Heather Guernsey, a Chanute Democrat, in November.
Slinkard hoped to involve parents in education more and promote patriotic curricula. She did not respond to a phone call and text message Tuesday night from Kansas Reflector requesting comment.
Gerken did not reply to emails and Facebook messages on July 13 and Tuesday night from Kansas Reflector requesting comment.
 
Western district
After a close race all Tuesday night, the district on Wednesday morning reported 51% for Clifford, a former state board member, retired Air Force attorney and Garden City resident, and 49% for Kelly Ancar, a nurse and nursing instructor from Hays.
Though only 772 votes determined Clifford as the likely winner, with all precincts reporting, the margin doesn’t demand a close-race audit or recount under the state’s standards.
Clifford’s campaign focused on improving local control, particularly in her district, the most rural and geographically largest state board district.
“I am grateful for the unofficial results from yesterday’s Republican primary and honored by the confidence the voters of District 5 have placed in me,” she said in an email.
Ancar said parents responded to her views on increasing parental involvement and teachers supported her plan for addressing behavioral problems in the classroom.
“I talked to a lot of teachers who shared that dealing with behaviors in the classroom was their No. 1 problem,” she said. “Some other states have gone to a three-strike rule, where if you have to remove a child from the classroom three times, there needs to be an alternative plan put in place.”
Clifford will face Lorie Wood, a Dresden Democrat and former teacher.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: As prediction markets grow, CT comptroller warns of ‘dark side’
description: Sean Scanlon's report found the platforms have led to gambling addiction and insider trading, and have been marketed to people under 21.
text:
The rapid rise of prediction markets has kicked off a wave of regulation in states across the country. The platforms are also driving deeper concerns about their potential economic impact, according to an analysis released this week by Connecticut officials. 
In its latest monthly economic update, the office of the state comptroller dedicated a section to prediction markets, online platforms that allow users to buy and sell contracts guessing the outcome of future events.
These platforms — which include Kalshi, Polymarket US, and smaller ones like ProphetX and Crypto.com — are rapidly gaining popularity, enabling people to buy contracts on everything from the outcome of dating shows to the results of local elections and the winners of sports events. 
As consumer use of the platforms has become increasingly common in Connecticut, Comptroller Sean Scanlon said he wanted to examine the role that plays in “shaping our daily life and economy.”
The report offers a short overview and basic primer on prediction markets, explaining how the markets work and their growth in recent years. It also points to a “dark side” of their rapid growth: a rise in gambling addictions among young men; marketing to people under 21; and the prevalence of insider trading. 
The study comes as state officials weigh regulation. Some lawmakers say the platforms are circumventing state gambling laws, particularly laws prohibiting those under 21 from gambling. 
The platforms have pushed back, arguing they’re entirely different from gambling, operating instead more like stocks. Not only are they legal, but regulation should fall only to the federal government, more specifically the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the platforms argue.
This tension is leading to a wave of litigation over the matter, including in Connecticut, which called for prediction market platforms to cease unlicensed online gambling operations in the state last year.
The comptroller’s report notes that as questions over the legality continue, and as state and federal lawmakers call for legislation to regulate their activity, people should understand how the markets affect Connecticut’s economy. 
Prediction markets are growing rapidly—but they come with drawbacks
While prediction markets have existed for decades, the latest iteration popularized by platforms like Kalshi, Polymarket and Robinhood are operating in ways that are less regulated and broader in impact.
The spread of prediction markets in sports is of particular concern to the state, which has closely regulated its own sports betting market. Connecticut legalized online gambling and sports betting five years ago. Under the 2021 law, businesses involved in sports betting must be licensed with the state and follow state regulations. 
Only three organizations are allowed to operate online gaming in Connecticut, including FanDuel (through a partnership with Mohegan Sun), Draft Kings (which is affiliated with Foxwoods Casino) and Fanatics (which works with the Connecticut Lottery).
Prediction market platforms, state officials argue, are violating state law by continuing to operate in Connecticut. 
Last December, the Department of Consumer Protection issued cease and desist letters to Kalshi, Robinhood and Crypto.com, instructing them to halt online gambling and sports betting operations in the state and adding that the sites were violating the state’s requirements that a person be 21 or older to participate in sports betting. 
“None of these entities possess a license to offer wagering in our state, and even if they did, their contracts violate numerous other state laws and policies,” DCP Commissioner Bryan T. Cafferelli argued at the time.
Kalshi countered by launching a lawsuit, arguing the platform has federal protections that allow it to continue to operate in Connecticut. The plaintiffs also said the state was incorrect in describing Kalshi’s services as gambling, saying the platform is instead trading a protected derivative — a form of traded contract like a stock, commodity or currency. 
Shortly after the lawsuit was filed, a federal judge temporarily blocked Connecticut officials from enforcing the gambling order. The case is still working its way through the court system.
Connecticut is part of a growing wave of resistance to prediction markets
As the platforms push back on state-level efforts to enact regulation, it’s creating new rifts between states and the federal government. 
Earlier this year, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced legal action against a handful of states, including Connecticut, saying the federal government has exclusive power to regulate prediction markets. The Trump administration has largely embraced the practice, with crackdowns on the markets limited to certain instances of insider trading.
As of May, some 16 states were involved in litigation over prediction markets. Last week, New York announced that it was suing Kalshi for violating the state’s gambling laws. 
Congressional efforts to enact new regulations on prediction markets have also faced hurdles. Multiple bills, including one introduced by U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal in March, have stalled. 
State officials in Connecticut say the markets have yet to produce a clear benefit, pointing to data showing very few participants win much money. The comptroller’s report highlighted a May 2026 Wall Street Journal analysis that found a small number of accounts on Polymarket and Kalshi actually win. In the case of Polymarket, 0.1% of accounts raked in 67% of profits generated through the online contracts.
The comptroller’s report goes on to say that the gap in profits highlights how the platforms are designed to benefit “sophisticated pros and trading firms, while casual traders are at a large disadvantage.”
But broader impacts on the state economy are less clear. Whether prediction markets are displacing the money generated by state-sanctioned online gambling and sports betting, a source of more than $110 million in tax revenue for Connecticut in 2025, is not yet visible in the data, according to the comptroller’s report.
Scanlon said the issue is worth keeping a close eye on. “Prediction markets are literally everywhere and are used to bet on anything which, to me, warrants a lot more attention from government but also all of us in society generally,” he said.

Free online program will help Delaware businesses understand market-entry strategies, financing options and commercial opportunities across the region
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware businesses interested in expanding internationally can learn about emerging opportunities in West Africa during a free World Trade Center Delaware program Monday, Aug. 10.
The August edition of the organization’s Global Power Hour, “West Africa: Opportunities for U.S. Exporters,” will be held virtually from noon to 1 p.m. The executive-level discussion is designed for businesses that are considering exporting for the first time as well as companies seeking to expand an existing international presence.
The session will focus on practical opportunities for American exporters, particularly in French-speaking West African markets. Topics will include market-entry strategies, trade facilitation, export financing and tools businesses can use to reduce the financial and commercial risks associated with international sales.
World Trade Center Delaware serves as the state’s international business resource, connecting Delaware companies with trade experts, educational programs and business networks around the world. The organization also provides import and export assistance, market research, referrals and other resources for companies exploring global growth.
Understanding an unfamiliar market
Entering a foreign market can present significant opportunities, but businesses must also navigate regulatory requirements, payment risks, transportation challenges and differences in language and business practices.
The Global Power Hour is intended to give company leaders a clearer understanding of those challenges before they commit substantial time or money to an overseas expansion.
The discussion will address opportunities in sectors including agribusiness, food products, logistics and related services. Participants also will learn about financing and risk-mitigation tools that may help exporters protect payments, secure working capital and manage transactions with international buyers.
Regional experience
The featured speaker will be Eric Schneider, founder and managing director of RéseauLink LLC, an international trade and development firm focused on commercial relationships between the United States and French-speaking West Africa.
Schneider helps businesses with market-entry planning, export readiness, regulatory compliance, business matchmaking, buyer engagement, and investment development. He works between the United States and Côte d’Ivoire and combines regional experience with relationships in the private sector and government.
A graduate of Fordham University, Schneider previously served as a Fulbright English teaching assistant in Côte d’Ivoire and as a bilingual program analyst for the U.S. African Development Foundation. He also received a U.S. Department of State-funded Mandela Washington Fellowship Reciprocal Exchange Grant.
A potential path for smaller businesses
International trade is sometimes viewed as an option primarily available to large corporations. However, export financing, trade counseling and local assistance programs can also help smaller companies determine whether their products or services are appropriate for overseas markets.
World Trade Center Delaware’s program will offer businesses a starting point for evaluating opportunities, identifying potential partners and understanding the preparation required before pursuing customers in West Africa.
The organization said the session is intended to provide information participants can use when deciding whether international expansion fits their company’s goals and capabilities.

title: McKinney unseats Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District
description: Michigan State Rep. Donavan McKinney has emerged victorious in the race for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, lodging a successful challenge against incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit). The Associated Press called the race for McKinney at 9:55 a.m. Wednesday. Unofficial results show McKinney received 51.9% of the vote, while Thanedar received[...]
text:
U.S. House of Representatives candidate and current state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks with a supporter ahead of his speech at a rally hosted by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-Vermont) at Mumford High School in Detroit, Mich. May 3, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceMichigan State Rep. Donavan McKinney has emerged victorious in the race for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, lodging a successful challenge against incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit).
The Associated Press called the race for McKinney at 9:55 a.m. Wednesday. Unofficial results show McKinney received 51.9% of the vote, while Thanedar received 48.1% with 99% of votes counted.
Michigan’s 13th Congressional District serves as a stronghold for Democrats and is made up of portions of Detroit, and its suburbs, including Allen Park, Hamtramck, Romulus and Wyandotte.
While Thanedar had the backing of U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), McKinney was endorsed by multiple progressive members of the Congressional Black Caucus, including Reps. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn) and Summer Lee (D-Pa.). McKinney also had the support of fellow Detroit-area Rep. Rashida Tlaib and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont).
Thanedar issued a statement on Facebook congratulating McKinney on the win.


“I want to congratulate Representative Donavan McKinney on a hard fought race. It was a tough election cycle and, in the end, the voters of the 13th District chose him to represent them moving forward,” Thanedar said. “It was the honor of my life to represent the 13th District in the United States Congress. I’m proud of all the work we did, from solving over 4300 constituent cases, to securing $45 million in funding for projects in every single part of the district, to leading the fight against Trump and his administration. I look forward to serving out the remainder of my term and wish Representative McKinney the best.”

U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Detroit, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party’s convention in Detroit on Feb. 22, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
McKinney’s upset win also came despite Thanedar’s large cash advantage, with campaign finance reports indicating the incumbent congressman had raised $390,276 over the course of this campaign cycle, with $5 million cash on hand. McKinney, in contrast, had raised $1.37 million, with $142,853 in cash on hand.
McKinney is almost assured to be elected to Congress in the reliably Democratic district. The only Republican candidate, T.P. Nykoriak, was sentenced in 2016 to 16 months in federal prison for stealing U.S. savings bonds from a church.
The Democratic National Committee released a statement Wednesday congratulating McKinney on his primary victory. 
“As a Detroit native who is serving his community in the Michigan Legislature, Donavan has spent his career fighting to expand opportunity for working families, lower costs, improve healthcare, and invest in local neighborhoods,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said. “Michigan Democrats have nominated a proven champion who will always put the people of his district first. The DNC is ready to work alongside him to lower costs and deliver for working families.”
This is a breaking story and will be updated.

Mike Rogers in the November general election. Unofficial election results show that El-Sayed was on track to win the race over contender […]

Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. The Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was too close to call at the time he spoke. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – After a grueling primary that saw attacks from Republicans and establishment Democrats alike, Abdul El-Sayed has won in his race to be the party’s nominee to face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the November general election.
Unofficial election results show that El-Sayed was on track to win the race over contender and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham). The Associated Press called the race for El-Sayed at 9:58 a.m. Wednesday.
El-Sayed, holding his election night victory party in Detroit, addressed his supporters at about 1 a.m. and said it was too close to call at that point. 
“Know that the billionaires, corporations, and the special interests-they weren’t going to give up light. We all knew they were going to spend their money,” El-Sayed said. “We didn’t know they were going to spend $70 million of their money. We didn’t know that they were going to outspend us $11 to $1. And yet we’re still standing.”
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), who had dropped out of the race in early July, endorsed El-Sayed based on NBC News making the call just before 2 a.m.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” McMorrow said in a release. “Take it from me — this was a brutal primary. But whatever differences there were between the candidates in this race, those differences are nothing compared to the contrast in November. Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are banking on all of us being too bruised, too proud, and too hurt to come back together to beat them. Let’s prove them wrong.”
Shortly after the AP called the race for El-Sayed, Stevens issued a statement of congratulations and support for the general election fight ahead.
“I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate. He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” Stevens said. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan.”
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (center) speaks at meet and greet event in Detroit with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (right) and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina (left). July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
El-Sayed,  the son of Egyptian immigrants, would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected in November.
The win sets up a showdown with Rogers, who ran uncontested in the Republican primary. Rogers has been able to gather resources, mainly cash, while the Democrats battled it out wire-to-wire.
Rogers — who lost his 2024 race against current U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) — has $4.41 million cash on hand according to pre-primary FEC filings.
Meanwhile, between April 1 and June 30, El-Sayed raised $4.57 million and spent $4.37 million, leaving him with $2.7 million cash on hand.
El-Sayed has carved out a lane that had pundits calling him both a Barack Obama-type figure for the Democrats and Michigan’s less-socialist Zohran Mamadani. El-Sayed routinely disavowed the democratic socialist label that followed some of his key policy planks, saying he was a capitalist who sees its inherent flaws and wants to fix them.
He did so by centering his campaign on Medicare for All, new leadership in the U.S. Senate, overtures on anti-corporate election interference and on upending decades of U.S. foreign policy — namely, military and diplomatic aid to Israel. While Stevens focused on kitchen table issues like affordability, resistance to the administration of President Donald Trump and rebuilding the might of Michigan’s manufacturing, El-Sayed captured the growing disdain within the Democratic Party for corporate money in politics and the U.S. relationship with Israel. El-Sayed was the first candidate in the race to declare his belief that Israel had committed genocidal actions in its ongoing war with Hamas in Gaza.

(Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Attendees of former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed's election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., await results in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, the Democratic candidate for Michigan attorney general, attends former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed's election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
As Stevens played to the middle, El-Sayed banked on Michigan’s Democrats joining his new coalition, which included young college-aged or college-educated progressives, union members, climate and anti-fascist activists, and women who were quickly becoming the core of the resistance movement against Trump and the actions of his administration.
Until just the last few weeks before Tuesday’s primary, El-Sayed had been framed as the race’s underdog. Although progressives had shown some strength this year with wins in New York for Mamdani and others, a great many pundits and election observers questioned whether the growing wave of progressive populism could find a root in Michigan, often called the purplest of Midwestern swing states.
El-Sayed had some name recognition from his 2018 Democratic gubernatorial bid, which he lost decisively to current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and his time as a progressive celebrity working in the Bernie Sanders sphere of influencers and podcasters. That attracted people like Sanders to his campaign effort, but also more controversial figures like streamer and commentator Hasan Piker.
Vote Abdul poster in Ann Arbor. August 2, 2026 | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
Whitmer, who had given Stevens a late endorsement, was quick to offer congratulations to all of the Democratic nominees following El-Sayed’s win.
“Congratulations to Jocelyn Benson, Abdul El-Sayed, and every Democrat who won up and down the ballot. They’ve got my support as we fight like hell, together, to win in November,” Whitmer said in a press release. “There was a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing—Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state. We’re all united by our shared goal: getting things done for the people of Michigan. We know there’s so much on the line this November—health care, costs, our fundamental freedoms. That’s why it’s time to come together, get to work, and win in November.”
For many Dearborn voters that Michigan Advance spoke with Tuesday, there was great enthusiasm to give a progressive like El-Sayed a chance.
Jalen Black, a security guard, said he was most excited to cast his ballot for El-Sayed after voting for him in 2018. Black said El-Sayed’s politics are the closest to his, pointing to his stance against Israel’s actions in Gaza, progressive policies on housing and healthcare, and focus on getting money out of politics. 
Black, 27, told the Advance outside of the Dearborn Administrative Center after casting his ballot, that he thought the Democratic Party was “largely out of touch” with people. 
“I think it’s mostly pandering at this point,” Black said.
Black said that politicians and the media have been Islamophobic and “weirdly antagonistic” towards Dearborn, referencing the response to the Uncommitted movement in 2024.
“Instead of actually making the attempt to understand Dearborn,” Black said, they were just “pointing the finger and making it seem like they’re irrational”
Gabriella Dias, a video editor, was also casting her ballot at the Dearborn Administrative Center late Tuesday afternoon. She said she was most excited about the Senate race.
“I think it’s an important thing as human beings to care about each other, and I think the first step is in local politics,” Dias, 24, said.
Dias said her generation isn’t politically involved enough, so she has been trying to get her friends to vote.  She said she’s “disillusioned” the with American political system and was glad to see a candidate like El-Sayed.
“I think a lot of people like miss the opportunity to be civically involved because they think it’s very complicated. But I just think it’s an important thing to do, and I think it’s morally right to do so.”
Aside from Stevens, who was framed as the race’s frontrunner and establishment favorite from the minute she entered the race, El-Sayed also faced McMorrow, who was trying her best through the race to carve out her own name ID and set herself apart from Stevens and El-Sayed.
That proved difficult for McMorrow, who at times played progressive by attaching herself to issues that El-Sayed championed, including an aversion to corporate campaign donations, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee,which Stevens openly accepted, while also supporting Israel’s right to exist as the Jewish homeland in the Middle East.
McMorrow dropped out in July leaving the race to just Stevens and El-Sayed. The battle to the finish line that ensued was intense and at times politically bruising. Stevens attacked El-Sayed on everything from his commitment to transparency and his treatment of women throughout his political career. El-Sayed in turn hit Stevens on her corporate campaign cash and her acceptance of help from AIPAC — which spent more than $40 million on the race to boost her.
The race was coming down to the wire until last week when several polls began to indicate El-Sayed was moving ahead.
El-Sayed ultimately claimed victory Wednesday morning, advancing the progressives in a key state, and one that mimicked other Democratic socialist upsets seen across the nation in the 2026 cycle. He will now have to turn his attention not just to Rogers in the general election, but also to mending ties with Stevens’ supporters, as Democratic unity will be essential if the party wants to hold the seat being left vacant by the retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Bloomfield Township).
Minnah Arshad contributed to this story.

title: Plaintiffs drop four-year-old lawsuit that alleged misconduct in Alaska’s foster care system
description: A New York-based child welfare advocacy group has dropped a lawsuit against the Alaska Office of Children’s Services that alleged widespread misconduct by the state’s foster care system. A Better Childhood, which represented 5 foster care children in the federal suit, told the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals last week that it was seeking to […]
text:
(Getty Images)A New York-based child welfare advocacy group has dropped a lawsuit against the Alaska Office of Children’s Services that alleged widespread misconduct by the state’s foster care system.
A Better Childhood, which represented 5 foster care children in the federal suit, told the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals last week that it was seeking to voluntarily dismiss the case.
The firm’s motion was accepted by the court on July 31. 
The group of plaintiffs filed a class-action suit in 2022, alleging systemic problems within the foster care system — including chronic understaffing, overburdened caseworkers and failure to find adequate placements — were creating a danger to children. 
Judge Sharon Gleason presided over an 11-day trial late last year and ruled against the plaintiffs, finding none had standing to bring the case and that none of the plaintiffs were either harmed or faced risk of harm.  
A Better Childhood appealed Gleason’s decision to the 9th Circuit but chose to drop that appeal. It isn’t clear why. A Better Childhood did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday afternoon.
In other states, A Better Childhood has filed successful lawsuits that resulted in court orders requiring specific actions by foster care programs in those states. 
The Alaska Department of Law — which represented the state’s defense — said in a statement that A Better Childhood’s decision to drop the case will allow the state to direct the foster care system without a court mandate.
“There is always room for improvement in how we support children and families,” said acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills. “But meaningful reform happens through thoughtful policy and cooperative innovation here in Alaska, not through expensive lawsuits brought by outsiders that drain already scarce public resources. (The) dismissal preserves Alaska’s flexibility to continue pursuing creative, practical solutions to the unique child welfare challenges our state faces.”
During this spring’s session of the Alaska Legislature, state lawmakers voted by a wide margin to mandate tighter regulation of hospitals that treat foster youth and to require stricter oversight of any psychiatric treatment. 
A separate lawsuit, alleging that the state is not adequately supporting older foster children, continues to advance in state court.

text:
Thomas J SmithRepublican voters in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District rejected Amir Hassan, the candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump, for the GOP nomination, choosing instead Thomas Smith, even though Smith suspended his campaign on July 16.
The district includes the tri-cities of Saginaw, Midland and Bay City, as well as the Flint area.
The primary, which has yet to be officially called by the Associated Press as of 9 a.m. Wednesday, was a three-way race between Hassan, a U.S. Navy veteran and former federal law enforcement officer, Smith, a retired General Motors engineer and small business owner, and Al Lemmo, an anti-abortion activist and retired mechanical engineer. When Smith suspended his campaign, he endorsed Lemmo, who has suggested that Hassan is a “trojan horse” candidate and a “lifelong Democrat.”
However, with 99% of the votes counted, Smith was polling 50.4% of the vote, while Hassan had 33.2%, and Lemmo with 16.4%. Despite his decision to suspend his campaign, Smith’s name remained on the ballot because he dropped out of the race well after the deadline to formally withdraw from the primary. 
Republican congressional candidate Amir Hassan | ScreenshotAl Lemmo | Campaign photo
Smith did not respond to messages asking how he intends to handle the results of the primary election.
The 8th District is considered by Republicans as a pickup opportunity in Michigan — it is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City), who was first elected in 2024 and is seeking re-election. The district was one of 13 congressional districts nationwide that voted for Trump in 2024 while simultaneously electing a Democrat to the House of Representatives. The 2026 election is considered a “lean Democrat” by the Cook Political Report. 
Trump endorsed Hassan late in the race, and he was one of the candidates that Trump spotlighted at a rally the week prior to the primary election. The rebuke of the candidate chosen by the president goes against the tides in the Republican gubernatorial primary, in which the Trump-backed candidate, U.S. Rep. John James (D-Shelby Township), defeated businessman Perry Johnson by a sizable margin. While Trump’s endorsement netted James the win, it did not do the same for Hassan.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Special episode: Unpacking the Legislature’s July 31 flurry, and what comes next
description: Beacon Hill made it through the traditional end-of-formals deadline with less chaos and upheaval than 2024 and 2022. But in the process, lawmakers left many big decisions for another day.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
GUEST: Chris Lisinski







FOR THE FIRST TIME since 2020, lawmakers finished their formal work on the even-year July 31 traditional deadline before the sun came up the next morning. This time around, they were done even before the clock reached midnight.
Legislative leaders had been arguing for weeks that the end of the month, which marks the cutoff for major new legislative business, would feel different than it did during chaotic all-nighters in 2022 and 2024. House Speaker Ron Mariano even suggested the key date would feel “more like a regular business day.”
Their expectation-setting exercises turned out to be successful, but that’s not to say Beacon Hill was idle. The week leading into July 31, and the day itself, still featured a flurry of action that put some major proposals on Gov. Maura Healey’s desk and teed up a dozen bills for ongoing House-Senate negotiations.
In a special bonus episode of The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon senior reporters Jennifer Smith and Chris Lisinski recap what happened, what didn’t, and what the next five months might look like with the Legislature still able to tackle some topics.
The significance of July 31 stems from internal legislative rules that the House and Senate adopt to govern their operations. For decades, the rules prohibited any formal sessions after July in the second year of the two-year term — designed to prevent lawmakers from tackling controversial measures during campaign season or in lame-duck, post-election activity.
This time around, with an eye toward averting the upheaval of the past two terms, lawmakers tweaked the deadline. Under updated rules, as long as the House and Senate each approve initial versions of bills by July 31, they can continue to negotiate compromises in the ensuing months, and return in a formal session to approve any final deal before the term officially ends on January 7, 2027.
A dozen bills are now in conference committee talks, where lawmakers will work to hammer out final agreements:
– A sweeping economic development package– Controversial public records reforms– An effort to ramp up investment in primary care– Data privacy protections– Measures banning cell phones in schools, and perhaps also limiting social media use by minors– High-profile energy affordability legislation– A bill dealing with pet safety– A bill enhancing teacher retirement benefits– A bill aiming to prevent violence against health care workers– A bill requiring more frequent campaign finance disclosures by ballot question campaigns– A borrowing bill to fund environmental investments– A measure funding higher education infrastructure
The only hard deadline moving forward is the end of the term in January, though Election Day might provide some motivation. Legislators might reach a deal on any of those measures in a week, or in four and a half months.
And the contours of negotiations carry big stakes. In their economic development bills, for example, the House and Senate took different approaches to artificial intelligence regulation, zoning requirements, happy hour, gambling, and more.
“It could be just a jobs bill. It could also be a housing bill and an AI bill and a tax policy bill and a juvenile jurisdiction bill,” Lisinski said. “We’ll find out.”
Two of the measures in conference committee might impact questions voters are already set to decide through the ballot in November.
The House and Senate each included language in their public records reform bills that seems designed to supersede any changes voters make when they weigh the same topic, and the Senate added language to its economic development bill tweaking the tax cap law that is already targeted in a ballot question.
It’s a contrast from prior cycles, when lawmakers have negotiated with proponents of ballot questions to find a compromise before the measure is put before the voters.  
“These are independent legislative attempts to end-run, possibly, around those ballot questions,” Smith said.
On this episode, Smith and Lisinski discuss bills that made it all the way to Gov. Maura Healey’s desk by July 31 (10:20), the complicated negotiations lawmakers will undertake (14:00), and proposals that appear doomed in the final five months of the term (25:00).

A voter leaves a precinct in Columbia, South Carolina, wearing an "I voted today" sticker after voting in the June 23, 2026, primary runoffs. (Seanna Adcox/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Early voting in South Carolina is underway for the Aug. 11 special GOP primary that will decide who replaces the late Lindsey Graham on November ballots.
Early voting centers are open from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Friday.
Ten candidates are on the ballot, as of Wednesday morning, after the state Election Commission complied with a judge’s order to add Danny Ford II to the list. However, it’s unclear whether he’ll remain on the ballot. The state GOP appealed Tuesday to the South Carolina Supreme Court.
Graham’s unexpected death July 11 triggered the special election’s timeline.
Most counties have just one early voting location open. By law, counties could open up to seven. But no county is doing that for the special election.
Lexington County, home to Sen. Darline Graham, has the most options with six locations. Beaufort and Georgetown counties each have four locations. Calhoun, Dorchester and Horry counties have three. Darlington, Lancaster, Richland and York each have two options. Voters can go to whatever early voting location is convenient for them within the county where they’re registered. For a county-by-county list of locations, click here.
On Tuesday, polls will open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
The candidates (in alphabetical order):

Walterboro attorney Duke Buckner
Upstate farmer Danny Ford II
U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, who represents the 7th Congressional District
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, sister of the late Lindsey Graham
Greenville businessman Mark Lynch
former Myrtle Beach Mayor Mark McBride
U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who represents the 5th Congressional District
retired Air Force reservist and Department of Defense budget analyst Glenda Gail Parker
former congressman and Gov. Mark Sanford
Lexington County scientist and inventor Sam Shepherd

South Carolinians who voted in the June 9 Democratic primary and/or the June 23 Democratic runoff can’t vote in the special GOP primary. The state Election Commission ruled it’s the same election cycle. Voters can participate if they voted in the Republican contests in June or didn’t vote in either party’s primary.
If no candidate gets more than 50% of the primary votes, the top two vote-getters will advance to an Aug. 25 runoff.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lawsuit alleging guards fatally beat inmate prompts calls for state review of prison deaths
description: More than eight months after 24-year-old Malik Avila died in custody at High Desert State Prison his family is still left with questions around the circumstances that lead to his death.  James Urrutia, an attorney at LJU law firm, which is representing Avila’s family, filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday seeking answers and alleging prison […]
text:
Attorney James Urrutia and the family of Malik Avila, who died with incarcerated in Nevada, announced a wrongful death lawsuit.
(Photo: Michael Lyle/ Nevada Current)More than eight months after 24-year-old Malik Avila died in custody at High Desert State Prison his family is still left with questions around the circumstances that lead to his death. 
James Urrutia, an attorney at LJU law firm, which is representing Avila’s family, filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday seeking answers and alleging prison guards fatally beat Avila.
“Malik Avila’s case is extremely disturbing,” Urrutia said Monday during a press conference on the steps of the Regional Justice Center in downtown Las Vegas. “We have again a case of an underlying beating of an inmate by guards.”
The Clark County Coroner’s Office classified Avila’s death as “natural” caused from a lack of oxygen and brain damage. The road to finding answers, and justice, has been plagued by obstacles from state and local officials. 
The Nevada Department of Corrections declined to respond to questions from Nevada Current, saying it does not comment on pending litigation.
NV prison system mortality report ‘sounds like a lot of unexplained deaths,’ legislator says

The litigation comes weeks after state lawmakers questioned corrections officials about the number of deaths in Nevada prisons. 
At the time of its July 16 presentation to the Interim Judiciary Committee, 166 people had died since 2024 while in NDOC custody, officials said. 
Two additional deaths have been reported since then, including another death Monday at High Desert State Prison, bringing this year’s death toll to 38 so far. 
Of the 166 deaths corrections officials presented to state lawmakers in July, 98 were classified as natural – just like Avila. 
State Sen. Melanie Scheible, who chairs the committee, said at the time the 166 figure  “sounds like a lot of unexplained deaths to me.”
When an incarcerated person dies in custody, it should be considered a “red flag,” Urrutia said. 
“There are so few inmates who have life sentences,” he said. “One of the challenges is that a prison controls the evidence. They are the ones telling the story to a coroner. And yes, the body tells a story. But it needs context. If the only context you’re getting is from the prison, they are not getting the proper context. It’s a huge problem.”
In an interview, Urrutia said the Nevada Attorney General’s Office should consider pursuing an independent investigation into all those who died in custody and review the manner and cause of death determined by a county’s coroner’s office. 
Alcinia Whiters, a spokesperson for the AG’s office, said the Nevada Office of the Inspector General is tasked with handling “investigations into suspicious deaths” at state prisons.
“Our office may become involved when a case is referred to us, including when an inmate’s death involves an alleged use of force by a correctional officer,” Whiters said in a statement. 
When asked under what circumstance would Attorney General Aaron Ford consider a broader holistic review of inmate deaths, the office said “prosecutorial decisions are made on a case-by-case basis.”
“We also regularly review and discuss broader issues that may affect inmate safety and deaths within Nevada’s correctional system,” Whiters wrote in an email. “Our focus is ensuring accountability where the evidence supports it while remaining attentive to systemic issues that may emerge through the cases we handle.”
The Current also asked Gov. Joe Lombardo’s office under what circumstances should the state review in-custody deaths. 
“To strengthen safety and support the Department’s mission of maintaining secure, humane facilities while preparing offenders for successful reentry, NDOC is evaluating additional measures to curb the flow of illegal substances while increasing surveillance, adjusting staff operations, and reviewing standard procedures regarding classification of offenders and housing practices,” Drew Galang, a spokesperson for the for the governor, said in a statement.
  ‘I will never understand’ 

Avila’s family joined Urrutia at the press conference Monday ahead of the lawsuit being filed. 
“I miss him so much,” Lucy Avila, Malik’s grandmother, said as she fought back tears. “Every single day I think of him. He had a beautiful smile.”
In 2019, a then-17-year-old Avila was convicted of second degree murder and began serving a 10-year sentence.




Quotation







“There are so few inmates who have life sentences. One of the challenges is that a prison controls the evidence. They are the ones telling the story to a coroner. And yes, the body tells a story. But it needs context. If the only context you’re getting is from the prison, they are not getting the proper context. It’s a huge problem.” 


– James Urrutia, attorney for the family of Malik Avila



Lucy Avila described her only grandson’s efforts to better himself in prison by taking classes and working as a porter serving meals to other inmates. The family mourns the person he could have become if he hadn’t died.
“For over a week, Malik had been requesting medical assistance,” the lawsuit reads. “Prison guards mocked him. Malik’s mom started calling the prison to seek assistance. Prison guards mocked Malik even more.”
A summary of the investigation included in the autopsy report says that a Correctional Emergency Response Team was dispatched to Avila’s cell at 4 a.m. Nov. 4 after a family member called the prison to inform staff he was having a seizure.The investigation alleges that Avila had access to an unauthorized cellphone. 
The report alleges Avila became “combative” and the CERT unit went “hands-on” and “took him down.”
Urrutia said the firm obtained a voice recording from a whistleblower within the prison system who captured the incident. 
“We know what his last words were,” Urrutia said. “‘Please stop. Please stop.'”
The autopsy report says Avila refused medical treatment and only began to have a seizure needing medical assistance nearly three hours later. The lawsuit alleges he was rushed to the infirmary immediately after the CERT unit entered his cell. 
“By 7:53 am, still in the infirmary, Malik began convulsing unconsciously; his brain damaged,” according to the lawsuit. 
A prison nurse called 911 seeking for Avila to be transported to the hospital after he began convulsing. During the call, the nurse described Avila as a “stupid young idiot.”
Though he arrived at Mountain View Hospital on Nov. 4, Avila’s family didn’t know where he was at the time, according to the lawsuit.  
“The family shouldn’t have to be searching all over the state of Nevada for where their son is.” Urrutia said. “And while they are searching, they don’t even know his status. They don’t even know why he is missing.”
Corrections officials “never told his next of kin that he’s on life support,” Urrutia said during the press conference. “It takes eight days for the family to finally find where Malik is laying unconscious on life support. How that is OK I will never understand.”
The lawsuit also alleges that the prison lied multiple times, telling the family officials “suspect he ingested a substance” and that “he wasn’t involved in any altercation.”
“How can we expect our medical staff to provide proper care when they are being told lies from the prison?” Urrutia asked. “It causes confusion with medical treatment. It causes confusion for the family?”
Avila died Nov. 22 according to the autopsy report. Urrutia questioned the determination as a “natural” death.
“If people have head trauma, they are not dying naturally,” Urrutia said in an interview, adding the family has waited eight months to receive a final autopsy report. “Families should not have to wait eight months to find out why their son died.”
Clark County didn’t respond to requests for comment. 
In conversations with the coroner’s office, “they just keep saying they are still investigating and that they sent Malik’s brain to a neuropathologist … and they are waiting to get that result back,” Urrutia said. “My understanding is they have gotten the results back but still aren’t letting us have access to the brain yet so we can do our own analysis.”
Following the 10 a.m. press conference, the Current emailed Clark County to confirm it hadn’t released the autopsy report to the family and explain the timeframe for releasing reports.
Urrutia said the family was sent the final autopsy report that night.
  ‘Justice has to be done’ 

In addition to a lawsuit on behalf of Avila’s family, Urruita also filed a separate lawsuit July 30 in the deaths of three other inmates in 2024. 
“It hurts my heart that we keep having to show up and talk about this,” Urrutia said. “We hope at some point our government officials will put more work into solving this problem.”
A deadly fight took place at Ely State Prison in 2024 and three people who were incarcerated died.
“The prison officials working that day watched as multiple men bled out and took no action to save their lives,” Urrutia said at the press conference. “It doesn’t make sense for a group of prison guards to watch men or women bleed to death.”
Monday isn’t the first time Urruita stood on the steps of the Regional Justice Center surrounded by grieving families searching for answers after loved ones died under unexplained circumstances while in NDOC custody. 
The attorney also represented the family Christian Walker, another inmate who died in 2023.
At the time the lawsuit was filed – April 2024 – Urruita said corrections staff “beat him and left him to die in a cell all by himself.”  
Walker’s family was awarded a $4.6 million settlement in October 2025 for his wrongful death.
His death – like Avila’s – was also determined to be natural, Alyssa Piraino, an attorney at LJU Law Firm, said.
In the Walker’s case, the Nevada Office of the Inspector General recommended criminal charges. 
“Up at the next level, at the attorney general’s office, the criminal prosecution division chose not to press charges,” Urrutia said. 
The Attorney General’s Office, which was defending NDOC in the wrongful death lawsuit, argued last summer there wasn’t enough evidence to bring criminal charges. 
The LJU attorneys said that three independent medical experts disagreed with that determination. But “the coroner’s office filed a motion for summary judgement,” said Piraino, ending the case.
All these incidents together should show a need for reform to Nevada corrections institutions, the attorneys said. 
“We need the camera system regularly inspected, unannounced,” Urrutia said. “The prison should not be the only one responsible for saving the footage. We need somebody independent to be monitoring the cameras and the footage.” 
In the meantime, the families still wait for answers. 
“We are just looking for justice,” Lucy Avila said. “Justice has to be done for the inmates who have lost their lives.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: IG report ignored the critical role of over-prosecution in straining the indigent defense system
description: Massachusetts cannot ignore the realities of how over-prosecution and overcharging are part of the reason for the price tag on indigent defense.
text:
THE OFFICE OF THE INSPECTOR GENERAL recently released its long-awaited report on indigent defense in Massachusetts, accompanied by grand announcements about a broken system for fulfilling the state’s obligations to uphold the right to counsel when accused of a crime.  
The report was conducted pursuant to legislation enacted to identify flaws in the current indigent defense system after a record number of court-appointed lawyers declined to accept new cases during the summer of 2025, citing inadequate payment rates, leaving thousands of individuals facing criminal charges without a lawyer. 
Despite taking a year to investigate the complex and nuanced issues involved in providing indigent defense, the 150-page report contains a glaring omission. The report places blame at the feet of the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state agency which is responsible for ensuring that people too poor to afford their own lawyers have representation when they are accused of crimes as well as the courts, the Probation Department, and the lawyers who provide this constitutionally required representation at a fraction of what they could be making in any other type of legal work.  
In its 42 findings, the report blames CPCS for not having full-time salaried staff attorneys take enough cases during the crisis as well as before and after. It proposes that CPCS conduct more audits of the work of court-appointed lawyers and cap the number of hours they can work on a case.  
The report blames the Probation Department for failing to adequately evaluate indigency when assigning lawyers and blames the courts for waiving fees charged to people so poor that they can’t afford a lawyer. What the report makes no mention of is the role over-prosecution and over-criminalization play in the state’s counsel crisis. 
The right to counsel is not universal. In fact, the right to counsel in Massachusetts is only guaranteed if the charge that the defendant is facing carries the possibility of incarceration.  
Every day, courtrooms across the Commonwealth are packed with people charged with low-level offenses, nearly all carrying the possibility of incarceration, and persons overcharged by overly aggressive prosecution. Charges that do not carry the possibility of incarceration are few. 
Individuals whose cases are so minor that they will never be incarcerated sit in the courtrooms waiting to be appointed a lawyer. Prosecutors across the Commonwealth regularly charge people as aggressively as possible to gain the upper hand in forcing a plea, creating in the process more work for the lawyers assigned to the cases. These charging decisions do not exist in a vacuum, and there has been much discussion in recent years about the racial disparities in the criminal justice system.  
A 2020 study conducted by The Criminal Justice Program at Harvard Law School found that racial and ethnic differences in the type and severity of initial charges account for over 70 percent of the disparities in sentence length.  Bringing both more serious charges than the facts warrant and charges in situations where criminalization is unnecessary adds to the financial burden on indigent defense. 
Prosecutors in Massachusetts wield broad authority. They decide whether to charge, what to charge, and how aggressively to pursue a case. When discretion is used to maximize exposure rather than to calibrate charges to culpability, it can not only distort outcomes but also add to the Commonwealth’s need for appointed counsel.  
Overcharging has become an accepted practice, and attention is rarely paid to charging decisions. A prosecutor can overcharge by adding multiple counts to a single incident or charging a more serious charge than the facts warrant.  
Both methods help prosecutors gain the upper hand in plea negotiations, but this very tactic requires the defense lawyer to spend more hours on the case. While charging decisions are complex, the fact that a report on indigent defense fails to address this variable in the system’s cost is a critical oversight. 
Any observer of the district and municipal courts, where most of the expense of indigent defense is incurred, knows that a large percentage of cases involve minor offenses that are unlikely to result in incarceration.  
For example, in 2025, there were 21,683 cases brought in the Commonwealth under laws that criminalize driving with a suspended or revoked license or registration and provide for imprisonment. In each of these cases, if the defendant was found to be indigent, a lawyer was assigned, and that lawyer was constitutionally required to spend time defending against the allegations. 
These hours and cases add up, and they can’t be discounted in any sort of accurate analysis of the indigent defense system. Decriminalizing lower-level offenses for which there is almost never an incarceration sentence would significantly reduce the number of people in need of appointed counsel. 
Future conversations about the indigent defense system in Massachusetts cannot ignore the realities of how over-prosecution and overcharging are part of the reason for the price tag on indigent defense. 
Shira Diner is a lecturer and clinical instructor at the Criminal Defense Clinic at Boston University School of Law.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: As forests burn across the state, a cluster of residential fires also takes a toll
description: Utah’s raging wildfires have burned fast and big in the backcountry, but cities and suburbs are also dealing with destructive fires.
text:
The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Utah’s raging wildfires have burned enough land in the backcountry to match the size of Salt Lake County this year. And along northern Utah’s urban corridor, a number of recent structure fires have also proved destructive, torching homes, displacing hundreds of people and forcing still more to evacuate. 
“Collectively, it’s been a very, very busy season,” Sandy Fire Chief Ryan McConaghie said Tuesday. 
The spate of house and apartment fires taking place from Cache County’s small city of Nibley to more densely populated West Jordan has kept firefighters hard at work as their departments focus on keeping them safe in this summer’s punishing heat. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And even if they sound like a broken record, city officials are urging Utahns to stay vigilant and on their best behavior, calling attention to this summer’s tinder-dry conditions. 
“We try to tell people, again: If you’re pulling trailers, try not to be dragging chains,” said Nate Cochran, spokesperson for Unified Fire Authority. “If you are smoking, try not to flick your cigarette butts out the window. If you are doing any type of barbecuing or outdoor fires — anything like that — making sure you have a water source with you.”
He noted firefighting agencies help each other out when backup is needed, but said if they get spread too thin, response times may stretch out a somewhat longer. 
McConaghie and Cochran said their agencies have been stocking up on electrolyte supplements and keeping a close eye on crews to help ensure they do not overheat as they battle blazes in scorching temperatures.
“We try to cycle guys into what we call ‘rehab,’ let them take their gear off, cool down, hydrate up, and then just really watching those work cycles,” Cochran said. 
The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)The North Union Apartments in Midvale are pictured on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, after a large fire days earlier displaced residents from all 220 occupied units. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)
But the high temperatures can still take a toll. Cochran said a Unified firefighter was treated for heat exhaustion last week after attacking an aggressive apartment fire in Midvale that tore through the building’s roof and top floor, displacing residents of more than 200 apartments. 
Thankfully, the agency serving unincorporated areas of Salt Lake County and the city of Eagle Mountain hasn’t recorded any major injuries this summer, Cochran added. 
But some residents have been severely affected by the fires. Two people in Sandy were hospitalized and a cat was killed in a house fire this week that was sparked by a candle, McConaghie said.  
He and Cochran agreed that while blazing outside temperatures don’t seem to intensify house fires, gusty winds will carry them quickly to other properties. And in an indirect result of hotter weather, overworked air conditioning units can also place stress on mechanical equipment that can lead to fires, they said. As for the cause of the Midvale fire, officials cited a mechanical issue but haven’t released further details. 
McConaghie said it’s fortunate his community is not experiencing the level of devastation seen in the Pacific Northwest. In Spokane, Washington, and its surrounding areas this week, hundreds of homes and other buildings were leveled and more than 65,000 people were told to evacuate because of wildfires. Officials there said Monday they arrested a man suspected of arson.  
With a focus on the potential for devastating wildfires where Utah neighborhoods meet rugged terrain, state lawmakers created a program to assess fees on homeowners in those zones and allow them to trim down that expense by taking steps to mitigate fire risk. Inspectors are expected to start visiting properties in coming weeks.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: National Dems to target GOP congressional leader in NC
description: North Carolina’s 9th district has long been considered a safe Republican seat.
text:
U.S. Rep. Richard Hudson (left), a North Carolina Republican, talks with state Sen. Bobby Hanig (right), a Republican running for North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, in Raleigh on Dec. 1, 2025. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is adding North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District to its “Districts in Play” program, targeting longtime Republican incumbent Rep. Richard Hudson. 
This program focuses on competitive districts held by vulnerable Republicans across the country as Democrats seek to regain a majority in the House, according to a Wednesday announcement. Other targets include Reps. Greg Murphy in NC-03 and Chuck Edwards in NC-11. 
It’s a bold move. Hudson has served as chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee for three years, raising money for the U.S. House Republican Caucus and deciding where it needs to spend that money to pick up or defend seats. 
North Carolina’s 9th district has long been considered a safe Republican seat. In 2024, Hudson defeated Democrat Nigel William Bristow by 18 percent of the vote. President Donald Trump carried the district that year by a similar margin. 
The GOP isn’t worried about the seat. Members view the addition as Democrats baiting them to spend more money in the district, diverting resources away from tighter races. 
“National Democrats know they can’t beat Chairman Hudson on his record, so they’re trying to buy what they can’t earn,” NRCC spokesperson Will Kiley said. “This is what desperation looks like with a checkbook.”
But Democrats are hopeful about Alamance and Guilford counties, which first became a part of Hudson’s district for the 2024 cycle. Democrat Josh Stein won both in the gubernatorial contest that same year. 
NC Congressman Chuck Edwards to face censure in US House for inappropriate conduct

DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus said North Carolina voters aren’t happy with Hudson’s record of attacking affordable health care and hurting working families. Democrats are also inspired by members of the party overperforming in special elections this cycle, although she said the DCCC has not conducted recent polling in the district.
“Voters know Richard Hudson is responsible for House Republicans’ disastrous anti-working family platform crushing North Carolinians,” DCCC chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. “A protector of corruption, and self-interested Republicans at the expense of North Carolina’s working families, Hudson does not work for this community.”
At the moment, Republicans hold a 218-212 majority in the House, with four vacancies. One independent, Rep. Kevin Kiley of California, caucuses with the Republicans. 
Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former Army major and West Virginia state senator, is facing Hudson in November. 
Ojeda spent about 15 years at Fort Bragg near Fayetteville during his military career. Upon moving to West Virginia, he won election to the state Senate in 2016.
He’s no stranger to running in Republican areas. Ojeda briefly ran for president in 2020, before dropping out and challenging U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito. He did not win the Democratic nomination in the primary election. 
After that, he returned to North Carolina. Ojeda has raised $2.2 million since he launched his campaign, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
“This race is winnable, and people are seeing that our hard work is paying off,” Ojeda said in a statement. “This district has been shifting, because people here are tired of having a member of Congress beholden to the MAGA machine in Washington.”
Hudson has been in office since 2013, with his district previously numbered as the 8th. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
New poll shows Whatley within striking distance of Cooper as GOP support coalesces

As NRCC chair, Hudson is the fifth-ranking member in Republican leadership and the highest-ranking Republican member of Congress from North Carolina in history, according to the committee.  
Hudson has raised $3.2 million so far during this election cycle, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
The Hudson campaign did not respond to requests for comment. 
Both parties are funding candidates across the Tar Heel State. 
The DCCC previously added Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, to its “Red to Blue” program, supporting his bid to oust Edwards in Western North Carolina. They’re also investing in Rep. Don Davis, an incumbent in the 1st Congressional District, the most competitive of the state. 
Republicans aren’t backing down. They’re aiming for NC-01 as well, adding Army Veteran Laurie Buckhout to the NRCC’s “MAGA Majority” program. U.S. House Majority Leader Mike Johnson, R-La., campaigned with Buckhout in the district this week.
Over in the Senate, Democrats view North Carolina’s open seat as one of their best pick-up opportunities in 2026. Recent polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley, with Cooper also well ahead of Whatley in fundraising. 
The general election takes place Nov. 3.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Paid Leave is helping workers — and businesses like mine
description: More than half of Minnesota Paid Leave applicants earn less than $78,000 a year, according to state data. These are the workers who staff our restaurants, clinics, retail counters and construction crews. These workers historically had the least access to employer-paid leave and the least cushion to fall back on when life happened anyway.  Before […]
text:
More than 38,000 approved applications for Paid Leave so far have been for new parents. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)More than half of Minnesota Paid Leave applicants earn less than $78,000 a year, according to state data. These are the workers who staff our restaurants, clinics, retail counters and construction crews. These workers historically had the least access to employer-paid leave and the least cushion to fall back on when life happened anyway. 
Before this program, an hourly employee facing a serious illness or a new baby often had two options: quit or return to work before they were ready. Unless they worked for my small business, which has paid out of pocket for loyal employees to get the care they need or to support those in need. These options are less than ideal for the employee and for the employer. 
For small businesses like mine, the Paid Leave program saves me money while providing a safety net that my employees deserve. To do some back-of-the-napkin math, an employee earning $78,000 would have a premium of less than $700 a year. And that $700 is the total; businesses can decide whether to split the premium equally or take on a bit more. In return, the employee can receive partial wage replacement while away. For a worker earning $78,000 a year, estimated weekly payments from Paid Leave exceed $1,000. The math is clear. This is a good deal. 
The geographic data reinforces why this matters beyond the Twin Cities. The Department of Employment and Economic Development, which runs the program, reports that 44% of applicants live outside the 7-county metro area. Greater Minnesota’s small businesses often operate with limited staff and fewer nearby job candidates to draw on than their metro counterparts; losing even one employee who has to care for an aging relative can mean weeks of scrambling. Without a return-to-work date, a small business owner might hesitate to hire a replacement, leaving them understaffed. Or they spend time, effort and money finding and training a new employee only to have them leave a few months later. A program that helps a rural clinic or hardware store retain the employee they already trained —  rather than searching a shallow labor pool for a replacement — is doing real economic work in exactly the communities that can least afford instability.
The gender breakdown deserves attention, too. Nearly two-thirds of applicants are women. This is unsurprising given that more than 38,000 approved applications so far have been for new parents. Much of the retail and hospitality industries are disproportionately staffed by women. Not to mention child care centers, home health and personal care aides, cleaning companies and educators. Small employers in these women-dominated sectors have long struggled to retain talent through pregnancy and early parenthood — not for lack of will but for lack of resources to hold a position open unpaid for months. Paid Leave gives them a tool they never had before: a state-administered benefit that lets them keep experienced staff on the books through one of the most common reasons people leave the workforce altogether — in exactly the industries that can least afford to lose them.
None of this is free, and small business owners are right to have asked hard questions about the premiums when the law passed. But the program was built with that concern in mind. Employers with 30 or fewer employees pay a reduced premium rate, and because the benefit itself is paid by the state — not the employer’s payroll — a small business no longer has to choose between funding a worker’s leave out of its own cash flow and letting that worker go. Grant assistance is also available to help smaller employers offset early administrative costs.
Six months of data is not proof of a program’s long-term success, and Minnesota should keep watching how Paid Leave performs as it matures. But the early numbers point in a clear direction: The workers using Paid Leave are disproportionately the ones small businesses most need to retain and who previously could least afford to hold on to. 
That is not a case against small business. It is a case for how far a modest, shared investment can go toward keeping Minnesota’s small employers competitive with the large ones down the street.
