title: Rick Brattin wins Missouri 5th District GOP primary amid uncertainty over district lines
description: A late endorsement from President Donald Trump boosted state Sen. Rick Brattin to the Republican nomination for Congress in Missouri’s 5th District Tuesday against former Boone County Clerk Taylor Burks. Trump was the instigator of Missouri’s gerrymandered redistricting map and issued his endorsement just before 5:30 p.m. Monday, after early voting had ended[...]
text:
State Sen. Rick Brattin, a Republican from Harrisonville, mingles ahead of Gov. Mike Kehoe's inauguration ceremony in January 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A late endorsement from President Donald Trump boosted state Sen. Rick Brattin to the Republican nomination for Congress in Missouri’s 5th District Tuesday against former Boone County Clerk Taylor Burks.
Trump was the instigator of Missouri’s gerrymandered redistricting map and issued his endorsement just before 5:30 p.m. Monday, after early voting had ended and too late to generate news stories on evening broadcasts.
The Associated Press called the race shortly after 9 p.m., with Brattin leading Burks 44% to 26%, with more than 60% of precincts reporting. There were four other candidates in the primary, only one of which, Brett Hueffmeier, had substantial funding. 
“I am honored to be the Republican nominee for the 5th Congressional District,” Brattin said, “and I look forward to working with President Donald J. Trump to keep his America First agenda on track.”
Brattin now faces 11-term incumbent U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Kansas City Democrat, and Randy Langkraehr, a Libertarian, in the November election. A court battle over Secretary of State Denny Hoskins’ denial Tuesday afternoon of a referendum petition will decide if the November election is held in the counties voting Tuesday or if the map will revert to the plan used in the 2022 and 2024 elections.
If the map drawn last year is used, Brattin has a clear advantage, based on Republican success in past elections. If the older map is used, Cleaver will have the advantage in a district where he has rarely received less than 55% of the vote.
Trump’s endorsement is meaningful whenever it is given, said Gov. Mike Kehoe after voting in Jefferson City. Kehoe, a Jefferson City resident, endorsed Brattin and is a constituent in the district drawn by lawmakers last year.
“Anytime President Trump weighs in, I think it can be powerful, whether it’s on time or not on time,” Kehoe said.
Brattin was carried to the nomination by the Club For Growth’s Win It Back PAC, which spent $2.1 million on his behalf, including $1.4 million on television ads attacking Burks. Outside groups spent $3.8 million total, more than four times what the candidates themselves spent.
Brattin is a two-term state senator who previously held office as a state representative and Cass County auditor. He is a Marine Corps veteran and owns a small construction company.
It is the second time Brattin has bested Burks in a congressional primary. In 2022, Brattin came in second and Burks finished fourth in the 4th District primary won by now-U.S. Rep. Mark Alford.
In an interview after he voted Tuesday morning in Ashland, Burks discounted the impact of the endorsement because of its late arrival. As he campaigned door-to-door over the weekend, he said, about half of voters had not yet decided.
“I don’t know what these national groups were telling the president or the White House and why he decided to weigh in at the last minute,” Burks said. “Most voters were already doing their research and trying to determine how they’re going to cast their ballot this morning anyway.”
The upcoming court challenge over Hoskins’ denial of the referendum will determine if the entire redistricting plan is suspended, which would throw Tuesday’s results into question and create uncertainty about the boundaries for most of Missouri’s eight districts.
Since the map was passed last year, court decisions have upheld it against every challenge. The uncertainty about the future if a referendum is ordered is based on the Missouri Constitution’s language that a state law subject to a referendum cannot take effect until a statewide vote.
The candidates filed for office knowing there is uncertainty about the redistricting plan, Kehoe told reporters after voting in Jefferson City.
“Those candidates went into this election in Congressional District 5 with their eyes wide open,” Kehoe said. “They understand that there probably would be some controversy over whether that goes. We’ll let the courts decide that. I think the map represents Missouri’s values.”

State Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield), speaking at a Lansing press conference to announce the reintroduction of the Michigan Voting Rights Act. May 19, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceState Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) has emerged victorious in a four-person race which will more than likely determine who will fill U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ empty congressional seat come 2027. 
The Associated Press called the race for Moss at 9:31. Unofficial results show Moss receiving 49.2% of the vote with 67% of the total vote counted.
Attorney Aisha Farooqi received 33%, Waterford School District Board of Education Vice President John Paul Torres received 9.6% and former Ford Engineer Don Ufford received 8.2 %. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a safe blue seat, the Democratic nominee is likely to prevail in Michigan’s 11th Congressional District. Troy Mayor Ethan Baker was the sole Republican candidate on the ballot, and will face Moss in November’s general election. 
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated Moss won on the win.
“Jeremy has fought for working families in the Michigan Legislature, and he will continue that fight in the halls of Congress. His commitment to lowering healthcare costs, tacking the cost of living crisis, and protecting our rights is as critical as ever,” Hertel said in a statement. “I’d like to thank each of the candidates in this Democratic primary for fostering a competitive and substantive race — primaries make our party stronger. As we look to November, I look forward to coming together to elect Jeremy Moss to Congress.”
A state lawmaker first elected to the state Legislature in 2015, Moss is the first openly gay member of the Michigan Senate and its only Jewish state senator. If he prevails in November, Moss could also be the state’s first openly LGBTQ+ representative.
As of July 15, Moss’ campaign has raised $1.49 million, with $352,516 in cash on hand. Baker, in contrast, raised $141,876 and has just over $121,000 in cash on hand heading into November.

text:
Michael Bouchard Jr. | Campaign photoThe matchup for November in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District is beginning to take form, as U.S. Army Captain Michael Bouchard Jr. secured the Republican Party’s nomination while the Democratic race was yet to be called.
With U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), opting against reelection to pursue the governor’s office, the 10th Congressional District is up for grabs, with a healthy field of Democrats and Republicans each vying to represent their party in the general election.
On the Republican ballot was Bouchard, Army veteran and construction manager Steffan Demetropoulos, and attorney Justin Kirk. While former prosecutor Robert Lulgjuraj was also on the ballot, Lulgjuraj suspended his campaign on July 14, following President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Bouchard.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Associated Press called the race for Bouchard at 9:17 p.m.. Unofficial results at 9:35 show Bouchard with 73.2% of the vote, Kirk with 17.3% and Demetropoulos with 3.7% with 18% of the total vote counted. 
Vying for the Democratic nomination are former special victims unit prosecutor Christina Hines, former Pontiac Mayor Tim Greimel and former Department of Commerce Attorney Eric Chung.
Looking towards November, Republicans hold the advantage in the 10th District, with the nonpartisan Cook Political Report giving it a “lean Republican” rating. However, Democrats still consider the seat a key target, with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the campaign arm for U.S. House Democrats, listing it as among their districts in play for 2026. 
The district covers southern Macomb County and parts of eastern Oakland County.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas voters reject constitutional amendment on judicial selection by wide margin
authors: Sherman Smith, Jacinda Hall, Tim Carpenter
description: TOPEKA — Kansas voters Tuesday overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to rewrite the state constitution and elect Kansas Supreme Court justices, spiking a plan long coveted by Republicans who want more conservative rulings on issues including abortion and school funding. About 64% of Kansans were voting “no” on the constitutional amendment with 443,296 votes cou[...]
text:
Amy Boucher, left, votes Aug. 4, 2026, in Eudora. Voters were asked to evaluate a proposed constitutional amendment that called for the election of justices. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas voters Tuesday overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to rewrite the state constitution and elect Kansas Supreme Court justices, spiking a plan long coveted by Republicans who want more conservative rulings on issues including abortion and school funding.
About 64% of Kansans were voting “no” on the constitutional amendment with 443,296 votes counted as of 9:30 p.m. Attorney General Kris Kobach, a supporter of the amendment, acknowledged it had failed while opponents declared victory.
“The billionaire political donors and politicians behind this amendment tried to buy our Supreme Court,” said Micah Kubic, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas. “They tried to turn our justices into politicians for sale, all so they could control the court’s rulings and take away our rights. But tonight, Kansas said no.”
Kobach, speaking at a GOP watch party in Wichita, said the vote “creates more certainty” that the current justices will decide cases that are making their way through the judicial system.
“If there had been a shift, there would be some question as to who would eventually be on the court that hears those cases,” Kobach said. “Now we know it’s probably going to be the justices right now, unless somebody retires.”
The primary ballot asked voters to evaluate a proposal that would spike a 68-year-old system for selecting justices for the highest court, a system born out of scandal from an era when justices were elected and the governor had total control over selecting replacements.
The amendment instead would give voters the power to vote on candidates for the Supreme Court, and mega-donors the power to influence court decisions.
Danedri Herbert, chair of the Kansas Republican Party, issued a stern warning Tuesday morning that the vote on whether to elect Supreme Court justices was “the most important election of our lifetime.”
“Yeah, I know everyone says that every year,” Herbert said. “This cycle, it’s true.”
Herbert, in a social media video, said the constitutional amendment “is the difference between Kansas becoming Detroit or Kansas becoming a land of prosperity.”
Conservatives have long raged against Kansas Supreme Court rulings that upheld constitutional rights to terminate a pregnancy and adequately fund public schools. They plotted to change the way Supreme Court justices are selected and, as a result, overturn those rulings.
With supermajorities in both the House and Senate, Republicans in the Legislature adopted a resolution during the 2025 session to place this constitutional amendment on the 2026 primary ballot. The goal was to hold the vote on a date when independent voters would have no other reason to show up at the polls. Republicans hold a sizable advantage over Democrats in the state in terms of affiliated voters who participate in primary elections.
The same gambit failed four years ago, when voters overwhelmingly rejected a constitutional amendment that would have removed abortion rights from the state constitution. That amendment failed by a 60-40 margin with 942,851 Kansans weighing in, just weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.
“I think a lot of people are just frustrated that we’re seeing this effort again to change the constitution because the state Legislature doesn’t like what the Supreme Court has done,” said Democratic U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, speaking with reporters after she voted Tuesday morning.
“There are plenty of us who disagree with court rulings on a regular basis, but you don’t completely change the way that we get Supreme Court justices just because you don’t like some of the rulings that they make,” she added.
Former Gov. John Carlin, right, gestures while former Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Lawton Nuss listens during a June 16, 2026, forum at Washburn University in Topeka. The forum was hosted by Kansas Appleseed to educate voters about the constitutional amendment. (Photo by Jessica Tufts for Kansas Reflector)
The ACLU of Kansas, Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes and Kansas Appleseed joined forces to form Kansas United for Impartial Courts in a campaign to oppose the constitutional amendment. They warned that the amendment would allow out-of-state billionaires to buy the court.
“So much was on the line tonight: abortion rights, voting rights, public education, workers’ rights, and the fundamental freedoms guaranteed to every Kansan,” Kubic said. “The politicians behind this amendment wanted a court they could control — a court that would do their bidding instead of following the law and the constitution.”
Kobach, though his PAC and various conservative groups, flooded airwaves and mailboxes with ads that criticized the current selection process.
At least $12.8 million, much of it dark money, fueled “vote yes” and “vote no” campaigns ahead of Tuesday’s primary.
“I hope that the people of Kansas, after over 50 years, will finally be able to once again be able to select our Supreme Court justices,” said Joshua Borman, who works for Americans for Prosperity, at a GOP watch party Tuesday night in Wichita. “I think it is very essential for us, especially with how much we are taxed in the state, that we start to have that representation back. It’s very important to be able to have the ability to elect our justices.”
The current system is the result of a notorious political scandal known as the “triple play.” In 1956, incumbent Republican Gov. Fred Hall lost his primary election, and Democrat George Docking defeated the Republican nominee in November. Supreme Court Chief Justice Bill Smith, a Republican, was prepared to retire midterm but didn’t want a Democrat to choose his replacement.
At the start of the new year, Smith resigned from the Supreme Court, Hall resigned as governor, and the new governor appointed Hall to take Smith’s seat on the court.
The following year, more than 70% of Kansas voters approved a constitutional amendment that created a merit-based system. It established a nominating commission, with attorneys choosing five members and the governor appointing four. The commission vets candidates for Supreme Court openings and sends three finalists to the governor, who chooses from those three.
Justices face retention votes in the next general election, and again every six years.
An election worker prepares to hand out “I voted” stickers to Johnson County participants in the Aug. 4 primary election to consider a proposed constitutional amendment and determine nominations for the Democratic and Republican parties. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
This year’s constitutional amendment would require justices to run for office like candidates for other political positions, and removes current restrictions on justices engaging in political activities or raising money for campaigns. The amendment authorizes the Legislature to determine how elections would be conducted — partisan or nonpartisan, statewide or by districts that lawmakers draw.
Proponents of this year’s amendment point out that no justice has ever lost a retention election.
Rep. Bob Lewis, a Garden City Republican, said in a video ad posted on social media that it was “balderdash” to claim that voters already get to evaluate justices.
“A retention election is not an election at all. It’s not competitive,” Lewis said. “Voters are given only one choice: Vote yes or no for this particular candidate. A true election, as we all know, is grounded in competition, giving the voters a choice.”
He said a retention election is “a rubber stamp.”
“It’s a rigged election, much like in communist countries,” Lewis said. “The result is foregone. You pick the guy the politburo has picked, or you pick no one.”
The video was paid for by Derby Republican Rep. Blake Carpenter’s reelection campaign.
Advance voting totals showed a dramatic drop-off from the historic turnout four years ago, when the anti-abortion amendment was on the ballot. This year, 176,703 Kansans had voted by mail or in person as of Monday. In 2022, 320,048 voted by mail or in person before election day.
The stakes were underscored when Christopher Jayaram, minutes before becoming the newest Supreme Court justice Monday, issued an opinion that strikes down numerous abortion restrictions under state law, some dating to 1997. Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly selected Jayaram, who was a Johnson County district judge, from the three finalists for an open seat on the high court.
“Tonight Kansans rebuffed a constitutional amendment that was designed to undermine access to abortion, mislead voters, and politicize the state’s Supreme Court,” said Emily Wales, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes.

Republicans hold a sizable advantage over Democrats in the state in terms of affiliated voters who participate in primary elections.
The same gambit failed four years ago, when voters overwhelmingly rejected a constitutional amendment that would have removed abortion rights from the state constitution. That amendment failed by a 60-40 margin with 942,851 Kansans weighing in, just weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.
“I think a lot of people are just frustrated that we’re seeing this effort again to change the constitution because the state Legislature doesn’t like what the Supreme Court has done,” said Democratic U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, speaking with reporters after she voted Tuesday morning.
“There are plenty of us who disagree with court rulings on a regular basis, but you don’t completely change the way that we get Supreme Court justices just because you don’t like some of the rulings that they make,” she added.
Former Gov. John Carlin, right, gestures while former Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Lawton Nuss listens during a June 16, 2026, forum at Washburn University in Topeka. The forum was hosted by Kansas Appleseed to educate voters about the constitutional amendment. (Photo by Jessica Tufts for Kansas Reflector)
The ACLU of Kansas, Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes and Kansas Appleseed joined forces to form Kansas United for Impartial Courts in a campaign to oppose the constitutional amendment. They warned that the amendment would allow out-of-state billionaires to buy the court.
“So much was on the line tonight: abortion rights, voting rights, public education, workers’ rights, and the fundamental freedoms guaranteed to every Kansan,” Kubic said. “The politicians behind this amendment wanted a court they could control — a court that would do their bidding instead of following the law and the constitution.”
Attorney General Kris Kobach, though his PAC and various conservative groups, flooded airwaves and mailboxes with ads that criticized the current selection process.
At least $12.8 million, much of it dark money, fueled “vote yes” and “vote no” campaigns ahead of Tuesday’s primary.
“I hope that the people of Kansas, after over 50 years, will finally be able to once again be able to select our Supreme Court justices,” said Joshua Borman, who works for Americans for Prosperity, at a GOP watch party Tuesday night in Wichita. “I think it is very essential for us, especially with how much we are taxed in the state, that we start to have that representation back. It’s very important to be able to have the ability to elect our justices.”
The current system is the result of a notorious political scandal known as the “triple play.” In 1956, incumbent Republican Gov. Fred Hall lost his primary election, and Democrat George Docking defeated the Republican nominee in November. Supreme Court Chief Justice Bill Smith, a Republican, was prepared to retire midterm but didn’t want a Democrat to choose his replacement.
At the start of the new year, Smith resigned from the Supreme Court, Hall resigned as governor, and the new governor appointed Hall to take Smith’s seat on the court.
The following year, more than 70% of Kansas voters approved a constitutional amendment that created a merit-based system. It established a nominating commission, with attorneys choosing five members and the governor appointing four. The commission vets candidates for Supreme Court openings and sends three finalists to the governor, who chooses from those three.
Justices face retention votes in the next general election, and again every six years.
An election worker prepares to hand out “I voted” stickers to Johnson County participants in the Aug. 4 primary election to consider a proposed constitutional amendment and determine nominations for the Democratic and Republican parties. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
This year’s constitutional amendment would require justices to run for office like candidates for other political positions, and removes current restrictions on justices engaging in political activities or raising money for campaigns. The amendment authorizes the Legislature to determine how elections would be conducted — partisan or nonpartisan, statewide or by districts that lawmakers draw.
Proponents of this year’s amendment point out that no justice has ever lost a retention election.
Rep. Bob Lewis, a Garden City Republican, said in a video ad posted on social media that it was “balderdash” to claim that voters already get to evaluate justices.
“A retention election is not an election at all. It’s not competitive,” Lewis said. “Voters are given only one choice: Vote yes or no for this particular candidate. A true election, as we all know, is grounded in competition, giving the voters a choice.”
He said a retention election is “a rubber stamp.”
“It’s a rigged election, much like in communist countries,” Lewis said. “The result is foregone. You pick the guy the politburo has picked, or you pick no one.”
The video was paid for by Derby Republican Rep. Blake Carpenter’s reelection campaign.
Advance voting totals showed a dramatic drop-off from the historic turnout four years ago, when the anti-abortion amendment was on the ballot. This year, 176,703 Kansans had voted by mail or in person as of Monday. In 2022, 320,048 voted by mail or in person before election day.
The stakes were underscored when Christopher Jayaram, minutes before becoming the newest Supreme Court justice Monday, issued an opinion that strikes down numerous abortion restrictions under state law, some dating to 1997. Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly selected Jayaram, who was a Johnson County district judge, from the three finalists for an open seat on the high court.
“Tonight Kansans rebuffed a constitutional amendment that was designed to undermine access to abortion, mislead voters, and politicize the state’s Supreme Court,” said Emily Wales, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes.

title: U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, United Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton to compete in November
description: TOPEKA — Incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall will face United Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in November’s U.S. Senate election, according to race calls from the Associated Press. Democratic voters participated in an unusually crowded primary with 11 candidates competing for viability, and Hamilton, who entered the race relatively late compared to other candi[...]
text:
Kansas Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall appears on April 2, 2026, at a National Guard armory in Kansas City, Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall will face United Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in November’s U.S. Senate election, according to race calls from the Associated Press.
Democratic voters participated in an unusually crowded primary with 11 candidates competing for viability, and Hamilton, who entered the race relatively late compared to other candidates, quickly became the frontrunner with record-breaking fundraising. 
Republicans have controlled both of Kansas’ Senate seats since 1939, and Marshall is favored to retain his seat in November. Marshall is running for re-election after a single term characterized by loyalty to President Donald Trump, pandemic critiques and questions about his primary residence.
Marshall led with 75% of votes, according to preliminary tallies, against his primary challenger, Pond Naramore of Lawrence, who did not immediately respond to Kansas Reflector’s request for comment. 
Hamilton held an early lead with more than 40% of votes, according to preliminary results, but only a fraction of precincts were reporting results when the AP called the race.
His campaign said in a statement Kansans are “tired of a Senator who only pretends to live in Kansas.”
“They’re tired skyrocketing prices for gas, groceries, and health care. They’re tired of a Senator who only pretends to live in Kansas,” the campaign said.
While the first candidates to challenge Marshall began announcing their campaigns roughly a year ago, Democrats found a strong fundraiser in Hamilton, who co-founded what is now the largest United Methodist church in the country. He rose to prominence later in the cycle after declaring his candidacy in late April, and since then, Hamilton has fielded attacks from fellow Democrats and Republicans. 
Most of the Democrats running lacked political experience. Marshall, a Republican from Great Bend, was a two-term Congressman in Kansas’ 1st Congressional District before running for the U.S. Senate in 2020.
Samantha Cantrell, regional press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, slammed Hamilton’s win.
“Adam Hamilton is a radical Democrat who would rubber stamp the new socialist agenda and tax hikes taking over the Democrat Party and Kansas voters will reject him in November,” she said.
U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand said Hamilton is running to be a voice “who will show up and bring people together to get things done.”
“As a fifth-generation Kansan and pastor, Adam has dedicated his life to caring for his community and putting people over politics,” they said. “Now, he’s going to take those values to the U.S. Senate – to fight for Kansas families, farmers, seniors, and everyone being crushed by higher costs of gas, groceries, and health care because of Roger Marshall’s toxic agenda.”
Hamilton was trailed by Christy Davis, a former federal employee from Cottonwood Falls, Noah Taylor, a veteran and small business operator in Kechi, and Anne Parelkar, an immigration attorney from Overland Park.
Candidates Damon Anderson, Jason Hart, Kevin Latz, Erik Murray, Sandy Spidel Neumann, state Sen. Patrick Schmidt, and Mike Soetaert trailed with 6% of votes or fewer.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters reject income tax phaseout, initiative petition changes
description: Missouri voters resoundingly rejected major Republican priorities on Tuesday as proposals to eliminate the income tax and change the way initiative petition majorities are counted lost by large margins across the state.  The Associated Press called the race for both amendments at 8:15 p.m., with Amendment 4 losing by 63 percentage points and Amendment 5 […]
text:
A yard sign opposing Amendments 4 and 5 in Columbia, paid for by the Boone County Democratic Party (Jason Hancock/Missouri Independent). Missouri voters resoundingly rejected major Republican priorities on Tuesday as proposals to eliminate the income tax and change the way initiative petition majorities are counted lost by large margins across the state. 
The Associated Press called the race for both amendments at 8:15 p.m., with Amendment 4 losing by 63 percentage points and Amendment 5 down 67 percentage points. 
Two other statewide ballot questions, Amendment 1 and Amendment 2, were projected to pass easily.
Amendment 1 extends the 0.1% sales tax that supports state parks and soil and water conservation. Amendment 2 will require that all county tax assessors be elected officials and affects only Jackson County.
Gov. Mike Kehoe, while projecting optimism about the chances for both amendments after voting Tuesday morning, said defeat was not the end, especially for the project to eliminate the income tax embodied in Amendment 5.
“I’m going to always look for ways to make the burden of government less on Missouri families and let them keep more of their own money,” Kehoe said.
Any discussion of tax changes needs input from across the political spectrum, people attending an election-night party in Jefferson City at the Missouri Association of Realtors office. The Realtors spearheaded the coalitions that defeated the two amendments, 
At the Ashland Optimist Club in Boone County, there was a steady stream of voters but little in the way of the usual jungle of campaign signs with a last appeal for candidates. There were some candidate primaries, but none that have generated wide interest and most voters wanted to talk about Amendments 4 and 5 as their motivation to vote.
Alan Helland said he opposed Amendment 4 because the initiative process is a way to check unlimited political power.
“It’s necessary, especially in a very partisan environment,” he said. 
Voter Steve Morton said he didn’t like the prospect of higher sales taxes that could have been the result of Amendment 5 passing.
“It’s going to tax away more than what my property tax and stuff is going to be expensive,” he said. “So I don’t want to pay more for everything else.”
The idea of eliminating the state income tax and raising revenue through sales tax appealed to Chad Cole, who said he voted for Amendment 5.
Cole said he expects to pay less in new sales tax than he would in income tax and that will boost the economy.
“I’ll have more money to spend,” he said.
The election was important enough that it brought Macie Reynolds, 18, to the polls for the first time. Outside the Optimist Club building, she hugged her father, Jason Reynolds, as they took a selfie to record the moment and her mother, Dana Reynolds, looked on.
They studied the ballot to prepare, she said.
“We just kind of talked through it and decided what priorities mattered to us, and kind of went with that,” Reynolds said.
What they decided, however, she would not say.
“I’ll keep that to myself,” she said.
Mark Jones, director of public affairs for the Missouri NEA, watches election results roll in on Tuesday at a watch party hosted by the Missouri Association of Realtors (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
The defeat of both amendments was engineered by the Missouri Association of Realtors and coalitions of activist groups on the left and right. During legislative deliberations on both measures, the Realtors made clear their group would provide funding and organizational strength to the opposition campaigns.
The Realtors have used the initiative petition process twice to amend the constitution. In 2010, the organization spent $4.3 million to pass a ban on taxing real estate transactions and, in 2016, $5.6 million later to ban any expansion of goods or services subject to sales tax.
“If we were willing to spend that much a decade ago, we are certainly going to fight to protect it,” Realtor lobbyist Jason Zamkus said after testifying against the income tax replacement bill that became Amendment 5.
Proponents of Amendment 5 came to the fight prepared and outspent opponents by a more than 2-to-1 margin and by an almost 4-to-1 margin in broadcast ads, according to The Independent’s tracking of state and federal campaign reports.
Missouri Promise PAC, the pro-Amendment 5 political action committee funded entirely by groups that do not disclose their donors, doubled its ad spending in many markets in the final week of the campaign in an effort to close the gap.
Opponents of Amendment 4 had the field almost to themselves in terms of big campaign spending. In addition to the group funded by the Realtors,  another opposition committee, Protect Majority Rule Missouri, raised $6.8 million and shared a website with the Realtors-backed committee.
The Realtors contributed $2.8 million to Missourians for Fair Taxation for the campaign to defeat Amendment 5 and $4.4 million of the $4.5 million in cash donations to Missourians for Fair Governance to defeat Amendment 4.
The funding for both campaigns generated some last-day sniping as Kehoe complained about the source of money for the opposition groups. Asked for a response, Scott Charton, a spokesman for both opposition campaigns, said Kehoe should be more careful with his criticism.
“No. 1, it’s easy to say no to anything,” Kehoe said. “No. 2, whoever’s putting a lot of money into that campaign obviously has some tax benefits and things that they like right now. I’m not saying that’s good or bad, but that’s usually how that works.”
Promoters of Amendment 4 tried to make it a grass-roots campaign, Kehoe said. 
The opposition to Amendment 4 came from “the outside interest groups who like to change our constitution, and we’ve seen it happen in 2020, 2022, 2024, where lots of outside money came to change our state’s constitution,” Kehoe said. “The whole point about Amendment 4 is our constitution should not be for sale.”
Asked if the Realtors are an “outside group,” Kehoe said they are “a special interest group, but there’s other funding coming from outside of the state for both of those questions, (Amendments) 4 and 5.”
Charton disputed the label.
“Helping working Missourians achieve the American Dream of homeownership for all is hardly a special interest,” he said. “It is everyone’s interest.”
The money the Realtors put into the campaigns against Amendments 4 and 5 came from the 25,000 Realtors throughout the state, Charton said. 
The money funding Missouri Promise is not disclosed.
“The source of Realtors’ money is Realtors,” Charton said, “but I cannot speak for the dark money groups who never recorded a single individual human donation from a Missourian.”
This story will be updated.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson handily wins Democratic gubernatorial primary over Swanson
description: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has easily won the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, defeating Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson. The unofficial result of the race was called by the Associated Press at 9 p.m., just after the last polls in the state closed, with unofficial results showing Benson leading 85% to 15%. Benson’s initial margins […[...]
text:
Jocelyn Benson speaking to supporters in Detroit after her resounding victory in the Democratic gubernatorial primary. Aug. 4, 2026 | Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan AdvanceMichigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has easily won the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, defeating Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson.
The unofficial result of the race was called by the Associated Press at 9 p.m., just after the last polls in the state closed, with unofficial results showing Benson leading 85% to 15%. Benson’s initial margins were widest in Kent County and Alger County, though as of 9 p.m., Swanson was not winning any county. 
“Tonight marks our opportunity to grow our coalition to include citizens in every corner of our state who believe, as we do, that the power of the people must always be greater than the people in power. My life’s work is about making that promise, that hope, a reality,” Benson said in her victory speech. “You all know who I’ll work for. All of you, and every Michigander in this state. Not the highest bidder, not corporate interests, not Donald Trump, you.”
She continued on to urge voter turnout and volunteer participation in the general election, saying, “Let’s take tonight’s landslide victory and deliver another one this fall.”
Benson consistently held a commanding lead in polls in advance of the primary, with polling from earlier in July giving her a 60-point margin over Swanson. 
“The people built this movement. You kept me going,” Swanson posted on X shortly after the race was called. “Thank you for believing that we could do politics differently. Thank you for walking this journey with me.”
Jocelyn Benson speaking to supporters in Detroit after her resounding victory in the Democratic gubernatorial primary. Aug. 4, 2026 | Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance
She similarly outperformed Swanson in fundraising. During the reporting period beginning Jan. 1, Swanson raised just over $722,000 and spent about $806,000, leaving him with roughly $187,000 cash on hand. Benson, meanwhile, raised $4.9 million and spent $2.1 million, leaving her with more than $6.4 million cash on hand heading into the general election.
National and statewide Democratic organizations were quick to congratulate Benson on her victory.
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel also thanked Swanson for his role in the primary, continuing on to say in a press release, “Michigan Democrats are fired up to elect Jocelyn Benson as our next governor and win a Democratic trifecta that will lower costs, expand healthcare, and invest in our public schools. Let’s go.”
EMILYs List President Jessica Mackler similarly emphasized that their group is “all in” to support Benson in the general election. 
Democratic Governors Association Chair Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said in a press release that Benson’s background as Secretary of State has set her up for success as governor. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is currently vice-chair of the organization. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Jocelyn understands the challenges families are facing, and she has been a fearless public servant who fixes broken systems and improves the lives of Michiganders,” Beshear said. “She’s already earned the trust of Michiganders by winning statewide twice, and the DGA will be all-in to make sure she wins this high-stakes race so she can keep standing up for the people of Michigan.”
The general election was initially expected to be a three-way race, with former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan running as an independent, but he dropped out in May. Though he had been pulling support from both Democrats and Republicans, some had been concerned about him playing spoiler for the Democrats in a general election, given the fact that Duggan was a Democrat for all 12 years in the Detroit mayor’s office. 
However, with Duggan no longer in the picture, Republicans will have to figure out how to single-handedly tackle Benson, who enters with more money on hand and without the baggage of facing the primary attacks that Republicans have been levying at each other for months. 
Three recent polls show Benson winning over both James and Johnson, though her margins were wider over Johnson than James. However, some in the Republican Party, including consultant Dennis Lennox, have argued that Johnson’s access to significant self-funding and his grassroots momentum would do more to boost down-ballot candidates in the state legislature than James would. 
As of 9:24 p.m., the Republican primary remained too close to call.


9:38 pmThis story has been updated with comment from Jocelyn Benson.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrats, Republicans firm up teams for statewide office contests
description: TOPEKA — Primary election results brought few surprises for statewide offices as most candidates ran unopposed. The lone exception was a skirmish between Democrats Jennifer Day and Samuel Lane. Day took a decisive lead as election results rolled in and the Associated Press declared her the race’s winner by 8:25 p.m. Tuesday. The Mission businesswoman, […]
text:
Rep. Pat Proctor, R-Leavenworth, shown here during a February 3, 2026, hearing in Topeka, will be the Republican nominee for Secretary of State and will face the Democrat who wins Tuesday's primary election, Jennifer Day or Samuel Lane  (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Primary election results brought few surprises for statewide offices as most candidates ran unopposed. 
The lone exception was a skirmish between Democrats Jennifer Day and Samuel Lane. Day took a decisive lead as election results rolled in and the Associated Press declared her the race’s winner by 8:25 p.m. Tuesday. The Mission businesswoman, who received Gov. Laura Kelly’s endorsement, will face Republican Pat Proctor of Leavenworth in the general election.
Proctor ran unopposed. A retired U.S. Army colonel, Proctor was elected to the House in 2020. He is among the Legislature’s advocates for election legislation, supporting President Donald Trump’s false claims about his 2020 loss to Joe Biden.
“Our elections belong to the people, not to any political party,” Day said in a news release after her win. “Kansans deserve a Secretary of State who will protect the integrity of our elections, support the professionals who administer them, and make decisions based on what is best for voters across our state.”
Also on the ticket in November will be Scott Morgan of Lawrence, who is running as a member of United Kansas, a new moderate political party espousing problem-solving over partisanship. Morgan is a fifth-generation Kansan who grew up in Shawnee and received degrees in journalism and law from the University of Kansas.
 
Insurance commissioner
Two experienced Kansas politicians will face off in the general election for insurance commissioner after both ran unopposed in the primary. 
Sen. Dinah Sykes, Lenexa, who has been in the Kansas Senate since 2017 and the Senate minority leader since 2021, will run for the Democrats. She was a Republican when entering politics but switched to the Democratic Party in December 2018.  
Sykes will face Rep. Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican, who has been in the Kansas House since 2013 and House speaker since 2023. 
Libertarian candidate Ric Koehn is on the ticket for insurance commissioner, but there has been little activity from his campaign. 
 
State treasurer
Democratic and Republican candidates for state treasurer ran unopposed in the primary. Juan C. Luengo, Olathe, will receive the Democrat nomination. He is the CEO of Engage Insurance Group and has worked in the private business sector throughout his career. 
On his website, he touts that he led Engage through a turnaround and says  the the state treasurer will need such skills.
Luengo will face incumbent Steve Johnson, an experienced politician who served in the state legislature from 2011 to 2023 before being elected state treasurer in 2022. Johnson was born and raised on a cattle and grain farm and has a background in ag economics. 
 
Attorney general
Democrat Chris Mann and Attorney General Kris Kobach will fight for the state’s top legal position in the general election, as each ran unopposed in Tuesday’s primary. 
Mann, an attorney, has a passion for representing drunk driving victims after he was seriously injured in his early 20s by a drunk driver. He was a prosecutor in the Wyandotte County District Attorney’s Office and also worked for the Kansas Securities Commission. 
Mann will face Kobach, who has made a name for himself nationally as a hardliner on immigration and a proponent of making significant changes to keep the election system safe. Kobach has been Kansas attorney general since 2023, and he served as secretary of state from 2011 to 2019.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Wesley Bell beats Cori Bush in Democratic primary for St. Louis congressional seat
description: Incumbent U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell staved off former Congresswoman Cori Bush in the Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District on Tuesday, ending the most expensive candidate primary in Missouri this year. The Associated Press called the race for Bell shortly after 8 p.m. Bell will take on one of two Republican candidates, Paul Berry […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell at a press conference in 2024 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Incumbent U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell staved off former Congresswoman Cori Bush in the Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District on Tuesday, ending the most expensive candidate primary in Missouri this year.
The Associated Press called the race for Bell shortly after 8 p.m.
Bell will take on one of two Republican candidates, Paul Berry III and Andrew Jones, neither of whom has formed a fundraising committee for their campaigns in the heavily Democratic district, and Libertarian Tom Schmitz in the November general election.
Bell and Bush’s political careers were shaped by the protest movement that erupted in Ferguson in 2014 and grew into a national reckoning over race and policing. 
But for the past several years, one main issue is putting them at odds — Bell’s support for Israel and Bush’s advocacy for Palestinian liberation.
Bell’s backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and other pro-Israel PACs led to his re-election spending to be seven times higher than efforts to re-elect Bush.
The 1st District race is the most expensive candidate primary in Missouri this year, with candidates and outside political action committees combining to spend $8.4 million — $7.2 million of that spent on Bell. 
Bell’s campaign has spent almost $3 million over the past two years, including $864,000 on broadcast ads in advance of the primary. Bush, who has spent almost $1.2 million, has only been able to afford $66,400 for broadcast ads.
Airest Wilson, 64, of St. Louis, speaks with former Congresswoman Cori Bush outside a polling place on Tuesday at the Natural Bridge Library in north St. Louis County(Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
AIPAC again worked on Bell’s behalf, spending $3.1 million, including $1.5 million on television ads in the St. Louis area through a PAC called the United Democracy Project. Another outside group, New Democrat Majority, has spent about $1.1 million to support Bell.
In 2024, the AIPAC and the other PACs spent more than $8 million backing Bell as part of a broader strategy by AIPAC to unseat Israel’s sharpest critics in Congress, including the “Squad,” which Bush was a part of. 
Bell was among the largest beneficiaries of AIPAC-related spending nationwide in 2024. The group, founded in the 1950s, has been criticized by progressive Democrats and some Middle East scholars for reflexively backing military escalation and indefinite occupation.
Bell said he disagrees with that criticism and characterization of AIPAC. 
“What they focus on is a strong U.S.-Israeli relationship,” Bell told The Independent in June. “I’ll be honest, I’m not a fan of the current (Israeli) Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, not a fan at all, but what I know about that group is that no matter who’s in charge, they’re going to support a strong US-Israeli relationship.”
Bell sits on the U.S. House Armed Services Committee, which oversees the Department of Defense, and was recently placed on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which oversees national security developments affecting foreign policy.
While Bell said he takes his role on the foreign affairs and armed services committees seriously, he said his priority is St. Louis.
“We have to focus on regional growth and development,” he said, “because I believe this region is a sleeping giant.” 
Patrick Brown, 58, of Normandy, voted for Bell, adding that he’s done a good job,
“I think Cori kind of fumbled the ball a few times,” he said, adding that he doesn’t think she brought enough funds back to Missouri.
Steve Oluokun, 70, stopped by his polling place in north St. Louis County to cast a vote for Bell.
“He does not hide his feelings about Donald Trump,” said Oluokun. He’s seen many TV advertisements for Bell that portrayed him as a “fighter,” which Oluokun said appealed to him.
This story will be updated.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Edwards faces pressure to depart congressional campaign following ethics probe
description: One of Congressman Chuck Edwards’ fellow North Carolina Republicans thinks the outcome of a U.S. House ethics investigation will make it hard for him to win reelection  in November. The U.S. House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it’s recommending that Edwards, a Republican representing North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, be censured for inap[...]
text:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC) departs from a House Republican Conference meeting in the U.S. Capitol Building on July 21, 2026 in Washington, DC.  (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)One of Congressman Chuck Edwards’ fellow North Carolina Republicans thinks the outcome of a U.S. House ethics investigation will make it hard for him to win reelection  in November.
The U.S. House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it’s recommending that Edwards, a Republican representing North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, be censured for inappropriate conduct toward two young women who worked in his office.
Multiple media outlets reported Tuesday that Sen. Ted Budd, R-North Carolina, told Edwards the race was unwinnable.
A spokesman for Budd told NC Newsline that while the Senator does not disclose his private conversations, he “finds the House Ethics report deeply concerning.”
“He believes Rep. Edwards faces a significant uphill battle in his reelection bid, given that he was already trailing in the polls and being outraised 9 to 1 even before this report’s publication,” said the spokesman in a statement to NC Newsline.
A spokesman for Edwards declined to comment on Budd’s comments to NC Newsline Tuesday night.
Ethics investigators found Edwards demonstrated a pattern of “inappropriate actions” toward the two young staffers, though it found no evidence he had inappropriately touched them or made explicitly sexual comments to them.
Both women received numerous gifts from the 65-year-old Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, “designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuums, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners,” according to the Ethics Committee’s report.
According to the report, the two female staffers were “uncomfortable with his behavior, but were put in an untenable position by virtue of his status as their boss and a Member of Congress.”
In May, Edwards said his office welcomed the investigation and called the allegations “baseless.”
In his response to the report, the congressman called censure “an extraordinarily harsh and infrequent punishment,” and insisted the investigation had not proven he broke any actual rules.
On Tuesday, Gov. Josh Stein said he had not read the full report but found the findings unsettling.
“To be clear, for Congress to take some action on a bipartisan basis indicates that what they know is very troubling,” said Stein.
NC Congressman Chuck Edwards to face censure in US House for inappropriate conduct

Edwards, who is running for his third term, faces a formidable opponent in Democrat Jamie Ager. Ager’s grandfather represented the 11th Congressional District from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991, following a stint in the state legislature. His brother Eric Ager serves in the N.C. House.
Even before the ethics probe, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced it would financially support Ager, as it viewed the seat in western North Carolina as one that could flip from Republican to Democratic with more resources and fundraising support.
At the end of July, election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball updated its assessment of the 11th congressional district from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: No immediate decision from judge on releasing probe of controversial UNC program
description: A coalition of news media organizations and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill will have to wait a bit longer to learn whether a lawsuit seeking the release of records from the school will go forward. An Orange County judge who conducted a hearing in the case Tuesday did not immediately issue a […]
text:
The historic old Orange County courthouse in downtown Hillsborough, built in the 1800s, has been replaced mostly by a newer courthouse across the street, but still hosts hearings in civil cases, Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo: Frank Taylor/ Carolina Public Press)A coalition of news media organizations and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill will have to wait a bit longer to learn whether a lawsuit seeking the release of records from the school will go forward.
An Orange County judge who conducted a hearing in the case Tuesday did not immediately issue a ruling.
The lawsuit from the news media organizations, including Carolina Public Press and NC Newsline, claims the state public records law requires the university to release a $1.2 million, 400-plus page report on its internal investigation into its controversial School of Civic Life and Leadership, or SCiLL.
UNC disagrees and has asked for summary judgment, which would effectively end the case.
Before issuing a ruling, Superior Court Judge John Morris said he will personally review the internal investigation report to help him decide whether to end the lawsuit or let the case proceed to trial.
Controversial UNC program
Since its inception in 2023, SCiLL has drawn criticism for its faculty turnover rate, connections to conservative scholars and hasty confirmation by the UNC Board of Trustees and the legislature.
On account of turnover, the university said it would bring in outside firm K&L Gates to conduct an “independent and impartial” review of SCiLL in September 2025.
UNC announced K&L Gates had completed its review of the school March 6 but swiftly denied public records requests seeking the full report, or even a summary, and issued a public statement that the report would not be released.
News media case
The news media coalition sued the university in April, arguing that it is a public record because it was paid for with taxpayer funds.
The parties failed to reach a consensus during a mandatory mediation session last month. Tuesday’s hearing was the result of UNC’s attorneys filing a motion for summary judgment, a request to end a lawsuit before it goes to trial on the grounds there’s no legal argument to continue.
UNC’s primary argument for keeping the report from public view is that its contents are trial preparation materials, and there is a prospect of litigation. It’s not clear what trial the university is preparing for in relation to the report, though UNC’s attorney Wes Camden said there have been allegations related to employment and hiring decisions and anti-discrimination laws like Title VII and Title IX.
“Every single page of this report was stamped by K&L Gates as being attorney work product, and that was done at the time,” Camden said. “That was done well before any of this was raised.
“So, respectfully, your honor, our position is the entire report is governed by trial preparation materials. It’s obviously why the report was commissioned. It’s why the report was prepared, and it’s frankly what the report does.”
The news media outlets’ attorney Mike Tadych referred to a statute in the public records law, G.S. 132-1.9, which says if a public records request is denied on an assertion that the public record is trial preparation material prepared for a legal proceeding that has not happened, the owner of the record should provide a written justification. There is no pending litigation, and a justification hasn’t been produced, Tadych said.
The university has also said the report is covered by attorney work product privilege and the state’s Human Resources Act. While such exceptions are not directly included in the public records law, the defense argued they still apply.
“Although the Public Records Act provides broad access to public records, that access is not absolute because ‘the Public Records Act contains various exemptions,’” the motion for summary judgment read.
“Some exemptions — like the exemptions for trial preparation materials and attorney-client communications are embedded within the Public Records Act itself. Others are scattered throughout the General Statutes but apply to the university as a public agency and state employer. Regardless of their location, exceptions and exemptions to the Public Records Act are construed narrowly.”
But Tadych said those “common law exceptions” not explicitly found in the public records law, have been found in previous case law to be insufficient, such as in McCormick v. Hanson.
Three of the news media outlets suing the university, Carolina Public Press, NC Newsline and the Daily Tar Heel, either did not make a request for the report or did not request it until after the lawsuit had been filed.
Camden said the news media organizations could not be denied the report if they had not requested it, which Tadych called a diversion, given the university had made it clear through denials to other news media outlets, which are visible on the university’s public records portal, and its statement that the report would not be released.
“What Mr. Camden did not tell you was that, had they received the report, I wouldn’t be standing in front of you,” Tadych said.
“So they too have been denied, and I think that’s a bit of a procedural red herring. Nobody in this room, other than counsel for the defendants and now you, your honor, has been allowed access to this report, in our understanding.”
The judge could opt not to recognize those specific news media companies in the case if he agrees with the defense’s argument about them, but there are other players whose claims would still have to be addressed, Tadych said.
A version of the 400-plus page report had already been provided to Morris by UNC’s attorneys ahead of the hearing. After arguments, Morris said he would have to review it himself, which he would be unlikely to complete within this court session, which is usually a week long.
“It will be an intensive legal inquiry and review,” Morris said.
Tadych told reporters the judge may come to a number of conclusions, such as the entire report should remain confidential or just parts of it should be redacted.
So far, not so much as a title page or an index has been released. Tadych speculates that’s in part because it would be a bad look for the university to release 400 pages blacked out with redactions. But that might be what the public records law obligates it to do, Tadych said.
There’s been a widespread push from faculty and students for the university to release the report. The UNC Faculty Council approved two resolutions April 17 calling for transparency related to SCiLL and the report, including a suggestion the university release it with redactions, if necessary. Students also protested shortly after the news media coalition filed the lawsuit, calling for the university to “release the SCiLL files.”
“If you look at their briefing, their position on it has been a lot about that the school’s taken on a lot of criticism, both internally and externally — this investigation using public funds was to address that,” Tadych said.
“Under the Human Resources Act, the university can say, ‘Well, this is important enough for the integrity of the program, or the services that the program delivers, that we can release the information.’?They’ve not availed themselves of that, and instead have said, ‘A thumbs up to everything, and that’s all we’re gonna say.’
“Having spent a million dollars plus on a report and having this new school created, it engenders some controversy. And if this report addresses that, then why shouldn’t the public be able to see that?”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont joins Elliott in exchange of attack ads in Democratic primary
description: With a week to go, the reelection campaign of Gov. Ned Lamont finally is putting some muscle behind a shot at Rep. Josh Elliott in an ad.
text:
With a week to go, the reelection campaign of Gov. Ned Lamont finally is putting some muscle behind a shot at “the other guy,” the governor’s standard reference to his challenger in next week’s Democratic primary, state Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden.
A new 30-second spot mentions 240 votes missed by Elliott, but the real hit delivered by a well-chosen surrogate, Rep. Toni Walker of New Haven, is the amplification of the governor’s larger claim that the 41-year-old Elliott just isn’t a player. 
“He was never there for us when we talked about ICE,” Walker says, speaking to camera. “He was never there when we talked about education in our schools, but he’s always there for that photo op. Josh Elliott cares about Josh Elliott.”
Walker’s mien is angry, her tone sharp. And it’s no accident the sharpest criticism to date of Lamont’s white liberal suburban challenger is not coming from the wealthy Greenwich governor but from a Black urban woman with deep progressive credentials. 
“He is not our guy, and he is not the person we want for the next four years,” Walker says of Elliott. “I want a governor who is battle tested, and that is Ned Lamont.”


Elliott said that, over the course of his 10 years in the legislature, he has been present for 95% of the votes taken.
“Appreciate that he is taking our campaign seriously. Only took him 13 months,” Elliott said in a text.
“He’s making his voice heard,” Lamont said “I got to take it seriously, and I got to go out every day and tell people I want this job.”
The governor’s campaign said the 240 votes missed by Elliott occurred over the entirety of his 10 years in the General Assembly, with 110 missed roll calls on the House floor and 130 in committees.
Elliott missed 43 floor votes in the most recent session when he was campaigning for governor; the other 67 were spread over the previous nine years, meaning he missed an average of fewer than eight votes a year over that time.
One of them was a roll call vote on a Republican amendment that would have weakened a police accountability bill that passed after an all-night debate in 2020. He had gone home to walk his dog and fell asleep.
The hostile amendment failed on a tie vote, 72-72, at 7:40 a.m., with Elliott among the seven who missed the vote. He was present to vote with the majority for final passage on an 86-58 vote at 9:03 a.m.
Lamont acknowledged the new tone of his advertising after a labor rally in New Haven, but he was not exactly in go-for-the-jugular mode — even after a series of recent Elliott ads questioning the governor’s ethics, his commitment to fighting the Trump administration and his values. One suggested he is not a Democrat.


Elliott’s ads were titled, “No More Ned.” The governor’s new spot was called, “Never There.”
“The other guy’s been punching me nonstop for the last six months,” Lamont said. “Maybe it’s time to stand up and tell him what we’re about.”
Maybe, indeed. Early voting opened Monday, and the primary is next week.
The only public tracking poll showed the race tightening since May, with Lamont still holding a 21-point lead, 48% to 27%.
Walker is the long-serving co-chair of the Appropriations Committee, a spot that often has put her in conflict with the governor over spending priorities, but ultimately requires a degree of pragmatism in getting a budget that can pass muster by diverse Democratic caucuses and their governor.
“Welcome to politics,” she said Tuesday.
Lamont said the no-nonsense message in the ad was Walker’s.
“The Toni ad was the Toni ad,” Lamont said. “You know, she stepped up, she said, ‘I want to do this. I know both players pretty well, and I’ll tell you why I support Ned Lamont, and he gets stuff done, and his door is open, and we see him all the time —unlike the other guy.’ I appreciate that.”
Lamont spoke about the ad after a labor rally in New Haven that underscored how a diverse labor movement has lined up behind the notion of continuing a constructive partnership with a governor whose personal brand is fiscal responsibility and whose great-grandfather was a Wall Street giant.
One of those who spoke was Ed Hawthorne, the president of the Connecticut AFL-CIO. He had blistered the governor for vetoing a bill that would have provided jobless benefits for strikers.
On Tuesday, Hawthorne ignored the veto and talked about the labor bills Lamont signed into law, including a measure that raised the minimum wage from $10.10 to $15 in roughly annual $1 increments, then indexed the wage to the cost of living.
It’s now $16.94. On Wednesday, Lamont will announce what the minimum will go to in 2027.

text:
U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, speaks Aug. 4 about issues raised by constituents during the primary election campaign after casting her ballot in a Johnson County polling station. Davids says 3rd District voters are keen to highlight concern about the rising cost of groceries, fuel, prescription medications and healthcare. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas won her primary against a liberal Democrat, according to the Associated Press. 
The AP called the Democratic and Republican primaries 15 minutes after polls closed for the Kansas City-area 3rd Congressional District for Davids and Eric Jenkins, a former Shawnee City councilman.
Davids said in a statement she was “deeply honored to earn the trust of voters.”
“I fundamentally believe the government should work for the people it serves — not special interests, big corporations, or partisan agendas,” she said. “Every single day, I hear from Kansans who are working hard, budgeting carefully and doing everything right, but are still getting squeezed by rising costs on everyday essentials like groceries, healthcare, and housing.”
All four Kansas U.S. House members appeared to lead their primary opponents, according to preliminary results. 
U.S. Republican Reps. Tracey Mann, Derek Schmidt, Ron Estes each had one Republican opponent, and Davids defeated Sarah Preu, a technology and communications professional from Fairway, who criticized Davids about issues such as Israel’s political influence, immigration enforcement funding and voting with conservatives.
Two Lawrence Democrats are competing to represent the 1st Congressional District. Colin McRoberts is a business law professor at the University of Kansas, and Lauren Reinhold is a lawyer who formerly worked for the federal government. 
Mann was ahead of Craig Musser, according to preliminary results.
Schmidt appeared to lead opponent Chad Young. Democrat, veteran and veterinarian Don Coover was unopposed in the Democratic primary.
A slate of Democrats lined up to challenge Estes, but some have since dropped out of the race to endorse Chris Carmichael, a veteran, and Katy Tyndell, a lawyer and oil and gas company owner. Estes led Frank McCollum, according to early results.
Trump endorsed each of the Republicans in similar posts to Truth Social on Monday.
