name: Daily Montanan
title: Upper Seven Law seeks class action in immigration case
description: A man who has lived in Montana for 10 years and faced pressure from federal authorities to deport himself is among 17 people being illegally detained in the Cascade County Detention Center, according to a federal court filing this week. Jesus Verde Hernandez, of Worden, faces no criminal charges, but U.S. Customs and Border Patrol […]
text:
Handcuffs illustration (Photo by Jernej Furman via Flicker | CC-BY-SA 2.0) A man who has lived in Montana for 10 years and faced pressure from federal authorities to deport himself is among 17 people being illegally detained in the Cascade County Detention Center, according to a federal court filing this week.
Jesus Verde Hernandez, of Worden, faces no criminal charges, but U.S. Customs and Border Patrol stopped him in Lewistown on Thursday, July 30, and arrested him without a warrant, according to his lawyers, with Upper Seven Law of Helena.
The same day, the lawyers asked the court to release him. A news release from the law firm says on Friday, the U.S. District Court of Montana set a hearing for Aug. 5 to consider releasing Hernandez.
Sunday, the lawyers asked the court to certify a class-action case. They argue Hernandez is one of approximately 17 men detained in the Cascade County jail on immigration holds and without criminal charges, and others in Montana are in a similar situation.
“Many class members will be unable to access the court because federal immigration officials will coerce them into self-deporting without adequately informing them of the legal consequences of doing so,” the court filing says.
An order Monday prevents authorities from transporting any of the others out of Montana before an Aug. 18 hearing in Missoula.
The petition was filed against Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter; Chief U.S. Patrol Agent Zachary Crosson of Havre; U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin; and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, among other officials.
Slaughter said the Cascade County Detention Center is simply the contract facility for the detainees. An online federal court system did not have the government’s written response filed by Tuesday afternoon.
The filing by the nonprofit law firm asks the Department of Homeland Security to release Hernandez and others it argues were detained without due process. The news release describes Hernandez’s arrest.
For 30 hours, Hernandez was offered only crackers and water, and he was denied the over-the-counter medication he takes to manage chronic pain, the news release said.
The court filing asks the court to immediately release Hernandez and all similar plaintiffs or hold hearings to show they’re a danger or flight risk.
The court filing says Hernandez lives with his partner of 14 years and their three children, 9, 6 and 4; his partner and children all are U.S. citizens; and he is a step-father to his partner’s two children from a previous relationship, both young adults and U.S. citizens.
“Jesus is a devoted father and member of the Worden community,” the court document says. “Recently, for over a year, he and his partner supported and took care of a homeless teen in the community.”
On July 30, Customs and Border Patrol arrested Hernandez and another man in Lewistown without a warrant, the court filing says. It says federal authorities took them to the local police station, “where they remained handcuffed for approximately two hours.”
Then, CBP drove them to Jordan, where they picked up a third detainee, and they took Hernandez and the two others to the Malta Border Patrol Station and incarcerated Hernandez and the others overnight, the court record states.
A news release from the law firm says Customs and Border Patrol pressured Hernandez to sign papers to agree to self-deport.
“Afraid of facing an even more prolonged separation from his family, Jesus felt pressured to sign,” the news release said. “Had his attorneys been unable to reach him, he would have agreed to voluntarily deport under false pretenses.”
On July 31, authorities took Hernandez and the other person arrested in Lewistown to the Cascade County Detention Center, where they remain among 17 men detained there without criminal charges, court records state.
“Jesus seeks to represent a class of noncitizens detained at CCDC or other detention facilities in Montana who, on information and belief, face prolonged, mandatory detention because of a draconian policy adopted by the Department of Homeland Security that prevents them from being released on bond while in lengthy civil immigration proceedings,” the court document said.
The lawyers believe the Department of Homeland Security intends to start removal proceedings for Hernandez and the others and will argue they are subject to mandatory custody —  but the policy was declared unlawful by the Ninth Circuit on July 30, 2025.
DHS officials argue that people such as Hernandez aren’t eligible to be released on bond during immigration proceedings, the court filing says.
However, Hernandez’s attorneys point out that the District Court of Montana, the Ninth Circuit, and “the vast majority of courts” have rejected the policy of treating people arrested in the interior of the country — as opposed to at the border — in a way that subjects them to mandatory detention.
“Jesus is neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk,” the court document says. “On information and belief, no other class member is a danger to the community or a flight risk.”
The lawyers allege the continued detention violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
They also note in recent months, “there has been a surge of immigration arrests in Montana,” multiple people are seeking relief from “this same unlawful interpretation,” and more petitions are likely to follow unless the court certifies a class-action case.
“Many class members … will be quickly boarded onto vans and planes and sent to neighboring states with ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) facilities and other far-off locations before they have a chance to seek help,” the court filing said, arguing for the necessity of the class.
After the hearing on Aug. 18, the court will determine whether the Department of Homeland Security will release the others being held from detention.
In a statement, Upper Seven Executive Director Rylee Sommers-Flanagan said Hernandez’s arrest is part of a pattern by federal immigration officials.
“And the quick transfer of detained individuals out of state without opportunity to contest their detention or consult with an attorney violates the law. The rule of law is for everyone, and we will fight to uphold it for our fellow Montanans, without exception,” Sommers-Flanagan said in a statement.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: After years of pleas to address water crisis, Morrisey begins two-day Southern WV listening tour
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday that he will be taking a brief listening tour around the state’s southern coalfields to hear about the persistent water issues residents in the region face.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces his two day water listening tour at a stop in Huntington, West Virginia on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. The governor is joined by Marshall University President Brad Smith (third from right). (Photo courtesy of Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s X account)Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Tuesday that he will be taking a brief listening tour around the state’s southern coalfields to hear about the persistent water issues residents in the region face.
The listening tour started on Tuesday and will go through Wednesday. Morrisey said during a news conference Tuesday morning that he will be stopping in four counties — Wayne, Mingo, Wyoming and McDowell — to meet with local officials and water operators and learn more about the challenges related to aging water infrastructure, poor water quality and struggling local utilities.
“We will be listening. We need to listen to learn about all the challenges that families are facing, and we know one of the big challenges that they’re facing deals with clean water,” Morrisey said. “… This isn’t about making speeches. This is about listening to what’s going on.”
The tour comes after residents in the coalfields have spent years — and, for some, decades — sounding the alarm on the crises unfolding in their backyards. Residents and advocates have shown up at the state capitol year over year begging for state-level attention on the issues, including increased funding to alleviate the challenges and a focus on correcting the root cause of some of them, like disturbances from nearby coal mining activities. 
Morrisey said part of the struggle for the state in addressing these concerns has come down to red tape: different agencies working on the same projects in different capacities, competition for funds and potentially overpaying contractors for work to correct problems. The governor did not provide specific examples of these situations.
The governor also touted the state’s recent investments in water and wastewater infrastructure. In the last 18 months, Morrisey said, the state has put more than $550 million toward those projects, with about $174 million of that coming from state grants.
But that money is less than a drop in the proverbial bucket that’s needed to correct the southern coalfield’s ongoing water woes.
According to the Infrastructure and Jobs Development Council’s 2023 statewide needs assessment survey — the most recent published — it’s estimated that nearly $18 billion is needed to upkeep and rehabilitate the state’s existing water and sewage infrastructure as well as to expand water and sewage service to all structures in the state.
As of that report, about 64,000 West Virginians are not connected to a centralized water service, while almost 254,000 residents go without sewage service. Of those who are served, thousands more live with inadequate service — leaky lines that lead to high water loss rates, persistent service outages, long-term boil water notices, contaminants that could impact health and more.
Water infrastructure is expensive to fix for even well-funded utilities under the state’s current funding structures. A majority of the money available comes from long-term loan funds, which can be difficult to pay off for small, already cash-strapped utilities. The cost of those loans is often directly passed on to ratepayers, as bills paid by customers are the only source of income for most of the state’s public water and wastewater utilities. That means residents are left to pay higher rates for services that are still inadequate.
As of Tuesday, there were more than 380 open boil water advisories active in the state. About 10% of those notices are for systems within the coalfield counties (generally recognized as Boone, Lincoln, Logan, Mercer, Mingo, McDowell, Wayne and Wyoming counties). Data for Boone County was not available on the state’s public boil water notice dashboard.
Some residents have relied on public water utilities that have been under boil water advisories — due to a lack of certified operators, consistently leaking pipes and persistent contamination, among other reasons — for years. 
And while the problem has centered on the southern coalfields — due to a combination of cash-strapped local governments as well as long term disinvestment from the state and private companies that, in previous generations, kept up the public services — water issues persist statewide.
In 2024, according to an analysis from the Charleston Gazette-Mail, more than 79% of the state’s public drinking water systems were found to have violations of the federal Safe Drinking Water Act. Nearly 30% of systems — the highest rate in the nation — had health-based violations.
Residents from affected areas have, for years now, shared photos and videos far and wide of what the water coming out of their faucets looks like. They’ve brought bottles to the state Capitol and hearings of the Public Service Commission, urging officials to take a drink if they don’t believe the issue is serious enough to warrant immediate response. Often that water is brown or yellow and murky. Sometimes it’s tinged with red, black or grey. The water stains clothes in the laundry, ruins expensive household appliances and, residents say, leaves some to develop skin rashes if used to bathe.
On Tuesday, Morrisey said he wants to hear directly from those who live with these challenges every day before moving the state forward with any sort of solution to the decades-old problem.
“The people closest to these challenges, they’re often the people with the best ideas for solving them, and that’s why we’re here … We want to hear directly from the people who know these issues the best,” Morrisey said. “We’re going to learn, and then we’re going to act and we’re going to do the right thing.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey will sign immigrant protections into law Wednesday
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The bill (H 5620) that cleared the House and Senate on split votes last Thursday would expand protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests to courthouses, public schools, child care centers and health care facilities.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY will sign a new immigrant protection measure into law Wednesday in Chelsea, saying the compromise bill lawmakers sent her last week “provides the strongest protections in the country against abuses by ICE, including keeping them out of courthouses, schools and hospitals.”
Lawmakers attached an emergency preamble to the bill, declaring it “an emergency law, necessary for the immediate preservation of the public safety” and arranging for it to take effect as soon as Healey signs it.
The bill (H 5620) that cleared the House and Senate on split votes last Thursday would expand protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests to courthouses, public schools, child care centers and health care facilities. It bars new agreements allowing state and local officials to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions, preserves the Department of Correction’s existing partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and codifies the Supreme Judicial Court’s 2017 Lunn v. Commonwealth decision which held that there is “no authority for Massachusetts court officers to arrest and hold an individual solely on the basis of a Federal civil immigration detainer.” 
“We started this effort by grounding our work in the belief that all Massachusetts residents deserve equal protection under both the United States constitution and Massachusetts constitution regardless of where they were born or their color, creed, or immigration status,” Sen. Cindy Friedman said Thursday before the Senate adopted the proposal. “And I would add that every single person in this Commonwealth, state, country, world deserve to be treated with dignity and respect. Nobody is illegal.” 
Friedman said the bill was a response to ICE, an agency that she said “has become violent, frequently disregarding the law, and often seems to revel in sowing fear and division.”
Joining Healey for the 9:45 a.m. signing ceremony at La Colaborativa on 6th Street in Chelsea will be Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll, Education Secretary Steven Zrike, Office of Refugees and Immigrants Executive Director Cristina Aguilera-Sandoval, Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez, La Colaborativa President & CEO Gladys Vega, public safety officials, advocates and others.
Healey said the bill was “top of mind” for her last week and expressed hope it would reach her desk.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia primary voters pick Mizusawa to face Warner, finalize key US House races
description: Virginians cast their ballots Tuesday in an unusually-timed primary that settled a statewide Republican contest for the U.S. Senate and determined several of Virginia’s most closely watched congressional matchups for the November election. Retired U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Bert Mizusawa won the GOP’s nomination to challenge longtime Democratic U.S. Senator Mark Wa[...]
text:
Virginia voters chose Bert Mizusawa as the Republican nominee who will challenge Democratic incumbent U.S. Sen. Mark Warner in this fall's midterm elections. There were decisive results in key U.S. House primary contests, as well. (Graphic by States Newsroom)Virginians cast their ballots Tuesday in an unusually-timed primary that settled a statewide Republican contest for the U.S. Senate and determined several of Virginia’s most closely watched congressional matchups for the November election.
Retired U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Bert Mizusawa won the GOP’s nomination to challenge longtime Democratic U.S. Senator Mark Warner, while incumbents and former members of Congress emerged victorious in a number of the night’s marquee House races. 
This year’s primary was held nearly two months later than usual, after Virginia lawmakers postponed the traditional June nominating contest to accommodate April’s redistricting referendum. The Supreme Court of Virginia later struck down the new map, leaving candidates to compete under the existing district lines. 
 U.S. Senate

Mizusawa defeated U.S. Navy veteran and political outsider David Williams with 50.71% to 29.54% of the vote, according to unofficial results reported by the Virginia Department of Elections at 8:35 p.m.
Businesswoman Kim Farington came in third with 19.75%.  
A former Pentagon official, Mizusawa built his campaign around his military and public service background, emphasizing national security, military readiness, federal spending and energy policy. He advances to face Warner, who is seeking a fourth six-year term in a state that has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since 2002. 
 1st District 

Democratic voters in the 1st Congressional District nominated Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor with 53.23% of the vote.
Taylor, Henrico’s top prosecutor since 2012 and an unsuccessful 2025 candidate for attorney general, will face U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, who has represented the district since 2007.
Taylor finished ahead of public-interest attorney Salaam Bhatti (19.93%), U.S. Navy Navy veteran and energy lobbyist Jason Knapp (9.95%), U.S. Army veteran Elizabeth Dempsey Beggs (6.71%), business lawyer Mel Tull (4.48%), environmental advocate Tim Cywinski (2.91%), and healthcare attorney Ericka Kopp (2.79%). 
 2nd District

Former U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria earned the Democratic nomination in the highly competitive 2nd District with 79.14% of the vote. The district remains Virginia’s most vulnerable Republican-held seat and is among 18 House races rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report. 
A retired U.S. Navy commander, Luria represented the district for two terms before losing to Republican Jan Kiggans in 2022. Tuesday’s victory sets up a rematch with Kiggans. 
Luria defeated physician Nila Devanath (17.53%), physicist and veteran official Bill Fleming (2.07%) and former U.S. Agency for International Development employee Patrick Mosolf (1.26%).
 5th District

Voters in the 5th District settled competitive primaries in both parties. 
First-term Republican U.S. Rep. John McGuire of Goochland secured his renomination with 85.74% of the vote, defeating Marine veteran and business owner Melanie Lucero (14.26%).
McGuire, a former Navy SEAL and state delegate, narrowly defeated then-U.S. Rep. Bob Good in the 2024 Republican primary before winning the seat that November.
On the Democratic side, former U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello prevailed with 78.24% of the vote. 
Perriello represented the district from 2009 to 2011, later sought the governorship in 2017 and served in diplomatic posts during the Obama and Biden administrations. He defeated physician Suzanne Krzyzanowski (15.49%) and writer Robert Tracinski (6.27%) and will face McGuire this fall.
 7th District

In the 7th District, Republican voters selected Douglas Ollivant with 56.42% of the vote to challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman of Woodbridge in November.
A retired U.S. Army officer and national security analyst, Ollivant campaigned on domestic manufacturing, energy production, job growth and reducing federal regulation.
He finished ahead of entrepreneur Philip Harding (30.77%) and pastor and construction company owner Rick Smithers (12.81%). Vindman, also a retired Army officer, was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.
 8th District

Six-term Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Beyer of Alexandria turned back four primary challengers in the 8th District, winning 66.89% of the vote. 
Beyer, a former Virginia lieutenant governor and U.S. ambassador to Switzerland and Liechtenstein, has represented Northern Virginia in Congress since 2015 and has focused recently on clean energy, artificial intelligence and assistance for displaced federal workers.
He defeated former Alexandria City Councilman and U.S. Labor Department attorney Mo Seifeldein (18.12%), former CIA officer and Marine veteran Adam Dunigan (9.22%), former U.S. State Department employee Michael Duffin (3.26%) and Stafford County teacher Lorena Bruner (2.51%). 
Beyer advances to face Republican Tony Sabio, who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination.
 9th District

Bedford County farmer and small-business owner Joy Powers captured the Democratic nomination with 49.30% of the vote in Virginia’s heavily Republican 9th District. Powers brings a background in agricultural development, foster care advocacy and leadership of the Bedford County Fair.  
She will challenge Republican U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith of Salem, who has represented the district since 2011 and was unopposed. 
Powers defeated Software developer Adam Murphy (38.50%) and United Methodist pastor and attorney Douglas Crockett (12.20%). 
 10th District

Retired U.S. Airforce Col. and former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense David Beckwith won the Republican nomination in the 10th District with 72.50% of the vote. 
Beckwith, who has centered his campaign on national security and government management, will face first-term Democratic U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam of Loudoun County in November. 
Beckwith defeated Fairfax County teacher and former state Senate candidate Julie Perry, who received 20.33% of the vote, national security and economics professional Anthony Suttles (5.54%) and retired U.S. Army Lt. Col. Sam Wong (1.63%). Subramanyam was unopposed for the Democratic nomination. 
The winners of Tuesday’s primary contest will go head-to-head in the midterm elections, set for Nov. 3.
Additional candidates who faced no primary opposition also secured their party’s nomination Tuesday, completing the lineup for Virginia’s remaining congressional races. 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott of Newport News will face Republican Ed Rivera in the 3rd District. Scott, the dean of Virginia’s congressional delegation, has represented the Hampton Roads-based seat since 1993. 
No Republican filed to challenge U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond, in the heavily Democratic-leaning 4th District. McClellan has held the seat since winning a 2023 special election.
Republican U.S. Rep. Ben Cline of Botetourt County will take on Democrat Beth Macy in the 6th District, while U.S. Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Fairfax, will face Republican Arthur Purves in the 11th.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC House approves election changes, budget additions over critics’ objections
description: North Carolina House Republicans on Tuesday approved wide-ranging changes to the conduct of elections, pushing past Democrats’ objections.   The House approved House Bill 958  in a 62-47 vote, with only Republicans in favor.   Among other changes, the Senate added a provision that would reduce the early voting period in primaries, run-offs, and special elect[...]
text:
North Carolina Legislative Building (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)A group protesting a bill changing North Carolina elections law is ejected from the House gallery as some chant, “The people united will never be defeated,” on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo: Claire Michal/NC Newsline)
North Carolina House Republicans on Tuesday approved wide-ranging changes to the conduct of elections, pushing past Democrats’ objections.  
The House approved House Bill 958  in a 62-47 vote, with only Republicans in favor.  
Among other changes, the Senate added a provision that would reduce the early voting period in primaries, run-offs, and special elections from 17 days to 10 days.
Republicans said turnout for those non-general elections is so low it doesn’t justify staffing polling sites for a full early voting period. 
The bill also allows challenges to ballots cast during early voting or by mail for up to three days after an election. People whose voter registrations are canceled because a federal database says they are deceased won’t have the chance to prove that their removal was a mistake. 
“Those databases we know are flawed,” said Rep. Phil Rubin, D-Wake.” We know they list people that are dead who are not dead.” 
The lack of due process will lead to lawsuits, he said. “It violates constitutional protections.”
Rubin said the measure also opens the door to strategic ballot challenges.
Candidates who appear to be losing on election night will have time to file strategic challenges in hopes of getting votes thrown out, he said.
Jefferson Griffin concedes in Supreme Court election

“We could call it the Griffin Rule, where you can actually wait to see the preliminary results of an election, see if maybe you need to get some changes made,” Rubin said, referring to former Republican state Supreme Court candidate Jefferson Griffin, who challenged thousands of votes in 2024 in an unsuccessful effort to reverse his loss to Democrat Allison Riggs. 
Loading up so many changes so close to the midterms is too much for voters to absorb, said Rep. Abe Jones, D-Wake. “The public will not have time to digest the changes before the elections take place in early November,” Jones said. 
The session paused briefly while protesters in the gallery, chanting “The people united will never be defeated,” were removed. 
House Bill 834, which focuses on ballot counting and obtaining missing voter signatures, passed with a vote of 74-35. Eleven Democrats and Rep. Carla Cunningham, U-Mecklenburg, voted with all Republicans. 
NC Senate approves controversial elections bill along party lines

The House also approved two small budget bills Republicans presented as corrections to the main state budget the legislature passed last month.
The larger bill, House Bill 268, rescinds some agency personnel cuts, adds millions in sporting events spending, and takes power away from executive branch Democrats. It passed 79-31.
The bill authorizes up to $40 million to secure at least four PGA Tour championship qualifying events for Greensboro. The Wyndham Championship is played each year at the Sedgefield Country Club in Greensboro. 
The bill would also spend $25 million on the Military World Games. The games are being held in North and South Carolina. Charlotte is the host for the games.
Rep. Marcia Morey, D-Durham, said that $65 million would be better spent to help Hurricane Helene victims, food banks, or Legal Aid.
“When you’re adding $65 million to an already existing sports program, that is not a technical correction, that is a big gift,” she said. “Let’s look to the people in need in North Carolina, and not the sports industry.”
One provision kicks Secretary of State Elaine Marshall off of a state commission that oversees local government finances. Another would force a governor’s Cabinet appointees out of their jobs if the Senate does not approve them during a two-year legislative session. 
Earlier Tuesday, Gov. Josh Stein told reporters that Republicans are “moving power to their friends” whether or not such moves make sense. 
“It’s all about trying, on a partisan basis, to take power away from Democrats, and it’s wrong,” Stein said.  
He referenced the controversial 2024 law that stripped state Board of Elections appointment powers from his office, giving it to Republican state Auditor Dave Boliek. Boliek hired a former state Republican Party executive director, Dallas Woodhouse, to a newly created job as an elections liaison to the counties. Woodhouse resigned from the office as controversies over his advice to counties on early voting times and locations swirled. 
“Government should be about serving people. What they’re trying to do is just move power to their friends” whether it makes sense for that person to have authority or not, Stein said. 
Asked for comment on Stein’s remarks, House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, didn’t disagree, saying only, “We’re taking [appointments] from his friends and giving them to our friends.”
The House also approved a smaller budget bill that includes an appropriation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy and approves an “America’s Semiquincentennial” license plate on a 99-11 vote.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Kalshi is subject to Utah’s anti-gambling law, judge rules
description: Utah may enforce its anti-gambling laws, even if they include bans of proposition betting, a federal judge ruled on Tuesday in response to a lawsuit from Kalshi challenging a new state law. The prediction market platform had described the law, which classified proposition bets within the definition of banned gambling, as “an intrusion into the […]
text:
In Kalshi's lawsuit against the state of Utah, a federal judge found federal commodities law does not override Utah’s anti-gambling mandates. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Utah may enforce its anti-gambling laws, even if they include bans of proposition betting, a federal judge ruled on Tuesday in response to a lawsuit from Kalshi challenging a new state law.
The prediction market platform had described the law, which classified proposition bets within the definition of banned gambling, as “an intrusion into the federal government’s exclusive authority to regulate derivatives trading on exchanges overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.” 
But, U.S. District Judge Robert Shelby disagreed, saying that the federal commodities law does not override Utah’s anti-gambling mandates.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“State regulation of its gambling laws does not prevent the CFTC from serving the public interest in regulating derivates markets, preventing price manipulation, ensuring financial integrity, protecting market participants, and promoting innovations,” the judge wrote in the order. “Kalshi has not met its burden of showing otherwise.”
Prediction market exchange Kalshi sues Utah over proposed prop betting ban

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who had vowed on social media to use every resource within his disposal as governor to beat prediction markets in court, applauded the news on Tuesday. 
“Prediction markets are gambling, full stop,” Cox said in a post. “They are causing tremendous harm to countless American families. Today’s ruling affirms that Utah’s anti-gambling laws are an appropriate way to protect our citizens and are not preempted by federal law.”
Jacki McGavick, a Kalshi spokesperson, said the company disagrees with the judge’s decision and will appeal.
“Multiple courts have already recognized that prediction markets fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction, and we will continue to defend that position,” McGavick said in an email. 
The issue of whether prediction markets, which allows people to bet money on the outcome of almost anything, fits the definition of gambling, has caused a stir all over the country. The debate is especially tense in Utah, where gambling has historically been strictly prohibited. 
Kalshi had argued in a lawsuit filed in February that because the company is a federally designated derivatives exchange, it should be under the exclusive oversight of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
“Kalshi offers consumers the chance to trade many types of event contracts, all of which are subject to extensive oversight by the CFTC, and are lawful under federal law,” the company said in its complaint. “The CFTC has the authority to initiate the review of, and under certain circumstances, prohibit the trading of, contracts listed on Kalshi’s federally regulated exchange. But the CFTC has since made clear that it views Kalshi’s offerings as legal and within its purview.”
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, however, contends Kalshi “can’t rebrand illegal gambling as a federal commodity,” he said in a statement. 
“Utah’s constitution bans gambling to protect Utah families, and my office will enforce that ban,” Brown said. “Gambling is gambling no matter what any company calls it.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: It doesn’t have to be like this, Montana
description: It doesn’t have to be like this. We can have it all:  A benevolent society that supports each one of us as we pursue the dreams of our lifetimes;  A thoughtful society that recognizes our inviolable right to a life of dignity; A compassionate society that provides quality medical care, child care, educational opportunities, effective […]
text:
Gov. Greg Gianforte signs a bill from the 69th Legislature. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)It doesn’t have to be like this.
We can have it all: 

A benevolent society that supports each one of us as we pursue the dreams of our lifetimes; 
A thoughtful society that recognizes our inviolable right to a life of dignity;
A compassionate society that provides quality medical care, child care, educational opportunities, effective aging services, agreeable housing, and decent workforce opportunities that pay a livable wage;  
An opportunity society in which each person has “a fair chance to make of himself all that in him lies,” as Teddy Roosevelt proclaimed in 1910. 

We can’t begin to approach these goals while wealth and power is concentrated in the tiniest portion of our population. The present tax structure facilitates this concentration of power. 
Thomas Jefferson set a high bar high with his famous words in the Declaration of Independence, and President Abraham Lincoln reaffirmed them 87 years later at Gettysburg. We are “all created equal” and we are all entitled to an equal opportunity in the game of life. 
Yet anyone with eyes can see how far short we have fallen. Everywhere, people struggle to get by, while a few amass fabulous riches and spend it on mansions, yachts and extravagances that are almost beyond comprehension. 
Franklin Delano Roosevelt warned us that “the test of our progress is not whether we add to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.”
With that in mind, since the Great Depression, the tax code has required the wealthiest to pay a higher share of their income to the government to support programs that advance the common good. This tax structure funded our public programs through the post-war era until the mid-’70s, yielding a period of unprecedented prosperity. 
Then came a new theory — trickle-down economics. It proposed cutting the taxes on the wealthy in the hope that they would create new jobs and revenue, lifting the living standards of the rest of us. Beginning with the Reagan presidency, this theory was put to the test. 
But it was too good to be true. The government cut taxes for the richest but the wealth did not trickle down. Instead it concentrated at the top 1% and the social safety net shrank. 
You would think that the trickle-down theory would be firmly buried by the facts. But you would be wrong. Gov. Greg Gianforte is preparing a new version called the “flat tax.” This proposal lowers the state income tax on those at the top while doing nothing for working people and families. Taxpayers who earn more than $575,000 a year already pay the lowest effective state and local tax rate of any category of taxpayers. Yet the flat tax would lower it even more. 
The governor’s tax cuts would decrease state revenue by $130 million a year, at a time when Montana sorely needs those revenues. That tax revenue protects Medicaid and rural healthcare, funds our public schools, addresses the affordable housing crisis, provides residential property tax relief, and cares effectively for our aging population. 
It’s easy to fall into the trap of hopelessness. But it doesn’t have to be like this, and there’s something we can do about it. 
It’s simple. We can vote. The elections this November can change the direction of our state and our country. We have the power to choose a new set of officeholders, folks who are committed to the belief that government should be used to provide for the general welfare of all and not just for the few.
The campaign for the midterms will begin in earnest after Labor Day. Find out where each candidate stands on the governor’s flat tax.
It doesn’t have to be like this. And we can do something about it.
 
Jon Ellingson serves as Vice Chair of the Board of Big Sky 55+. He is a former state legislator and was Senate Majority Leader during the 2005 session. His career includes work with former Attorneys General Mike McGrath and Steve Bullock and as the legal director of the Montana ACLU.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s Democratic nominee for US Senate drops out
description: South Dakota’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee ended his campaign Tuesday. “In recent weeks, my family has faced extraordinary personal challenges,” Julian Beaudion said in a written statement. “As many of you know, we experienced a devastating house fire while continuing to navigate significant personal financial hardship.” The deadline for the state Democra[...]
text:
Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls businessman and former state trooper, speaks at the downtown Sioux Falls library on April 7, 2025. Beaudion announced Tuesday that he's withdrawing from the race for U.S. Senate. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee ended his campaign Tuesday.
“In recent weeks, my family has faced extraordinary personal challenges,” Julian Beaudion said in a written statement. “As many of you know, we experienced a devastating house fire while continuing to navigate significant personal financial hardship.”
The deadline for the state Democratic Party Central Committee to nominate a replacement candidate is next Tuesday. The party issued a news release Tuesday evening that did not say whether party leaders will pick a new nominee. Instead, the news release said the party “respects Julian Beaudion’s decision to suspend his campaign for U.S. Senate” and added that he “would have made an outstanding U.S. senator for South Dakota.”
Party officials did not immediately provide a response to South Dakota Searchlight questions on Friday evening.
Podcast: Rhoden’s victory, a quote that doomed Doeden, and a Democrat’s ‘uphill battle’

Beaudion is a businessman and former state trooper. He had been receiving support from party officials, but some other Democrats had been calling for Beaudion to drop out, saying they believe the independent candidate in the race, Brian Bengs, has a better chance to beat incumbent Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as the Democratic nominee against Republican U.S. Sen. John Thune in 2022 and received 26% of the vote.
Beaudion alleged in his statement that “an opponent and those associated with the opponent, hit my family and I with intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”
“Those attacks were personal and never about politics,” Beaudion’s statement said. “The mental and physical safety of my family is my priority and for this reason alone, I step aside.”
The Bengs campaign replied to Searchlight questions by sending a written statement from Bengs.
“I have never spoken ill of Julian, and I won’t start now,” Bengs’ statement said, in part. “He is a patriot and I applaud his action. We were both under a great deal of stress, but I entirely reject the notion that there was some behind-the-scenes conspiracy. Nobody has been attacked or threatened.”
The effort to force Beaudion out of the race included American Muckrakers, a website operated by a North Carolina man.
American Muckrakers published articles in recent weeks praising Bengs and sent an email to South Dakota media outlets in June containing allegations about Beaudion, with references to some of the personal struggles Beaudion ultimately alluded to in his statement Tuesday.
The Bengs campaign, in response to earlier Searchlight questions, said it has no formal relationship with American Muckrakers or its author.
Several people who spent decades working in Democratic politics had also been calling for Beaudion to leave the race. They included Steve Jarding, a former executive director of the South Dakota Democratic Party; Steve Hildebrand, who was the deputy national campaign manager for then-Sen. Barack Obama’s successful 2008 presidential campaign and worked on earlier campaigns for former South Dakota U.S. Sens. Tom Daschle and Tim Johnson; and Drey Samuelson, who was Johnson’s chief of staff for 28 years.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hildebrand had said there’s a stigma associated with the Democratic brand in South Dakota that would prevent Beaudion from winning, and Jarding said “the Democratic brand in South Dakota is dead.” They said Beaudion should drop out to consolidate votes and resources behind Bengs. Beaudion said in his statement Tuesday that he will not endorse Bengs or Rounds.
Democrats have not held a statewide office in South Dakota since January 2015, when Sen. Johnson — who was slowed by health problems — left office after opting against a reelection campaign. Rounds, a former governor, won the race for Johnson’s Senate seat and has held it ever since. 
The gap between registered Republican and Democratic voters in South Dakota has widened in recent years, and Republicans now outnumber Democrats 2.5 to 1. The Democratic Party has been further subjugated by the rise of independents and voters who list no label or affiliation on their registration, who now collectively outnumber Democrats in the state.
South Dakota Democratic Party Chairman Shane Merrill, in an interview with Searchlight prior to Tuesday, disagreed with the assertions by Jarding, Hildebrand and Samuelson that the party’s brand is too damaged to win statewide elections in South Dakota.
“I find it rich that the folks that made their living off the South Dakota Democratic Party are now running away from the brand instead of trying to help build and strengthen the brand,” Merrill said. “If we would all work together, we could probably accomplish more.”
Rounds has used the Democratic feud over Beaudion to raise campaign donations, sending emails to potential donors saying “the Democrats are running a fake independent to flip my seat.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Libertarian Party to hold 3rd District nominating convention after Battaglia ends campaign
description: The Libertarian Party of Iowa will hold a convention Sunday to nominate a new 3rd District candidate to appear on the November ballot after Libertarian Marco Battaglia ended his campaign. The state party announced Monday Battaglia was ending his campaign because of a medical emergency. “Our thoughts are with Marco and his family as they […]
text:
Libertarian candidate for the 3rd District Marco Battaglia blasted Republican Party officials who are challenging his right to be on the November ballot in a speech to the Iowa State Fair crowd (Photo by Jack O'Connor/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Libertarian Party of Iowa will hold a convention Sunday to nominate a new 3rd District candidate to appear on the November ballot after Libertarian Marco Battaglia ended his campaign.
The state party announced Monday Battaglia was ending his campaign because of a medical emergency.
“Our thoughts are with Marco and his family as they focus on his health and recovery,” Iowa Libertarian Party Chair Stephanie Berlin said in a statement. “Out of respect for Marco’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details. Right now, our focus is on supporting Marco while ensuring the party fulfills its responsibilities under Iowa law and continues to provide voters with a Libertarian choice on the ballot this November.”
Before ending his campaign, Battaglia was in a legal battle to make it back onto the November ballot after being removed by the State Objections Panel in June. The panel had ruled Battaglia did not qualify for the ballot because the name he was running under differed from his legal name, Mark T. Anderson. The candidate had appeared on the ballot using the name “Marco Battaglia” in previous elections.
Battaglia, as well as the Libertarian gubernatorial ticket of Nicholas Gluba and Jules Cutler challenged the State Objections Panel decision to remove them from the general election ballot in court. A Polk County District Court judge upheld the panel’s decisions, but both Gluba and Battaglia said they planned to appeal the ruling. While Battaglia’s appeal may not go forward, the Libertarian Party of Iowa said in a statement the party will continue to support Gluba and Cutler “pursue ballot access through the legal process.”
Because Battaglia ended his campaign, the party is set to hold a nominating convention to replace Battaglia on the ticket Sunday, Aug. 9 — meeting the deadline under Iowa law for political parties to hold conventions and replace candidates that withdraw by Aug. 14. This candidate is set to compete against incumbent U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, a Republican, and Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Community rallies after death of Plainfield man in ICE custody
description: A crowd gathered at a Highland Park church Tuesday urged officials to close Delaney Hall after a detainee died in custody Saturday.
text:
Ashley Cornejo, 12, the daughter of Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, and Maria Cornejo, the mother of the 39-year-old detainee at Delaney Hall, cry during a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026, days after Cornejo’s death. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)HIGHLAND PARK — On the lawn of the Reformed Church of Highland Park Tuesday, nearly 100 people rallied to call for the closure of Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall after the death of a 39-year-old man in ICE custody Saturday.
Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo’s family made pleas to Gov. Mikie Sherrill and the Attorney General’s Office to investigate his death and called for the release of his medical records, while urging the federal government to cease the detention of undocumented immigrants. Cornejo was detained at Delaney Hall for six weeks before his death.
“I’m going to grow up without a father,” said Ashley, Cornejo’s 12-year-old daughter. “They didn’t even let him see me one last time before he died.”
For roughly two hours, the crowd in front of the church prayed, chanted for the closure of Delaney Hall, and heard stories from people who have loved ones held at the Newark detention center.
Cornejo was a Salvadoran immigrant who lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years, according to his family. They said he had diabetes and high blood pressure and was not being given his medication regularly since he had been detained June 18. His mother said she has still not been contacted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials or Geo Group, the private company that runs Delaney Hall.
ICE, which said Cornejo was deported in 2006 after crossing the border illegally, stated that Cornejo received “proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals” while in custody. His official cause of death is still pending.
His brother disputes that Cornejo was receiving the medical attention he needed, noting he was on daily medication. Cornejo told his brother in jail phone calls that to get Tylenol for a headache, he had to fill out a form, and often wouldn’t receive it for two or three days.
“Nothing will bring back my brother,” he said in Spanish. “It’s not right, everything that happened. And no one knows, no one speaks up because of fear, but sometimes we need to lose our fear to get justice.”
Jenny Garcia, an activist with American Friends Service Committee, said that Delaney Hall detainees have complained about being given the wrong medication or being told they have to split medication because there isn’t enough for everyone. She alleged that ICE is not being truthful about whether detainees are seen by doctors or given the medicine they need.
Maribel Encalada said her dad is one of those people who is denied medical care. Her 58-year-old father, who came to the U.S. over 40 years ago, has been in detention for several weeks. He’s been denied medical attention for his high blood pressure and a painful toothache that’s developed since he arrived at the jail, she said. He’s also been fed moldy bread, she said.
“Every day that he is denied proper medical care is another day that his health is put at risk,” she said. “Access to basic medical treatment is not a privilege, it’s a basic human right — and my father’s story is not the only one.”
Cornejo’s death comes amid a rising death toll in ICE custody nationally. At least 22 ICE detainees have died in the first seven months of the year, according to the agency’s national data. At this point in 2025, ICE had reported 12 in-custody deaths.
Up until June, ICE policy required the agency to report deaths of detainees who die within 30 days of being released from custody, but it now no longer does. Advocates said the change makes it harder to track deaths tied to medical neglect that surfaces after someone is released or transferred.
Several activists expressed concerns about whether there could be more deaths linked to Delaney Hall than ICE has reported publicly.
After an unannounced visit to the jail Monday, Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08) said that in July, a person who was being processed at Delaney Hall was having a medical episode when ICE released them from custody, and they later died at University Hospital in Newark. His office said it is working to learn more about the circumstances of the death and other medical emergencies that have occurred inside the facility, noting an ambulance was on site Monday morning.
People gather for a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Members of the Cornejo family comfort each other during a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A person holds a sign at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gabriela Soto, whose husband is detained at Delaney Hall in Newark, speaks at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A person holds a sign at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Jorge Torres, an organizer with National Day Laborers Organizing Network, speaks at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A sign is seen at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The Rev. Seth Kaper-Dale speaks at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The family of Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo arrives at a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Analilia Mejia speaks during a rally at the Reformed Church of Highland Park on Aug. 4, 2026, days after the death of 39-year-old Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, a detainee at Delaney Hall. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
An unsigned statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said all immigrant detainees are provided with medical care and downplayed in-custody deaths as just “0.008% of the detained population.”
“As bed space has rapidly expanded, we have maintained higher a standard of care than most prisons that hold U.S. citizens — including providing access to proper medical care. For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives,” the statement reads. “Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now.”
Sally Pillay, a longtime volunteer with Eyes on ICE, on Tuesday called detention centers “death camps.”
“We have so many people right now in immigration custody at Delaney Hall who have been detained for over a year in that facility, who have medical issues, medical concerns. We have a number of individuals who are diabetic, who are not getting their medications in time, and they are not getting food,” Pillay said.
She said she’s “pleading and begging” lawmakers to help get medically vulnerable people out of detention as soon as possible.
Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-11), who said her mother was once undocumented, called on ICE to be abolished. Mejia urged her colleagues to continue to visit the detention centers, press federal officials, and enter all that they discover into the congressional record.
“I will do my part, you will do your part, and I know that together we will demand and we will win the kind of justice that, sadly, Edwin was not given,” she said. “Shut it down.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri redistricting referendum blocked by secretary of state, drawing lawsuit
description: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins blocked a public vote on the state’s new congressional map Tuesday, declaring a referendum petition unconstitutional a few hours before polls closed in the primary election. He refused to tell reporters at a Jefferson City press conference whether the petition had enough valid signatures to qualify for the November [[...]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on Tuesday said two measures proposed by petition, to force a referendum on a congressional map and to hold a vote on changes to the initiative process, are unconstitutional and will not be on the November ballot (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins blocked a public vote on the state’s new congressional map Tuesday, declaring a referendum petition unconstitutional a few hours before polls closed in the primary election.
He refused to tell reporters at a Jefferson City press conference whether the petition had enough valid signatures to qualify for the November ballot. It didn’t matter, he said, because the Missouri Constitution does not allow a referendum on redistricting.
“Whether they had one signature or 500 million signatures doesn’t really matter because they are unconstitutional,” Hoskins said at a news conference.
The political action committee People Not Politicians turned in more than 300,000 signatures in December, and local election authorities spent hundreds of hours verifying whether the people who signed were registered voters.
Hoskins also rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to limit legislative power to change measures passed by initiative. That proposal, which would have been Amendment 6 on the Nov. 3 ballot, violates the requirements that ballot measures be limited to a single subject and amend only one article of the constitution, he said. The Respect MO Voters committee also submitted more than 300,000 signatures, and Hoskins declined to disclose that count as well.
Local election officials go with Missouri’s gerrymandered congressional map despite uncertainty

Hoskins’ decision brought an immediate court challenge from People Not Politicians. It will be the final case in the seemingly endless litigation over whether Missouri’s gerrymandered redistricting plan will be subject to a referendum.
The Missouri Constitution’s referendum power does not contemplate a vote on redistricting plans, Hoskins said. The U.S. Constitution, he said, gives state legislatures the power to set the rules for congressional elections, and a referendum would violate it.
Hoskins’ announcement came on the last day he had legally to rule on whether measures submitted by petition will be on the Nov. 3 ballot.
He said he waited because he wanted every possible bit of information before making a decision.
“According to Missouri state law, I had until today at 5 p.m. to certify those signatures,” Hoskins said. “As a certified public accountant, I want to make sure all my ‘i’s are dotted and T’s are crossed.”
After meeting with reporters, Hoskins released opinion letters from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway laying out the legal reasoning for rejecting the petitions. On the referendum, Hanaway wrote that the state constitution is silent on authority for a referendum.
“In order to authorize such referenda, the Missouri Constitution would need to speak through a clear statement divesting the legislature of its authority under the U.S. Constitution’s Elections Clause,” Hanaway wrote. “But the Missouri Constitution includes no such clear statement.”
People Not Politicians executive director, Richard von Glahn filed the lawsuit in Cole County Circuit Court late Tuesday.
“Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” von Glahn said in a news release. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year, and we won’t stop now.”
The petition has enough signatures to make the ballot and the courts will uphold the referendum power for redistricting, von Glahn said.
“People will have the final say in November and the chance to vote no to politicians desperate power grabs,” he said.
The Democratic leader in the Missouri House, state Rep. Ashley Aune of Kansas City, said Hoskins is showing he is a Republican partisan, not an impartial official.
“Every step of the way, Denny Hoskins has engaged in obstruction and dishonesty to stop Missourians from exercising their constitutional right to decide whether the mid-decade partisan gerrymander Republicans forced through last year should become law,” Aune said. “As a result, his latest act of contempt against Missouri voters should surprise no one and provides further proof that he is unfit to serve as the state’s top election official.”
The lawsuit filed Tuesday is simple — it argues that Hoskins is wrong and the Constitution does not prohibit a referendum. Only appropriation bills and laws enacted on an emergency basis are exempt, the petition states.
The redistricting plan “falls into neither of those categories,” it argues.
In previous litigation over the congressional map, the Missouri Supreme Court has upheld Gov. Mike Kehoe’s power to convene the legislature in a special session, the legislature’s authority to revise the map at any time and the constitutionality of the map as a basis for elections.
It has not ruled on the question of whether the Constitution allows a referendum. In a May ruling, the court hinted that if it finds the referendum power applies, the map would have never taken effect — meaning Tuesday’s primary was conducted in district boundaries that were never legal. 
“Because the secretary’s certification process…is ongoing and has not been finally determined, it is impossible to say as of this opinion whether the Dec. 9 referendum petition filing was ‘legal, sufficient, and timely’ and, therefore, whether (the 2025 map) went into effect on Dec. 11 or whether (the map) was referred to the people as of Dec. 9 and can only go into effect when approved by a majority of the votes cast thereon,” Judge Ginger Gooch wrote.
In the case over the legislature’s authority to revise the map, opponents said that because the Constitution doesn’t explicitly allow it, lawmakers did not have that authority. The high court rejected that argument.
Hoskins said the same silence in the constitution cuts the other way on referendums — that the absence of explicit authority means one is not allowed. He said he did not see a parallel between the two provisions of the Constitution and its silence on a key point.
“Here we’re trying to compare apples and oranges,” Hoskins said. “Also the Constitution doesn’t say that Denny Hoskins should make a million dollars a year absent that. So I would disagree with that analysis, and I would say that the Constitution does not specifically say that a referendum or an initial petition can be done on congressional redistricting.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: County Republican committees, lawmakers and candidates file brief in lawsuit against state GOP
description: Two weeks after a district court judge held a hearing on whether new Montana Republican Party bylaws are unconstitutional, a group of 67 individual Republicans, plus representatives of three county GOP central committees, filed a brief supporting the lawsuit.  In an amicus curiae brief, the group, collectively known as “Montana Grass Roots Republicans,” argu[...]
text:
State GOP Chairman Art Wittich talks to Republicans at the party convention in Missoula in June 2026. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)Two weeks after a district court judge held a hearing on whether new Montana Republican Party bylaws are unconstitutional, a group of 67 individual Republicans, plus representatives of three county GOP central committees, filed a brief supporting the lawsuit. 
In an amicus curiae brief, the group, collectively known as “Montana Grass Roots Republicans,” argues that constitutional danger arises when a political party “elevates the will of the party above the will of the people.”
In the lawsuit, filed in early July, two county central committees and several individuals, including sitting lawmakers and a former Montana GOP party chairman, argue the bylaws adopted by the party at its convention in June take power from voters by letting the party leaders remove members at will.
Lewis and Clark District Court Judge Michael McMahon issued a temporary restraining order against the bylaws while the suit played out in court, later narrowing it to just a few  sections of the bylaws.
The sections at the heart of the lawsuit include those defining the characteristics of Republican membership, term limits for precinct officers and central committee officers, and the suspension or removal of members.
State GOP chairman Art Wittich has defended the new party bylaws, saying they passed with  97% of the delegates at the party convention voting in favor. 
“There is a difference between self-identifying as a Republican and voluntarily participating as a full member of our party, a political association with its own rules, responsibilities and authority,” Wittich previously said.
Montana Grass Roots Republicans includes the Glacier, Pondera and Teton County Republican Central Committees, as well as 11 sitting state representatives, six state senators, 12 Republican nominees for the legislature, and 38 elected or appointed precinct committee representatives. 
Republicans in 13 counties across Montana are represented, including more than 20 from Ravalli County, which has been a pressure point for Republican infighting in recent years. 
The group is not seeking to join as a party to the lawsuit, but “provide the Court with a perspective grounded in the offices and organizations directly affected by the challenged provisions.”
Among the arguments the grassroots organization supports, is that the state GOP cannot remove voter-elected precinct representatives from office nor terminate party membership or participation of precinct representatives or duly-elected Republican nominees. 
The new bylaws, the brief states, allow the state party to exercise tight control over its members, including limiting party support or endorsement for members who aren’t in “good standing,” or removing them from office altogether. 
“The Montana Republican Party transforms private membership discipline into a power over positions and nominations created and filled through Montana’s election laws,” according to the brief.
In its post-hearing brief to the court, the state GOP said the overwhelming support of the new bylaws during the vote shows the rules are not a “power grab by a few,” and instead establishes due process for internal disciplinary actions. 
The party also argues that the plaintiffs cannot show that any individual, nor county committee, has suffered harm due to the new bylaws, and that it’s a First Amendment right for the party to decide whom to associate with.  
If the court granted an injunction against the bylaws, it “would force the Party to lend its name and its treasury to speech and candidacies it has chosen not to support,” according to court documents. 
The court has not indicated when it will issue a ruling on the requested injunction.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Judicial Branch launches court records search tool
description: Searching through court records in Idaho just got easier. A new interface for accessing court documents was rolled out across local courthouses Tuesday morning, according to the Idaho Judicial Branch. Computer kiosks at Idaho’s county courthouses have been updated to enable users to search case information and hearings without entering a party name or case [[...]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Searching through court records in Idaho just got easier. A new interface for accessing court documents was rolled out across local courthouses Tuesday morning, according to the Idaho Judicial Branch.
Controller declares ‘Idaho Transparency Month’ with stakeholder discussions, government access tips

Computer kiosks at Idaho’s county courthouses have been updated to enable users to search case information and hearings without entering a party name or case number.
Each of the 44 county courthouses is equipped with at least one computer that allows the public to access case information and records from across state courts. Court records from across Idaho can also be accessed at the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise.
Idaho law requires the state to make public records open to inspection “at all reasonable times.” The code protects the right to make copies of documents, whether physically or by photography. The government is allowed to charge for the cost of copying documents.
Information and records from cases of interest across Idaho, including the 2022 University of Idaho student murders and the trial of Andrea Shaw, who is charged with killing her twins in 2025, are available online at the Idaho Judicial Branch website.
