name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s Catholic diocese has plenty of shame to go around
description:
Decades of Vermont bishops, not just the current ones, bear responsibility for hiding clergy abuse.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s Catholic diocese has plenty of shame to go around.
text:
Dear Editor,
I’m writing to thank VTDigger reporter Kevin O’Connor for shining a light on corruption in the Roman Catholic Diocese of Burlington in its effort to prevent justice for survivors of clergy sexual abuse in Vermont. There is plenty of shame to go around.
Let’s start with Vermont’s former bishop, Christopher Coyne, and his once second-in-command, John McDermott. According to a whistleblower, a woman who applied for the position of chief financial officer of the diocese, Coyne and McDermott moved the diocese’s money so they could claim that the diocese was broke when it came time to pay the many victims suing them over clergy sexual abuse. If not for the courageous actions of the whistleblower, who said she was pressed by both Coyne and McDermott about whether she would be comfortable moving money, the public and the courts would never have known of these efforts. What did Coyne and McDermott get for apparently trying to shield assets from victims and the courts? They were promoted by the Catholic Church, with Coyne becoming archbishop of Hartford, Connecticut, and McDermott being named bishop in Vermont.
Then there are the diocese’s legal bills: $2 million in the last two years. But how much did the diocese pay attorneys for decades to avoid doing penance for their sins? The judge in the bankruptcy case is concerned that there will be nothing left for victims after lawyers get their large piece of the pie.
Coyne and McDermott are no better than their predecessors. Bishop John Marshall was an architect of the cover-up and recently had his name removed from a Catholic school in Morrisville, partly because leaders there didn’t want their fine school named for a man who covered up for child molesters. Bishop Salvatore Matano was the first money mover. He was so brash about it that he even wrote a letter to Vermont Catholics to inform them of his plans. And now, a recent Rhode Island attorney general’s investigation has detailed a pattern of cover-up by Providence church leadership — including Auxiliary Bishop Kenneth Angell — during his time there. He did the same thing in Vermont. It was under Angell that the plan was hatched to pay survivors of St. Joseph’s Orphanage a pittance to stop them from suing the diocese or even talking about the abuse they suffered.
So where do we go from here? First, I ask other Vermont media to report on this story, too. To Saint Michael’s College, I say: Why are you willing to host the bishop’s chancery offices in light of what the diocese is doing? 

READ MORE

I also call on Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark to investigate the obvious attempt to hide money from victims. Those abused deserve justice.
Maura Labelle Colchester, Vt.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judge tosses Cherry Hill schools’ lawsuit targeting records requester
description: Suit tossed under law meant to prevent court-assisted censorship after judge finds no evidence for district's harassment claims.
text:
The Cherry Hill school district is suing Ben Shore, alleging that he has filed numerous and "vexatious" public records requests with the district. (Shore photo by Ben Shore; school bus photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A Superior Court judge has tossed the Cherry Hill school board’s lawsuit against a records requester it claimed had harassed them by submitting an average of one records request per month over 18 months.
Judge Michael Mikulski dismissed the suit, which sought to bar Benjamin Shore and his journalistic outlet, Shore Investigates, from submitting requests for public documents for one year, with Mikulski citing a New Jersey law aimed at barring lawsuits meant to censor or chill political speech.
“Plaintiffs have shown no evidence of any ill-intent of Defendants here. In fact, the record reflects defendants’ willingness to cooperate with the board in making the requests less intrusive,” Mikulski wrote in the seven-page ruling.
New Jersey’s Uniform Public Expression Protection Act allows judges to dismiss lawsuits meant to chill speech or political engagement on an expedited basis. The court must award attorney’s fees and costs to the defendant if a suit is dismissed under the law.
The court found Shore’s request to toss the case as a strategic lawsuit against public participation met all three required bars.
“This is the right outcome. No public agency should sue anyone, let alone reporters, because they file an OPRA request or two a month,” said CJ Griffin, an attorney specializing in public records who represented Shore. “Public records belong to the public and no one should live in fear that they will be sued for seeking basic transparency.”
Griffin has represented the New Jersey Monitor in a range of legal matters.
Because Shore was acting in a journalistic capacity, the case centered on a matter of public concern, the judge wrote, satisfying the first prong, while the second prong was automatically met because he did not work for the government. He said the third prong was met because the school board submitted no evidence to support its claim that Shore filed Open Public Records Act requests with the goal of burdening or harassing board staff.
“Here, the intent is the dispositive factor, which the court finds none in the evidence presented,” Mikulski wrote. “The court finds the amount of time the board must expend in order to respond to the requestor OPRA requests is not a valid reason for its action.”
The judge further dismissed claims that a website Shore set up to assist with filing records requests with the Cherry Hill Board of Education could mislead residents into believing the site belonged to the district.
No facts backed up that assertion either, the judge said, noting the website was noncommercial and included at least two disclaimers that said it was not affiliated with the school district.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Madison officials, cops clear protesters from encampment at police shooting site
description: Madison city workers, police and state patrol officers cleared protesters from the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets early Tuesday morning, putting an end to the encampment that had blocked off the major east side intersection since a Madison police officer shot and killed Corey Ruiz there July 22.  Starting around 5 a.m., officials […]
text:
Protesters began their occupation of the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets after Corey Ruiz was shot and killed July 22. On July 23, a vigil was held in honor of Ruiz and protesters remained barricaded on the streets until city officials cleared the intersection August 4. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Madison city workers, police and state patrol officers cleared protesters from the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets early Tuesday morning, putting an end to the encampment that had blocked off the major east side intersection since a Madison police officer shot and killed Corey Ruiz there July 22. 
Starting around 5 a.m., officials announced through loudspeakers that the barricades blocking the streets would be removed and the gathering dispersed. Videos posted to social media show a chaotic scene at which police grappled with protesters and deployed pepper spray. City officials also towed away the replica George Floyd fist statue that was brought to the intersection last week. 
Dylan Brogan, a spokesperson for the city, said the city planned to let non-police city staff lead the effort. 
“The plan was for this to be led by non-law enforcement city agencies,” he said, adding that the unhoused people staying at the site would be given the opportunity to stay in a hotel and that people’s belongings would be available for pickup at Demetral Field, located about 2 miles northeast of the protest encampment site. “The message was delivered loudly that people had to get their things together.” 
The city announced that the intersection was open to traffic at 9 a.m.
In a statement released Monday evening, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway warned that the encampment would be shut down on Tuesday — stating that Ruiz was “no longer at the center of the current crisis our city faces.”
“For almost two weeks now, City of Madison staff and elected leaders have been on the ground and communicating to and through community leaders to peacefully resolve extremely complex, emotionally fraught circumstances that started with the police taking the life of Corey Ruiz,” Rhodes-Conway stated. “Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive. A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately.” 
She added that the protesters at the site were making demands that city officials have no authority to meet, only extending the closure of the intersection which had begun to take a toll on the businesses in the culturally important Willy Street corridor. 
“There are too many residents and local businesses suffering because of the occupation, and it’s become increasingly clear that unsheltered people are being used as leverage for demands that, frankly, the City of Madison cannot deliver because we do not have the power to deliver them,” Rhodes-Conway said. “As we and others have repeatedly explained, the City cannot make an arrest or bring criminal charges — that authority rests with the Dane County District Attorney following an independent investigation by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. The City does not control this timeline.”
“I’m increasingly alarmed that those supporting the occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street are either purposefully ignoring the harm being done, or deliberately hoping that the situation spirals further out of control,” she continued. 
After the raid at the encampment, protesters marched outside Rhodes-Conway’s home, video posted to Facebook by local activist organization Freedom Inc. shows.
“If we don’t get no sleep, you don’t get no sleep,” the organization said in its post. “How dare Mayor Satya send her goons to raid the Corey Ruiz Memorial Encampment full of women, children and pregnant people.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Aquarium receives accolades after hosting marine veterinary medicine workshop
description: Veterinarians and students participated in the marine veterinary medicine program this summer at the Mississippi Aquarium in Gulfport.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here..   

Since 1999, the MARVET, Marine Veterinary Medicine Team, has introduced veterinarians and students to aquatic medicine with an emphasis on the ecosystem and the inclusive One Health model, typically hosting two international workshops per year.
Our session this summer, which for the second consecutive year was hosted by the Mississippi Aquarium in Gulfport, was among our most remarkable experiences yet.
Mississippi Aquarium’s critical watershed connection to Gulf waters and its proximity to other regional marine facilities make it a perfect and dynamic venue for teaching the One Health model, highlighting the bonds between human, animal and environmental health.
Students examine a penguin earlier this summer during marine veterinary medicine workshop at Mississippi Aquarium in Gulfport. Credit: Courtesy photo
This summer, the beautiful, world-class facility brought together students and expert instructors from diverse backgrounds and institutions from across the globe, including institutions from Alabama, Cornell, Iowa, Disney, Florida, Gulf Coast Research Laboratory (The University of Southern Mississippi), Mississippi State University, Dauphin Island Sea Lab, with students coming from Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Minnesota, Texas, Wisconsin, Brazil, Grenada and the United Kingdom.
The success of the workshop was driven by Alexa Delaune, the vice president of Veterinary Care, and her outstanding team. Delaune volunteered her time to lead high-energy clinical lectures and critical hands-on labs for experiential learning – including an extraordinary opportunity for our group to observe the release of two sea turtles back to the wild, following their successful rehabilitation by the Mississippi Aquarium veterinary care team.
The entire staff inspired us with their genuine enthusiasm, warmth and willingness to share their knowledge on marine species and the marine environment.
Gulfport and the entire Mississippi Gulf Coast should be incredibly proud of the Mississippi Aquarium. It is a vital asset to both the local community and the global scientific field. Because of this exceptional partnership, we are already planning to bring MARVET back to the Mississippi Aquarium in 2027.

Christine A. Curry is a passionate advocate for environmental stewardship, combining science, creativity and community engagement to drive change. An experienced project and product developer, she has spearheaded initiatives in marine conservation and sustainable agriculture and now collaborates across Iowa and the Mississippi River watershed to protect clean water, restore ecosystems, improve soil health and strengthen climate resilience. She is co-founder of MARVET, the Marine Veterinary Medicine Team, and a trustee of the nonprofit “Institute for Global Health and Health Policy”, which sponsors MARVET as an educational outreach.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: House and Senate set Aug. 19 Veto Day, amid Ayotte’s record vetoes
description: The New Hampshire House and Senate will meet Aug. 19 to take up 31 of Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s 33 vetoes this year, after the Republican governor broke a modern record for vetoing the most bills in one year passed by a Legislature of her own party. This year’s Veto Day, which will occur 20 days […]
text:
Republicans hold a 16-8 majority in the New Hampshire Senate. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)The New Hampshire House and Senate will meet Aug. 19 to take up 31 of Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s 33 vetoes this year, after the Republican governor broke a modern record for vetoing the most bills in one year passed by a Legislature of her own party.
This year’s Veto Day, which will occur 20 days before the Sept. 8 state primary, could highlight profound disagreements among moderate Republicans, conservative Republicans, and Democrats. Many of the bills Ayotte vetoed touch on incendiary cultural issues.
Three vetoed bills are nearly identical: Senate Bill 268, Senate Bill 552, and House Bill 1442 would all allow businesses to require patrons to use bathrooms, locker rooms, and other facilities that correspond to their biological sex at birth — and require that separation in state jails, prisons, and hospitals. Republicans have repeatedly submitted the legislation, known as the “bathroom bills,” despite Ayotte’s previous vetoes, arguing they want to send a message. Democrats and LGBTQ+ advocates have denounced the bills as attacks on transgender adults, and Ayotte has said they would cause discrimination. 
Lawmakers will also take up Ayotte’s vetoes of Senate Bill 434, which requires public schools to adopt procedures to allow books to be challenged and removed; House Bill 1358, which would create a study commission to explore converting public schools to charter schools; House Bill 232, which would expand the “rights of conscience” of medical professionals to refuse to assist in abortions; House Bill 1422, which would allow convicts to introduce new evidence to prove their innocence beyond the current three-year limit; Senate Bill 627, which would raise turnpike tolls for drivers without New Hampshire E-ZPass transponders; House Bill 2026, the 10-year transportation improvement plan that also raised tolls; and House Bill 1336, which would allow landlords to request an additional month’s rent security deposit for tenants with low credit scores or lacking landlord recommendations.
Most of the Republican-led legislation will likely not be overturned. Lawmakers need a two-thirds majority of all elected members of both the House and Senate in order to override a veto. Senate Republicans, who hold a 16-seat supermajority in the 24-member chamber, can achieve that threshold without Democratic votes, but House Republicans, who hold a smaller majority, need Democratic support. 
The bills will be taken up by the body in which they originated: Senate bills in the Senate and House bills in the House. They will advance to the other chamber only if they pass the first chamber by two-thirds. 
The House has already voted on and failed to override two of Ayotte’s vetoes this year: House Bill 349, which would have allowed optometrists to perform certain laser procedures, and House Bill 451, which would have required paint manufacturers to operate and pay for a recycling system.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas voters put mark on competitive GOP, Democratic primaries for governor
description: Kansas' primary election is here at last, and Republican voters are choosing from among seven candidates and Democrats are picking from among three rivals.
text:
Stacy Rogers, a Wichita business owner and candidate for the Republican Party's nomination for governor, is competing in a seven-candidate primary Tuesday. Kansas voters also are responsible for selecting the Democratic Party's  nominee for governor from among three options. In 2026, it's an open seat due to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly being term limited. (Submitted)TOPEKA — Stacy Rogers was the first to officially file as a candidate in the 2026 campaign for Kansas governor.
In a dark-horse bid for the Republican nomination launched in February 2025, Rogers defined herself as a Wichita business owner frustrated by politicians who depended on lobbying and campaign cash to bulldoze aside the interests of many Kansans. Rogers set herself apart from more prominent candidates by refusing to pay the $10,000 fee to participate in debates sanctioned by the Kansas Republican Party.
Rogers focused on a grassroots campaign drawing energy from retirees, farmers, teachers, business owners, veterans and others eager to share what they wanted of government.
“Their stories are different, but their hope is the same,” Rogers said. “They want a government that listens. They want leaders who keep their word. They want opportunities for their children and grandchildren. This campaign has never been about one person. It’s about all of us working together to restore confidence that our state government can once again serve the people.”
Rogers is among seven Republican gubernatorial candidates appearing on Tuesday’s ballot.
The list also includes Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson of Andover, former Johnson County Commissioner Charlotte O’Hara of Olathe, self-described underdog Nick Reinecker of Inman, Overland Park businessman Philip Sarnecki, Secretary of State Scott Schwab of Overland Park and Kansas Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt of Topeka.
Schmidt, who completed two terms as insurance commissioner after serving in the Kansas Senate, said it was important voters understood they held outsized influence in primary elections because turnout was smaller than in general elections.
“I listened to a lot of Kansans this year,” she said. “The mom rationing a prescription because the grocery bill went up again. The town watching to see if its hospital makes it another year. That’s who I’m doing this for.”
Perception of the GOP contest has been shaped by President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Masterson, who has served in the Legislature for 20 years. Trump’s decision led to the surprising termination of former Gov. Jeff Colyer’s campaign.
As the primary wound to a close, the clashes between Masterson and Sarnecki intensified.
“Even President Trump gets bad advice sometimes,” Sarnecki said in an ad. “So, he has endorsed one of the career politicians who has driven Kansas into a ditch. It happens.”
In the Kansas Democratic Party primary, voters taking part in the gubernatorial election have the option of Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog, state Sen. Cindy Holscher of Overland Park and state Sen. Ethan Corson of Fairway.
Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly endorsed Corson early in the race. The final chapters of this primary delved into questions about candidate electability and the governor’s role in tipping the scale against Holscher and Skoog.
While Holscher and Corson initiated their candidacies in 2025, Skoog waited until June to jump in. Skoog justified the delayed entry to a determination that Holscher’s political views would limit her appeal in November and that Corson struggled to gain traction in the primary.
Holscher offered herself as an anti-establishment candidate dedicated to funding K-12 public education, protecting communities from the data center craze, legalizing cannabis and restraining use of tax breaks to drive economic growth.
“I’m not attached to the establishment. I’m attached to working people,” Holscher said. “I’ll take on anyone, regardless of party, who stands in the way of lower costs, better schools and a government that works for everyday people. I won’t be bought by billionaires, bullied by special interests and insiders, or pressured by the political establishment.”
Corson, an attorney who worked at the U.S. Department of Commerce before entering the state Senate, said he was the only Democrat with a strategy for responsibly lowering property taxes. He would authorize a $250 vehicle registration tax credit for every vehicle registered in the state.
“We would freeze property taxes on even more of our fixed-income seekers,” Corson said. “We would bring back in the one-third of Kansans who rent into our property tax relief program.”
He promised to veto “pork” projects thrown into the state budget by the Legislature and reject bills designed to undermine abortion rights affirmed in a statewide vote in 2022.
Kansas voters have a tradition of cycling between Republican and Democratic governors. Kelly, the two-term Democrat, followed Colyer, who finished the unexpired second term of GOP Gov. Sam Brownback. Brownback won the governorship after departure of Democratic Gov. Mark Parkinson, who completed the last year of Democratic Gov. Kathleen Sebelius’ second term.
In 2022, Kelly dominated a two-candidate primary with 93% of the vote. She went up against then-Attorney General Derek Schmidt, who won the GOP nomination with 80% of the party’s vote. In the general election, Kelly won a second term by outrunning Schmidt by a margin of 49.5% to 47.3%.
Kelly prevailed in 2018 by winning a five-candidate primary in which she scored 51.4% of the vote. Her top competition came from former Wichita Mayor Carl Brewer with 20.1% and Josh Svaty at 17.4%. Then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach won the GOP primary against Colyer by 343 votes out of more than 250,000 cast. In the general election, Kelly secured 48% of the vote to Kobach’s 42.9%.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Masterson scores victory in GOP primary for Kansas governor; pair of Democrats go to the wire
description: Kansas GOP nomination for governor goes to Senate President Ty Masterson, while a pair of Democrats Ethan Corson and Cindy Holscher prove every vote counts.
text:
Stacy Rogers, a Wichita business owner and candidate for the Republican Party's nomination for governor, is competing in a seven-candidate primary Tuesday. Kansas voters also are responsible for selecting the Democratic Party's  nominee for governor from among three options. In 2026, it's an open seat due to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly being term limited. (Submitted)TOPEKA — Republican Ty Masterson rode President Donald Trump’s endorsement to victory Tuesday in a volatile seven-candidate gubernatorial primary, while Democrats Cindy Holscher and Ethan Corson continued to slug it out for their party’s nomination.
Masterson, the Andover president of the Kansas Senate, built an early lead with 40% of the GOP vote as results began rolling in from precincts statewide. He ran away from businessman Phil Sarnecki and Kansas Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt and Secretary of State Scott Schwab. Sarnecki had no previous political experience, Schmidt was vulnerable to attacks for a series of moderate votes on abortion as a member of the Legislature and Schwab never found his footing in a crowded field of conservatives.
“I didn’t just talk about conservative values. I’ve delivered,” Masterson said. “We cut income taxes, eliminated the state tax on Social Security, cut property taxes, axed the grocery tax, protected girls’ sports, defended the unborn and stood up to federal mandates when it counted.”
He said a top opportunity for change on the horizon was finding an answer to surging property taxation that had a detrimental effect on home ownership and business success.
The roster of other Republicans in the race included former Johnson County Commissioner Charlotte O’Hara of Olathe, Nick Reinecker of Inman and Wichita businessperson Stacy Rogers.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ethan Corson, a state senator from Fairway, speaks to reporters after voting Aug. 4 in the state’s primary election. Corson is recipient of Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s endorsement in his race against state Sen. Cindy Holscher of Overland Park and Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
In terms of Democratic voters in the gubernatorial race, Holscher and Corson — both state senators from Johnson County — fulfilled expectations for a close race once the polls closed. Early in the counting, Holscher had 47% of the vote to Corson’s 41%. The third option, Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog, had 12%.
While Corson claimed the outgoing Democratic governor’s endorsement and relied on heavy spending on television advertisements, he struggled to connect with voters concerned about his electability in November. There was a sense among some Democrats that Holscher’s mix of public policy positions and a combative campaign style were better suited for challenging the GOP nominee.
Holscher offered herself as an anti-establishment candidate dedicated to funding K-12 public education, protecting communities from the data center craze, legalizing cannabis and restraining use of tax breaks to drive economic growth.
“I’m not attached to the establishment. I’m attached to working people,” Holscher said. “I’ll take on anyone, regardless of party, who stands in the way of lower costs, better schools and a government that works for everyday people. I won’t be bought by billionaires, bullied by special interests and insiders, or pressured by the political establishment.”
Corson, an attorney who worked at the U.S. Department of Commerce before entering the state Senate, said he was the only Democrat with a strategy for responsibly lowering property taxes. He would authorize a $250 vehicle registration tax credit for every vehicle registered in the state.
“We would freeze property taxes on even more of our fixed-income seekers,” Corson said. “We would bring back in the one-third of Kansans who rent into our property tax relief program.”
He promised to veto “pork” projects thrown into the state budget by the Legislature and reject bills designed to undermine abortion rights affirmed in a statewide vote in 2022.
Kansas voters have a tradition of cycling between Republican and Democratic governors. Kelly, the two-term Democrat, followed Colyer, who finished the unexpired second term of GOP Gov. Sam Brownback. Brownback won the governorship after departure of Democratic Gov. Mark Parkinson, who completed the last year of Democratic Gov. Kathleen Sebelius’ second term.
In 2022, Kelly dominated a two-candidate primary with 93% of the vote. She went up against then-Attorney General Derek Schmidt, who won the GOP nomination with 80% of the party’s vote. In the general election, Kelly won a second term by outrunning Schmidt by a margin of 49.5% to 47.3%.
Kelly prevailed in 2018 by winning a five-candidate primary in which she scored 51.4% of the vote. Her top competition came from former Wichita Mayor Carl Brewer with 20.1% and Josh Svaty at 17.4%. Then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach won the GOP primary against Colyer by 343 votes out of more than 250,000 cast. In the general election, Kelly secured 48% of the vote to Kobach’s 42.9%.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Amazon abandons plans for a data center at Calvert Cliffs
description: Amazon Web Services is abandoning its plans to develop data centers on the campus of the Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, a move that comes after fierce voter pushback against hyperscale data centers in Calvert County’s June primary election.
text:
The Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant Units 1 and 2 are located near Lusby. (Photo courtesy the Nuclear Regulatory Commission)Amazon Web Services is abandoning its plans to develop data centers on the campus of Southern Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, according to a news release issued Tuesday by Calvert County government.
It comes after fierce voter pushback against hyperscale data centers in Calvert County’s primary election on June 23.
The three county commissioners who previously voted against a pause on data centers were all ousted in their primaries by candidates who took issue with the trajectory of data center development in the county thus far. The commission president and vice president, Todd Ireland (R) and Mark C. Cox Sr. (R), both lost their races, as did commissioner Earl F. “Buddy” Hance (R).
The Amazon proposal was for “multiple data center campuses” at Calvert Cliffs, covering 2.4 million square feet, according to a planning document published on the Calvert County government website. The company submitted its proposal to Calvert in early May.
“Calvert County Government remains committed to transparency and will continue to provide updates on significant development proposals and application activity,” read Tuesday’s news release. “Keeping residents informed through accurate, timely and accessible communication remains a priority.”
On Aug. 18, the county will host a public meeting to consider a “temporary six-month moratorium on site plan approvals for data center development projects,” according to another news release issued Tuesday.
Data center frustrations cause upheaval in county primary elections

“The proposed ordinance would establish a temporary moratorium to allow time to review and adopt regulations and zoning ordinance text amendments related to data centers and heavy industrial use conditions, and to complete any necessary studies or analysis,” the news release reads.
Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday afternoon, nor did Constellation, the owner of the nuclear plant.
In addition to the proposal for a data center on the Calvert Cliffs site in Lusby, another company, called Natelli Holdings, has also proposed a data center close by. That facility, if built, would be located along Route 4 near Calvert Cliffs State Park, as well as an existing landfill, wastewater treatment facility and county-owned gun range.
The electoral result in Calvert was perhaps the most acute example statewide of data centers’ growing impact on local politics, though voters in Frederick County also ousted their council chair, Brad Young, after the council voted to expand an existing data center zone in Adamstown, while restricting data centers in other parts of the county.
After the election, Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater enacted, via executive order, a pause on data center development through the end of the year. In a statement, Fitzwater said that during the pause, county officials hope to educate voters about data centers and the zoning change during a series of public meetings. But county leaders still plan to move forward with the data center campus, currently planned at 2,500 acres.
In other counties in Maryland, the pauses, or moratoriums, are longer-term. Prince George’s County currently has the longest ban, a two-year hold that was enacted in July.
According to a news release issued last month by the Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN), nearly 77% of Maryland’s population currently lives under some kind of data center moratorium.
Many of the state’s most populous counties have adopted measures, including Montgomery, Prince George’s, Baltimore County and Baltimore City. Harford County enacted a ban with no time limit.
Smaller and more rural jurisdictions have also adopted one-year pauses, including Queen Anne’s County on the Eastern Shore and Washington County in Western Maryland.
“Grassroots outrage from across the state has made it clear that a moratorium is the most reasonable course of action that can be taken right now,” said Brittany Baker, Maryland director at CCAN Action Fund. “The playing field has quickly shifted in the last few months, which is why I expect the Maryland General Assembly will likely take a serious look at statewide moratorium bills during the 2027 session.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ICE, CoreCivic to open Appleton immigrant detention center this year
description: Immigration and Customs Enforcement will pay private prison company CoreCivic more than half a billion dollars to reopen a defunct 1,600-bed prison in rural western Minnesota as an immigrant detention center.  CoreCivic said in a press release the company expects to begin receiving detainees in the fourth quarter of 2026, and that it expects to […]
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has contracted with CoreCivic to reopen Prairie Correctional Facility as an immigrant detention center. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Immigration and Customs Enforcement will pay private prison company CoreCivic more than half a billion dollars to reopen a defunct 1,600-bed prison in rural western Minnesota as an immigrant detention center. 
CoreCivic said in a press release the company expects to begin receiving detainees in the fourth quarter of 2026, and that it expects to generate approximately $75 million in revenue per year for its role in facilitating the mass deportation agenda of President Donald Trump. 
A notice posted on the federal government’s award management website lists the total contract value: More than $536 million over the next five years.
The detention center will be the first of its kind in Minnesota, which until now has housed immigrant detainees in local jails or shipped them to facilities out of state, most often to Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas. ICE also holds immigrants for short periods in the cells at the Whipple Federal Building, home to the agency’s regional headquarters. 
The acquisition of the 1,600-bed prison, known as the Prairie Correctional Facility, is part of the agency’s push to expand detention capacity to historic highs since Trump began his second term. In July, the average daily population of immigrant detainees in ICE and Border Patrol custody surpassed 65,600, up from 39,000 when Trump took office, according to agency data. 
The former prison in Appleton has been on ICE’s radar for at least a year. The Washington Post first reported ICE was considering reopening the facility on Aug. 15, 2025, sparking protests from immigrant rights activists and a handful of residents of the 1,400-person city. 
CoreCivic runs some of the country’s largest and most infamous immigrant detention centers, including the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, which holds families with children, including, at one time, little Liam Conejo Ramos. (The image of him in his floppy-eared hat and Spiderman backpack outside a federal vehicle became synonymous with the immigration crackdown here.) Disease outbreaks, lack of medical care, inedible food and lack of outside time are common complaints of detainees. 
Appleton is about a three-hour drive from the Twin Cities, near the border with South Dakota.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming DEQ investigates foul odor coming from Jim Bridger Power Plant
description:
Rocky Mountain Power says ‘smell has been on and off since the ‘80s’ and results from power plant scrubbers removing sulfur dioxide and other pollutants from exhaust.
The post Wyoming DEQ investigates foul odor coming from Jim Bridger Power Plant appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
ROCK SPRINGS—The Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality has initiated an investigation into the Jim Bridger Power Plant and a foul smell that seems to be coming from the plant’s evaporation ponds.
Residents living near the power plant have considered the operation a good neighbor, but over the last 12 to 18 months, an increasingly foul odor resembling sewer gas and rotten sulfur has left the nearby communities of Superior and Point of Rocks demanding action.
Residents and an elected official took their concerns over air quality and environmental impacts stemming from the industrial evaporation ponds at the plant — and the foul odor and white powder that is allegedly coming from the ponds — and reached out to the DEQ.
‘Unbearable’ smell
For Point of Rocks resident Roger Varley, whose family has lived in the area for 60 years, the change in air quality has altered daily life.
“All they had to do was open the windows and let the fresh, cool air in,” Varley said of his parents’ home, which lacked air conditioning. “We can’t do that now. It smells like rotten sulfur, and it’s unbearable. I have a 3-year-old granddaughter, and I’d like her to breathe fresh air.”
While the plant has maintained a strong relationship with the community for many years, the management of its wastewater and evaporation ponds has become a major sticking point, Varley said.
The industrial evaporation ponds hold liquid waste, including wastewater and soda liquor — a concentrated alkaline solution used in plant scrubbing operations, he said. Because of the massive volume of water present, relying on natural evaporation to dry out the beds so heavy equipment can drive on and cap them could take decades.
“There are days we feel we can’t live like this,” Varley said, stressing that engineers and specialists must account for the immediate human impact on small communities as they find solutions. “I’d like them to reassure us that it’s temporary.”
Superior Mayor Dominic Wolf said he received his first complaint regarding the smell roughly a year to a year and a half ago. Since then, the issues have escalated from sporadic nuisances to an ongoing problem.
“You notice the bad sewer smell more when the wind blows,” Wolf said, noting visiting construction crews at first thought the odor was a sewer backup.
The smell became particularly severe in late July, prompting Wolf to reach out to state regulators directly.
“We’ve been doing a water study for the last couple of months, and the crew said they couldn’t stand the smell. So I had enough and called the DEQ,” Wolf said. “I just wanted to be proactive and make sure everything’s protected.”
Wolf expressed worry for plant workers breathing the fumes daily, as well as local wildlife, noting a recent influx of sage grouse in the area.
He said he hopes everyone’s involvement will help bring health and environmental risks back down to safe levels, restoring peace of mind to residents.
Sweetwater County Board of Commissioners Chair Keaton West said Wolf reached out to the commission. The commission contacted the DEQ Air Quality to put its officials in touch with Wolf and also forwarded Wolf the contact information for the Air Compliance Inspector in Lander.
“Our latest understanding was that an investigation was initiated and inspectors would likely be out soon,” West said. “Although this is a DEQ matter, we share the same concerns for health and safety and want to ensure residents and workers in the area are safe and well-informed.”
In response to public inquiries, the Wyoming DEQ emphasized the importance of community involvement when environmental concerns arise.
Keith Guille, outreach manager, said it is crucial for residents and local leaders to reach out whenever something seems amiss.
“It’s our job to ensure the public is safe from the type of things that we regulate, but if we’re not the regulatory agency on that, we try to work with other partners as well,” Guille said. “If there’s ever a concern or something they see doesn’t make sense, they can always reach out to us, and we will definitely look into it.”
According to Guille, the DEQ has initiated an investigation. The Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission will be involved as well.
The DEQ acknowledged reports of a white powdery substance blowing over several areas. Guille said the smell and the substance are not connected.
Soda liquor is a concentrated liquid solution made of alkaline chemicals — typically sodium carbonate (soda ash) or sodium hydroxide (caustic soda), Guille said. 
In local industrial uses, such as coal-fired power plants, it is used as a neutralizing liquid in flue gas scrubbers to strip sulfur dioxide (SO2) out of power plant exhaust before smoke leaves the stack. It creates a white powder when soda liquor spills or drains into evaporation ponds and dries out. High winds can whip up the leftover dry crust, dispersing a fine white, dusty powder across the area.
Guille said while soda liquor residue creates the visible white powder blown by wind, state regulators note it is odorless, meaning any separate sulfury or “rotten egg” smells in the area stem from a different source.
Jona Whitesides, a spokesperson for Rocky Mountain Power, said he was unaware of an upcoming investigation but noted the utility regularly coordinates with the DEQ, as waste streams and ash ponds require continuous monitoring.
“The smell has been on and off since the ‘80s,” Whitesides said. “Anytime you have a power plant and the scrubbers remove the sulfur dioxide and other pollutants from the exhaust, it doesn’t eliminate the odor, so you get that smell.”
He added that wind direction and weather conditions can make the odor stronger on given days.
“There are pros and cons to living near a power plant,” Whitesides said. “Your electricity is close and it employs a good workforce, and then there’s the smell from coal and other industry smells — it is an industrial facility.”
Whitesides said to remain environmentally conscious and comply with state and federal laws, scrubbers on the coal units actively strip sulfur dioxide and other pollutants from exhaust, which naturally generates a sulfur smell.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Feds approve disaster declaration for Arthur, Mississippi’s third of 2026
description: Flooding in Hancock County from Tropical Storm Arthur.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Just over halfway through 2026, Mississippi received its third federal disaster declaration of the year. 
President Donald Trump approved the declaration on Tuesday to help the state recover from Tropical Storm Arthur.
From June 18-20, Arthur brought dangerous flooding, tornadoes, straight-line winds and severe weather to south Mississippi, damaging 532 homes and killing one person in Franklin County. 
“I’m grateful to President Trump and his administration for assisting Mississippi as we recover from the storm,” said Gov. Tate Reeves said in a statement Tuesday. “This declaration will further strengthen our recovery efforts and deliver additional support to Mississippians. We continue praying for every community impacted. The state of Mississippi will continue to assist for as long as it takes.”
The storm brought 30 inches of rain to the state over five days and forced several rivers into major flood stages, threatening multiple dams, according to the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency.
Hancock, Harrison, Pearl River and Stone counties all are approved for individual assistance, which provides direct aid to affect residents. Approved for public assistance, which sends grants to support local governments, are Covington, George, Greene, Hancock, Harrison, Pearl River, Stone and Wayne counties.
The declaration marks the third one Trump has approved for the state this year, following Winter Storm Fern in late January and seven tornadoes that struck south Mississippi in early May. It marks the most federal disaster declarations the state has received since 2020. Mississippi saw six declarations approved that year, including for Hurricane Zeta and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Impacted residents in counties approved for individual assistance can apply for support by registering online at www.DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-FEMA (3362), or by using the FEMA app. They can also visit the MEMA website for more information.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Judge keeps NJ’s ‘assault weapon’ ban in place pending Supreme Court review
description: New Jersey’s so-called assault weapons ban dates to 1990 and prohibits 66 rifles and shotguns plus those with things like a pistol grip.
text:
New Jersey’s so-called assault weapons ban dates to 1990 and prohibits 66 rifles and shotguns plus those with things like a pistol grip. (Photo by Aristide Economopoulos/New Jersey Monitor)A federal appellate judge has ordered New Jersey’s longstanding ban on certain semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines to remain in effect until the U.S. Supreme Court decides whether to consider the case.
The U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals’ full bench struck down the ban in a ruling last month. But the state asked the court last week to pause that order, citing contradictory appellate rulings in other states they hope the nation’s top court will review and resolve.
Tuesday, Judge Arianna J. Freeman agreed to do so in a brief order, staying the 3rd Circuit’s July ruling until the nation’s top court either decides to let it stand or intervenes to issue its own final decree.
Attorney General Jen Davenport applauded the decision.
“We are thrilled that the Third Circuit this morning stayed its ruling in our assault weapons/large-capacity magazines case while our petition to the US Supreme Court proceeds,” she said in a statement. “That ensures this 36-year-old law will remain in place as litigation continues — providing much-needed stability on the ground. We will continue to stand up for common-sense gun-safety laws in court.”
New Jersey’s so-called assault weapons ban dates to 1990 and bars ownership of 66 listed rifles and shotguns and similar firearms plus those with certain characteristics, like a pistol grip, a threaded barrel meant to accept muzzle devices like flash hiders and suppressors, or folding or telescoping stocks.
Its high-capacity magazine ban bars any magazine that can hold more than ten rounds of ammunition.
The Association of New Jersey Pistol and Rifle Clubs brought the suit.
Gun owners have also challenged a more recent New Jersey law that bars firearms in an array of locations. A divided three-judge 3rd Circuit panel upheld most of the law but gun owners want the court’s full panel of judges to rule on their challenge.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Opponents ask New Mexico utility regulators to review whether PNM waived multimillion payout
description: An Albuquerque anti-poverty nonprofit is asking state utility regulators to order a hearing over whether the parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider forfeited a $350 million payment from the private equity firm looking to acquire it.
text:
Regional bulk transmission lines crisscross the area between Golden and Madrid along New Mexico Highway 14. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)An Albuquerque anti-poverty nonprofit is asking state utility regulators to order a hearing over whether the parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider forfeited a $350 million payment from the private equity firm looking to acquire it.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a filing with the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission Monday, attorneys for Prosperity Works argue that TXNM Energy Inc., which owns PNM, could have collected $350 million from private equity firm Blackstone Infrastructure in July when regulators shot down a controversial stock sale between the two companies.
Commissioners last month voted 2-1 that a $400 million stock sale between TXNM and a Blackstone subsidiary violated state law because the parties did not first obtain PRC approval. After the vote, the commission ordered both sides to unwind the deal. In the Monday filing, Prosperity Works’ attorneys argue that the merger agreement between TXNM and Blackstone includes a provision to let TXNM collect a $350 million merger termination fee if the stock purchase did not go through.
Prosperity Works attorney Steve Michel said that PNM’s share of that would be $240 million. He argued that it would translate to a yearlong 16% rate reduction for PNM customers.
Since PNM and Blackstone announced plans for the $11.5 billion acquisition in 2025, officials from both companies have often said it was the best way to inject cash into New Mexico’s outdated electric grid.
“You’re a company that’s perpetually complaining that you don’t have enough money, and you’re just walking away from this $350 million cash infusion?” Michel said.
New Mexico residents turn out to UNM campus to weigh in on proposed private equity takeover of PNM

A spokesperson for Blackstone declined to comment. A spokesperson for PNM in an email to Source NM called Michel’s arguments “incorrect.”
“We did not have a legal basis to collect a termination fee from Blackstone Infrastructure,” the statement said. “We will respond through the Commission process and look forward to demonstrating the long-term benefits of the transaction to New Mexico and the communities we serve.”
A hearing will only move forward if the PRC schedules one. Prosperity Works successfully pushed for one related to the controversial stock sale earlier this year.
Prosperity Works and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez earlier this year raised questions about the $400 million stock sale’s legality, which prompted the commission’s hearing examiners to open an investigation into the matter in March and to hold a lengthy hearing in April.

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Blanche nomination for attorney general advanced by US Senate panel on party-line vote
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was one step closer to permanently leading the Justice Department Tuesday, after two skeptical Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans voted to advance his nomination given Blanche’s signed promise that President Donald Trump’s nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund is dead.Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who had been withholding support for Blanche, voted with other members of the committee along party lines, 12-10, to send Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate. It is unclear how soon the Senate will vote on the confirmation.Blanche, Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer, issued a brief signed statement on social media Sunday night promising the fund is “rescinded,” and an attached unsigned memo stated the tax immunity deal for Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization only applies “retroactively.” Trump did not sign the documents, and the president has defended the fund in recent days.Cornyn said ahead of the vote Tuesday he and Tillis came to an agreement with Justice Department officials on an “agency interpretive guidance document that reaffirms what Mr. Blanche said in his sworn testimony” that the tax audit immunity is limited to the parties and subject matter in Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against his administration’s own IRS.Trump voluntarily dropped the lawsuit in May in exchange for tax enforcement immunity for him, his sons Eric and Don Jr., and the Trump Organization, as well as the creation of a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” fund that could potentially pay out to violent, but now pardoned, Jan. 6 rioters who assaulted police.“Given this agreement with Mr. Blanche, I expect the department to live up to this in future litigation, and I will vote to advance him out of the committee today,” Cornyn said at the opening of Tuesday’s meeting.Tillis said the question over the “payout pot for punks” was settled.“I've never liked this 1776 fund. It made no sense to me, and I thought it was an insult to the police officers and the people that defended us on January the 6th. It's done, it's been rescinded, and I am satisfied,” Tillis said.Tillis argued “both (sides) have a problem” and he hopes Blanche will attempt “a bending of the curve of this absurdity.”“If you want to talk about weaponization, take a look at the Biden administration … Maybe it's a little bit more intense in this administration than the last one, and that a little bit more intense than the prior administration, and so on and so forth. But folks, we've got to end this stuff,” he said.He added the “bonehead” DOJ official in North Carolina who is prosecuting former FBI Director James Comey for a social media post of seashells on a beach spelling out “8647” — a nod to a restaurant kitchen term to get rid of something — “better damn sure have information to back it up because if all it is is a picture, that person should lose his or her job.” Dems united in oppositionAll committee Democrats followed ranking member Dick Durbin of Illinois in delivering remarks opposing Blanche’s nomination. The panel’s minority members hammered concerns about Blanche’s handling of the Epstein files and meeting with convicted sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell, federal lawsuits for states’ voter records and a promise to faith leaders that the DOJ will make the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn federal abortion protections “permanent in every single state.”The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment about the criticisms.Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey chastised his Republican counterparts for comparing the Trump administration’s actions to the Biden administration, including President Joe Biden’s pardons of his son Hunter and other officials just hours before leaving office.“That is like being obsessed and using a magnifying glass to study the stain on the living room carpet when behind you is a mountain of excrement covering the living room couch and coffee table,” Booker said. He added that Trump’s recent financial disclosure revealed he made nearly $2 billion in crypto and foreign investments, and pointed to his sons’ Eric and Don Jr.’s backing of defense tech business ventures.“The lack of proportionality going on (by) my colleagues, it is laughable,” he said.Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse described Blanche’s two-paragraph signed statement and unsigned memo in response to Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns as “decorative.”The Rhode Island Democrat said the Trump administration could reverse course and create a similar fund.“Nothing in this document prevents anything like that from happening,” Whitehouse said.Durbin accused Blanche of lying under oath when he denied during his confirmation hearing a comment he made about the “anti-weaponization” fund during a pre-hearing meeting with Durbin.“Mr. Blanche told me he made, quote, ‘a mistake,’ end quote, by creating the January 6th slush fund. Where did he say it? In my office, with witnesses on my staff to what I'm about to say. When I asked him about this under oath, Mr. Blanche falsely claimed that he never made this statement,” Durbin said.Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., slammed Trump for suing the Internal Revenue Service in the first place. The contractor who leaked Trump and his sons’ and organization’s tax information to reporters in 2019 was sentenced for the crime in 2024.“He waits til he’s president. He sues the IRS for $10 billion. In a stunning act of self-dealing, he purports to settle with himself. He's represented by his personal lawyers on the one hand, and by his other lawyers at the Department of Justice on the other hand,” Schiff said, highlighting the Florida federal judge’s order that Trump used his presidency to “manipulate” the court for his benefit. “Now there was an effort, and I appreciate my colleagues from Texas and North Carolina making an effort to try to rein in this tax settlement. But what they attempted to achieve has not been achieved,” Schiff said.Epstein survivors disappointedBlanche’s nomination vote drew criticism from outside the committee as well.In an open letter Tuesday, 18 survivors of abuse by the now deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and convicted sex trafficker Maxwell called the vote “a profound disappointment.”Survivors have slammed Blanche’s handling of the Epstein files release, which unmasked several survivors' names and images in the process “while he concealed the identities of alleged abusers and others connected to Epstein's trafficking network,” the letter stated.“When we met with Blanche (after his confirmation hearing), he interrupted us. He told us to ‘get to the point.’ He told us to report what happened to us to the FBI. We already have. Some of us have been reporting these crimes for decades,” the survivors wrote.In another line of criticism, the legal advocacy organization Democracy Forward said in a letter to the Justice Department Monday that Blanche has refused to provide a sworn statement in federal court that the “anti-weaponization” fund will not accept and pay out claims.Democracy Forward is representing several plaintiffs in a lawsuit over the fund, including a former federal prosecutor who alleges he was fired in June 2025 for his involvement in Jan. 6 prosecutions.“The American people are not fooled by this latest move, and neither are we. The Trump-Vance administration cannot ask the public or our clients to accept a late-night social media post in place of legally binding action,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward in a statement Monday.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Wiggins rallies around Hood Industries workers after mill closure
description: An aerial view shows Hood Industries' Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill, which is expected to permanently close at the end of August 2026 after Tropical Storm Arthur caused significant damage to the facility.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
STONE CCOUNTY — As Hood Industries prepares to permanently close its Wiggins plywood mill at the end of August, community organizations are working to help approximately 250 displaced employees find new jobs and connect them with financial, mental health and other support services. 
A two-day job fair for former Hood Industries employees will be held Aug. 14 from noon to 6 p.m. and Aug. 15 from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College’s Perkinston campus. The event is part of a coordinated rapid response effort following the company’s announcement that the mill would close after Tropical Storm Arthur caused significant damage to the facility. 
The mill has operated in Wiggins for 56 years. 
“We are part of the rapid response team,” said Rachael Kunz, associate vice president of workforce solutions at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College. “Rapid response starts immediately after the announcement of the closing of an industry partner … as a community college, we want to serve our community.” 
Screenshot Credit: Courtesy of Rachael Kunz
Kunz said the job fair was organized within a week of Hood Industries announcing the closure July 7. 
The rapid response team includes Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College, the Mississippi Department of Employment Security, the Mississippi Department of Human Services and Stone County Economic Development. In collaboration with MGCCC, Stone County Economic Development has also launched a website connecting residents with job opportunities, school supply assistance, mental health resources, food assistance and other community services. 
Kunz said the effects of the closure will extend beyond the mill’s workforce. 
“It’s not just the employees,” she said. “Suppliers, restaurants and other small businesses throughout the community will also feel the impact.”
Hood Industries said approximately 250 employees are affected by the closure. Company President Jay Galloway called the decision difficult.  
“We are well aware of the impact this decision will have on the Wiggins employees, their families and community,” Galloway said in a statement. 
The company said affected employees will meet with Hood Industries representatives to discuss transition assistance and opportunities at other company facilities. Employees will continue receiving pay through Sept. 5 as part of the company’s transition plan. 
Former Hood Industries employee Joseph Fairley worked at the Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill for 25 years before being laid off July 24, 2026. Credit: Courtesy of Joseph Fairley
For longtime employees, the closure marks the end of decades of work. 
Joseph Fairley spent 25 years at the mill as a lift driver before being laid off July 24.
“It was sad because I just never thought that it would close,” Fairley said. “It’s been there so long. I didn’t see it coming. It didn’t hit me that day … but the next day it did.” 
Fairley said the facility needed repairs before Tropical Storm Arthur damaged the mill, including work on the roof, but he hoped the problems would eventually be addressed. 
Lew Douglas Schuit, who worked at the mill for 13 years as a machine and forklift operator before also being laid off July 24, described hearing the news as “a sinking feeling.” 
“I wasn’t necessarily expecting it,” Schuit said. “With what they had said was the cause, it’s something I knew would happen eventually. I figured it would be able to be reconciled.” 
Former Hood Industries employee Lew Douglas Schult worked at the Wiggins, Miss., plywood mill for 13 years before being laid off July 24, 2026. Credit: Courtesy Lew Douglas Schult
Hood Industries is also expanding operations elsewhere in Mississippi, with a new sawmill in Wayne County and a new plywood mill in Perry County expected to be completed later this year. Fairley believes those investments influenced the company’s decision not to repair the Wiggins facility.
“I don’t think the owner wanted to put a lot of money in here because he put a lot of money into the new mills,” Fairley said. 
As the community prepares for the mill’s final weeks, Fairley said he is focused on taking time to recover before deciding what comes next. 
“Right now, I’m going to take some time off, just for my mental health,” he said. “I’ve been working so long. I’ve raised my kids through that mill, so I’m going to take a couple of months off.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Legal Marijuana NOW candidate will stay on fall ballot for Nebraska US Senate
description: Mike Marvin, one of the candidates accused of being a “plant” for Dan Osborn, didn’t submit the paperwork to drop out of the Nebraska U.S. Senate race.
text:
Signs in the bowels of the Nebraska State Capitol advocate for legalization of marijuana. Aug. 2, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s U.S. Senate nominee Mike Marvin will stay on the ballot after all. 
Marvin, one of the candidates accused of being a “plant” for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn, didn’t submit the paperwork to drop out of the Senate race, the Secretary of State’s office confirmed Tuesday. The deadline for a candidate to drop out was Monday. 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., center, faces nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn, left, and Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Mike Marvin in Nebraska’s Senate race this fall. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
Marvin has denied being a plant for Osborn. On his website, Marvin said he would “work with other candidates to make sure” to have a “united front against Pete Ricketts.”
Former Democratic nominee Cindy Burbank paid Marvin’s $1,740 candidate filing fee earlier this year. Burbank dropped out of the race one day after Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot were verified by the Secretary of State. 
While the race technically has three candidates, Osborn and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts are considered the leading candidates. 
There could also be two new state political parties that could get candidates on the U.S. Senate ballot, depending on whether their signatures are verified. 
The race between incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and Osborn, which has turned Nebraska politics upside down with allegations that candidates are “plants” for other candidates, multiple lawsuits and new political parties emerging.  
The race has drawn national attention for its nontraditional political dynamics. The election is Nov. 3.
